VERY YOUNG AND EARLY SONGS-Cat Stev- ens-Deram DES -18061 Packaged somewhat like a can of LeSeur brand peas, these morsels of nourishment have a taste quite different than the more mature variety, but you can readily tell they stem from the same legume. Of the ten titles, "The Tramp" tastes most like the new variety of Cat, and the furthest thing from it is "Image Of Hell," perhaps Stevens' attempt to dupli- cate "Crying In The Chapel" and establish an r&b ballad tradition across the Atlantic. The rather lavish orchestrations put the artist in a now unfamiliar light, but these are h:s roots. And there will be many musical gard- ners interested in a grafting or two. LIVE-EVIL-Miles Davis-Columbia G30954 Miles Davis has transcended any musical category except to be classified as Miles Davis. Springing from his fame in the jazz idiom, he has proven again and again that he can broad- en his horizons far beyond the realm of pre- conceived notion. He has the magnetic charis- ma to instill his vision into his topflite back- up men such as saxist Wayne Shorter, drum- mer Jack DeJohnette, guitarist John McLaugh- lin and pianists Joe Zawinul, Chick Corea, Herbie Hancock and Keith Jarrett. And the total image is vivid for the listener on "Double Image," "Little Church" and others, including a narration by Conrad Roberts. JULIE & CAROL AT LINCOLN CENTER-Julie Andrews and Carol Burnett-Columbia S 31153 The concert took place in New York last July, and it can now make winter that much more bearable. The highlight is a 47 song medley of the top songs of the 60's, and it's a flatter- ing reminder of the Mary Martin -Ethel Merman TV medley of so long ago. Two talented charm- ers in comedy and song. STANDING OVATIONS-Gladys Knight & The Pips-Soul S736L Surely one of the most resilient acts in the business (they've been going strong since "Every Beat Of My Heart" in 1960), this LP should prove a worthy successor to their "If I Were Your Woman" package. Standards are given that special touch of Pip ("Fire And Rain," "Help Me Make It Through The Night," "The Long And Winding Road") and two strong new entries ("Master Of My Mind," "No One Could Love You More") should prove success- ful follow-ups to their currently charted "Make Me The Woman That You Go Home To" which leads this set off to a fully royal Knightly start. CAT STEVENS MIf JULIE %\I) CliO1. U1.1\( :I H \ Cl;\ 17:R HOT ROCKS 1964-1971-The Rolling Stones -London 2PS 606/7 The Stones have their own label now but the work they did on London during these seven years continues to live on. This two rec- ord sep could serve as a handy primer for groups who would become international leg- ends. "Time Is On My Side" gets things go- ing and Jagger and company take the listener on up through "Satisfaction," "Ruby Tues- day," "Honky Tonk, Women," "Gimme Shel- ter" and more than a dozen more. Sure to be a top selling album in record time. STRAIGHT UP-Badfinger-Apple 3387 Badfinger is pointing straight up and its aim is accurate. This new Apple album is sure to get fast spin-off from Badfinger's involvement in George Harrison's Bangla Desh affair, as well as the group's other work with Paul Mc- Cartney and Harrison. But Badfinger isn't go- ing to make it on Beatle karma alone. Listen to "Baby Blue," "Suitcase," "Flying" and "Perfection" and hear the group's inherent quality that attracted the heavies to start with. The LP was produced by Todd Rundgren, with four cuts produced by Harrison. MARK -ALMOND II-Blue Thumb BTS -32 You put this album on the turntable, and out of necessity, the rest of the world draws a rosy -colored blank. Few artists are as suc- cessful in creating a totality of mood, one which can extend from opening to closing band on one side of the LP and still compel you to flip it over to begin the cycle anew. If this be understatement, then may we be forever destined to walk softly and carry one Mark -Almond LP under each arm, should one lonely phonograph approach us in the dis- tance. No doubt it will soon want to bring along a friend. If life can't be a dream, at least this jazz/folk/rock concept can approach the ideal. DYNAMITE-The Supremes & The Four Tops- Motown M745L When two of the hottest and finest groups around get together, dynamite is the word to describe what happens. Once again the Su- premes and the Tops team up and the results are splendid. "If," "It's Impossible," "Hello Stranger" and "If I Could Build My Whole World Around You" are included. There are six more cuts-all incredible. Should glide up the chart with ease. CHER-United Artists UXS-88 With "Gypsys Tramps And Thieves" and a new TV series, she's back on top again. United Artists has an attractively priced double -LP set here which collects her early hits like "All I Really Want To Do," "Bang Bang," "Alfie" and "You'd Better Sit Down Kids" as well as her fantastic readings of "Sunny," "Elusive Butterfly," "You Don't Have To Say You Love Me" and "Homeward Bound" just to name a few. Certainly one of the finest programs the thrush has ever assembled in one package and one that's bound to cause re-newed inter- est in the material. SUPERSTAR-Vikki Carr-Columbia C31040 You can always depend on this songstress to come up with pleasantly diverting fare. Her latest entry in the MOR category is chock full of songs which are beautifully tailored to the Carr style. "The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down," "How Can You Mend A Broken Heart?" "Loving Him Was Easier," and "Crazy Love" are four of the really standout cuts but the whole album is a treat. 100 Cash Box - December 25, 1971 www.americanradiohistory.com

UA Sales Forces Meet in LA To Hear New 16 LP Lineup LOS ANGELES - United Artists Records held a three-day national sales meeting here last weekend (Jan. 7-9) at the Beverly Hilton Hotel, at- tended by the company's regional and local sales representatives. Also in- vited were regional promotion men, as well as key members of UA's na- tional staff. Sessions were opened with a cocktail party Thursday night (7). Label president Mike Stewart, who hosted the gathering, introduced 16 new LPs, including the Nitty Gritty Dirt Band's "All the Good Times," the group's first new recording in over a year; Canned Heat's "Historical Fig- ures and Ancient Heads"; "Strange Fruit," initial presentation from Ike Turner's band Family Vibes; and "Mozartmania," follow-up set by Waldo de los Rios to his chart success "Sinf onias. " A highlight of the UA program was the debut presentation of the la- bel's Legendary Masters Series, two - record sets collecting now -historic material by Fats Domino, Eddie Cochran, Ricky Nelson and Jan and Dean. The late Junior Parker was rep- resented by "I Tell Stories Sad and True I Play the Hamonica Too. I,t Is Very Funky," as was the original off- Broadway cast recording of "Touch- stone" by Tarot, and the first album by UA country artist Penny De - Haven. UA's jazz subsid, Blue Note Rec- ords, offered a debut LP entitled "Flute In" by Young Bobbi Humphrey, who has had major na- tional television exposure during re- cent months, and UA Latino, the firm's ethnic label, showcased a quar- tet of new albums-"Chucho Con Amor" by Chucho Avellanet, "The Tito Rodriguez Superpak," "La Vio- letera" soundtrack starring Sara Montiel, and "Orquestra Revolution '70" from a new Puerto Rican band. "Traffic Month," all-out campaign in January on the six UA LPs by the English supergroup, was also presented to the organization's na- tional and local staffers. Stewart Address Stewart keynoted the meeting with an address in which he expressed great satisfaction for the way the la- bel began the year as one of the nation's hottest disc and tape com- panies. Stewart cited Don McLean, currently on top of the national best- seller charts, plus fast-moving and fast -rising product from WAR, Bobby Womack, Dory Previn and Shirley Bassey, the instant success of Poppy Bowing New Product NEW YORK - Poppy Records intro- duces its winter/spring releases at the UA/UDC regional sales meetings. Harold Friedman of Poppy will in- troduce the product via a presentation designed by Milton Glaser of Push Pin Studios. This is Poppy's largest simultaneous release and includes first releases by new Poppy artists Linda Cohen; "Leda," Doc Watson (accompanied by his son Merle) "The Elementary Doc Watson," and Don Bandi "The Don Randi Trio + 1 At The Baked Potato." "Don't It Drag On," Chris Smither's second Poppy album will also be introduced. Rec- ords will ship in Feb. The first UA/UDC Sales Meeting will take place in New York City on Jan. 14, followed by meetings in Cleveland (17) Atlanta (18), Chicago (19), Dallas (20) and Los Angeles (21). soundtracks from "Fiddler on the Roof" and "Diamonds Are Forever," plus the continued growth and ac- ceptance of jazz subsidiary Blue Note. Stewart also noted the firm's in- volvement with the forthcoming Da- vid Merrick Broadway production of "Sugar," musical version of the film "Some Like It Hot." "Sugar" will star Robert Morse, Anthony Roberts and Cyril Ritchard. An original cast LP is expected in March. Likewise cited was a 15 -city tour by Shirley Bassey, her first in America, and the immediate overwhelming na- tional response to the latest James Bond film and UA soundtrack, "Dia- monds Are Forever," in which Miss Bassey sings the title tune. Stewart also noted UA's plans for the release of a debut LP by television star Da- vid Frost. Elektra Launches 10 LP's At First Annual Confab PALM SPRINGS - Elektra Records hosted its first national sales conven- tion last weekend. The gathering, which met at the Riviera Hotel and Country Club in Palm Springs, California, brought to- gether the key Elektra exec staff with personnel from the eight branches of the W -E -A (Warners-Atlantic- Elektra) Distributing Corp. as well as personnel from Kinney of Canada and Kinney of England. During his five year tenure, one of his main functions was purchasing masters for the label. Vanderbilt was head of na- tional promotion at Laurie for two and a half years when he and Morris, in Jan., 1970, struck out on their own with the formation of Big Tree. Uttal, Vanderbilt, Morris `Product Is Theme' At Polydor Meet HOLLYWOOD - Polydor Inc. feels that "the product is the theme." Using the slogan as a theme for a recent sales meeting at the Beverly Hilton Hotel. The bulk of the meeting was de- voted to audiovisual presentations of Polydor's new pop product, including product from distributed labels, Sire, Spring and Deutsche Grammophon. Also, the promo drives planned for Manfred Mann & His Earth Band and James Last were unveiled. The Polydor release comprises "Manfred Mann's Earth Band," "Teenage Licks" by Stone The Crows, "Love, Luck and Lollipops" by The Bells, a group called Ram, "Music From Across The Way" by James Last, "Mothor Motor" by Bobby Gosh, "The Paul Simon Songbook" by Arthur Fiedler & The Boston Pops. Coming out on Sire will be "Tight- ly Knot" by the Climax Blues Band and "And Other Short Stories" by Barclay James Harvest. At the meeting, Deutsche Grammo- phon's classical division director, Fred Dumont, presented an outline of the label's plans for the year, includ- ing upcoming product. New releases include two new LPs by pianist Ar- turo Benedetti Michelangeli, Herbert von Karajan conducting the Berlin Philharmonic in a new recording of Tchaikovky's "Swan Lake Suite" and "Sleeping Beauty Suite" and a dou- ble -disk set of Mahler featuring "Songs of A Wayfarer" coupled with "Symphony No. 5". manager Bill Harvey and art director Bob Heimall. The show utilized 4 slide projectors and a small digital computer. The resultant collage which spotlighted the music, rather than a specific sales approach, used the songs to create a complete show via techniques of cuts, dissolves and ani- mation. Holzman Talk Addressing the meet, Elektra pres- ident Jac Holzman said that "commit- ment" was a byword at the company. "By commitment we mean a high, to- tal energy dedication to our artists. You have probably already discovered that very little is routine with us. When we produce and deliver to you what we believe is a hit artist or record and you in turn bring it home for us, our excitement each time is like it's the first time. And we can go back to our artists and tell them that our commitment to them is shared by you." Several Elektra artists were also presented in concert. The convention, which ran from Thursday, January 6 to Sunday, Jan- uary 9 also included various seminars for salesmen, regional and local pro- mo men and branch managers to dis- cuss upcoming merchandising and promotionals campaigns. RCA/Musicor's Pact On Jones NEW YORK-Musicor Records and RCA Records have formed an agree- ment whereby the recordings made by country music artist George Jones will be released on the RCA label in the U.S. and Canada and through RCA's record and tape clubs. The an- nouncement was made by Art Tal- madge, Musicor's president, and Harry Jenkins, RCA Records divi- sion vp of country music. Talmadge explained that the deal covered Jones' entire catalog of 230 tunes already released on Musicor as well as 58 sides that were recorded under Jones' Musicor contract but not released as yet. Therefore, RCA's product will be a number of reissues of Jones' Musicor sides in addition to some cuts never previously issued. Jones recently switched labels from Musicor to Epic Records, so the RCA- Musicor deal only covers what he had recorded before leaving the label. Talmadge stated that his label made the deal because of its conviction in RCA's distribution strength. Jenkins verified that RCA intends to give full promo treatment to all product, start- ing with the initial release of the first single under the pact, "A Day In The Life Of A Fool." Talmadge said Musicor Records will continue its own label distribution of its other product, concentrating its ef- forts to develop new artists through its current distrib facilities, as in the past. Maxin Exits E.H. Morris NEW YORK - Arnold Maxin has resigned his post as general profes- sional manager of Edwin H. Morris Co., effective immediately. The vet publishing/recording exec joined the company last June. He said he would announce his future plans at a later date. He can be reached at (212) 581-0030. VIRGINIA-There was so much action last summer along Virginia Beach, especi- ally among the young set who discovered the play fun of a table soccer game called foosball. The popularity of the game prompted the formation of a Tide- water Foosball Association and with the assistance of Southern Musements Co., they sponsored a foosball derby the last weekend in November at Virginia Beach Dome. Coordinator Bruce Thompson says that there were over 175 entrants and nearly 1,000 attended the three day meet. The matches proved highly exciting for the competitors as well as for the spectators, says Bruce. The 2/4 player game is styled after the German soccer term fussball. Each player controls a set of rods in positioning players and it takes plenty of concentration and swift re- flex action in blocking and shooting. The winners in the men's doubles were John K. Hayes, 23, and Paul Nipper, 21, and John Hayes captured men's champion honors. Michelle Artese a Virginia Beach Junior High 8th grader took women's division honors. Bobby Taliaferro a junior took the junior men title. A series of prizes included a motorcycle for John Hayes and a racing motorcycle for the junior men's champ, Bobby Taliaferro. Michelle collected a $200 clothing certifi- cate and there was also a round trip air ticket to Florida for the men's doubles. Bruce says the turnout and excitement of this event is a clue to future events. D BE SURE TO CHECK BUSINESS CLASSIFICATION ABOVE A CM%1110wx/ Round The Route EASTERN FLASHES The local trade was saddened to learn of the death of Frank Selinger Wed. the 2nd, due to heart failure. Frank, husband of MONY's popular Sophie Selinger, was known to many in the industry from his appearances as Sophie's escort to many of our trade affairs over the years. Those wishing to send condolences may write to Sophie at 1020 Neilson St., Far Rockaway, N.Y. 11691 .... Just after we learned of Sophie's loss, we received a call from Arnold Kaminkow of General Vending in Baltimore, informing us that company founder George Goldman also passed away Wed. (3rd). See story elsewhere this issue on George. QUALITY CONTROL-WHERE ARE YOU?-Seems to be a serious problem brewing with 45rpm singles right now, concerning the technical quality of the disks themselves. We've received several letters and calls lately, from both opera- tors and one stops, screaming about unnecessary service calls due to record deficiencies, one stops are up -to -here getting tired of hearing operator's gripes and say the real complaint should be lodged with the offending record companies. Many operators do write these lables, listing problems they've had with records, but it seems the complaints are going unanswered. Chief among these deficiencies are: record warpage (increasing, they say), mislabeling of records (some disks come labeled with two 'A' side labels, others have the labels from the record they want on a completely different disk also issued by the same firm). thin vinyl (one very prominent label's disks have been described as "paper thin"), the perennial favorite-bad start -in groove, and last but obviously not the least-the hole being off center. This last one really takes the cake. When we first heard it out at the MOA seminar we thought it impossible to press a record with an off -center hole, but certain pressing processes used by some labels today can do this if the quality control don't do their job. Worst of it is the midnight service calls that take an operator ten miles or more from home, just to find that the sensitive jukebox mechanism won't abide the eccentricities of a defective single. That's time and money unnecessarily spent and it's no wonder the one stops get so much steam. Hope the record companies responsible wake up to the fact that the technical performance of a single is as important, if not more important, to the operator than its artistic performance. OFFICIAL SOCCER UNION, NEW JERSEY - United Amusements International, Inc., has announced the release of a new 2/4 player soccer game, `U.A.I. Official Soccer'. The game, premiered at the MOA convention and the recently held International Park Show, is manufactured by United Billiards, Inc., and shipments are being made to United's distributors. The game is housed in an all mica cabinet and United Amusements ex- ecutive Barry Feinblatt states that decorator colors are available at no extra cost. Additional operator features include a slide -out drawer unit for easy access to the inside of the machine, a separate cash box, coin drop chute with flexibility of pricing plus a "Zenith" mechanism providing an automatic ball release at the drop of the coin to start the game. No outside electrical connections or cords are needed for operation of the game and a spare energizer is packed with each game. Fast -paced play action is offered with full spin goalies. Easy glide telescopic all steel rods are bearing surfaced mounted in all aluminum housings for easy maneuverability. Continuous ball movement is practi- cally assured with a contoured playfield to minimize dead spots. Soc- cer scoring is automatic in picture frame on the playfield. A glass top is standard equipment and the glass is removable if desired. Feinblatt also reminded that the ad- justable leg levelers are rubber based to absorb play shock. The shipping weight of the game is 250 pounds. The game is 4 feet and 7 inches long; 2 feet and 5 inches wide and 3 feet 2 inches high. Operators are requested to stop by their United Billiards distributor and see why `U.A.I. Official Soccer', is "one of the big attractions of the season for top location profit," com- mented Feinblatt. Dalton says the unit acts as a miniature computer and when placed in a machine will register all coins (dimes, nickels, quarters). The unit is removed by the routemen and returned to a central machine which reads out and then erases the tape. The unit can then be replaced in the machine. The unit can also be programmed to register the records items vended along with the cash. Dalton further informed that the unit is being made to sell for less than one dollar, it is unknown at this time the cost of the complete assembly. Plessey Inc., is still negotiating the assembly package. Lee Morgan Fatally Shot NEW YORK-Lee Morgan, the jazz trumpeter, was shot and killed while performing here at Slugs on Sat., Feb. 19. Police said a woman, Helen More, described as his common-law wife, shot him. She was held with- out bail until action by a grand jury. Morgan, a star on the Blue Note label, toured in the 50's with Dizzy Gillespie and the Art Blakey Jazz Messengers. Morgan, 33, recorded 12 albums for Blue Note. Set B. B. King Bio Col Album On Big Sur Fest Columbia Records has released "Big Sur Festival-One Hand Clapping." The album was produced by Bobby Colomby and Roy Halee and features Joan Baez, Blood, Sweat and Tears, Kris Kristofferson, Taj Mahal and Mickey Newbury. One cut, Kristoffer- son's "Me and Bobby McGee," is per- formed by the entire Festival includ- ing Big Sur Choir, John Cooke, Mimi Farina and Tom Jans, Larry Hankin and Lily Tomlin. The recording comes from the eighth and probably the last Big Sur Festival. Produced by Nancy Carlen, the Festival was held at Esalen In- stitute with the performers appear- ing for Union scale-$50. Columbia Records paid Festival expenses. The album contains a large color poster featuring Festival performers and a note from Ivan Illich and Friends: "We call on you to discover, together with us, what we must do to use mankind's power to create the humanity, the dignity and the joyfulness of each one of us; to be responsibly aware of your personal ability to express your true feeling and to gather us together in their expression. We can only live these changes" we cannot think our way to humanity. Columbia plans an extensive cam- paign to promote "Big Sur Festival" with in-store displays, print advertis- ing and a unique series of rotating time buys. Belkin Buys Plato Club CLEVELAND - Mike Belkin, presi- dent, Belkin Prod., has announced company's acquisition of the Plato, 1500 -seat club in Cleveland being re- named the Threshold. Following re- furbishing, Belkin will operate on a Friday & Saturday night policy, at proposed low -admission prices. His plan is to book top -name bands with one of two shows per night, depend- ing on the act. Groups already set for Threshold are Lighthouse (17-18), Malo (24-25), Sweathog (31-4/1), Cheech & Chong (11-13) and Canned Heat (21-22). Besides the "name" gigs, Belkin promises to provide oportunities to young groups in need of added ex- posure, with an eye toward grooming attractions to appear at his recently leased Akron Rubber Bowl. Belkin kicks off yearly series of summer con- certs at the Bowl June 16 with 3 Dog Night. Income before taxes and amortization of intangibles was $1,046,000 for the year ended Dec. 31, compared to $2,- 056,000 for 1970. Net after-tax earn- ings were $506,000 or 520 per share as compared to $986,000 or $1 per share the previous year. Fields reported that, mainly due to the fact that many major artists chose percentage income rather than guaranteed income, commission in- come for 1971 was $9,277,000 com- pared to $11,310,000 in 1970. Client billings were $108 million in 1971 and $135 million in 1970. One of the world's leading talent agencies, CMA is active also as a packager of motion pictures and tele- vision shows. Fields anticipates a good future for the entertainment industry and CMA both in the United States and abroad. He said, "I foresee a year of in- creased cooperation internationally. This will be a year of profits and growth. The recession from which we are hopefully emerging has demon- strated that show business-in bad times as well as good-is a vital, dynamic aspect of the American economy." It asked the Court to enjoin the enforce- ment of Section 1137(r) of the Texas Penal Code enacted last year. The suit alleged that the statute is void since the enactment of the anti -piracy amendment to the U.S. Copyright Law (P.L. 92-140) takes precedence and was in conflict with the newly - enacted State statute. U.S. District Judge Joe E. Estes dismissed the suit, holding that the plaintiff should seek its remedy, if any, in the state courts; that great and immediate irreparable harm had not been demonstrated, and that the U.S. District Court should not interfere under the circumstances with the state criminal courts enfor- cement of state law. In the Chicago action, a suit asking for a preliminary injunction, an ac- counting of profits, damages, court costs and other relief was brought by Mercury Records, MCA Records, United Artists Records, Capitol Rec- ords and CBS, Inc., against McKenna Industries, Inc., Carl Manelli and Her- bert Levin, charging the piracy of recordings by such artists as Rod Ste- wart, Buddy Miles, Elton John, Neil Diamond, Barbra Streisand, Santana, Janis Joplin, Don McLean and George Harrison. McKenna Industries, Inc. operates under the name of Stereo City Stores and Stereo City, Inc. Judge Walter P. Dahl, in handing down the temporary restraining or- der, scheduled a hearing on the mo- tion for a temporary injunction for March 20. Col Suit (Cont'd from p. 7) tors have violated state law on unfair competition. Count II of the counter- claim alleges that the record and tape duplicators have damaged the reputa- tion of the record companies as pro- ducers of high -quality albums and tapes by selling reproductions of in- ferior quality which the public is led to believe are the product of the record companies. The counterclaim seeks $150 million in actual damages and $100 million in punitive damages under Count I, and a permanent injunction against unau- thorized record and tape duplication under both counts of the counter- claim. Congress recently amended the copyright laws to grant copyright protection against unauthorized du- plication, but the new law, which be- came effective on Feb. 15 of this year applies only to recordings completed after that date. Protection from unau- thorized duplication of recordings made prior to that date has been ac- corded in the past through individual court orders issued by state courts in New York, California, Tennessee, Illi- nois and in many other states. Jazz Jamming At Radio City NEW YORK - Radio City Music Hall will be the site for two midnight jam sessions when the Newport Jazz Festival -New York makes its debut July 1-9. On July 3 and July 6, climaxing the evening activities, over 60 famous musicians will participate in the jam session. The roster of artist who will appear at the jam sessions includes Dizzy Gillespie, Thelonious Monk, Art Blakey, Barney Bigard, Ben Webster, Lionel Hampton, Benny Carter, Elvin Jones, McCoy Tyner, Sonny Rollins, Cannonball Adderley, Thad Jones, Woody Herman, Stan Getz, Charlie Mingus, Billy Taylor, Gene Krupa, Teddy Wilson, Illinois Jacquet, among others. Radio City Music Hall will also be used for a concert of gospel music on Sunday morning July 9. This is the first time in the theater's 40 year his- tory that a jazz concert will take place on the great stage. The jam sessions and the gospel concert at Radio City Music Hall are only three of 27 events presently scheduled. Other festival events in- clude nightly concerts at both Phil- harmonic Hall and Carnegie Hall July 1-6 and large outdoor concerts at Yankee Stadium July 7 and 8. For complete information, write Newport Jazz Festival -New York, P.O. Box 1169, Ansonia Station, New York, New York 10023. Grammy Awards (Cont'd from p. 7) go, Nashville and Atlanta. Many Acts The 1% hour telecast, which inci- dentally, had tough competition in NBC -TV's presentation of the first TV showing of the movie version of "West Side Story," was loaded with artist representation, a notable failing of which has been noted at previous shows. There was a segment by the cast of "Godspell", a Grammy winner as Best Score from an Origi- nal Cast Album, and performances by B. B. King, Jerry Reed, Freda Payne, the Carpenters, Tammy Wynette, Bill Evans Trio, 3 Dog Night, Andy Williams and the 5th Dimension. Artist "presenters" included the 5th Dimension, Kris Kristofferson, Anthony New ley, Richard Harris, the Temptations, Conway Twitty, Loretta Lynn, Bobby Darin, Florence Hender- son. The telecast also featured special awards, one a Governors Award to Leonard Bernstein, who was on hand to receive the award, and other a Trustees Award to the Beatles, who, of course, are no longer a single enti- ty in music. Also, a special Bing Crosby Award was given posthu- mously to Mahalia Jackson and Louis Armstrong, both of whom died over the past year. Home viewers also saw a segment of the "Bangladesh film" featuring George Harrison. Carole King could not be present, since she recently gave birth. Lou Adler, president of Ode Records, dis- tributed by A&M, and her producer accepted all her awards. Besides Carole King, other multiple Grammy winners included Lou Adler, Isaac Hayes, Charley Pride and Bill Evans, who all had two Grammys each. Also, Aretha Franklin's showing for Best Rhythm & Blues Female Per- formance on "Bridge Over Troubled Water" was her fifth straight Gram- my award, a streak that started in 1967 with "Respect." Hughes LP Via Double -Shot HOLLYWOOD - "Will The Real Howard Hughes Please Stand Up ?," a comedy album featuring Dave Bar- ry & Company, is being rush -released by Double -Shot Records here. Both the Smith brothers write, pro- duce. arrange and play keyboards and guitar. All three share vocals. Ben Smith Hospitalized NEW YORK, NY - Ben Smith, veteran musician and arranger, has been admitted to the Sydenham Hos- pital at 565 Manhattan Avenue. Smith, suffering a partial paralysis, entered the hospital March 8. His condition is listed as satisfactory, ac- cording to Hospital spokesmen. Currently, with offices at 1697 Broadway, Smith has been offering professional music services to count- less performers and writers since en- tering the local scene in 1934. He has also been producing independently as well as producing for other record labels. Smith is allowed visitors and visit- ing hours are obtainable by checking with the Sydenham Hospital. Broido, who joined the music publishing firm as president in 1969, is also chairman of the board of its subsidiary company, Elkan-Vogel, Inc. Broido previously served in execu- tive posts for Boosey and Hawkes, Inc., Mercury Music Corp., Edward B. Marks Music Corp., Frank Music Corp. and the Boston Music Co. He was a member of the board of direc- tors of the Music Educators National Conference from 1966 to 1968, pres- ident of the Music Industry Council from 1966 to 1968, and served on the Rockville Centre, New York, Board of Education from 1963 until 1969. CONDOLENCES-Attorney Ben Haskell, partner of Teddy Blatt in the law firm of Haskell and Blatt, died a couple of weeks back. Ben was fairly well known to the local trade, having assisted Teddy in the numerous documents they've pre- pared over the years for the association (MONY) and its member operators. Ben and Ted, in business together over 40 years, originally met in law school 50 years ago. He was also active in Jewish charity affairs and as president and board chairman of his temple in Laurelton, L.I. raised quite a bit of donantions for UJA. He was 67 when he died. PUBLICATION OF THE YEAR'S BIGGEST HITS TO DATE Because Cash Box is continually asked to supply a list of the year's leading hits to A&R men, record producers and radio stations, etc., Cash Box offers a continuing feature that lists the year's Top 50 titles as of the date the feature appears. The feature is published in the last issue of each incnth and is compiled from the Cash Box Top 100 Sales Chart. Point system operates as follows: For each week a song is m1 on the Top 100 it receives 135 points. Each record is awarded 123 points. No. 3 gets 122, No. 4 gets 121, No. 5 gets 116. From No. 6 thru 10 songs get 115 to 111 points respectively. No. 11 songs get 90 points and so on down the line till the No. 50 song which gets 51 points. Atlantic Rushes Daniel LP & Promo NEW YORK-"Take A Sad Song ...", the first album recorded by the rock group, Godfrey Daniel, will be rush - released by Atlantic Records. Plans for Godfrey Daniel include an advertising, publicity and point -of - sale merchandising campaign as well as a continued public appearance tour of the nation. Their recent dates in- clude Coney Island, Nathan's Green Room; Tampa, Granby's Celler; Mia- mi, Wolfie's; Atlantic City, Harry's Penny Arcade and Tad's Steak House in N.Y.C. `Medicine' As CBS Book -Album NEW YORK - Columbia Records has released "Medicine, Mind and Mu- sic, a Consideration of Their Links Through the Centuries," thirteenth in a series of book -and -record sets in the CBS Legacy Collection, prepared under the direction of Goddard Lie- berson, CBS senior vice president. "Medicine, Mind and Music" is a two - record set with a deluxe 53 -page illus- trated book. "Medicine, Mind and Music" was produced by Lieberson. Fred Karlin and Meg Welles Karlin did the musi- cal research and Fred Karlin was mu- sic director. Mr. Karlin has recently been working in Hollywood, where his song "For All We Know" from "Lovers and Other Strangers" won an Academy Award and his score for the movie "the Baby Maker" was also nominated for an Oscar. The performers range from the blues team of Sonny Terry and Brownie McGhee to the distinguished classical harpsichordist Igor Kipnis. Meg Welles Karlin is heard in several English songs. Dial: Tex Gold And Allmans LP CHICAGO - Dial Records is working on a number of projects simultane- ously, rather than concentrating on one specific item, reports Buddy Kil- len, vp of the Nashville -based label that is distributed by Mercury Rec- ords. He claims, "We're in a position to pursue a lot of different direc- tions." What gave them the position to move is Joe Tex's "I Gotcha," which was recently certified by RIAA as a million -selling single. A new Joe Tex album, entitled "I Gotcha," is com- pleted and set for release soon, ac- cording to Killen. Also coming soon is a package re- corded in the late 1960's by Duane and Greg Allman (The Allman Brothers) when their group was called Allman Joy. Also set for release soon are the singles by rock artist Dutch Ross and country act Donald Wayne. Other artists on the Dial roster in- clude Gunilla Hutton of "Hee Haw," the Nashville Edition and Johnny Lee. Bettye Swann To Atlantic NEW YORK - Bettye Swann has been signed to an exclusive recording contract with Atlantic Records. The deal was arranged between Jerry Greenberg, senior vice-president and general manager, and Rick Hall of Fame Records, Muscle Shoals, Ala- bama. Hall who is producing Miss Swann's recordings, has worked with Clarence Carter and the Osmond Brothers. Miss Swann's first single for Atlantic, "Don't Be a Victim Of a Foolish Heart" was written by George Jackson and will be released soon. Miss Swann first became prominent with the success of her soul hit "Make Me Yours", in 1967 on the Money Records label. SESAC Vote Salute At NAB Confab NEW YORK -A salute to America's 1972 Presidential elections and the national "Get Out The Vote" cam- paign will provide the theme for SESAC's popular hospitality suite (Room 900) at this year's annual con- vention of the National Association of Broadcasters, to be held at The Conrad Hilton Hotel, Chicago, April 9-12. Designed to highlight the role that America's radio and television broad- casters will again play in this Pres- idential election year, SESAC's Suite 900 at The Conrad Hilton will feature portraits of the presidents, from George Washington to Richard Nix- on, displayed in a colorful patriotic motif reminiscent of political rallies of years gone by. Live entertainment will be provided nightly by Chicago pianist Eddie Fritz, a favorite of SESAC suite visitors to the N.A.B. two years' ago, who will bring back a repeat of his "sing -along" stylings. In addition, a photographer will be on hand to photograph the individual convention delegates in the suite and then mount their photos on plastic - covered "campaign buttons" and award them as souvenir mementos. One room of the three-room suite will be decorated as an old fashioned Chocolate Shoppe where, in cooper- ation with the Chocolate Manufactur- ers Association of the U.S.A., dele - vates will be invited to "Explore the World of Chocolate" and to enjoy hot chocolate and other "goodies" as they learn how these delicacies were first discovered more than 400 years ago. 1972 marks the 23rd consecutive year that SESAC has opened the doors to its hospitality suite at the annual N.A.B. get-togethers. This year, the suite will be open daily be- ginning Sunday, April 9, through Wednesday, April 12, from 9:00 AM to 10:00 PM. SESAC representatives scheduled to be in attendance include: A. H. Prager, executive vice president and managing director; Salvatore B. Candilora, vice president and execu- tive administrator; Signey H. Guber, director of marketing services; Nor- man Odlum, director of copyright ad- ministration; Charles Scully, director of information services; Aleene Jack- son, public relations coordinator, Nashville office; John Eckenrod, of the Broadcast License department, and field representatives Harold Fitz- gerald, Bob McGarvey, Glenn Ramsey and Tom Snowden. Last Chance Revives Rock Classics NEW YORK - Last Chance Records has been formed by Paul and Michael Scialod and Stephen Green. CAShÓOX/ Round The Route EASTERN FLASHES ON THE AVENUE-Lou Wolberg, Runyon sales exec, returned Tuesday from a 15 day trip he and the Missus made to Israel and to say that Louie was im- pressed would be an understatement. The Wolbergs, along with 38 other tourists, did the bus thing all over the country, visiting the religious shrines, the farms and even the war front along the Lebanese border and the Golan Heights em- placement in occupied Syria. Lou discovered (or re -discovered) his linguistic talents during the tour, using his excellent French, his okay Yiddish and of course his New York English. He heartily recommends the trip to one and all and no doubt will be returning himself one of these days. . . . RECORD EVENTS-Columbia's jukebox coordinator, Ron Braswell, says that Andy Williams new single, "Love Theme From 'The Godfather' ", is already on the way to becoming another 'Love Story' giant. HERE AND THERE-An operator's work is never done, (additional work, that is) and on February 1 the operator was given an additional workload. That is the date that the new cigarette tax went into effect and from reports on the grape- vine, many an operator is still puffing about trying to get all those cigarette ma- chines (converted). In this case it's a price conversion (upward naturally) and painful for all concerned. Some machines presented more problems than others. For some machines, operators reported, it was difficult, and often impossible, to find conversion parts. Again, operators also said there were long delays before receiving ordered parts; also after a long delay, some operators were informed that the conversion parts were unavailable. At any rate-many an operator is still involved in the conversion problems. CONDOLENCES-We just recently learned of the death of Milton Nagler who had passed away last November. Nagler, although he had been retired for some 8 years, served as the parts department manager for 20 years at the Mike Munves Corp. We are passing this sad information on, and we belatedly express our sym- pathy to the Nagler family. NEW ENGLAND NEWSNOTES-Big do in the area was Bob Jones lavish open houser weekend before last. Second place honors went to L.O.O.M. (team #2) from Norwich, N.Y. Third place was won by Bernadini's Restaurant of Winooski, Vermont. Fourth place was taken by L.O.O.M. Bridgeport, Conn.... Cash1101x/ Round The Route EASTERN FLASHES ON THE AVENUE-Midway's 'Dune Buggy', a single player novelty drive game, has lots of driving thrills, says Lou Wolberg (Runyon Sales Co.), and operator reports indicate lots of location play. The game features a hazard car known as 'Freddy Fender Bender' that cruises up and back over the driving course at vary- ing speeds. The player must try to avoid the hazard car while at the same time guide the 'Dune Buggy' over a perilous course, says Lou. The players' score is determined by the number of completed course runs in the allotted playing time. Fun and action, says Lou. The new Bally entry, 'Hill -Climb' shipments are expected within a couple of days, reports Lou, and Hill -Climb features motorcycle thrills and spills. Should be quite a spring with two exciting entries, back to back, says Lou . . . Albert Simon, Inc., is also a scene of busy activity, trailer trucks con- taining the new United's 6 -player shuffle, "French Quarter" are being unloaded. Sy Lipp (Simon) reports that the initial test pieces of 'French Quarter' got tre- mendous plaudits. Op's can view the new piece on the showroom floor. The Williams -United Shuffle is destined to be a big demand item, and, says Sy, the orders should be placed quickly . .. Murray Kaye (Atlantic New York Corp) says that the pace has been considerably quickened with the advent of spring and seasonal locations are uppermost on the operators' minds. The Seeburg Bandshell 'Firestar' has the today styling and today sound, says Murray, and in any location the 'Firestar' has that magnetic (Play Appeal) coin pulling power ... cashboxitalenton stage cash boxRrlbum ar1eriews Mike Nesmith CASTAWAYS, NYC - Kenny, who runs this upper east side musical oasis continues to select from among my personal and as yet, unsuperstar- ry favorites without prior consulta- tion. This gives me a lot of faith in the future of the bar/club scene. The most recent bravo is connected with his booking of RCA's Mike Nesmith, a man who has a profound under- standing of both people and music himself. It's now four, going on five LPs past the Monkees. The screams have been supplanted with quiet admira- tion. No one owns just one Nesmith LP, and those who have heard him collect them like we used to favor baseball cards. Fanatics, yes-and for good reason. Here is an artist whose music is about rather than simply is. The object of his focus is western music, which reflects more fo1ky roots than what Nashville and Bakersfield presently call their own. Nesmith is one of the few still writing in this style, and one of a handful who can put across its most memorable stan- dards. "Jo -Ann" was his biggest self - recorded hit and he's still revered for "Different Drum," but before he cut one note for RCA, he had assembled nine LPs worth of originals, other new fangled portraits and time- honored canvases of the art and is just beginning to reveal the complex clockwork inside his mind. His stage presence is a very posi- tive yet laid-back thing which no one should miss. His methods cannot fully be dealt with here, so watch the "In- sights & Sounds" feature for further illumination. But we had a real good time that we defy anyone to sit through a Nesmith set and label him just another Monkee who don't stop no show. r.a, David Pomeranz Revival TOWN HALL, NYC - The crowd was small but committed. At this point, so is the relative standing of Decca's David Pomeranz in the pop pantheon. But while so many singer/ songwriters are retreating into self- made wombs of introspection and in- troversion, a few (Polydor's Ellen Mcllwainne also comes to mind) are not only rebels, but have cause. David does not put on an act, but he sure knows how to put on a show. He opened on guitar with "You Can't Do That" and encored with "Jailhouse Rock." And during each, you hardly were conscious of John, Paul, George, Ringo or Elvis. They came across vibrantly fresh and per- sonal, tinged with the jazzy enthusi- asm that might be of future extension of Cat Stevens when and if he should decide to gamble on a new sound that'll keep his present fold while im- pressing the formerly aloof. David mostly plays piano, but is also gifted with David Mason in his quartet, giv- ing himself the freedom to play either keyboard or guitar. His originals are all fine, all different. So are his moods. Many artists are pleasant to hear, few are interesting. Pomeranz is a "few" who in time shall be discovered by the many. Opening the show, Buddah's Re- vival. They are spirited, but have seemingly chosen to limit their base of operations to the electrified exten- sions of pre -progressive folk-rock. Things kind of get louder than this description might imply, and certainly funkier, but the core is unmistakably neither nostalgia nor what passes for normalcy on the current rock scene. Dig their attitude, dig their sound. It's that simple. Their music requires an open mind. r.a. Bobby Goldsboro WESTSIDE ROOM, L.A. - It was Bobby Goldsboro's debut at this Cen- tury Plaza Hotel supper club, and the United Artists singer handled the oc- casion to nearly its-and his-best advantage. Sitting on a stool, guitar in hand and backed by the string and horn -laden Al Pellegrini Orchestra and three of his own rhythm players, Goldsboro whisked through a dozen songs, of which eleven were hits ei- ther for or written by the singer him- self. His patter was interesting and assured, and his guitar playing was considerably stronger than just "functional." During the show, it became clear that Goldsboro is perhaps a greater talent than the music press generally gives him credit for being-"See the Funny Little Clown," "I'm a Drifter," "Broomstick Cowboy," "With Pen iii Hand" and the more recent "Califor- nia Wine" are really good songs, and Goldsboro wrote them all. Other tunes performed included Sonny Curtis' "Straight Life," plus "Love the One You're With," "Watchin' Scotty Grow", "Your Song" and, inevitably, "Honey." All came through strong and clear in Goldsboro's versions. t.e. Billy Joe Royal P.J.'s, L.A. - Billy Joe Royal, the man with the biggest sob in his throat since Johnnie Ray's heyday, made an all -too -infrequent appear- ance in this Vegas lounge -styled room and proved that he's every bit as good as he's always been. Backed by a seven -piece band (three horns) called Thunderchicken, Royal combined several of his hits ("I Knew You When," "Hush," "Cherry Hill Park" and "Down in the Boon- docks") with several current successes by other artists. The high quality of Royal's versions of "Without You," especially, and "Honky Tonk Wom- an" and "Superstar" (the Murray Head number, not the Carpenters') indicated that Royal's recent "cool" period might be due more to lack of the right material than to any lapse in his considerable vocalizing ability. t.e. Honk SANTA MONICA CIVIC AUDITORI- UM, L.A. - Being the warm-up band for a surfer movie isn't exactly ideal exposure for a group, even if they did the soundtrack for the film. Honk had the opportunity and, though they're a fine band, muffed it badly. The group opened with "When I'm Dead and Gone," and the McGuinness - Flint jumper was the only uptempo tune of the long set. The rest of the program consisted of some nice but slow-paced originals, a brace of Jack- son Browne tunes, and "When Roose- velt Came to Trinidad," which they took from the most recent Ry Cooder album. The set was as dreary as it was long; the sound was without doubt the least definitive, boomiest, bassiest ever heard in these parts (and that's saying a lot), and the audience was quite justifiably unap- preciative. All that is unfortunate, though, be- cause the group is obviously quite good. Your basic country -rock instru- mental line-up with especially good vocals and part singing, they add spice to their sound with harmonica, accordion and steel guitar. The drum- mer is especially strong, able to gen- erate a nice Allman Bros, shuffle that, under other circumstances, would be nearly irresistible. The group would do well to sit down, listen carefully to the first Buffalo Springfield album and learn how to plan a set. Then . . . watch out. t.e. Pop Best Bets BAGS & THINGS-Dennis Lambert-ABC/Dun- hill DSX 50119 The title obviously refers to Lambert's dis- taste for musical labels like "pop" and "rock," and the music inside attests to the talent be- hind that way of thinking. As part of the Lam- bert/Potter writing duo, he's been connected with charttoppers like "Two Divided By Love" and "Don't Pull Your Love" but this LP fea- tures none of these. His newies are potentially as gigantic however, the best being "I Didn't Sing (In The New York Subway)" and "Some- body Found Her." This is his first album as a singer, but he paid his dues in the early sixties on quite a few single efforts and the experience thus gained makes a potentially shakey coming out sound more like a reunion. LOU REED-RCA LSP-4701 The underground rock movement started with many groups to be sure, but Velvet Under- ground certainly was a cornerstone and Lou Reed its fountainhead. On his first solo effort, Reed continues to take that almost deadpan but always brilliant voice of his and use it to its fullest and most unique level. Assisting him are Yes' Rick Wakeman and Steve Howe as well as Hookfoot's Caleb Quaye, among others. Musically, he has become something quite distinct from the Underground, but no doubt he will be able to build upon their support. As close to a rock magician as you'll find anywhere, he will establish an occult cult of his own in no time. CELEBRATION-El Chicano-Kapp KS 3663 The "Viva Tirado" boys are at it again in an aptly named LP. Third album for the band features a reprise of that hit number, some hi-jinks with the likes of "La Cucuracha," and some cooking versions of Van Morrison's "Brown Eyed Girl," the Cream classic "I Feel Free," Horace Silver's "Senor Blues," and "In A Silent Way," which was written by Joe Za- winul. Throbbing rhythms and top notch ar- rangements make El Chicano a special type of group. PARIS ENCOUNTER-Gary Burton & Stephane Grappelli-Atlantic SD 1597 Two musicians of unquestionable creden- tials have gotten together for an album which is a rare listening experience. Vibraharpist Bur- ton works neatly with the legendary Grappelli over a course of nine songs. There's a touch of the old ("Daphne" and "Here's That Rainy Day") and flashes of the new as in Steve Swallow's "Eiderdown" and "Falling Grace." Grappelli's own "Arpege" gets a lovely render- ing too. Swallow and drummer Bill Goodwin round out the ensemble. A must for every serious collector of jazz music. LOOSE & FIERY-Roger Whittaker-RCA LSP- 4652 Roger Whittaker has been an international favorite for some time but has remained on the brink of American success. This may well be the album which puts him over the top here. It's a beautiful assortment of tunes, with Roger's solid vocalizing holding them all to- gether like a cord. His version of "Mammy Blue" is unforgettable and other gems in- clude "A Taste Of Honey," "By The Time Get To Phoenix," "Scarborough Fair" and "You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling." Hang on, Roger, your "new world" is coming. SON OF MY FATHER-Giorgio-Dunhill DSX- 50123 International singing star Giorgio clicked on the American singles front with "Son Of My Father" and he could easily duplicate that suc- cess in the album field with this identically named set. The material here is every bit as fascinating as the face of the dog on the jacket. Listen to "London Traffic," "Spanish Disaster," "That's How I See Her" and "Watch Your Step." *ANY INNItiOn tTtWHIAIMIi altAPPIKLt MRS 1101Cl0lr!ttTtlR Cash Box - April 15, 1972 35 www.americanradiohistory.com

cashbox! Round The Route EASTERN FLASHES ON THE AVENUE-Murray Kaye (Atlantic New York Corp.) said that he was looking at the calendar as he was talking, and there was a puzzled tone to his voice. The significance of April 11th finally occurred to him, it was his Birthday. We didn't seriously feel that Murray had forgotten, but as with many of us, there is a point when you stop counting. We do take this opportunity to ex- press our wishes for many, many more, Birthdays. The first good signs of spring had Murray thinking about the golf course for the coming weekend. Murray also reports that the Seeburg showroom has been a beehive of activity; operators are looking for vending and cigarette equipment. The Seeburg To- bacco Shop is a popular choice, along with the Choice Vend can vendors, says Murray, and where permissible, the Gottlieb 2 -player 'Outer Space' is doing a great job for the operator ... Lou Wolberg (Runyon Sales Co.), getting back into the swing of things after an highly interesting and enjoyable trip to Israel, says there is plenty of action going on at the Runyon Avenue headquarters. Lou sas that the Rowe Fresh -Vend Candy Vendor is moving very well. The model 479 has man outstanding features, handles all sizes and great pricing flexibility from 5¢ to $1.00. Importantly, the first -in/ first -out system and delivery from beginning of the cycle to the end, is a couple of seconds, one of the fastest in the industry, says Lou. Recent visitors at Runyon included Seymour Pollack, Tarrytown, N.Y.; Sam Singer and Steve Hodges (Atomic Music). Lou also says that there is plenty of operator interest in the new Bally 'Hill -Climb', a single player with a motorcycle motif. The game has lots of built in thrills as the player steers the motorcycle along tricky runways which twist up a steep and rugged hillside. The player also governs the speed with a simple twist -control on the right handlebar; driving as fast as possible to build up run -points, at the same time trying to avoid wrecks. Running into rough areas or driving at excessive speeds both cause point -loss wrecks. Lou says that the game is an eye-catcher as well as a profit catcher. THE BROOKLYN BEAT-Big news item from the Musical Distributors Corp. showroom on Rogers Avenue is the new Chicago Coin 'Twin Rifle'. There's no question about the game having a decidedly new and different (look, says Mel Achiron, and the operator reaction has been highly favorable. Two players are competing simultaneously, as they fire at a single target as fast as they can pull the triggers. The player with the quickest and most accurate shot gets the target. And, Mel says that shipments are arriving in plenty of time for the coming arcade season ... We finally had an opportunity to catch Len Schneller (U. S. Billiards) at the Amityville, N.Y., headquarters. Len only returned from one of the top pool tournaments in the country at Lake Geneva, Wisconsin. Len says that a great crowd was on hand for the Empire Distributing sponsored event. Roger Dahlgren, last year's Class A winner, has repeated as Class A champion. Roger gathered in a $1,000 prize and also the famous U. S. Billiards champion blazer. And, we understand that Roger won the fifth and final game in a stunning manner. The 8 -ball dropped in the side pocket on the break to clinch the match for Roger. operator was North Shore Novelty (Cristiano & Albanfonte) representing Stubbs Tavern in Kenosha. Len says that the '72 Red & Green Pepper table line is getting a fantastic reception from U.S. Billiards distributors throughout the country. Len also reports that the response to the new U. S. Billiard 'Electric Pro Soccer' has been sensational. AROUND TOWN-Belam vice president Marc Haim is off on another sales trip to the Orient this week; stops include Japan, Okinawa, Taiwan and Manila. Should be back at the Madison Ave. desk end of the month.... Charles Steindecker, na- tional distributor for the Rene Pierre table soccer line, proudly notes that his Virginia dealer Peabody & Sons will be holding another football tournament May 15-17 in Virginia Beach. Lots of cash prizes await skilled table soccer players, Charles says.... Insiders who attended the April 10th hearing at the Consumer Affairs Dept. feel the City will permit the existing Four Aces, Extra Innings and Planets to stay on location but will probably ban further sales and installations of these pieces, while being more stringent on similar games that might come out in the future. We understand that Rufus King, the attorney who represented Gottlieb & Williams at the hearing, really knows his nuts and bolts about the pingame situation around the country and made some good points for the trade. THE JERSEY BOUNCE-Send your get well wishes to American Shuffleboard's Tony Oliveri who was stricken by a heart attack week before last and is resting up in Christ Hospital on Palisades Ave. in Jersey City. The factory is anxious to get Tony back in a hurry; orders on shuffleboards and coin tables are quite back- logged. . . . ARAVEN's Herb Sternberg enjoyed phonecall from New York State Assn. president Millie McCarthy last week while the latter was in the City; dis- cussion centered on legislative matters affecting the trade from both Albany and City Hall. LOTS OF ACTIVITY AT Williams Electronics, Inc.-reiterating our statements of a couple of weeks back, "when you're hot, you're not!" 'Spanish Eyes' has really captured the one player market, according to Williams' Billy DeSelm. "The game's creating all kinds of excitement at the factory and we're running daily overtime production schedules to meet the demand." They're also swamped with orders for 'French Quarter', another of the very recent entries from Williams. As for 'Winner', suffice it to say, "it's stampeding in popular acceptance world-wide," as Bill further relates, adding that "25¢ play is very obviously the predominant pricing on our products." FROM THE DAILY PAPERS: In as much as alcoholic beverages are a no -no in US vending machines, it was interesting to read in Chicago's Parade last Sunday (8) that such is not the case in Japan. Two prominent distillers there offer their whisky to the public thru vending machines. The price of a two -ounce shot is about 35¢ in American money. FOR YOUR INFORMATION: A Duke Ellington Festival will be held on the University of Wisconsin -Madison campus this summer from July 17 thru 21. The famed musician -composer, who was awarded an honorary degree by the university last year, will have his full orchestra with him for the festival. Among the activities scheduled are a series of public concerts in Madison and Mil- waukee; various clinics conducted by key players of the Ellington orchestra; rehearsals with university and community music organizations; and a lineup of classes taught by the Duke himself. For further info please write the School Of Music, University of Wisconsin, Madison 53706. ûisiglsl&sound NEW YORK-IMUS-IN-THE-MORNING: TALKIN' DIRTY AND PLAYIN' THE HITS Those who have been flipping FM dials waiting for the next innovation in radio have missed it. And those who feel it could never happen in New York have been proved dead wrong. WNBC's newest staff addition, Imus-In-The-Morning is not a breeze of fresh air-he's an entire hurricane season. The world is his straight man, so everybody duck. Careering as dj for less than four years, Imus is now the morning man on New York's fastest growing AM station; it seems they are building it all on his shoulders. In many cases, their long-established air personalities have had their time slots, even their days changed to fit into the "progressive MOR's" new image. He has been called an "impudent little bastard" and other more colorful phrases. Well, he is a verbal exhibitionist-Archie Bunker turned liberal side out, Don Rickles in overalls and Old Glory shirts. And now, thanks to the release of his RCA LP "1200 Hamburgers To Go," a recording star. The album features a sampling of the characterizations and outrageousity that have brought him from Palmdale, California to Cleveland and onto the big one, New York. Folks interested in a master success plan for dj's will have to get it from somewhere else, for Imus isn't working according to any he'd admit to. "My mother-I support her; I'd like to mention that-asked me how I kept my plans secret from everyone for so long. But I just fell into everything in radio. I had a plan, and still do, but to be a rock and roll star." First signed to Dooto Records in 1959 as their first and only white act (which seemed logical wince he first won his recognition at an all -black talent show at LA's Club California), he never waxed an official release for them. He moved over to Arvee Records, a logical spot he thought to get The Olympics to record his "Gunfight On Sunset Strip" as a follow-up to "Western Movies." Instead the label released his master of the tune. HOLLYWOOD-DON BUDAY: CHICANO FOR A DAY It's all too seldom that we can pick up an album for the first time, put it casually on the turntable (in this case, killing time before a movie), and find ourselves jumping up and down with excitement. In the case of EI Chicano's new Kapp LP, "Celebration," we were so excited that we damn near missed the movie. Surprised we were, and pleased too, that the album was produced by old friend and fellow rock-and-roll journalist, Don Buday. Naturally, we called him to find out what's up. "I've been a music critic for about ten years. I was writing about jazz for Down Beat in 1963, and I've written for the L.A. Free Press, the Staff and various men's magazines. I knew jazz very well and was asked a couple of years ago to produce for Limelight. But it would have entailed moving to New York, and be- sides, I thought that jazz was dead. I still think it's gone so far underground that it's not important anymore. "I'd first seen EI Chicano at a promotion party. I liked their music but felt they could be doing it even better. So I told them what I thought. They didn't pay any attention, so I wrote a review, outlining my thoughts." A series of events, articles and other meetings transpired, the result being that Kapp's Johnny Musso and the group asked Don to produce their third album for the label. "They only had two tunes when I came in. I brought in some things that I had written, but it turned out that they just didn't fit, and I wanted to put the best possible tunes on the album. "I felt that the group had no identity and no identification, and so I wanted to establish one with them. I tried to get the kind of material any radio station could program-and now I'm finding that some very conservative MOR stations are playing 'In a Silent Way,' for instance. "I tried to pick tunes that had a certain kind of 'Latin credibility,' if you will. The IMUS: In The Morning DON BUDAY: Celebration Up until this current RCA LP, his best review was a B+ in Cash Box for his Challenge recording of "I'm A Hot Rodder And All That Jazz." Soon after release of that record, he found himself in Arizona pumping gas. There he met his wife ("who whipped out two kids from a previous marriage .. . I keep 'em in up in the attic now: they don't get as much to eat as the two younger daughters and only have a black and white TV"). After jobs as a uranium and copper miner and railroad man, back to L.A. and the Don Martin School of Radio. (Lest you be taken in by the similarity in names with a certain character in Mad magazine, rest assured that there is such a place and that it has turned out, in addition to Imus, Don Steele, Bob Eubanks and Tom Kennedy.) Before completing his course work, he landed a weekend job at a 5 kw rocker, KUGY in Palmdale and ever since the morning man "skipped town, on a bum check or something" he's been a morning man. A morning man who has pub- lished 300 songs with Tree Music, and who still wants that big hit for himself. For his next album, he'd like to do a bit of an update on Jimmy Reed B sides. "Imagine J. J. Cale singing with The Blossoms backing. That's what it would be like. I'm a dynamite r&b singer, and my brother Fred is a strong blues guitarist. I'm learning the blues harp now, gettin' ready. There's nothing better than doing a session." Right now, he's at a point where he's just beginning to believe that while (Cont'd. on P. 32) band itself can play anything it wants to, but a lot of people expect them to play certain things. They can boogie, they can play fantastic blues, and they jam like few bands do. I picked 'Senor Blues,' thinking that it would be a 'Viva Tirado' type thing for them. I'd thought of it before even meeting them. It turns out that they'd thought of doing it, too, but had never quite dared to. I tried to give them more of a rock-and-roll identity by getting them to do 'Brown Eyed Girl' and 'I Feel Free.' I tried to leave room for flexibility-picking material that would be new to them and new to me, too. We found a place where our tastes could meet, and none of the tunes would become old hat. "I made absolutely sure that all composers' names-their full names-were on the album jacket, right on the outside where the disk jockey or customer could see it. I used to manage a retail record store in Baltimore, and that probably affects the way I look at the packaging of records. Horace Silver's name is there to attract the jazz audience. Van Morrison's name is there for his audience. So few people bother to consider that when putting together an album, but I think it's vital." We asked Don his reaction to producing, the first time around. "I thought (Cont'd. on P. 32) 14 Cash Box - April 29, 1972 www.americanradiohistory.com

Japan 2nd to U.S. In Venders on Location TOKYO - Japan has surged ahead of West Germany and now ranks sec- ond to the United States in the num- ber of vending machines at work on location. Although the traditional tea cere- mony will endure as long as Japan does, Japanese office workers by the thousands take their workday tea from vending machines. It's a trend that is less souless than it appears. Tea vending machines, the Japanese point out, relieve women from having to serve it and frees them to do "more productive" jobs in a country strapped by a shortage of labor. Vend- ing machines generally are helping to ease the tight labor market. Nearly 1.4 million vending ma- chines were operating in Japan at the end of 1971, an increase of 30 per cent in a year, according to a survey of the Japan Automatic Vending Ma- chine Manufacturers Association. Ma- chines in Japan dispense virtually ev- ery daily necessity from food and cig- arettes to railway tickets and cash, daily swallowing some $4.3 million. One out of every ten stations in the Japan National Railway system has ticket vending machines that dispense $123 million worth of tickets a year. Some banks have installed automa- tic cash machines that roll out money and record the withdrawal in the de- positor's bankbook by merely insert- ing a special plastic card and punching the proper buttons (see photo above) . Meters are replacing at- tendants in parking lots and sound an unmistakable warning when time runs out. CHAMPION SOCCER Germany's Finest Fussball ARIZONA AUTOMATION, INC. 8900 N. FROM THE MOUNTAINS-About 250 operators and guests of the three regional a'-sociations enjoyed a real fine weekend May 5-7 in the Catskills, celebrating their combined anniversaries. Friday night's industry symposium was quite excel- lent, concerning the amount of meaty information exchanged. We learned the New York Consumer Affairs Dept. has decided to order those previously -legalized "flipper" games off location May 15th, but that trade attornies were slated to meet with them sometime last week and make some kind of informal appeal. The subiect of machine rotation and equipment upgrading got a fine address by At- lantic distributor Meyer Parkoff, who chided some of the tradesters for operating old equipment even in some of their best stops, warning that such stuff is actually detrimental to the reputation of the route (service -wise) and a sure way to crimp collection potential. Columbia Records' Paul Smith informally moderated a ques- tion and answer session between operators and the score of record people in attendance. Principle topic was the lack of communication between operator -one stop -label and the only answer anyone could come up with was a better record sampling service between the manufacturers and the operators direct. Social -athletic activities included the traditional golf match and distributor vs operator softball game. Meyer Parkoff and Mr. and Mrs. Nugitelli scored high golf - wise; the operators soundly trounced the distributors for a change, thanks largely to the heavy bat of Eddie Goldberg of Archie's Amusement. Louie Wolberg won first prize in raffle then redonated the electric ice crusher to the associations for a re -raffle in the name of Runyon Sales. That's very ice of you, Lou. Plenty of cock - tailing went on both nights, we can tell you, and the food was absolutely excellent at the Grant. Great affair and congrats to the three associations and their reps. Rich, Brokaw Industry NEW YORK-RCA recording artist Buddy Rich, and Kurt Brokaw, man- ager of creative advertising and sales promo at RCA Records, recently gave a combined presentation to an audi- ence of 300 promo executives in Chicago. The presentation, "Artistry in Pro- motion," was part of a three-day Idea Workshop sponsored by Advertising & Sales Promotion Magazine. In ad- dition to Rich and Brokaw, the Work- shop featured a 40 -member "faculty," which included numerous promo men in many business areas. "With the counterculture dying and younger people desperately trying to cut through loneliness and anxiety to find some sense of community and maybe a little piece of nature some- place, the record industry has to be puzzled and jittery," said Brokaw. He described new trends in contemporary music, RCA's internal advertising op- eration ("it saves time, money, and- most important-it saves face"), and the philosophy behind RCA's custom record business. Brokaw defined the major problem confronting the industry as "reaching a restless customer. People are plow- ing around in snowmobiles and taking quickie European vacations and stand- ing in line to see 'The Godfather' .. . they're bored and worried and uncer- tain, and that means music has a lower priority today then last week, or two years ago." Drummer Rich, just off a nation- wide tour with his big band, com- mented on the changing face of to- day's audiences, saying that "honesty is the thing that keys the people that come to hear us play, and the music we play as well." Ad Reprints Available The NARM office has made avail- able to its members, reprints of the advertisement which appeared in the music industry trade press, placed by the National Music Publishers Asso- ciation and the Harry Fox Agency. Headlined "Attention Record and Tape Dealers", the advertisement is a strong statement regarding legends such as "All copyright royalties paid", which appear on much pirated prod- uct. Dealers are cautioned that these statements are misleading, and that those retailers selling such unauthor- ized recordings (despite what is printed on the package), are liable for severe penalties under the law. Malamud states: 'Reprints of the ad- vertisement are available in any quantity necessary to NARM mem- bers, for distribution to dealers in their areas. We commend the National Music Publishers Association and the Harry Fox Agency for this forthright statement, and for disseminating it on an industry -wide basis. The NARM membership is grateful to the music publishers and their representatives for their staunch and continuing fight against bootleg product." New LP's From Capitol HOLLYWOOD - Headlining Capitol Records' June release is "Begin- nings," the U.S. debut album by Rick Springfield, winner of Australia's best singer -songwriter and best guitarist polls, along with "Obscured by Clouds," Pink Floyd's score for the film "La Valee," and "Maybe This Time," a Liza Minelli reissue contain- ing her original recording of the love ballad from "Cabaret." "Modern Times" contains a musical score composed by Chaplin, conducted by Alfred Newman, and arranged by Edward Powell and David Raksin, in- cluding the standard "Smile." "Modern Times" is currently being shown in theatres throughout the na- tion as a result of the interest engen- dered by the presentation of an Oscar to Charlie Chaplin on the recent Academy Awards show. Jethro Tull's Gold `Brick' NEW YORK - "Thick As A Brick," the recently released Reprise album by Jethro Tull, has been certified gold by the R.I.A.A. signifying sales of over one million dollars. Cities covered in the latest Tull tour include Boston, Philadelphia, New York (Nassau Coliseum), To- ronto, Minneapolis, Milwaukee, Edmonton, Vancouver, Seattle, Las Vegas, Houston, Los Angeles, San Diego and Phoenix. There are twenty- nine dates in all covered by the two month tour. "Aqualung" and "Benefit," Jethro Tull's last two Reprise albums, were also certified gold. Duke Ellington's "Latin American Suite" is the second album for the label by the composer, following his "Second Sacred Concert" release of last year. The music was written by Ellington following a tour by his or- chestra of several South American countries in 1968, and was recorded by the full band, including the late Johnny Hodges. "Slow To 20," is Jim Post's second Fantasy album and features the com- poser's friend, guitarist Jim Schwall of the Siegel -Schwall Band. Redwing's debut album was well - received by critics in North America and Europe, where they toured last November. The new album is titled "What This Country Needs." Seven of the ten songs are originals and two are Chuck Berry standards. Rudy Ramos is new to recording but had a regular role in the "High Chapparal" TV series. His band is called Hard Knocks and Bad Times, which is also the title of his first Fantasy album. Pianist Richard Bell, who works regularly with Judy Col- lins, is also featured. Blakey has recently completed several new original compositions for his first album for the label, now in production at Rudy Van Gelder's studio in Englewood Cliffs, New Jer- sey. Chappell Bolsters Drive On Contemporary Sounds Lee Chief Of New Effort NEW YORK - Chappell Music has launched a new drive to strengthen its contemporary look in the U.S. and Canada. The program, being spearheaded by George Lee, vp, who joined the com- pany as international vp, but, under the new Polygram setup, will devote more time to the stimulation of Chap- pell's contemporary division within the U.S. and Canada. Ohe of the immediate signs of suc- cess in this area, the firm notes, is the "Brandy" disking by the Looking Glass (Epic), number 65 (with a bul- let) on this week's Top 100. Due to his extensive background in record production and music publish- ing as vice president and general manager of Warner Bros. Records, Lee's program will be aimed at both the signing and development of con- temporary writers, artist/writers and self-contained groups, plus the strengthening of Chappell's indie rec- ord production affiliations. Internal Production Staff Through publishing agreements with a number of major independent producers, Lee is constructing a built- in production staff available for the recording of Chappell artists and songs. Lee is coordinating efforts in both the areas of artist signing and pro- duction agreements with the Chappell professional staff: Tommy Mottola, Chappell -New York; Jon Devirian, Chappell -Los Angeles; Jerry Rene- wych, Chappell -Toronto; Henry Hurt, Chappell -Nashville. "This young team," Lee said, "will be functioning on a much broader scale than ever. Their combined talent and experience in the fields of pub- lishing, record production and promo- tion is already being fully utilized. They are also involved in present production affiliations and will be further involved in the expansion of this area."
