Grammy Awards Entries Screened NEW YORK-Dozens of the record- ing field's producers, musicians, ar- rangers, composers, record company execs, reviewers, authors and trade paper representatives gathered in New York's Essex House on Nov. 9 for a full day screening of thousands of entries submitted for this year's Grammy Awards competition. The purpose of the record Academy's (NARAS) annual event was to in- sure proper category placement for recommendations submitted by mem- bers and companies and also to screen out. all ineligible material. Throughout the morning, separate committees met to review all entries in their specific fields, occasionally huddling with other committees to discuss duplicate entries. In the after- noon, the various committees com- bined forces to solve all remaining category problems and also to review all entries for the Best New Artist category. The pop, rock and folk committee meeting was supervised by Atlanta's Bill Lowery, assisted by Mary Tall- ent. Chicago sent Bill Traut; Los An- geles winged in Jack Daugherty and Don Ralke; Nashville supplied Don Gant and John Sturdivant. The trades were represented by Bob Adels of Cash Box, Mike Sigman of Record World and Sam Sutherland of Bill- board. Nancy Ehrlich sat in for Rec- ord Source International, while Co- lumbia and RCA sent over Mickey Eichner and Bruce Summerfield, re- spectively. Chicago producer Sam Brown su- pervised the rythm and blues screen- ing with able assistance from Jim Delehant of Atlantic, Cecil Holmes of the Buddah Group, Phil Jones of Mo- town, Buzzy Willis of RCA and Tim Whitsett of Stax, along with Tony Heilbut, author of "The Gospel Sound: Good News and Bad Times," and producers Joe Kennedy and. Hor- ace Ott. Dan Morgenstern, editor of Down Beat and a New York chapter Gover- nor, piloted the Jazz committee that included Atlantic's Michael Cuscuna, CTI's Gregg Hall, trumpeter Joe Newman and reviewers Stanley Dance, Ira Gitler and Father Norman O'Connor. Musicologist David Hall again chaired the Classical committee screening, aided expertly by producer Jim Frey, Scott Mampe of Philips and Tom Shepard of Columbia. And once more this year, author and teacher Henrietta Yurchenko and historian Ray Kennedy reviewed all the entries on the Ethnic/Traditional category. BIG BYRD-UA biggies congratu- late Blue Note Records' Donald Byrd upon his successful engagement at The Lighthouse, west coast jazz mec- ca at Hermosa Beach just outside of Los Angeles. (Left to right) Joseph Ende, vice president and treasurer of the United Artists parent film com- pany, Byrd, and Mark Levinson, vice president of United Artists Records. 3rd Child For Neil Bogarts NEW YORK-Brad Bogart is the name of the third child born to Mr. & Mrs. Neil Bogart. Beth, wife of the co -president of the Buddah Group, gave birth on Thanksgiving Day (23) at New York Hospital. The couple also has a girl, Jill, and a boy, Timothy. SLEEPER SIGNS-Greene Mountain Record president Charles Green (right) has signed Mississippi singer/composer Jeremiah ("The Sleeper") Griffith (middle) to an exclusive, longterm recording and publishing contract. Man- agement consultant Tony Ricco (left) looks on. The Sleeper's single, "Four Dried Beans (From The Lord Above)" will be the label's first release, slated for early January. Sea Cruise To St. Louis ST. LOUIS-Ken Keene has moved his central base of operation to this city after a tenure in New Orleans and Nashville. The company has re- tained its representation in those two key cities, while the new headquarters is more centrally located. The move involves Sea Cruise Productions and Briarmeade Music Unlimited and their affiliated companies. Ken Keene is personal manager of such established artists as Frankie Ford, Robert Parkey, Apocalypse, Carolyn Porter, and Billy Joe Duni - ven. Ford is a partner in the firms; it was for his million -seller disc of "Sea Cruise" a few years back, that they derived the name of the produc- tion company. Ford has just been signed to a re- cording agreement with Cinnamon Records, which is headed by Johnny Morris. The label's first sessions with 5 Douglas Sets Released By UA HOLLYWOOD - Five more LP's from the Douglas Collection series of albums are being shipped immediately by United Artists Records. Among the major jazz artists represented in the UA quintet are Bill Evans and Jim Hall ("Undercurrent"). Herbie Mann ("Brazil Blues"), Charlie Mingus ("Wonderland"), Kenny Dor- ham ("Matador"), and Betty Carter ("Inside Betty Carter"). Previously, another five collections had been is- sued in early October. These were Bil- lie Holiday's "Lady Love", Art Blak- ey's "Three Blind Mice," John Col- trane's "Coltrane Time", King Plea- sure's "Moody's Mood For Love", and "Money Jungle" which combined the talents of Dike Ellington, Charlie Mingus and Max Roach. The Douglas Collection consists of a series of recordings originally pro- duced by Douglas in 1962 for the label. Five To Serve Music Conference HOLLYWOOD-The group Chicago, Henry Mancini, Benny Goodman, Arthur Fiedler and Doc Severinson have been invited to serve on the Spe- cial Advisory Council of the Ameri- can Music Conference, a non-profit organization representing all seg- ments of music. The goal of the AMC is to instill within young and old the desire to become involved with and understand music. Ford have been completed and a single, "When I Stop Dreaming" b/w "I'm Proud of What I Am" is sched- uled for immediate release. George Cooper III of Country Collage has been retained to handle national pro- motion for Cinnamon Records. On the international scene, Keene has leased a master by Narvel Felts to Southern Sound Records in London. The single, "Tongue Tied Jill' b/w "Lola" has already received attention in Sweden, Germany, England and Denmark. The sides have never been released in the United States or Canada. Apocalypse will be returning to the studio next month to record their next single. Keene is also currently negotiating for a tour of England for Robert Parker who has toured there twice before. He has had sev- eral hit records there, including his "Barefootin" for which he received a gold record. Parker is also an in- strumentalist; his saxophone has been heard on countless hit records including "Rockin' Pneumonia and the Boogie Woogie Flu" written and recorded originally by Huey Smith, and "Sea Cruise" by Frankie Ford. For deejay copies, and additional information about any of the Ken Keene artists, contact Sea Cruise Productions, P. O. Box 11387, St. Louis, Missouri 63105. Phone 314/ 865-0714. NEW DEAL-The songwriting team of Dennis Lambert (L) and Brian Potter (L) approve of their new BMI contract being signed by BMI vice- president, Ron Anton. The deal, through their Soldier Music Publish- ing, was negotiated by their attorney, Bruce Grakal. The Lambert & Potter team has been riding high with a number of successes ("Don't Pull Your Love," "Sooner or Later") and are currently watching their "Keeper of the Castle" hit by the Four Tops climb .the charts. The duo also pro- duced the tune (and the album of the same name) , with Steve Barri, for ABC/Dunhill. Paul Williams In Mini -Pilot HOLLYWOOD -A "mini -pilot," something new for television, is being peddled to networks and syndicators, the show starring singer -composer Paul Williams. Pilot is being handled by Pierre Cossette and Jerry Frank of Hollywood, who put on the Johnny Mann "Stand Up and Cheer" show. A nine -minute segment of Wil- liams' appearance on that program was lifted and edited "to show a taste of Paul's personality," according to his manager, Denny Bond. The vi- gnette shows Williams singing, and talking. Pilot show is being offered as a late -night, primetime TV vehicle, since the A&M recording artist is well known in that time slot, having guested many times on the "Tonight" show. The segment was shot at KTLA studios in Hollywood, with John Mof- fitt directing from a script by Rod Warren and Ken Shapiro. Starday-King Boot Promo NEW YORK-Starday-King Records has initiated a promo contest for its distributor promo men involving a new album by Boot, who record for Starday-King's subsid label, Agape. Each promo man has been sent one boot (compliments of Acme's famous Golden Eagle) with his initial ship- ment of "Boot" albums. As soon as a promo man secures album airplay on his local FM -Underground station, he will be sent his other boot. Boot, a band from the Tampa -St. Petersburg section of Florida, signed with King Records' progressive Agape label in mid 1972. Chi War Fete CHICAGO-A busload of Chicago and Milwaukee radio, TV and press people were taken out to the High Chaparal club here in town for the Thanksgiving Eve performance of War, highlighted by the group's re- cording of a live album session to be released in the near future by United Artists Records. Label's Marty Cerf came in from Los Angeles to join local representa- tives Jim Bryant, Walter Paas, Otis Jones and Hilary Johnson in hosting the event. The entire program was aired live via radio station WVON, one of this area's top r&b outlets, and emcee'd by the station's program director E. Rodney Jones. Music Etc's. 4th OKLAHOMA CITY-Music Etc. has opened its fourth store in Oklahoma. The new store carries discount rec- ords and tapes, as well as a wide se- lection of auto and home stereo equipment. The new location at Quail Plaza will be holding its grand opening through Nov. Pat Sherburne is man- ager. The large tape and record re- tailer has three other locations in Oklahoma. Memphis Comm. We Need Order-Chi Lites-Brunswick Melvin's Gold NEW YORK - Harold Melvin and the Bluenotes, one of Philadelphia In- ternational's most popular recording acts, have struck gold with their smash single, "If You Don't Know Me By Now." The record has been certified gold by the RIAA, signifying sales of over one million units. "If You Don't Know Me By Now" was produced by Ken Gamble and Leon Huff, and was culled from Har- old Melvin and the Bluenotes' current chartclimbing LP on the Philadelphia International label, "I Miss You." 16 Cash Box - December 2, 1972 www.americanradiohistory.com

Stigwood Forms RSO Label In U.S.; Bienstock Chief Atlantic Dist Key Acts To Co. NEW YORK - Robert Stigwood has formed RSO Records in the U.S., and has named Johnny Bienstock as man- aging director. Bienstock was former- ly head of singles sales for Atlantic Records, which will distribute the new label. It's understood that RSO will kick - FRONT COVER: "Man of La Mancha" is the latest in the continuing saga of hit soundtrack albums from United Ar- tists Records, which has firmly estab- lished itself as a leader in motion picture music during the past decade. - "Man Of La Mancha" follows hard on the heels of UA's "Fiddler on the Roof," one of the best-selling film LPs of all time. Inspired by the Spanish classic by Cervantes, "Man of La Mancha" is an original work by Dale Wasserman, who has brilliantly combined the character and spirit of Cervantes with the splendid lunatic fantasies of the author's fictional creation Don Quix- ote. "Man of La Mancha," adapted for the screen by Wasserman, has been described as a musical within a play, but it actually defies convention. Au- diences around the world, however, have agreed that it is a unique dra- matic experience. Peter O'Toole as Cervantes/Don Quixote, Sophia Loren as Dul- cinea/Aldonza, and James Coco as Sancho Panza, inherit roles per- formed in theatrical productions presented in 22 languages in 45 coun- tries. The original stake version opened in New York on Nov. 22, 1965, and later swept the Tony and Drama Critics Awards as Best Musi- cal. It has been brought to the screen with its prize-winning songs and mu- sic, inciding such favorites as "The Imposslble Dream" and "Dulcinea." For pr ducer-director Arthur Hiller, "Man Of La Mancha" caps a career that indludes, "Love Story" and "The Hospital." Bienstock At Chicago Meet: Indie Distributors Vote To Seek Gains In NARM Framework NEW YORK - Dispelling rumors of a separate indie distributor organiza- tion, a group of indie distributors meeting in Chicago on Fri., Dec. 8, voted unanimously to work within the framework of NARM, the merchan- diser -manufacturer association. The meeting of 22 distributors was called in the wake of problems faced by this segment of the business, which in recent years has been con- fronted with the growth of branch operations and charges by labels util- izing such a network that indie dis- tributors are failing to provide sufficient promo support on product and are slow in payment of bills. The Chicago meeting also saw plans developed for an expanded role of the indie distributor in NARM, originally organized to serve the rack -jobber area, but which has evolved as an association of wider industry purpose. The first order of business at the Chicago meeting was a unanimous vote of the 22 distributors present to remain in NARM, and to continue to work as members of NARM, for the best interests of their segment of the industry. Plans were developed whereby the indie distributors could achieve their objectives within the framework of the established industry association. Working with Jules Malamud, NARM exec director, Dave Press, NARM president, and Earl Kintner, general counsel, who attend- ed the meeting, the distributors present worked out a set of initial plans for their expanded role in NARM. Foremost and of the most immediate importance was the role MCA Shows Video Disk; Sees Pricing Along Lines Of LP UNIVERSAL CITY - MCA Disco - Vision, Inc., unveiled its eagerly antic- ipated video disk last week for the MCA board members, industry execs and press, highlighted by a seven - minute demonstration drawn from the Universal Pictures archives. The record itself proved to be a paper -thin, 12 -inch silver mylar disk with a playing -time capability of at least 40 minutes, at 1800 r p.m., for either color or black -and -white pro- gram material, thus far outdistancing the capabilities of existing audio- visual disk systems. It can be pro- duced for about 40 cents and pressed in virtually the same way an ordi- nary LP record is pressed. It is also just about indestructible. Price to the consumer will be along the lines of LP pricing. Opening the first public demonstra- tion was Lew R. Wasserman, pres- ident and chief exec officer of MCA, Inc., who aster a few brief remarks introduced the newly appointed pres- ident of MCA Disco -Vision, Inc., John W. Findlater, a veteran MCA senior officer and vice president. Said Findlater, "We believe we've achieved the ultimate concept in home entertainment and information storage and retrieval systems, and that both the hardware and the soft- MCA's Video Disk Player ware will be sold to the consumer at popular prices." $400 Unit Indications were that the sinc'le- record playback unit would be priced in the $400 range, and that a multi- ple -disc player/changer would cost around $500. Pi's Paul To Give Col Top Single Of '72 NEW YORK - Billy Paul's "Mr & Mrs. Jones," on the Columbia - handled Philadelphia International label, will probably end its sales run as Columbia's top -selling single of 1972. The deck has already been awarded an RIAA million -selling gold disk, and sales are heading toward the 2 million mark, according to the label. In addition, the LP spin- off on the hit looks like it will emerge as the first million unit seller for the hot PI label, owned and pro- duced by Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff. PI has sold some five million sin- gles over the past three months. Dis- tributed through the Epic and Columbia Custom Labels, PI has had gold showings from Paul, the O'Jays ("Back Stabbers") and Harold Mel- vin & the Blue Notes ("If You Don't Know Me By Now"). 2nd 'In Concert' Scores In Ratings NEW YORK - Don Kirshner's "In Concert" rock shows on TV continue to show rosy ratings. With national Nielsens' yet to come, the second show, featuring the Allman Bros., Chuck Berry, Blood, Sweat & Tears and Poco, got a 32 share of audience in Los Angeles, outdistancing the CBS late -night moive (22) and the Johnny Carson Show (21) . In New York, the show posted a 22, double that of the Dick Cavett Show, one of the ABC presen- tations sharing the 11:30 to 1 am time -slot. The next "In Concert" TV'er takes place Jan. 19, and will feature the Grand Funk Railroad concert from Madison Square Garden taking place this week (23). cashbox! dbwn reviews MORE HOT ROCKS (big hits & fazed cookies) -Rolling Stones-London 2PS 626/7 What's a fazed cookie? Perhaps it's only a rhetorical question, since everyone in the in- dustry knows by now what a hot rock is. This is volume two of the successful Stones hit LP of the past year; with the inclusion of eight tracks never before available in the U. S., it could even surpass its predecessor. In addi- tion to the aforementioned cuts-mostly good ole r&b-there's at long last, "We Love You," a single B-side, never before on LP. That track kind of sums up the national reaction to the most consistently popular band around. RE-FOCUS-The Monkees-Bell 6081 Bell has come into the rights of the Colgems catalog, and the first repackage is, not sur- prisingly enough, a Monkees offering. It's a compenium of their best singles and LP cuts, including material by Boyce & Hart, Mann & Weil, Neil Diamond, Goffin & King, John Stew- art and their own Michael Nesmith. The group brought a lot of happiness to a lot of people with their music a not too far back once upon a time. The label that's done so well with marketing the Partridge Family should have another chart item here. JUST FOR YOU - Bobby Sherman - Metro- media MD 1060 Bobby Sherman has a lot more competition now on the pre -teen market than he had when he first hit big, but don't count him out of the picture. There are a number of tracks here that could give him yet another hit single and he still commands a substantial share of the LP market. The best of the lot is "Unborn Lullabye (Let Your Mind Be Your Captain,") which Bobby himself arranged. The Tokens' hit, "She Lets Her Hair Down" is also one his fans should quickly latch onto. ELLA LOVES COLE-Ella Fitzgerald -Atlantic SD 1631 Cole Porter, of course, with Ella updating and, in some cases, adding to the wonderful Porter set she did for Verve Records more than a decade -and -a -half ago. Norman Granz is still the producer, and Nelson Riddle supplies his usual vocal -perfect orchestral settings. Ella and Porter are unbeatable, so look for Ella -Porter fans swarming to pick up copies of this smart set at their dealers. KEITH MICHELL SINGS BROADWAY-Spark SPA -03 Michell, whose towering performance in "The Six Wives of Henry VIII" TV series im- pressed viewers on both sides of the Atlantic, possesses a strong, aware baritone voice. His "Broadway" material ranges wide, from Steven Sondheim's dramatic "Being Alive" to the effervescent "She Loves Me." Peter Knight's arrangements (on most cuts) for a big orches- tra are always apt. Michell, who played Broadway before, deserves more vehicles on the Main Stem, and this LP bears witness to it. POP PICKS TN WNW MU 11111MITINT DEVIL WITH A BLUE NESS ON BREAKOUT TURN ON TOUR LOVEUGHT GOT 00U ,I FEEL GOAD) 000E IT TO ME BABY JENNY TAKE E BIDE LITTLE LATIN WPE LO TOO MANY FISH IN TIE SEA I UBE IT LAKE TIAT TARIM ALL I CAN GET SLUE ATAIL FEATHER POP BEST BETS KEITH MICHELL - AIMCA BZC'DWAY CLASSICAL PICKS THE MELODIYA ALBUM - Melodiya/Angel SRBR-4123 The Capitol distributed classical line has just renegotiated its arrangement with the Soviet Melodiya label (the ONLY label in the U. S. S. R.), and takes this opportunity to celebrate the nation's 50th anniversary in music. The sampler of some of the greatest moments in the Melodiya/Angel catalog includes perform- ances by David Oistrakh, Sviatoslav Richter, Irina Arkhipova, Emil Giles, Ivan Petrov, Msti- slav Rostopovich, the Soviet Army Chorus & Band and others. From ballet to balalaika, a complete view of Soviet recording. SUNNY DAYS - Lighthouse - Evolution 3016 Canadian rockers Lighthouse are coming off their most successful single yet, "Sunny Days." It serves as the take-off point for what could easily be their biggest LP to date. They are very tight and very commercial throughout, even on the extended cuts which provide much of the interest: "Beneath My Woman" and "You Give It To Me." The single most likely to follow-up their latest sounds like "You Girl," with an instrumental intro that should be a topic for many a dj rap. Ten men, one hit sound all their own. MITCH RYDER & THE DETROIT WHEELS GREATEST HITS-Virgo SV 12001 First LP release for the Roulette -distributed label is one long awaited. In the late sixties, this quintet kept the spark of American rock and roll alive with a sound that was both heavy and commercial. They were especially fine in med!ey form: "Jenny Take A Ride" ("See See Rider" with Little Richard's "Jinny Jin") and "Devil With A Blue Dress On/Good Golly Miss Molly." Like the early Raiders, they were responsible for getting the previously uninitiated into the boogie club for the first time. Album is a perfect compromise between apt production and pure passion. MR&TDW can still sock it to ya, baby! MERMAN SINGS MERMAN-Ethel Merman- Stanley Black & the London Festival Orchestra & Chorus-London Phase 4 XPS-901 The vocal electricity still possesses high voltage, so who could really ask for anything more when La Merman revives those incredible songs she's introduced over the years? With big, brassy, swinging ork-chorus backdrops, the star offers supercharged versions of "You're the Top," "There's No Business Like Show Business," "It's D'Lovely" and nine other greats. It's wonderful to hear the sheer joy of singing again. GASOLINE-Chip Taylor-Buddah BRS 5118 Chip, one third of Gorgoni, Martin & Taylor, has released his first solo LP. Mixing the down-and-out insights of a Kristofferson with the more joyous aspects of a Lobo, Taylor puts himself in a rather commercial, yet very individualistic and personal groove. His own version of the self -penned "Angel Of The Morning" is the album's highlight. The entire production bears the mark of much thought and carefully directed talent. CHARADE-Buckwheat-London XPS 621 The quintet's been experimenting some with Delta soul and other varieties since their last LP. They are quite righteous borrowers of both Sly ("Hey Little Girl"-our favorite track) and Delaney & Bonnie ("Old L. A."); but you couldn't call what they do stealin' by any definition. They have developed an interesting choral vocal approach which helps to sprinkle enough of the original out of each soulshaker they pick up on. And Uncle Bucky Smother - man's keyboards are more than proficient. JAZZ PICKS THE BEST OF JOHN COLTRANE, HIS GREAT- EST YEARS, VOL. 2-Impulse AS -9223-2 It was obvious from the start that even a double -LP best of album was insufficient to capture Trane's spirit. So here's specially priced set #2. This one contains tracks record- ed from '61 to '67, including "India," "Miles' Mode" and "Manifestation." Assisting in the flow: Eric Dolphy, Pharoah Sanders, Archie Shepp, Freddie Hubbard, McCoy Tyner, Alice Coltrane, Duke Ellington, Elvin Jones and others. The man is his own best tribute. 20 Cash Box - December 30, 1972 www.americanradiohistory.com

NASHVLLLE - Nashville Talent and Booking Co., a division of B.I.B. Pro- ductions Inc., is now actively booking acts from all aspects of the entertain- ment business. Owner and president James (Jim) Berry also announced the appoint- ment of musician/singer, Hal Jackson, as vice president of sales for the booking agency. Berry deemed the formation of his business the "realization of a life- long dream" and said the corporation is designed to eventually include pro- duction, publishing and promotion. In the interim, he said the booking agen- cy will be "booking and promoting acts on an equal opportunity status while elevating its standards in growth to its best capabilities." Berry received a BS degree in per- formance engineering from Purdue and later, received a degree in man- agement and administration. Follow- ing an Air Force stint and discharge at the rank of Captain, he spent years traveling around the country as an equipment performance engineer for the Chrysler Corp., later joining Ken - worth of Tennessee as a field sales engineer. With music and songwriting a con- tinuing hobby, Berry began working with talented youth, which led him to hosting the Greater East Nashville Talent Show this past year and, even- tually, formation of his company. Jackson began playing guitar at age 12. Beginning professionally at 14 as part of the house band for KFH Radio and playing the following year at KAKE-TV in Wichita, he entered the service at 17, continuing to make personal appearances throughout his tour of duty. Marriage, a course in business administration and forma- tion of his own group ensued. 'New Era Adds Member CHICAGO - Vocal -instrumental group, The New Era, who recently signed a disk pact with Expo Records, have added a new member to their unit. She's Penny Lee, former Miss Wyoming and Miss U.S.A. runner-up. Group, now numbering six mem- bers, is preparing for an extensive college tour in conjunction with the release of their first single by the label. Purcell Mgmt For A. Williams NEW YORK - Composer -singer Ann Williams, formerly with the Sweet In- spiration group, which performed with Elvis Presley the past year and backed on records many top artists, has signed for personal management with GWP Associates, according to Jerry Purcell, president of the organi- zation. Purcell added that an album of original material by Miss Williams is scheduled for Feb. WELL KNOWN-Columbia Records president Clive Davis joins Philadelphia International's creative team, Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff in presenting Harold Melvin and the Blue Notes with gold record awards for their million and a half selling single, "If You Don't Know Me By Now." Pictured at the presentation held for the group at New York's Plaza are (1. to r.) Teddy Pendigrass, Bernie Wilson, Larry Brown, producer Kenny Gamble, Harold Melvin, Lloyd Parks, Clive Davis, producer Leon Huff and Logan H. Gavin '72 Musical Summary Sees Soft Sound Triumphant HOLLYWOOD - Hard rock took a back seat to smoother sounds in the realm of popular music during 1972, according to the annual summary prepared by Bill Gavin, publisher of the weekly guide to radio program- ming, the Gavin Report. "A glance at the year's top 100 hit singles will show that fewer than 25 per cent are in the real tough rock category," Gavin noted, pointing to "mellow ballads" as the kind of music America liked best. The trend toward slower and senti- mental songs also was evident in the rhythm-and-blues field, he said, while the traditionally -conservative non - rock radio stations became less so and programmed a higher percentage of current hits. Country music contin- ued to thrive, according to Gavin. The Top 10 pop hits of 1972, based on weekly findings filed by Gavin Re- port correspondents: 1) First Time Ever (Roberta Flack); 2) Horse With No Name (America); 3) Alone Again (Gilbert O'Sullivan); 4) Precious & Few (Climax); 5) Nice To Be With You (Gallery); 6) I'd Love You to Want Me (Lobo); 7) Without You (Nilsson); 8) Summer Breeze (Seals & Crofts); 9) Brandy (Looking Glass); 10) Lean on Me (Bill With- ers). Rockless Hits: 1) Alone Again (O'Sullivan); 2) I Can See Clearly Now (Johnny Nash); 3) Nice to be With You (Gallery); 4) First Time Ever (Roberta Flack); 5) City of New Orleans (Arlo Guthrie). Rhythm And Blues Hits: 1) If You Don't Know Me By Now (Harold Melvin and the Blue Notes); 2) I'll Be Around (Spinners); 3) I'll Take You There (Staple Singers); 4) Me & Mrs. Jones (Billy Paul); 5) If Loving You Is Wrong (Luther Ingram). Country Hits: 1) Happiest Girl in the U.S.A. (Donna Fargo); 2) My Hang -Up is You (Freddie Hart); 3) If You Leave Me Tonight (Jerry Wallace); 4) Funny Face (Donna Fargo); 5) It's Not Love (Merle Haggard). Gavin's Yearly Summary contained 100 hits in each of the above catego- ries. UA Services Disk Jazz Show to FMs HOLLYWOOD - United Artists, in order to reach further markets with their Douglas Collection jazz series has produced an hour-long radio show geared specifically for the col- lege and FM media. The program, produced and written by Martin Cerf of UA's creative services dept., and Colman Andrews (editor of Coast Magazine) will be pressed on disk and serviced to FM and college radio outlets nationally early this month. Rosenberg New RKO Gen. Veep HOLLYWOOD - Hal Rosenberg, General Manager of KRTH, has be- come a vice president of RKO Gener- al, Inc. He is the only FM general manager in the RKO system to dou- ble as vice president. Since becoming general manager, Rosenberg has built up the station's sales and led it through changes in call letters (from KHJ-FM to KRTH) and format (to classic gold rock n' roll of the fifties and early sixties). Atlantic Best Year (Cont'd from page 10) Nash & David Crosby;" "History Of Eric Clapton;" Bee Gees-"To Whom It May Concern;" Joni Mitchell-"For The Roses." Atlantic's custom labels also re- leased albums by their biggest stars. The Rolling Stones double LP, "Exile On Main Street," was issued by Roll- ing Stones Records; Little David Records released George Carlin's "FM & AM" and "Class Clown," and Flip Wilson had "Geraldine." Atlantic also released new product by its outstanding jazz artists: Herbie Mann, Eddie Harris, Les McCann, Rahsaan Roland Kirk, Yusef Lateef, David Newman, Hubert Laws, Dave Brubeck, and The Modern Jazz Quar- tet. Rahsaan Roland Kirk made his debut as a producer for Atlantic with an LP featuring a great Chicago jazz musician, Von Freeman. The first al- bum in the commodore label's classic jazz series was issued in October, Bil- lie Holiday's "Strange Fruit." One of the new groups signed to the label was "The Chicago Art Ensemble," whose records will be produced by Michael Cuscuna. Although Led Zeppelin did not have a new album during the year, their fourth album, released in late 1971, continued to be a big seller through- out the year, passing the million unit mark in total sales. The tours and concert appearances by top acts helped spur sales of both singles and albums. In addition to the Rolling Stones tour during the sum- mer, such important artists as Gra- ham Nash & David Crosby, Stephen Stills and his new band Manassas, ELP, Yes, Roberta Flack, Donny Hathaway, Led Zeppelin, George Car- lin, and many others appeared in au- ditoriums, arenas, theaters and clubs during the busy year. The Nash -Crosby tour was the first for either artists in over a year. Ste- phen Stills had a very busy schedule, with five tours, including one in Eu- rope, in the six months from June to December. In the fall of the year Atlantic re- leased the second album featuring Ar- chie Bunker and his TV family "All In The Family, 2nd Album." The first "All In The Family" album was a smash in 1971; the second album was a strong seller in 1972. Atlantic Records and its custom la- bels signed many talented artists dur- ing 1972. Among the artists joining the label in 1972 were: Bettye Swann, Jackie DeShannon, Dave Brubeck, New Heavenly Blue, Daryl Hall & John Oates, Good God, Lenny Welch, Ramatam, Margie Joseph, The Spin- ners, Stiller & Meara, Doug Sahm, Bette Midler, Bobby Austin, Willie Nelson, Eric Justin Kaz, and Sam Dees (Clintone). Asylum Records added to the strength of its roster with the signing of Linda Ronstadt, and the all-star rock group, The Ea- gles. Ronstadt's first album will be released next year. Atlantic signed a recording con- tract with its own West Coast region- al promotion director, Big Johnny Fisher. His first single was released in November. The English super -group, Yes, made a personnel change in 1972 when Alan White succeeded Bill Bruford on drums. Bruford left Yes to join King Crimson. The Persuaders, one of Atlantic's top -selling vocal groups were signed to a new, long term exclusive contract with Atlantic Records, under the su- pervision of vice president of promo Henry Allen. Atlantic Records merchandising de- partment under Rick Willard came up with a number of unusual merchan- dising ideas that helped enhance At- lantic releases and artists. In the STATION BREAKS: Guy Lombardo Department: With New Year's Day just behind us, and a whole New Year ahead, now is the best time. Not just to make resolutions, but to see if we can really keep them. Regardless of the arbitrariness involved in shipping the endless ribbon of time into neat, twelve-month strips for wrapping our memories and past hopes into compact little packages, January is indeed a new beginning. With the holiday tidings and busi- ness spurt also comes the subse- quent lull in music trends, and in policy decisions in general. But in- genuity can't take a holiday. We have no control over January be- ing a cold month, but it doesn't have to be a dull one. Jocks, mds, pds, and gms must prove their stuff now more than ever before. Lest old acquaintances be forgot. Radio is so easily taken for granted. Only the excitement you bring to the medium can continu- ally reactivate the efficacy of a true friendship, a real, not imag- ined communication between you and your audience. They'll give a damn only if you do your damnest. In the words of the President who just passed his last Christmas- give 'em hell! It seems that the "program" in "pd" may be in for a new mean- ing. Lee Abrams has left his pd - ship at Detroit's WRIF with an idea he'd like to see realized. He's been working with the computer meaning of the word "program" for some time and now has over 75,000 research pages of input ready to be turned into output for the right rocker. (Much of his data comes from ARB analyses.) He can be reached at (313) 356-2698. Meanwhile the ABC FM outlet is looking for a replacement for Abrams ... Charlie Greer, former jock on WABC moves his business address closer to home as he as- sumes the 9 -noon slot at Spring Valley's WKQW. New faces at Richmond Hill, On- tario's CFGM. Bill Anderson is the new pd, coming from CJCB in Syd- ney. John Hart is the new public service director, from Montreal's CKGM and CFCF; and Bob Mc- Adorey has returned as morning man from a two-year hiatus at Toronto's CFTR ... Dave Turner is the new night news editor at Charlotte's WAME. Many smaller cities within shoutin' distance of larger urban areas often have an inferiority complex. It can spread to the sta- tions in these smaller metropolises as well. But not always. Reading and WRAW is a case in point. With Philadelphia so close, the station still gets pulse numbers like 33 in morning drive and 50 in afternoon drive. Doug Weldon is pd there, while at sister station in Allentown it's Gene Werley. Both are important men when there is a record to be broken in Philly. Aircheck: Imus In The Morning, WNBC. Before interviewing Joey Heatherton on the air: "I'd do anything for her. Anything. I'd even play her record." robert adels spring the firm issued a series of pos- ters of top artists illustrated by the famous artist Stanislaw Zagorski. Posters featured Aretha Franklin, Roberta Flack, Wilson Pickett, Les McCann, Eddie Harris, The Bee Gees, Stephen Stills, David Crosby, Graham Nash, Herbie Mann, Keith Emerson, Greg Lake, and Carl Palmer. Two of the posters, David Crosby and Keith Emerson, garnered awards as best posters of the year in a contest sponsored by Print Magazine. The merchandising department also initiated a new in-store monthly leaflet called Atlantic Album Review with reviews of new Atlantic prod- ucts. Stores all over the country were using the Atlantic Album Re- view as stuffers and giveaways. Atlantic received an outstanding achievement award in the 30th annual exhibition of the New York Metropol- itan Printing Industries for its Led Zeppelin display. Two completely re -packaged oldies single series were issued by Atlantic in 1972. Called the Oldies Hit Series and The Collectors Series, they were introduced in early Oct. The two series contain 166 singles, all with back to back hits. The collectors series features such artists as Ray Charles, Sticks McGhee, The Clovers and Joe Turner. The oldies series features Lavern Baker, The Coasters, Aretha, Otis Redding, The Bee Gees, Led Zeppelin, and Crosby, Stills & Nash. These recordings are offered in two browser boxes, one called The Real Beginning, the other The Gold Bin. Atlantic used both slide shows and films to introduce its new product to dealers this year. It's "Soul Ex- plosion" release in Jan. 1972, show- cased new product in a 30 minute film created by Joe's Lights. In the fall the firm introduced new product in Au- gust and October with slide shows created by Ron Naar Associates and written by Atlantic's own advertising manager, Elin Guskind. A 12 -page booklet, A Short His- tory of Atlantic Records was also made available in 1972 for the con- sumer. The 1200 word story with a list of all gold records was written by advertising and publicity vice pres- ident Bob Rolontz. A number of polls were won by Atlantic during the year. The firm was voted the company that gives the best service to college radio stations by the nationally circulated College Radio Report, and also by Format, the Mid -Western newspaper of the In- tercollegiate Broadcasting System. Atlantic initiated its own service for college broadcasters by acting as a clearing house for college students who wanted to get into broadcasting. Resumes sent to Atlantic are passed on to commercial radio stations by Gunter Hauer, Atlantic Records col- lege promo director. Bullard succeeded O'Gilvie in jazz promotion; Dolores Seymour was named exec assistant to Henry Allen. Rick Willard was appointed merchandising manager, a new post for the company; Johnny Bienstock was appointed singles sales manager, and in Dec. he joined RSO Records as U.S. label manager. Sal Uterano was appointed album sales manager. Paul L. Johnson was named eastern re- gional promo manager; Phil Rauls was appointed southern & regional promo manager; Paul Ahern joined Asylum Records as head of promo. Michael Cuscuna joined Atlantic as a staff producer. Dede Sparico was appointed to the post of foreign production coordina- tor; Bob Defrin joined Atlantic as art director, advertising. LeBaron Taylor joined Atlantic as A&R head for R&B product. Rick Sanjek left BMI to come with Atlantic as country music administra- tor. He was also made manager of Atlantic's first Nashville office. Sets New Mktg Concept At NY Meeting NEW YORK-"Communications '73", a major Atlantic Records marketing convention was held here recently at the Plaza Hotel for more than 50 sales, promotion, advertising and publicity executives from the field, the west coast and the New York home office staff. Chaired by senior VP and general manager, Jerry Greenberg and marketing VP Dave Glew, the meetings were held to initiate Atlan- tic's new domestic sales and promo- tion concept: the formation of five national marketing teams, each com- prised of one sales and two promo- tion managers, which will be respon- sible for all Atlantic activity in their territory. Topics Discussed In the course of the two-day meet- ings, many major developments and re-structurings of Atlantic's market- ing operations were revealed. "In creating the marketing teams," said Greenberg, "regional sales and pro- motion can now be supervised in con- junction with the eight Warner- Elektra-Atlantic distribution branch- es, and local retailers, radio sta- tions, rack jobbers and one -stn's with new facility and efficiency. When a record is introduced into a market under our new system, all pertinent information concerning airplay, sales activity, artist appearances, invento- ry, advertising and publicity will be immediately in the hands of all terri- torial executives-and available for home -office direction." To Clive Davis, Columbia's Black Experience is Obtaining A Universal Audience NEW YORK - Columbia Records' enormous penetration of the black recording market with marked cross- over impact is seen as a greater reali- zation of the label's commitment to establish a "universal audience" for all areas of the pop music scene. Through the Epic and Columbia Custom Labels, the company is presently going through a remarkable surge in black acts making huge gains in the black market and across- the-board as well. The sources include the Columbia - handled Philadelphia International la- bel, which is owned and produced by Ken Gamble and Leon Huff; a dis- tribution deal with the Stax label; and, via England, Johnny Nash's "I Can See Clearly Now" on the Epic label. And to come is a label distribu- tion deal with Thom Bell's new com- pany. Bell is the producer of such stellar black acts as the Stylistics and the Spinners. Clive Davis, president of Columbia, looks at 1972 as one of the label's most gratifying years, partly as a result of moving into an area of "pri- mary significance, black music, which has provided a tremendous burst for us." This penetration proves to Davis that "when you have the right mar- riage of creativity and marketing prowess that you can move into any area, and there is no reason to have barriers setup." Davis, of course, points out that Columbia has always had black per- formers. This time around, however, the label's black successes are true definitions of "black market records," that is recordings that start to break on black radio and, hopefully, cross- over into Top 40. Davis notes that about a year ago, he held meetings with Gamble & Huff on the possibilities of a distribution tie, making clear to them not only the immediacy of a hit single, but to look at a market beyond, and to think of albums as well. To Bruce Lundvall, vp of marketing at Columbia, the black market itself has proven to contain a "superstar structure that spreads into pop." "The black market itself," Lundvall adds, "is enormous and concentrated. In the album area, there is a remarkably small return factor." Ron Alexenburg, vp of Epic & Columbia Custom Labels, sees the black market boom as a case in point that "you can't categorize music any longer." "Top 40 radio," he explains, "has really looked at black stations and realized that it's one world of music. They want records by black acts as quickly as R&B stations. For a label, it means that now you can position records in an entire city. We have had to establish a greater, more direct re- lationship with new dealers and one - stops." It's Alexenburg's "gut feel- ing" that 1973 will see an even greater dominance of black acts from the industry as a whole. For Epic and Columbia Custom Labels, Alexenburg reports that the division will realize a 200 to 300% increase in volume this year over 1972. "What we're gearing to do is to take the same care as we do in product in building the images of these artists so they do not just appeal to the black (Cont'd on p. 10) Cerro Drops Tape Club; Sues In Calif. NEW YORK - The Cerro Corp. is dropping its Stereo Tape Club of America operations, while bringing suit against a national accounting firm involved with STCA, financial statements. Cerro, which acquired a majority interest in the firm in 1971, alleges that it was furnished with false and misleading statements by Touche Ross & Co., a national accounting firm, in a $14 million damage suit in Federal District Court for the Central District of Calif. The complaint al- leges that the audited financial state- ments were misleading in that they overstated the accounts receivable of STCA, leading to overstatements of assets and earnings. Also involved in the suit as defen- dants were former directors of the Club, Joseph DeFranco, Andrew D. Berkey, Sidney Steinberg, William F. Staunton and Ralph Weinstock. Cerro said it would incur an after- tax loss of $3,973,000 for 1972. Hollywood N.A.A.C.P Honors RCA HOLLYWOOD - RCA Records was honored as "The Record Company of the Year" at the sixth annual Image Awards presented by the Beverly Hills -Hollywood Branch of the N.A.A.C.P. before an audience of 1500 persons at the Hollywood Pal- ladium. In commenting on the award, Pres- ident Junius Griffin said, "For some two decades the social revolution in this nation has received a great deal of its thrust and support from the music industry in general and from the recording industry in particular." He emphasized that the award to RCA Records was "in recognition of its artistic excellence and outstanding contributions toward the furtherance of brotherhood and the maintenance of dignity of minorities in the enter- tainment industry." Redd Foxx, who also won an Image Award for his role in "Sanford And Son" for NBC-TV, acted as master of ceremonies and presented the "Record Company of the Year Award" to Winston Wills, Director of Rhythm and Blues Music, RCA Records. Redd Foxx-Winston Willis OPERATION PUSH Black businessmen gather at a spe- ' cial reception hosted by John H. Johnson, President of Johnson Pub- lishing Co., Inc. to open Operation PUSH's Cross Fertilization of the Black Economy Seminar held in Chi- cago, December 6 and 7. Welcoming the seminar participants (shown 1. to r.) are Al Johnson, President of Al Johnson Cadillac in Chicago and Co - Chairman of the Cross Fertilization Seminar; A. Romeo Horton, President of the Bank of Liberia; Rev. Jesse L. Jackson, President of Operation PUSH; Al Bell, Executive Vice Pres- ident of Stax Records in Memphis, Tenn.; and Alvin Boutte, President of the Independence Bank of Chicago and Co -Chairman of the Cross Fertil- ization Seminar. Jerry Butler Headlines At Copa NEW YORK CITY, NY - Jerry But- ler, Mercury recording artist, along with Brenda Lee Eager & Peaches opened Thursday, Jan. 4 at the Co- pacabana. Jerry has been riding high with, "One Night Affair" and with the recently released "Melinda," a movie with a powerful score and a delivery of the title theme that lives up to the ice man standard. `Spice of Life' was also one of his recent top selling al- bums. The Copa stint promises to be an exciting one for New Yorkers; and visitors. Corp. in Elmhurst, NY.-DD ON THE '73 HORIZON STEPHANIE MILLS CONNIE THOMAS `Black Arts' Receives Emmy Nom. NEW YORK-Black Arts, an in-depth look at creative Black talent, has been nominated for an Emmy program award, it was announced by the New York Chapter of The National Academy of Television Arts and Sciences. Dr. Roscoe Brown, Jr. Director of the Institute of Afro-American Affairs at New York University, is host of the weekly series which first aired on January 2nd, 1972 and is presented each Saturday at 2pm on Channel Two. Roy Allen, who also produces Sunrise Semester, is the producer/director of the show. Dr. Brown says he tries to spotlight a different art form each week-drama, dance, mu- sic, photography. The program has featured such Black talents as the cast of "We, Us & Company"-described as a youth cultural happening; author, John Killens; musician, Billy Taylor, and Ed Spriggs, of the Studio Museum of Harlem. Shown (Left to Right) Dr. Roscoe Brown and Fred Beauford, Editor of Black Creation. Rust Brown Hosts Toy Drive NEW YORK - The Christmas spirit abounded last week at the posh Rust Brown Restaurant. Owners Lloyd Brown and former television sports- caster, Art Rust, Jr. were host to a toy drive sponsored by Operation P.U.S.H.-only one part of their mas- sive campaign to collect food, cloth- ing and toys for 10,000 needy families in the area. Such emminent personages as Man- hattan Borough President, Percy Sut- ton; Emmy nominee, Dr. Roscoe Brown, host of WCBS's Black Arts Show; and P.U.S.H. New York co- ordinator, Joyce Ware Thomas were on hand to meet and greet guests. The party attracted several hundred enthusiastic people-each with a toy- to the upper westside restaurant and was hailed as an enormous success. 16 Cash Box - January 13, 1973 www.americanradiohistory.com

KsotsotsotsotsC=cX=XX=t>{ s:=1t.<=tt0tx=D4rottoex cashbox/talent on stage ' roeoctocsotrocsoWsot?_ x_ s '4t o:_s<=soWsotaocsoisocsc The Spinners The O'Jays APOLLO THEATRE, NYC-Opening Jan. 10, The Spinners and the O'Jays drew an overflow audience for the last two shows of the night. And, to ac- curately describe what happened could fill a book. The O'Jays, super soul personalities all the way, absolutely destroyed the place with a fantastic rendition of, "Listen To The Clock On The Wall," and believe me, there was barely a soul who wasn't listen- ing with all their hearts. "Back Stab - hers" was another selection that had everyone clapping and singing to this rhythmic fantastic tune. Another out- standing selection was, "You Are My Sunshine," a very beautiful number on the order of, "Peace In The Valley Of Love". "You Are My Sunshine" is a heartstopper in every way. And, as if that wasn't enough, one of the biggest reactions to a song that this reviewer has seen, when the group went into, "Love Train" everyone was aboard. The Apollo was ringing with the music and lyric of the tune. It was super. The Spinners are a group that could melt an ice- berg, and coming on after them, you had better be with it. There isn't much lacking in the way of dance routines. Their individual talents, their all around performance capabil- ity, their experience and professional- ism really makes them one of the outstanding performing groups. The Spinners are together and more than proved it with this Apollo perform- ance. "It's A Shame" was one of their opening selections. Also, their new single release, "I'll Be Around" came across with zip and fire. The group also does fantastic impressions of other groups and artists and they do it with class. Phillipe Wynne, newest member of the group, is one helluva tenor lead singer. He really gets down. The other 4 members are origi- nal members and they go back some 17 years. Their repertoire consists of soul ballads, grooving songs such as "I Need Somebody Soon" and also the flip side of "I'll Be Around", "How Could I Let You Get Away" even had this reviewer as well as everyone yelling for more. They are indeed a family and this was one of the best shows of '73 and there are more to come. Iii Four Tops arbara Mason COCONUT GROVE, L.A. - The Four Tops, who have been spinning gold records for over a decade, satiated their opening -night audience. They opened their rousing, precisioned act with their brand new ABC/Dunhill single "Ain't No Woman," and it was plain to see that there was no woman or man in the capacity crowd who could resist the infectious beat. It would take an applause meter to discern which one of their string of hits is most outstanding. In fact it's their long list of hits that make an audience anticipate a great show even before the curtain goes up. The Four Tops, one of the best quartets around, fulfill every expectation. In- cluded in their flawless performance was "Baby I Need Your Loving" (their first hit, circa '61), which if rereleased today, unaltered, would probably become a hit all over again. That's been the secret of their suc- cess-production, cosmopolitan mate- rial, and exceptional vocals. The un- mistakable lead voice of Levi Stubbs can make practically anything sound good. The group was adept on "Still Waters," a superb Jobete copyright which should be covered by other ar- tists. The also sang the title tune from their last Motown album, "That's the Way Nature Planned It," but then devoted too much time to other less significant songs from the same album. Their hit ABC/Dunhill single, "Keeper Of The Castle," didn't quite keep the pace associated with the record. It seemed a little slow. Nevertheless the Four Tops remain 'keeper of hits.' Also on the bill was Buddah Rec- ords' Barbara Mason. She has a unique voice which is also very sexy. Unfortunately she's just a bit too em- phatic about the latter quality. A sex kitten doesn't have to growl. Miss Mason succeeds with her hits "Bed and Board" and of course "Yes I'm Ready." Also strong was her offering of "Me and Mr. Jones" (which brought to mind why no one has written an answer song to "Me and Mrs. Jones") and her new single "Gimme Your Love." This tune can make Barbara Mason a household name again. r.b. d.d. Orphan Jay Hersh Keith Sykes BITTER END, N.Y.-A show featur- ing London recording artists, Orphan and two yet well polished but undis- covered folkies, proved to be a bill well worth attending. The show opened up with Jay Hersh, who at one time had an album out on Atco Records. He was booked for the evening at the last minute but yet by his performance I could not understand why. His set had two out- standing numbers, "Foggy Night On The Road" and an appropriate song entitled "New York City." He is pres- ently at work on another album which should prove stimulating. Keith Sykes followed, and he really kept the audience captivated. He has vocal characteristics of Arlo Guthrie and Bob Dylan and he also has the humor of the Smothers Brothers. He stood out on a song called "Stay With Me" and combined some daz- zling vocals with a touch of witty humor. Orphan, a country -rock group, proved to be well polished. They played some songs from their first album, "Everybody Lives To Sing" and some new cuts from their forth- coming London album, still untitled and to be released in mid -February. Two very interesting offerings were, "Places I've Been" and "Everybody Lives To Sing". Eric Lilljequist and Dean Adrein share the guitarist and vocalist chores and they are backed by Steve Abdu on bass, and Rich Adelman on drums. Eric seems to have a strong career ahead as a song- writer. It should be noted that J. Geils and his band and also the likes of Don McClean first played small clubs such as these but they are now pack- ing them in, all over the country in much bigger places than these. Or- phan, a country rock band with a Boston sound is surely destined for greater recognition than they are now receiving, and with the release of their new album it should clearly happen. The next time I see them, I hope it will be at Carnegie Hall. b.e. Harold Melvin & The It lue Notes Luther Ingram Tommy Tate APOLLO THEATRE, NYC-Koko re- cording stars Luther and Tommy and those vet performers Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes completed a suc- cessful stint at the Apollo, Jan. 3-9. Luther, backed by 12 pieces, including 6 horns, saying it with song opened with, "It's All Here In My Song" and although Luther comes across beautifully on record, it would have to be said, especially with this per- formance, that Luther performs rather low-key. But, the audience was with him all the way and his offerings of, "I Love You," and "I'll See It Through" were exemplary of his sing- ing talent. Of course, the top offer- ing was "If Loving You Is Wrong, I Don't Want To Be Right" and with material of this nature, Luther will grow in stature. Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes, second on the bill, are a together group and they wowed the audience with, "What's Happen- ing Brother," "Just Be For Real" and "Whatcha Doin To Me". Their dance routines and deliveries are par ex- cellence. "Mercy, Mercy Me" was given a super cool delivery. The group just seems to explode at the audience and the reaction to, "If You Don't Know Me By Now" had the Apollo rocking from stem to stern. And, "I Miss You" continued the reaction to a total screaming and screeching af- fair. The gals rushed to the front of the stage. This is the kind of re- sponse they got, and deservedly so. Tommy Tate, first on the bill, op- ened with "Let's Stay Together" and "School Of Life" the latter number was delivered beautifully. "More Power To You" and the big Chicago hit, "Does Anybody Know What Time It Is" were also included in his set. Aquarius, an 8 piece band, percus- sion, horns and conga, supplied plen- ty of super back up power. And, this opening night had another big sur- prise for the audience when soul brother number one arrived at the Apollo. James Brown was given a rousing ovation when he was brought on stage for a brief introduction. Through the years and week after week the Apollo has been instrumen- tal as a spawning ground for the launching of talent both amateur and professional. Wednesday, the opening night is also amateur night and often an act will show the necessary ingre- dients to become a star of tomorrow. The Apollo is a right -on institution, and the above show was another ex- ample. d.d. Al Anderson FOLK CITY, NYC-The relationship between Vanguard's Al Anderson and Kama Sutra's NRBQ is a variation on the Rod Stewart and Faces theme. Anderson is a part of the group, but they change character when Al gets the booking, or makes a solo record. Lots of folks remember Al as the lead force in Vanguard's Wildweeds, perhaps the finest cult country -rock- ers in the history of the form. While there's still the blue sky and open spaces in his presentation, by far the biggest influence now is a kind of independently -styled blues, previously best exemplified by Little Milton. That's in the vocal depart- ment. His guitar technique is a devil- ishly clever amalgam of everything from Berry to country, and the ulti- mate result is a tight and commer- cially electric presentation (on record as well as live). It got a New York press crowd to scream "encore" with the fervor normally reserved for the word "fire!". Also in the audience was British singer -songwriter Ian Matthews who has recorded a number of Anderson songs. One of them was "Mare, Take Me Home"-and when Al broke into it, Ian went all smiles. But then so did everyone else. It's obvious that the Wildweeds LP reached a lot of people in a very personal way, and Al's new LP will do likewise. Some of the highlights of his set from his new LP included a blues shuffle called "We'll Make Love" and a funky "Be My Woman Tonight." NRBQ performed with generous tal- ent, uniformed in identical plaid flan- nel shirts and masks. (Jeans too, lest you think this a new kind of thea- trical adventure.) The music is not masked-it's out - in -the -open excitement. So what you get is more than what you see. And what you hear is dynamite. r.a. . VV. Stevenson FOLK CITY, NYC - New York a trendy city? Not on your life, at least when it comes to turning on to what's happening in the Texas singer -song- writer scene. But those press folks who did turn up for B. W.'s set and party got a good, and probably un- expected time for their modicum of trouble in challenging the current cold wave. B. W. stands for Buckwheat. His music stands for itself. Although the room seemed to be wired to duplicate the acoustical fa- cilities of a toilet bowl, B. W.'s act came off as strongly as we seem to feel we all sound in a shower. Like fellow Texan Michael Murphey, Ste- venson has a pleasingly and correctly invoked falsetto, so that the melodic range of his songwriting skills can be fully appreciated. When rapping, he's a bit like Arlo Guthrie, but never quite enough to be blatant about it. His songs about Texas, highways and a freer state of mind don't sound at all misplaced on his first visit to the Big Apple. If the city has any sense (and B. W. the desire), he'll be back. The RCA artist already has a band that understands. The audi- ence is sure to follow. r.a. Nitzinger WHISKEY, L.A. - Nitzinger is a fast -rising Capitol act with a great deal of potential for establishing themselves as one of the top hard - rock groups in the U.S. Their style centers around the lead guitars of John Nitzinger and Bugs Henderson, who incorporate each other's work smoothly into sections that focus ei- ther on soloing or a weaving of both guitars together. The percussion of Linda Waring and bass of Curly Ben- ton nicely added the needed depth, giving the group a very complete sound. At times Nitzinger ventured away from their hard rock format, and seemed to lack some of the "Orig- inal" luster that is their forte. Yet when they returned to rock, the mo- mentum that had been lost was im- mediately regained. C.C. 24 Cash Box - January 20, 1973 www.americanradiohistory.com

iflf4ih1#SSOlI1WI continued NEW YORK: JERRY BUTLER (Cont'd. from page 22) by Chappell Music). Jerry and his staff devote several hours once each week going over material that has been submitted from producers and writers involved with the workshop. The material is rated on a point system-one to ten-and consideration is given to whether its a writer, producer or vocalist. The analysis is then given to the artist. He can then work in those areas that need to be further developed. Terry Callier, one example, of the bright talents who has participated in the workshop, is now writing and producing professionally. "We are working to encourage more black youths to participate and although there has been an increase of black material submissions to the workshop from throughout the country," Jerry says, in '73 he is going to try and increase the Black representation. His own recording and live performance career is, of course, of major concern to Jerry and he is constantly striving to broaden his own acceptance scope. This is beginning to happen for Jerry, who can be described as a golden -voiced crooner with the right combination of commercial eloquence and soulful force; he has recently completed a successful two-week engagement at the Copacabana in NYC. Jerry has surrounded himself with an outstanding rhythm section, appropriately called, "The Ice Man's Band" and they have their own instrumental albums. Robert Bowles serves as musical director for Jerry. Charles McMillan, a genuinely together man, serving as general manager and personal aide to Jerry, is another example of Butler's ability to surround himself with the right people and that is the key to any man's success. The back up vocal group, "Peaches" and "The Ice Man's Band" complete the package known as, The Jerry Butler Revue. Both as an artist and as a man, Butler is special. And, when Brenda Lee Eager steps out to share the vocal on, "Close To You", it gives one a powerful example of the Butler brand of spice. "The Iceman" is totally together. don drossell HOLLYWOOD: NEW SEEKERS (Cont'd. from page 22) corporate, polish, and perfect many channels of amusement. The outcome of these is a cabaret act that includes singing, comedy, acting, and dancing. And their goal of reaching this broad audience with such a style is a matter of record. In their home country, England, they have established themselves as one of the top sources of entertainment available. In 1971, their single, "I'd Like To Teach the World To Sing," won them a Gold Disk Award, the first record in three years to sell more than a million copies in Britain. Since they they have become regular attractions on television throughout that country. In the United States they are now in the process of building similar, wide- spread, recognition. This fact is quite apparent in their bookings. From concerts at Disneyland over the past Christmas holiday to gigs at the Bitter End, the St. Regis Hotel, and the Troubadour, the New Seekers have been reaching varying audiences with consistent success. And from appearances on the Sonny & Cher Show to last Friday's Inaugural Performance for President Nixon, their potential here seems to know no bounds. The New Seekers are a flexible act that can shift emphasis as fast as they can perform. This is their key to success. They can give the people whatever they want, no matter who they are. From T-shirts to tuxedos the New Seekers deliver the goods. charles copien NEW YORK-FOCUS: NEW WAVE IN THE MAKING The problem with most new groups these days is that they all try too hard. There's a difference between being able to make music -and actually making it. Many are able to piece together bits of songs thinking that they have indeed created music. Others, however, have a talent for composition. Two of the bright- est prospects for super -success in '73 are Genesis and Focus. Note the names if you will: Genesis ... the beginning and Focus ... the point towards which we turn our attention. By no means accidental! We have already discussed Genesis in earlier columns, so let's now focus on Focus. Like most groups, Focus have had their share of personel changes and general problems. But now, they are a unit. And as such, they have created a most inventive, most unusual kind of music. Right now, Focus is the most popular group in Holland, but their popularity is fast spreading to other parts of the globe including these United States. Though the group is heavily" influenced by Elvin Jones, Charlie Parker, Miles Davis, John Coltrane, and Buddy Rich, the rock in them shines through. Focus is determined to have audiences listen to their music and appreciate the thought that went into it. Composed of Jan Ackerman (guitars and Lute), Thijs Van Leer (organ, flute, vocals), Pierre Van Der Linden (drums), and Bert Ruiter bass and vocals, the group has just released their most recent LP entitled "Moving Waves" on the Sire label. In all probability, the LP will only serve to introduce the group to the American audience-but if you have the time, listen to a single track called "Hocus Pocus." That will explain it all. There's no doubt that we'll be hearing a lot from Focus in the coming year. cash bo,r/ aftiwn redeem DOUG ZAHM AND BAND Black Girl POP PICKS DOUG SAHM AND BAND-Atlantic SD 7254 One of the few people capable of bringing the Tex-Mex sound to a rockin' acceptance in year's past, this year present finds Doug Sahm with a broad base of music under his belt. Harris Heads Columbia's 'Artist Careers' NEW YORK-Steve Harris has been named to the newly -created post of director of artist development for Columbia Records. At the same time, Harris has named Josephine Mori as his assistant. Harris will report directly to Bruce Lundvall, vp of marketing, in the planning and execution of artist career building programs for artists on the Columbia label. Harris will also supervise the concert booking ac- tivities of all assigned artists, evalu- ate and counsel with artists on their in -person performances and work closely with other departments within marketing in planning overall sup- port campaigns for assigned new art- ists. Harris will be responsible for the artist relations area for all Columbia artists and will supervise the activities of the artist relations staff. Before coming to Columbia, Harris was vice president of artist develop- ment at Elektra Records and was in- strumental in planning the artist de- velopment activity for such artists as Judy Collins, the Doors, Bread, Harry Chapin, Mickey Newbury and Carly Simon. He has actively been involved in the recording industry for the past 10 years. Ms. Mori, before assuming her present position at Columbia, was a publicist for Trans -Lux Corp. She later assumed the post of director of publicity at Elekra Records before be- coming Harris' assistant at that label. She has been voted one of the top 100 "Heavies" of the American Rock and Roll scene by Esquire Magazine. Steve Harris `Fat Albert' Track Rights To RBB&B NEW YORK - The soundtrack rights to the CBS -TV animated series, "Fat Albert & The Cosby Kids," has been awarded to Ringling Bros. Barnum & Bailey Records. The announcement was made jointly by Ringling Bros.' Joe D'Imperio and Filmation Studio toppers Norm Pres- cott and Lou Scheimer. Filmation Studios, a Teleprompter company, produces the weekly show. "Fat Albert & The Cosby Kids," which began airing on the CBS Net- work in Sept., has received the highest ratings ever for a children's program in the Saturday A.M. time slot. The show leans heavily on edu- cational and moral values. D'Imperio and Lenny Scheer of Ringling Bros. are currently in negotiation with a major label for release of the materi- al. In addition, the coordination of concert and fair appearances for the real, `live' Fat Albert has begun in conjunction with upcoming pop single releases by the real Fat Albert. New Talent Combo: Purcell, Friedman NEW YORK - Jerry Purcell of Gerard W. Purcell Associates, Ltd., and Budd Friedman, owner of the Im- provisation Cafe in New York City, have made a cooperative arrangement whereby they will join together in the development and personal manage- ment of selected new talent. Under Friedman's direction, many stars have developed out of the Im- provisation including Ace Trucking Company, Dave Frye, Rodney Dan- gerfield, Bette Midler, Marvin Braver- man, Dave Brenner, Robert Klein, Daphne Davis and Stiller & Meara. Gerard W. Purcell Associates, Ltd., will present and showcase artists it manages at the Improvisation on a regular schedule of appearances for as long a period as is necessary to develop the artists' potential talents. These appearances will give the man- agement from the opportunity to showcase talent for recording compa- ny execs, entertainment and talent di- rectors of TV and night clubs. It will also afford an opportunity for concert promoters and college buyers to view Sicilia Exits Buddah Group; Merenstein VP Post NEW YORK - Dominic Sicilia, who for the past year and a half has acted as vice president and creative director for The Buddah Group, has resigned his position with the company to con- centrate on his personal business. Neil Bogart and Art Kass, co - presidents of The Buddah Group, stated: "We will continue to use Dominic's services on special proj- ects." Sicilia currently manages three acts on The Buddah Group's Kama Sutra label: Stories, Ray D'Ariano, and Dust. Lewis Merenstein has been named the new vice president and director of creative services at Buddah, effective immediately. Merenstein began his career as a recording engineer in jazz. The names of the artists with whom he has worked read like a Who's Who, in- cluding Dizzy Gillespie, Herbie Mann, Cecil Taylor, Stan Getz, Lee Morgan, and Thelonius Monk. Most recently Merenstein has been active as a pro- ducer, including Van Morrison's "As- tral Weeks" and "Moondance" al- bums. Other artists that Merenstein has produced include Mama Cass, The Association, Glass Harp, Barry Gold- berg, John Cale, Mike Bloomfield and George Burns. Looking forward to his activities with The Buddah Group, Merenstein noted: "With the enormous amount of product presently being released on so many labels, marketing and mer- chandising is equally important as ra- dio airplay. At The Buddah Group, they will enjoy the same input of creative energy and excitement as now characterizes the Buddah promo- tion staff." The other members of the creative and marketing departments under Merenstein will remain unchanged. Concurrent with his new position, Merenstein will continue to produce and to fulfill his production agree- ments. Merenstein the artists while performing before the public. Purcell and Friedman will not only jointly personally manage the per- formers (in which area, Purcell will devote most of his energies), but they will advise and counsel performers while appearing at the Improvisation on the development of their per- formances. In this area, Friedman, who is a seasoned vet of the night club scene, will devote most of his energies, since, as the operator of the club, he is there each evening. Murray Becker of Gerard W. Pur- cell Associates Ltd., will act as coor- dinator in both areas of personal management and development of tal- ent at the club. Philosophy Messrs. Purcell and Friedman be- lieve that this is a "most innovative step in the development of talent that fills a void that has come about due to the closing of night clubs all over the country." By giving new acts the opportunity to work regularly for uninterrupted periods, the pair feels that they can gain a confidence and practical experience in a relatively short time that might take years to reach in the intermittent bookings that are now possible because of the scarcity of personal -appearance op- portunities. The Improvisation is located at 358 West 44 Street, New York, N.Y., and Gerard W. Purcell Associates Ltd., headquarters at 133 Fifth Avenue, New York, N.Y. Johnson Atlantic's R&B Promo Chief NEW YORK-Henry Allen, vice president in charge of promo for Atlantic Records, has announced the appointment of Paul Johnson as Na- tional R & B promo director for the company. A vet of more than 15 years ex- perience in the music industry, John- son is perhaps most familiar to the public from his days as a radio an- nouncer when he starred as "Fat Daddy" on stations WWIN, WSID and WITH in Baltimore for many years. During this time he also held the posts of music and program di- rector for these stations. In the course of his radio career, Johnson was named the "most influ- ential disk jockey" in the United States by Business Week Magazine, and one of the top three D.J.'s in the country by Time Magazine. Johnson orginally joined Atlantic in 1971 as part of the New York pro- mo staff, and has also served with the company's Artist and Repertoire Department. 1 /N \ IMAM \11 iCashBox ùssicjhl&sound NEW YORK: SHEL SILVERSTEIN-HE'S THE BALD ONE It was raining on Shel Silverstein's clean and free -being head the day we got together for a bite and a rap. (No, he really doesn't bite.) According to Shel, rain and bald do not go together well. That's probably the only time he might opt for a full head of hair; but after joking about how much easier it is for him to dry off his top, he didn't seem at all envious. Shel's been known to the industry for quite some time, not so much as a recording artist but as a songwriter. But music in any form hasn't always been his life. He sold his first cartoon to the Crib Diaper Service magazine some years back an an art student and worked his way up to one of Playboy's most respected illustrators. From cartoons, he got into children's books, thence to full-fledged songwriting. He's got a number of hits under his belt: from The Irish Rovers' "The Unicorn" onto Johnny Cash's "A Boy Named Sue" and just about every- thing Dr. Hook & The Medicine Show would ever think of doing-including their biggest "Sylvia's Mother" and their current "Cover Of 'Rolling Stone'." Shel has recorded before-for Elektra, Atlantic, and RCA. Now, he's got a chart LP for Columbia, "Freakin' At The Freakers' Ball." A cut from the album, a Dr. Seuss-ian narrative called "Sarah Cynthia Sylvia Stout Would Not Take The Garbage Out" is breaking out of Seattle and looks like a real left -field giant. The darn thing was charted at KJR even before it was released. Shel Silverstein is a man of many talents. The "Sarah" song might well be another "Rubber Duckie"-but the kiddies get a rather uniquely titled B-side for the same money, "Stacy Brown's Got Two." And if they get to the alarm, there's more R-rated goodies for their immeasurable pleasure and teehee-ing. Columbia finds this an interesting state of affairs, but their minds are open. Shel's mind opens up at the drop of a suggestion. In a very non-egotripping way, he's quite opinionated on many subjects. Having followed the scene around the country (quite literallj', having lived since 1955 where it was ever happening at the time of peak excitement), Shel's now moored in a house boat in Sausalito, HOLLYWOOD-JIM WEATHERLY: SUNNY FORECAST RCA Recording artist Jim Weatherly is a tunesmith who can thank his twisted toe. You see, if Weatherly, once a quarterback for the University of Mississippi, hadn't twisted his toe during a tackle, he might have gone on to play pro. How- ever had he done this, he probably wouldn't have become the singer he is, signed to RCA, nor would he have written the new Gladys Knight and the Pips hit, "Neither One of Us." Truth of the matter is "neither one of us" will ever know what might have happened if circumstances had been different, though it's always fun to play hypothetical merry-go-round. The days when he was an all-American candidate, and selected along with Joe Namath as quarterback for the Southern Eastern Con- ference, have long been played and passed. However it was during those days, maybe in quarter time, that he got involved playing in a band. The group called themselves the Gordian Knot. When Jim made up his mind, with the help of his toe, that, he would no longer aspire to be a pro football hero, he went off to score in another field, that of recording and performing. The Gordian Knot was soon thereafter signed to MGM-Verve. They had one album, a segment on a Fred Astaire TV special where they did "Top Hat," some un- memorable singles, some good club dates, and some dives, and that was it. Making it big was something the Knot did not. There was a short abeyance in Jim's career, but he didn't give up. By now it was clear to him that performing and writing were his life. So he continued to tackle music. It wasn't too long after, that he became a writer for Jim Nabors' publishing firm where he really learned how to concentrate on writing and developing an original style. Jim Weatherly confesses that up until his association with Jim Nabors he had always written songs as a hobby. As a writer for Nabors, he recalls deliberately working hard. He drawled, "If I'm taking a man's money, I've got to do him a day's work." The guy who had been known to make a touch down in two minutes now SHEL SILVERSTEIN JIM WEATHERLY waiting for the next place to happen. Meanwhile, his songs are doing things to people's heads (bald or hirsute) wherever they may be. Silverstein doesn't believe in reviews on a personal level. He just won't read them. Being fairminded, he feels that if you're going to go up on the highs of favorable press, you also have to sink with slings and arrows of raging fury and discounted from the same quarter. Doesn't believe in the representative form of doing business either. Those who have done Shel's songs have gotten them be- cause Silverstein has visited them with his game himself. Chet Atkins first brought him down to Nashville and showed him around ... now folks like Loretta Lynn don't regard him as anything but one of the gang down there. If he's freaky, he's also earthy, forthright and personably honest. That cuts a lot of mustard with musicians of all persuasions. Shel is also of the Harry Nilsson school of the performing arts-he won't, except on record. He's not against a fan club though, should any of our readers be so organizationally inclined. He claims that while he's not complaining about his sex life, to date there is no true example of a Shel Silverstein groupie. Some- body really ought to help him find out. Can't think of anyone who wouldn't be curious to see the result. robed adels PASSING REMARKS-"Buckle Your Body Down" is not Totie Fields new theme song but rather a song penned by Casey Anderson for the California Highway patrol's seat -belt campaign.
