POP PICKS iiiimosamo is6sqIlItt4osusd continued NEW YORK: ALAN PRICE (from p. 22) was, for the most part, performed "live" in the film and the muscians were "borrowed" from the Georgie Fame TV series in England. Bringing it all back home, Alan claims to owe a good deal to Eric Burden on his blues background. He admits that Burden taught him enough to understand and make music a bit easier to perform as a result. The future for Alan Price? Well, Alan says he plans to go into the studio one of these days and record an album of original material that he has been writing along the way. The ambitious performing gesture, he relates, is to be augmented with the use of a full horn section, which ras he puts it, would be a new experience, but a quite fulfilling one. At the age of 31, Alan Price has seen and done a lot, but I have this funny feeling that we're going to be seeing and hearing a good deal more from the man in years to come. A very talented individual, this Alan Price. arty goodman HOLLYWOOD: HENRY MANCINI (from p. 22) The cigar -a -day composer was probably contemplating the title tune of "Sun- flower,'' a film of a few years back that was one of his finest compositions but which never shot -off any commercial fireworks. But it is usually conceded, with few exceptions, that the success of the music is in direct correlation with the success of the picture. But Mancini views this as being the story of any com- poser's life as well as the fact that many pieces that the composer feels are of consequence are not acknowledged and accepted as such by the public. In his own case, "Soldier in the Rain," "Two for the Road" and "Nothing to Lose" (with Don Black) have been the bafflers. But the man himself is a bafflement. The closest scrutiny of his music re- veals no tricks-no borrowing from himself, no sequential writing, no hard to follow melodies or ones that can't be put down on a lead -sheet, as is often the case with r&b. Instead, the anagrams of his notes are arranged with a con- grunecy and conciseness whether the framework is structured around the som- ber, the sweet, the light or the heavy. The same can not always be said for his counterparts in the rock camps. His belief is that the early days of rock and roll were primitive, apart from being a neophyte, in that the music was very, very simplistic in harmony, melody and lyric. "There was a whole section in there, prior to The Beatles, that was naive beyond words. And The Beatles, themselves, had a transition period. They started out imitating American artists such as Chuck Berry until they started finding new approaches around the "Sergeant Pepper" LP. In fact, up until that time, any of their songs could have been from a 1940's Warner musical. They were so straight out of tin -pan alley. At about the same time, the male vocal sound became higher which accounted for groups like The Beach Boys. And then the females came along --Carol King, Joni Mitchell-and they took off in another direction entirely. In general terms, people started coming -in with orchestras and choral back-up which precluded arriving in the studio with only a chord sheet. And so with the attention to arrangements and vocal blending, groups like Three Dog Night and Bread appeared on the scene with some really beautiful numbers. We're now in the center of a very broad music arena with a lot more scope and potential than previously realized." When asked what corners he sees being turned in today's market, the RCA artist answers as uncomplicated as the melodic language he uses in his compo- sitions: "Jazz. It is coming about with Mahavishnu and Focus who are out and out rock -jazz groups that just use a different language to communicate with." Henry Mancini will be communicating in his own language July 25-29 at the Universal Amphitheatre with Johhny Mathis.-barry mcgoffin Coming Next Week: WILLIAM POPSIE' RANDOLPH The End of An Era Caedmon Sees Lewis LP Tie -In With Watergate NEW YORK - Caedmon Records has just released an album entitled "It Can't Happen Here" which is based on the Sinclair Lewis novel first pub- lished in 1935. The album is narrated by Michael Lewis, son of the au- thor. In view of the current Watergate hearings, the label feels that Lewis' story, written almost 40 years ago is again topical. The LP, edited by Bar- bara Holdridge, contains almost an hour of narration, and according to a Carr To IFA NEW YORK - Bud Carr has joined International Famous Agency's New York concert department, reports Herb Spar, IFA's New York concert vice president. Carr comes to IFFA from CMA where he was responsible for such major performers as Grand Funk Railroad, Stephen Stills, Jim Croce, among others. label spokesman, copies of the LP are being serviced to all political colum- nists as well as to every member of the Senate Watergate investigation committee. RRMIITIIM 1N APRIL CAME THE DAWNING OF THE RED SUNS SUNRISE, SUNSET-Tony Bennett-Columbia -C 32239 Tony has long been one of the smoothest crooners in popular music, singing the best of all available material in both live and on re- corded performances. This latest cellection is yet another indication of the man's huge talent as a vocalist. In offering such top flight ma- terial as "The Party's Over", "Days Of Wine And Roses", "(Where Do I Begin) Love Story" and "Put On A Happy Face", Tony once again dazzles. Simply, the man is all performer and this collection perfectly demonstrates that fact. EL CHICANO-MCA-312 When the '70's brought with it the firiest of Latin and the coolest of brass, El Chicano was there to combine the two and create a smooth, yet intense medium that has come to be known and loved as "Latin Rock". This latest El Chicano collection is going to finally show this spirited conglamoration's talents to the world. In delivering such solid, yet graceful covers of "What's Going On" and "We've Only Just Begun", the group demonstrates a pop sense defying comparison, but the true es- sence appears on such Latin oriented material as "Un -Mundo", "Cha Chita" and "Tell Her She's Lovely". Watch El Chicano take off with this one. The time is definitely right. THE SMOKER YOU DRINK, THE PLAYER YOU GET-Joe Walsh-Dunhill-DSX 50140 Since leaving the James Gang to solo, Joe Walsh has been seemingly more creative than ever. This, his second solo flight (Barnstorm was his first) is a very tight musical congla- moration of rock and blues that should score heavily (in fact it's already begun to rack up points). Leading the way here is the dynamic "Rocky Mountain Way" and other strong tracks such as "Bookends," "Meadows" and "Midnight Moodies." For those who think he made a mistake leaving a successful group to solo, Joe Walsh is proving those skeptic to be as wrong as can possibly be. Truly a solid performer with the talent to make it on his own. IN APRIL CAME THE DAWNING OF THE RED SUNS-Ramatam-Atlantic--SD 7261 If you can remember back to a hard rock- ing, fast driving debut by Ramatam a while back, this second collection by the group will come as a pleasant surprise. The highly poetic nature of this album's title is only the begin- ning. For the most part the material is highly melodic, in a softer sense and is quite enjoy- able as a result. It's as if the group is embark- ing on a brand new career. Listen to "The Land" and "Rainy Sunday Evening" as well as "Bounty On My Table" and be reintroduced to a fine "new" band. FINGERS-Ai rto-CTI-6028 It has been accepted fact for some time now that Airto, the Brazilian percussionist, is one of the finest (if not the finest) at his craft in all the world. This collection of fine jazz -pop ori- ented material should do much to increase his already dedicated large following. As single re- leases, "Parana," "Tombo in 7/4" and "Merry Go Round" would seemingly have little prob- lem in pleasing a vast audience, but the collec- tion is strong enough to stand on it's own. Check it out. It's definitely worth the while and a true representation of the artist's genius. SUPER OLDIES-Trip-TOX 60 What this series actually is (and it is a series)) is ten perfectly representative albums of "solid gold" from the '50's and '60's. The '50's segments (2 2 -LP sets) and the '60's segments (8 2 -LP sets) include the biggest hits of the day and each "set" has more memories than can possibly be imagined. A prime example of the power of this collection is the '60's Vol. 8 collection which includes "Sweet Talkin' Guy" by The Chiffons, "Crim- son and Clover" by Tommy James & The Shondells, "Hooked On A Feeling" by B. J. Thomas and "Alfie" by Dionne Warwick. The entire set is a perfectly nostalgic trip and a very pleasant sentimental journey. Cash Box -July 14, 1973 41 www.americanradiohistory.com

Cash Box/R(JB News Report Blue Note Logo LOS ANGELES - Sparked by its new logo designed by United Artists Records' art director Mike Salisbury, Blue Note Records has initiated an all-out sales push for both new and catalog product. Included in the Blue Note campaign are full -age ads in the music trade publications, a brochure specially tai- lored for radio stations and reviewers containing biog data on the current artists roster of the label, catalog stuffer for retail outlets, a new Blue Note stationery and graphic image. Image posters for 112 artists on the roster are currently being shipped, as are store decals of the new logo, plus special Blue Note order pads. Slick books featuring new and cur- rent hit collections are being made available to salesmen, and print ad- vertising aids are being made avail- able to dealers. Blue Note jackets and tank tops are also being manufac- tured for wide distribution. The Blue Note new release con- sists of "Sassy Soul Strut" by Lou Donaldson, "Mr. Jones" by Elvin Jones, "Sweet Revival" by Ronnie Foster, and a debut set from The New Heritage Keyboard Quartet. Blue Note ASCAP Honors Eckstine NEW YORK-The American Society of Authors, Composers and Publish- ers (ASCAP) honored Billy ("Mr. B") Eckstine, Stax recording artist, with a special tribute commemorating the singing star's 35th anniversary in show business and for his "outstand- ing contribution to the music world as a pivotal figure in jazz music his- tory," it was announced by Stanley Adams, president of ASCAP. Academy Award winning songwrit- er Sammy Cahn made the ASCAP presentation to Eckstine at the New- port Jazz Festival held at Hollywood Bowl. "Billy Eckstine is one of the out- standing music artists responsible for the current world-wide recognition of jazz music as an esthetic American cultural contribution to the world," Cahn stated. "Noted as both an instrumentalist and as a singer, Eckstine stands high on the roster of great jazz artists. Kendrix Re -Signs i / as TOGETHER - Tamla (Motown) re- cording artist Eddie Kendricks (c.) gets together with Frank Wilson (I.), producer of Kendricks' new Tamla LP, "Eddie Kendricks," and Cash Box' Ron Baron at a party in the Beverly Hilton Hotel to celebrate Kendricks' re-signing with the Mo- town label. Billy Bass To RCA Post NEW YORK - Billy Bass has been appointed Regional R&B promotion manager RCA Records. In his new post Bass will be based out of the company's Cleveland office, and will cover the mid -western part of the country. Bass's appointment was an- nounced by Tom Draper, National R&B promotion manager, to whom he will report. Bass, one of the best known air personalities in Cleveland was last with WMMS-FM in that city where he was General Manager and Program Director of the station. He was also an on the air personality at WMMS. Before that he was Program Direc- tor of WNCR, also in Cleveland, and previous to joining WNCR, he was the 6 to 10 PM disc jockey at WIXY, again in Cleveland. Bass got this start in the record business managing a number of rec- ord stores in Cleveland for Stark Rec- ords. In making the appointment, Draper cited Bass's extensive background in radio and community service. In Cleveland, Bass was partially respon- sible for putting on numerous free concerts in Cleveland's Edgewater Park. He was also involved in setting up the Cleveland free clinic for that city's underpriviledged. BILLY BASS CTI Opens Cana Branch NEW YORK - CTI Records has an- nounced its entry into the interna- tional market with the opening of its first company outside of the United States, CTI Records of Canada Ltd. In making the announcement, Creed Taylor, president of CTI, said that the move came as a logical step in the company's desire to deliver uniform quality to its consumers the world over. The opening of the branch was her- alded by ads in the Canadian trade press. In a letter to all Canadian rec- ord dealers and radio stations, Vic Chirumbolo, vp of marketing, stated that the entire CTI catalog, cmmprised of CTI, Kudu, and Salva- tion products, would become immedi- ately available in Canada, and that new products would be simultaneous- ly released in the U.S. and Canada. All of the merchandise, which will be shipped by CTI Records of Cana- da, will be newly manufactured in Canada under CTI's specifications. Operations began July 3, 1973, with CTI Records of Canada, Ltd,,, official- ly becoming the sole authorized dis- tributor of the company's products. CTI Records of Canada, Ltd., is lo- cated at 2372 46th Avenue, Lachine, Quebec. The telephone number is (514) 636-8700. R LI B INGREDIENTS-A wrap-up of the recently held Newport Jazz Festival New York is featured in an action photo page in this issue of Cash Box. And, this reviewer wishes to thank photographer Ronnie Brathwaite who caught the name artists While they were doing their thing. Ronnie also does the R&B covers for London's Blues & Soul Magazine ... Jazz is once again becoming significant in major centers of Canada. Cities of Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg and Vancouver are reporting increased sales of Jazz re- cordings. Of course, DJ's are programming more product in the jazz area. Jazz programs now being heard over FM stations in the major markets include, Bob Smith, CBC Vancouver; Lee Major, CBC network originating in Winnipeg and Ted O'Reilly, CJRT Toronto. Artists such as Herbie Hancock, Keith Jarrow, John McLaughlin, Weather Report and Mahavishnu Orchestra are having an influence on the new jazz buyers . Revelations Movement, who recently appeared at Art D'Iugoff's Village Gate in NYC, is certainly one of the out- standing gospel groups. The group, a part of the New York Community Choir is under Benny Diggs direction. The Revelations choir, composed of 15 voices and a five piece rhythm section, puts plenty of fire and get -down rock in the gospel message. They are highly contagious. Benny Diggs is an inspired and exciting director . Roberta Flack has announced a concert tour next Feb- ruary of nine West African countries to raise funds for Africare, a Washington, D.C. based organization concerned with health standards in Africa. Miss Flack commented, at a press reception hosted by the Embassy of Niger, "being a successful entertainer can only be partially fulfilling unless one is also pre- pared to share the fruits of her labor with other individuals." Other top -name entertainers will also be participating in the fund-raising tour ... It has also been announced that rights conflicts with the "Bessie" flick have been re- solved. And, Roberta Flack has been signed by producer Porter Bibb for the title role in "Bessie," the forthcoming feature on the life of famed blues singer, Bessie Smith. Production will begin in early 1974 with Gordon Parks, Sr. directing. Academy award nominee Lonne Elder III will write the screenplay, which will be based on Chris Albertson's best-selling biography, "Bessie" (Stein & Day, 1973) . Manu Dibango, "Soul Makossa" artist, is coming to the U.S. for personal appearances, according to Atlantic Records. Newport In New York AF ETRA FRANKLIN ROBERTA FLACK DONNY HATHAWAY STEVIE WONDER The Newport Jazz Wrap-up NEW YORK-Kicking off at Noon, Friday, June 29, at Wollman Amphi- theater in Central Park, and closing out at the Nassau Coliseum in Long Island on July 8th, the 2nd annual Newport Jazz Festival to be held in New York City, offered every form of music. More than 60 events were scheduled throughout the city and its suburbs. Well over 300 musicians par- ticipated in the events including per- formances by almost all well-known jazz figures. There was also a musical tribute to the late Louis Armstrong and a ceremony renaming the Singer Bowl to the Louis Armstrong Me- morial Stadium. George Wein, pro- ducer of the event, presented a fes- tival that has to be described as a rewarding and enriching experience. For those New Yorkers who turned out to witness the concerts and artists in action. Most will agree that stand- ing ovations were not uncommon. From -gut blues-New Orleans style -swing-avant garde-contemporary -electronic to get -it -on soul, the city and environs was ablaze with sights and sounds. The original Benny Goodman Quar- tet got together at Carnegie. Teddy Wilson, on piano; Lionel Hampton, on vibes; Gene Krupa, on drums, and Goodman on Clarinet are the original four. Bassist Slam Stewart joined them in the Carnegie set and it was an enjoyable excursion of musical fare of the late '30's and '40's. They played the Goodman standards, in- cluding "Moonglow." Duke Ellington, at Philharmonic and also on the closing night at Nas- sau Coliseum, rolled it out with some exciting rockin' rhythm that knocked the audience out. The Swedish vocal- ist, Alice Babs working with the Duke is an absolutely incredible performer, her "Checkered Hat" offering is a work of art. The Duke included, "Per- dido," "C -Jam Blues" and it was foot- stompin' sound all the way. The great Count Basie Band of the '50's was reunited in a program en- titled: "Basie Now and In Retro- spect." Singers Joe Williams and Helen Humes held forth with Snooky Young, Benny Powell, Henry Coker, Al Grey, Marshal Royal and many others who comprised the Basie band of the '50's. Many of the great artists per- formed more than one date. Ray Charles was honored at Carnegie with a tribute to Ray written by Baldwin. But, it was at Nassau where Ray Charles with the full band and his five Rayettes came on after Donny Hathaway and proceeded to do his thing. He absolutely took the place apart with an SRO audience going wild. It was a no-nonsense lets get -it - on performance. And, it was every bit of that. Aretha, with 26 pieces behind her and the Prima -Donna group, proved without question that she is still the number one female with a performance so compelling even the orchestra became spell- bound. Shea Stadium was the scene for Stevie Wonder, Staple Singers Grover Washington, Ramsey Lewis, Freddie Hubbard, Roland Kirk, Roberta Flack and War. The performances were flawless. A Thirties Ball was held at Rose- land and some 3500 dancers were on hand to dance to three different bands-Woody Herman, Duke Elling- ton and Count Basie. Dave Brubeck, Ella Fitzgerald, Sarah Vaughan, Stan Getz, Eubie Blake, Elvin Jones, Chico Hamilton, Max Roach, Earl Hines, Clark Terry, Archie Shepp, Charles Lloyd are also among those who performed their particular brand of music. Sarah Vaughan, with Michel Le- grand and Stan Getz, ran the gamut from blues to scat singing and a vocal duet with Legrand "Watch What Hap- pens" proved that Sarah still rates as one of the top jazz singers. Also, on the same program was Tom Scott's L. A. Express, which gave goers a taste of West Coast Jazz. Michel Le- grand, writer of the music for the film, "Lady Sings the Blues" directed the orchestra backing Sarah and Stan Getz. The New York Musicians Festi- val as part of Newport held several events at Alice Tully Hall. These con- certs given by musicians who are con- sidered experimenters and innovators are a vital function in jazz offerings. The Charlie Rouse Sextet; Danny Mixon Trio; Abdullah; Walter Bishop, Jr. Quartet and Byard Lancaster - sound of liberation were some of the groups offering original material; of- ten exciting. The famed Apollo Theatre in Har- lem was turned into a Jazz mecca. Some of the artists appearing, in- cluded: Irene Reid; Dizzy Gillespie Quintet; Kenny Burell Trio, Dakota Staton, Charles Mingus, Louis Jor- dan; Herbie Mann, Two Generations of Brubeck; Roy Haynes Hip Ensem- ble and the Jazz Opera Ensemble, plus many more. Max Roach, Ruth Brown, Robin Kenyatta, Elvin Jones, Charles Earland and Stan Getz with the Eleo Pmare Dance Company closed out the five day event. From the opening afternoon fea- turing Gerry Mulligan, Gato Barbieri, Charles Lloyd and Wein's own group, the Newport Ensemble and Margie Joseph, to the final wrapup at Nassau Coliseum, the festival would have to be termed as an artistic success. Over 16,000 were jammed into the Coliseum to get turned on by Tito Puentes, Duke Ellington, Ray Charles and Aretha Franklin. These formidable artists just simply had the Coliseum rocking from the very first note. There was an intermission following the Duke. Then, Donny Hathaway picked up the pace and it was full steam ahead. "Donny socked it to 'em with his latest, "Love, Love, Love." Ray Charles gave the audience what it wanted to hear and included, "I Can Make It Through The Day." But, the icing on the cake was the fantas- tic performance by Aretha Franklin who was in top form and top voice. "Day Dreamin," and her new release "Angel," written by sister Carolyn helped to turn the evening into a magical event. A true black experi- ence. The Newport Festival, after 18 years in Newport, is now history in its second year in New York. Despite steamy heat, often rain, and minor sound difficulties, most of the 60 events went off on schedule, whether held indoor or outdoor. It was cer- tainly an event in which music held the top-drawer for ten days. The crowds were orderly and eager. Let's hope this is only the beginning of an era and that this kind of dynamic start can flourish for years to come. Bravo! to one and all. Armstrong Stadium ASCAP president Stanley Adams was among those present at the cere- morial Stadium. He was accompanied Festival, that saw the Singer Bowl re -named the Louis Armstrong Me- moarial Stadium. He was accompanied by Lucille Armstrong, the jazz great's widow, and Mayor John Lindsay. .,. ., Vr" Miror...."-erj= MAVIS STAPLES RANDY WESTON MAN DRILL The Onlookers: ar. +i.a.' mein,r...w.w r_ 26 Cash Box - July 21, 1973 www.americanradiohistory.com

Dripping Springs Draws Young Crowd DRIPPING SPRINGS - It really "happened" at "Willie Nelson's First Annual 4th of July Festival at Drip- ping Springs, Tex. Unlike the "reu- nion" of the previous year where the hot sands of Texas parched every- one's enthusiasm, the springs not only "dripped," they flowed with suc- cess. At least 50,000 fans are known to have attended the fest. Approximately 20,000 couldn't even get in the grounds. An array of talent was on hand to entertain the crowd of orderly, well- mannered fans who attended because of their love for, and interest in, country -oriented music. Most of those in attendance were 25 -years -of -age or under. The artists who appeared through- out the day were Willie Nelson, Kris Kristofferson, Tom T. Hall, Charlie Rich, Leon Russell, Waylon Jennings, Rita Cooledge, John Prine, Billy Joe Shaver, Jerry Jeff Walker, Kenneth Threadgill and Johnny Darrell and each played from 45 -minutes to an hour. There was even a wedding when Paul English, who plays drums in Willie's band, was married on stage. Contractual problems made it im- possible for Atlantic Records to se- cure and release an album of this year's fest, even tho' it had been ear- lier reported to be a possibility. Coor- dinators for the one -day affair were Sam Uretsky, Neil Reshin, Nick Hunter and Willie Nelson. Choctaw Fair Features Country Music NASHVILLE - The Annual Choctaw Indian Fair has been set for July 18-21 with an expected attendance in excess of 100,000. The Fair, to be held near Philadelphia, Mississippi, 38 - miles northwest of Jackson, Mis- sissippi, will feature Indian arts and crafts and native ballgames, dances and pagentry. A highlight of the entertainment will be a country music review con- sisting of some of the top artists in the entertainment field. Coordinator for the Fair is Bob Ferguson, executive producer for RCA and whose wife, Martha, is a Choctaw whose family boasts a num- ber of Chiefs in the Indian nation. Elektra's July Picnic A Success NASHVILLE - Fisherman's Pier on Old Hickory Lake near Nashville was the site for the 4th of July picnic hosted by Elektra Records. The fami- ly -type get-together got it all togeth- er with a wide array of food, old fashioned "visiting" and watersports. There were three houseboats, plus an assortment of run -abouts for the pleasure of the almost 200 music ar- tists and executives who attended. Even a tremendous thunderstorm could not dampen the good time. Hosts for the day were Jack Holzman, president of Elektra; Russ Miller, vice-president and A&R; Mike Nesmith, president of Countryside; Dave Mack, Elektra national promo chief; Pete Drake, producer, and Elektra artists Mickey Newberry and Linda Hargrove. Son- ny James and The Southern Gentle- men top the list of headliners that also includes Johnny Paycheck and The Cashiers, and Diana Trask. Mack Trucks Uses Disk For Promo NASHVILLE -A nationwide radio campaign for Mack Trucks Inc. of Allentown, Pa., featuring country ar- tist Dave Dudley has been initiated by Lieberman -Harrison, Inc., an Allen- town, New York, and Toronto adver- tising agency. The six-month campaign is geared to reach an audience of nighttime truck drivers with a message em- phasizing the availability of quality Mack parts and service at key loca- tions around the country. Key to the campaign is Dudley's recently recorded hit "Keep on Truck - in'." Authorized Mack distributor- ships and service centers are offering free copies of the record to drivers via the commercials. The 60 -second messages themselves feature Dudley singing about and directing drivers to quality Mack parts and service. The novel idea is Mack's first major radio promotion. The campaign began July 10 over 30 stations which feature predomi- nantly country and western program- ming. Cash Box -- July 28, 1973 39 www.americanradiohistory.com

J0B I f All Family of Music' For 1973 EWiS8 L> Cited Area 20 Acts Showcased At Meet SAN FRANCISCO — More than 20 SAN FRANCISCO — Paying: tribute to the companies’ promo men in the field, Columbia, Epic and the Colum- bia Custom labels held a special sin- gles presentation at the labels’ 1973 Convention. Called “There’s No Hits Without You,” the presentation provided both audio and visual highlights of the year’s past chartmakers and a pre- view of sounds to come. Assembled by Steve Popovich, Columbia vice pres- ident of national promo, and Stan Monteiro, director of national promo at Epic and Colubmia Custom labels, “There’s No Hits Without You” was scripted by Bob Adels, narrated by WFIL’s George Michael and recorded at Columbia’s New York studios and James Guercio’s Caribou ranch. The multi-media fete offered in- sights into the behind the scenes as- pects of the recording careers of such chartbreaking “newcomers” as Earth Wind and Fire, Edgar Winter and Albert Hammond. Opening with the Manhattans singing the title song, the singles review previewed forthcoming music by Albert Hammond, Johnny Mathis, Mac Davis, Eric Andersen, Blood, Sweat and Tears and Dr. Hook among others. Artist Interviews In addition, interviews with various artists were incorporated into the event, tracing their hit-making de- buts. A history of Earth, Wind and Fire was presented, reviewing the Welcome To The Confab 'Cabaret' Via Chip Monde SAN FRANCISCO—The transforma- tion of the Fairmont Hotel’s Grand Ballroom, scene of the dinner/shows at the Columbia/Epic 1973 Conven- tion, into an intimate, cabaret-style room was the result of the activity of Chip Monck, who has done eleaborate staging for the Rolling Stones and other major groups. Monck, who also staged Columbia’s “Week To Remember” at the Ahman- son Theater earlier this year, had the challange of converting the Grand Ballroom of San Francisco’s Fair- mont Hotel into a concert hall big enough to accommodate a 32-piece orchestra, yet intimate enough to cater to the more down-home feel of some of the labels’ country acts. Joined by Abe Jacob, sound consul- tant for the convention, Monck began working against deadlines in order to achieve his desired transformation. While Monck was busy getting into details about smoke machines, being able to change the levels of the stage some 32 inches in 12 minutes and wondering how to spin certain stage areas around in a swivel motion, sound expert Jacob was attempting to put together a sound system that would sound just as clear reverber- ating the sounds of acoustic guitar strumming as it would blaring out heavy rock rhythms. “We were faced with a problem of putting together a truly flexible PA system,” he revealed, “one that would accommodate any artist. We began to assemble equipment furnished by McCune sound and .Swanson sound and, aided by the Record Plant, we put together something quite innova- tive. All the concert performances here were heard in quadraphonic sound. It’s the first time we’ve ever used live quadraphonic sound at a convention and all the acts, from country to r&b, seemed to adapt well to it.” group’s success in 1972-73. The Log- gins and Messina story featured singer-songwriter-guitarist Jim Mes- sina commenting on the duo’s forth- coming album. Clint Holmes, a smash with “Playground In My Mind” offered his personal thanks to all the “guys in the field” who helped him attain popularity. Edgar Winter was represented by manager Steve Paul, who, in a taped phone conversation, traced Edgar’s development as an artist. Mac Davis was interviewed before previewing his “Kiss It And Make It Better” release. Epic Records, which declared 1973 as “Charlie Rich Year,” was lauded by the hit-making artist for its efforts in making “Behind Closed Doors,” his biggest pop single ever. The Manhat- tans and Intruders were spotlighted in a success story relating to the suc- cess of Columbia, Epic and Custom Labels in the area of black music, and which stressed the creativity of such producers as Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff, Thom Bell, Barrett Strong, Jim Stewart and Joe Wissett. The special singles presentation also lauded the promo men for their “unflagging dedication” on behalf of the labels’ releases and closed with a special preview of “Tell Me,” a single culled from Chicago producer James William Guercio’s forthcoming film “Electra Glide In Blue.” Sung by Chi- cago’s Terry Kath, the tune rep- resents Guercio’s first writing effort in over five years. Col/Epic Promo, SAN FRANCISCO — Columbia and Epic honored top members of their promo and sales staffs during the la- bels’ Convention. The promo awards were announced at a midweek luncheon hosted by Steve Popovich, vice president of na- tional promo, for Columbia; Stan Monteiro, director of national promo for Epic and the Custom Labels; and Logan Westbrooks, Columbia’s na- tional director of special markets. The sales awards were announced by Jack Craigo, vice president of sales, and Ron Alexenburg, vice president of Epic Records and Columbia Custom Labels. Awards were presented to Sal In- geme of the northeast region for Columbia regional promotion Man- ager of the Year and Lennie Petze of the Northeastern Region for Epic/ Custom Label Regional Promotion Manager of the Year. Also recog- nized was Gene Denonovich of the southeast region, a two time winner, for his ‘continued dedication’. Columbia’s Branch Promotion Man- ager of the Year award went to Ed Hynes of the Boston office, while Mike Atkinson of the Los Angeles office was designated as Epic’s Branch Pro- motion Manager of the Year. And he can sing. Making a simple entrance to the song “Thus Spake Zarathustra,” adapted from “2001: A Space Odyssey” he held the audience by each breath, note and gesture for one hour during which he ranged from country to rock to gospel to just plain serious Elvis Presley sing- ing. His selections included “Faded Love,” “Blue Suede Shoes,” “Fever,” “You Ain’t Nothing But A Hound Dog,” “Help Me Make It Through The Night,” “Something,” “I Can’t Stop Loving You,” “The American Trilogy,” “Love Me Tender,” “I Can’t Help Falling In Love With You,” “You Gave Me A Mountain,” and “How Great Thou Art.” Dressed in a white suit with high shirt collar encrusted with multi- colored studs he introduced each member of his band, and paid tribute to a few of his friends who have, and still, contribute to his career friends and associates such as Chet Atkins and Felton Jarvis. Donning a white cape lined with the same blue as the scarves he threw on occasion to the crowd, El- vis Presley finally bowed to his “sub- jects,” facing north, east, south and west in the auditorium, the lights went out and he was gone—back to his hotel to rest before he faced the evening sellout audience of scream- ing, flashbulb-popping, shoving peo- ple who have contributed to his leg- end spanning the best of two de- cades. Opening the show was comedian Jackie Kahane who tailored his re- marks to the crowd who accepted his light patter courteously as they waited with almost unbearable antic- ipation for the appearance of their “idol.” The Sweet Inspirations, who worked along with J. Sumner and the Stamps Quarter as backup singers, gave a well-accepted review of rhythm and blues numbers. 90,000 people that wanted to see the show couldn’t get tickets. j-j- Loleatta Holloway THE WHISKY, L.A.—GRC’s Loleat- ta Holloway looks like a black version of Playboy Magazine’s satiric herione Little Fannie Annie and possesses a voice equally as provocative. Her ver- satile singing abilities seem to be rooted in a gospel background, as in- dicated by occassional, almost ecstatic crescendos. She sounded particularly nice on “Neither One of Us,” “I’ve Got Love,’ and her own “Our Love.” This latter tune sounds like a hit. Loleatta is quick to establish a rapport with her audience which sus- tains through out her entire act. What an audience wants, Loleatta gives. She was backed by a group called Home Grown. r.b. what is BaeEmam^Tuiimeir WHISKEY, L.A.—No fireworks, may- be, but Motown’s Edwin Starr and his eight-man band are a brightly- beated lot who splash much color around with their vocals, garb and movements. Stunningly superior in their choreographing of themselves and even their instruments, the effect pays off perfectly—you can’t take your eyes off of them. And that’s al- ways half the battle. One minute everything is heavy brass and the next it is all rhythm, with little re- conciling between the forms. Yet it is Starr’s unpretentious way of throw- ing those great, gut-level r&b sounds at you that sews-up the evening. He ambled along easily with “Walk on By” but did a superlative job on his own composition, “You and Me.” It was—for comparison only—a Barry White type of piece that musically swung in broad, latitudinal moves while simultaneously being heightened by his vocals. Bachman Turner Overdrive opened the show. They were all there, in tune, and played to beat the band. But they just couldn’t walk-off with any prizes. A new group from Canada, the Mercury artists are a hard-rock act, and they certainly lived-up to the expectation. Much of what they sang, though, was just screechingly hurled at the audience which acheived an impact rather than a welcomed acknowledgement. But to be fair, they showed determination in what they played and a definite capability of smoothing themselves out to be a good, good act. b.m. Melissa Maiieliester TROUBADOUR. L.A.—Ms. Melissa Manchester: now and then she sounds like Della, piano-plays like Carol and stylizes like Bette, yet the lady is the very essence of originality—or is it unpredictability? Whatever it is, she is a fascinating protector of the free enterprise system of singing, parting her material the way it suits her while brushing it with breathless conviction and agility. There are little pockets of climaxes that are built into each number with her unaccount- able way of whispering the words into intense statements. And she is also theatrical, giving impassioned em- braces to songs like “Since I Fell for You” as though they were carrying a torch for her rather than the other way around. That song, sans back-up (dnimmer/Kirt Bruner & bassist / Cooker LaPresti) except for electric guitarist John Sholle, and “Never Never Land” (from “Peter Pan”) were both actually quite revealing in that they unmasked the simplicity and elo- quence just dying to be retreived in her repertoire. And there is certainly nothing wrong with ANYTHING she sings. Most of it runs as swiftly as it does strongly, as with “Easy” and “Funny That Way,” both of which she wrote. In fact, her new Bell LP, “Home To Myself,” features solely her material and is a melange of moods fused to- gether into a beautiful package—just like her performance. Headliner Donald Byrd (Blue Note) swooped-in with his appealing jazz- jive and walked-off—as David Mer- rick would be apt to remark—with mixed reviews. A fairly large group seven members, the emphasis seemed to be loud, long and loose in every- thing they played. And though this sort of extravagance is welcomed whenever the opiates of the evenings require such, this was just unreserved indulgence. Nonetheless, some nice interesting rhythms circulated here and there, especially with “Black Bird,” Byrd’s super-seller of late. b.m. Spammers Miracles Eddie Kendricks Edwim Starr THE FORUM, INGLEWOOD— Re- cently Don Cornelius’ Soul Train packaged a kinetic, entertainment- filled evening of soul reminiscent of those gala Apollo line ups. This kind of event, featuring a lengthy roster of performers, is a revered novelity here and growing practically extinct elsewhere. The show thus had a built-in appeal. This line up opened with a promis- ing newcomer act called the Jackson Sisters and- segued to Motown’s Ed- win Starr. Edwin is back on the rise with his o\Vn hit, “There You Go.” Starr also made points by performing his “25 Miles.” Eddie Kendricks, a former Tempta- tion next proved that girls find him tempting as ever. Although the Soul Train was precisioned non-stop, Kendricks managed to stop the show a few times with his “Can I’ and his latest smash, “Darling Come Back Home.” When it was time for the train to bring on the Miracles, there was no Smokey in the engine room. There former lead sat in the audience with his wife, Claudette, and watched new Miracle Bill Griffin handle solos. It was interesting to sit behind Smokey and watch his response to the entire performance. He approved.) The Miracles sang all of their hits but with slightly newer arrangements. Although Griffin simulates the voice of his genius predescessor (who’s now a solo act) , the different orchestra- tions and phrasing makes them the Miracles of ’73. Especially nice was a cut off of their new Renaissance LP called “What Is the Heart Good For?” After a brief intermission the show resumed with the Sylvers, who brought their spectacular eclat to the stage. Dressed in harlequin costumes, they mesmerized the crowd with cos- tumes, choreography, and songs like “Stay Away From Me.” Finally the caboose brought out the headliners of the night, the Spinners. Jazz Great Eddie Condon Dies Col. Released Tribute LP Before His Death NEW YORK - Lee Wiley sang "Back Home Again In Indiana," backed by Earl "Fatha" Hines, Wild Bill Davison, Johnny Windhurst, Vic Dickenson, Kenny Davern and Cliff Leeman. Then, on a blue note, the 40 -minute funeral service ended Wednesday (8) for guitarist Eddie Condon, purveyor of Chicago jazz and strong spirits, who died Aug. 4 after a long illness. He was 67 years old. Credited with helping organize the Chicago jazz style and influencing the many muscians who played his New York City night spot over the years, Condon worked and played with the giants of jazz in a career that began in the early 1920s. He recorded for Decca and Commodore, among oth- ers. A native of Indiana, he grew up in the mid -West. His night club on Manhattan's 52nd Street, on the fringes of Times Square district, was the most well-known of the jazz and strip clubs that lined the street in the days when jazz was king. Dixieland and Chicago were the idioms the crowd favored and Con - don's attracted the foremost practi- tioners of both styles. The club moved to new quarters nearby some years ago. Condon is survived by his wife, Phyllis; two daughters and a broth- er. Eddie Condon's unexpected death came only days after Columbia Rec- ords had released "Eddie Condon's World of Jazz," a two -record featur- ing Eddie and his favorite musicians. The Columbia project, produced by Michael Brooks and sponsored and inspired by executive producer, John Hammond, was to coincide with the release of the book, The Eddie Con- don Scrapbook of Jazz, on which he collaborated with Hank O'Neal, to be published next month by St. Martin's Press. Condon is actually heard very little on this Columbia release. Most of the material on the album features those musicians and the style of music which Eddie espoused during his long and full career as not only a musician, but as advocate, organizer and wit. Performances by Louis Armstrong, Bobby Hackett, Henry Allen, Bix Biederbecke, Bud Freeman, Bunny Berigan, James P. Johnson, Hot -Lips Page, Pee -Wee Russell, Jack Teagar- den, Fats Waller and Lee Wiley, among many others, are an integral part of the album, as they were of Eddie's life. In all, 27 tunes from Eddie's past are presented in the double LP set. "One of the less important facets of Eddie Condon's career was the fact he played guitar," reminisced John Ham- mond a few days after Condon's death. "He was sharp, witty, and I should add, quite devastating. I first met him in 1930 in a basement speakeasy where he had a band with Red McKenzie, Joe Sullivan and Jack Bland-they were called the Mound City Blue Blowers." "His contributions to the art were many. He had the first integrated band to go into a recording studio. He also had the first jazz television program, which introduced such peo- ple as Ella Fitzgerald, Jack Teagar- den, Louis Armstrong and a dozen others to a wide audience. He was instrumental in bringing jazz to two generations of bibulous and not - necessarily musical New Yorkers. "He helped more muscians than any other man associated with jazz through his concerts, night-club per- formances, recordings and other en- gagements. This album contains some of his merciless comments (in the ex- panded liner notes) and some of his favorite musicians, sometimes playing with his non -favorite vocalists." NEW DEAL-Jesse Colin Young (center) signs an exclusive recording con- tract with Warner Bros. Records. With Jesse are Joe Smith, WB president, and Mo Ostin, chairman of the board. Studio Honors Motown Staff LOS ANGELES - Motown Records was the recipient of a party thrown in its honor by the Village Recorder to show the label just what the studio did with the sound on Willie Hutch's new LP. "We invited Motown's creative de- partment to a champagne party and listening experience to Willie's album which was recorded here," says gener- al manager Dick LaPalm. "It's the first time we did anything like this and it gave us a chance to let off some of the excitement we felt after doing the project." LaPalm arranged the party through Hutch's producer -manager Ed Theo- dore. Besides inviting vice president Suzanne DePasse, the studio also played host to over one dozen Mo- town people plus a number of press and radio representatives. Grunewald Music Sold To Pianist NEW YORK - The oldest music store in New Orleans, the 121 -year - old Grunewald Music Co., owned by the Grunewald Family since 1852, has been sold to local pianist Ronnie Kole. Pierre B. Clemenceau, president of the Grunewald Music Co., Inc. will remain as chairman of the board and chief executive officer. Ronnie Kole has been installed as the new president. S. J. Olivier will continue in his capacity as vice pres- ident and director of piano sales, along with James Stubban, vice pres- ident and director of the Band Instru- ment Department. The board of direc- tors of the Company are Messrs. Cle- menceau, Kole, Olivier, Stubban, Re- mus Hebert, and Everette Link, Jr. Assoc. Booking Plans Oct. Move To Beverly Hills HOLLYWOOD - Associated Booking Corporation has sold its building at 9477 Brighton Way in Los Angeles and is moving to new quarters, a half floor, at 9595 Wilshire Boulevard, Beverly Hills, on October 1st. Oscar Cohen, president of ABC, has switched Tony Pappa, v.p. in charge of the Dallas office, to head the new California setup. Dave Bendett, brought from Florida to California last year, has been dropped. Pappa plans to spend three weeks a month in L.A. and one week in Dallas. His associate, Ernie Powers will run things in Texas while Pappa is attend- ing to duties in California. The first new agent to be added to the Beverly Hills office is Dan Spellens, who'll work in the contemporary dep't. CBS Expands Studio Set -Up HOLLYWOOD - Creation of a new division of Chuck Blore Creative Ser- vices (CBCS), the Great Scott Re- cording Studios, was announced this week by Milt Klein, president of the company. The new entity consists of the original recording studios owned and operated by CBCS, combined with new recording, dubbing, post produc- tion and mixing facilities. The studios are not available for rental. Moody Blues Seek 'Long Hair' Music Reviews NEW YORK - Because of requests made since the Moody Blues an- nounced their 1973 international tour, Threshold Records has announced that it will invite classical reviewers to attend the Moody Blues concerts in the United States in addition to the pop and rock reviewers normally in- vited to the group's concerts. This is the first time a rock group has made such a gesture. The Moody Blues began as a rock and roll band and have never deserted that catagorization (their most recent hit single was called "I'm Just A Singer In A Rock And Roll Band"). However, ever since their album "Days Of Future Passed," was re- leased in 1968, recorded with the Lon- don Symphony, the Moody Blues have received critical acknowledgement from all segments of the musical spectrum. The decision to invite classical mu- sic reviewers is a response to that interest. Rather than categorize the Moody's music, Threshold is inviting all music reviewers to the Moodys concerts in keeping with the group's wishes that their music not be limited to any one particular audience. The Moody Blues have also been invited to lecture at the prestigious Eastman School of Music in Rochester, New York. Rick Nelson To Aid In Heart Campaign HOLLYWOOD - Rick Nelson, MCA Records artist, will be "National Youth Spokesman" for the 1974 Heart Fund Campaign. Nelson will record promotional spots for Top 40 radio and network television stations to include 4300 AM and 1800 FM sta- tions. The spots will also be tied in with the release of Nelson's new forth- coming album scheduled to be re- leased by MCA this fall. ? Cash Box - August 18, 1973 www.americanradiohistory.com

Cash Box/R(IB News Report Atlantic `Gold' From NATRA (Thom Bell Top Producer) NEW ORLEANS - Atlantic Rec- ords' superstars came away from the 1973 National Association of Televi- sion and Radio Artists (NATRA) Golden Mike Awards Show in New Orleans last week toting a respecta- ble share of the gold bullion under their arms. Winning four Gold Mike Awards out of the seventeen categories, At- lantic took the Best Duo of the Year- Roberta Flack and Donny Hathaway; Best Female Vocalist of the Year- Aretha Franklin; Best Male Vocal Group of the Year-Spinners; and the Best Producer of the Year- Thom Bell. Thom Bell is the highly talented, independent producer who Atlantic contracted to produce the Spinners album titled, "The Spinners." The re- sults were three gold singles and a gold album (all RIAA certified) for the group. The eloquent Paul Johnson, Atlan- tic's national promotion director or R&B who accepted the Golden Mike Awards for the "heavies", described the momentous occasion as the "phan- tasmagorical mind -mesmerizer of the year!" (L To R) Paul Johnson and Thom Bell Baccus & Vogelhut Form R&B Pdtn's NEW YORK - Barbara Baccus and Reid Vogelhut announce the opening of the New York office of R & B Productions, a multi -service concert promotion, management and adver- tising venture. Nationally, the pair will produce their own concerts, coordinate the acquisition of major acts for colleges and universities and develop new talent. Prior to the organization of R & B Productions, Ms. Baccus served as di- rector of the concert division of Mu- sic Fair Enterprises, Inc., in charge of booking and producing contem- porary and variety attractions for the chain of East Coast theatres -in - the -round. Ms. Baccus was also re- sponsible for the management of Sly & The Family Stone, Genya Ravan, Peaches and Herb for a number of years. Vogelhut, who has produced many concerts throughout the country, will remain as president of Nazz Advertising, located in Baltimore, Md., handling advertising and promo- tion campaigns for R & B projects. Previously, he was with Tract Adver- tising in Philadelphia, heading up their concert advertising accounts. R & B Productions is located at 527 Madison Avenue, Room 700-16, New York, New York 10022. Tele- phone (212) 753-6108. 'Lady A', Founded Stax Back In Biz MEMPHIS - Mrs. Estelle Axton, long recognized as one of the leaders in Memphis Music for many years, re-entered the music business after a five year absence. "Lady A" as she is fondly referred to, founded Stax Records with her brother, Jim Stewart, in 1958. From a humble beginning on East McLemore in a renovated theatre, Estelle Axton and Jim Stewart created the giant rhythm and blues studio known all over the world. Such recording art- ists as Isaac Hayes, Rufus and Carla Thomas, The Mar -Keyes, Otis Red- ding, Staple Singers and many others began their record careers under the watchful eyes of this brother/sister duo. Now Estelle Axton is beginning a new music career. Long a strong be- liever in new talent, Mrs. Axton has established a company dedicated to discovering and developing new promising talent. Songwriters will form a strong nucleus of new talent but it will not be limited to songwrit- ers. A subsidiary of Fretone Music is being formed entitled Discovery Un- limited. "We believe that Discovery will fill a basic need in our communi- ty" said Mrs. Axton. "Many of our talented people have no one to see or hear their work and this is what we will endeavor to do. In addition to songwriters, we intend to see and hear singers, musicians, actors, an- nouncers, and models for films. We have an "open door" and "Open Mind" policy to anyone that has tal- ent in the recording, film, TV, or related industries. We do not promise you stardom, only a chance to be heard. If you have what it takes, we will do what we can to develop that talent," stated Mrs. Axton. Ted Cunningham, former general manager of the Memphis Symphony Orchestra for many years and a staff member of Trans Visual Productions, will co-ordinate Discovery Unlimited. `Black Caucus' Reception "MEET THE BOSS': That's what Isaac Hayes seems to be saying as he introduces his new bride to Congress- woman Barbara Jordan (D., Texas). Photo was taken at a recent press party in Washington in connection with the Congressional Black Caucus Dinner to honor Mayor Tom Bradley. Hayes, who won an Acade- my Award for his score for "Shaft," will headline an array of stars that will appear at the benefit dinner to be held at the Washington Hilton Hotel on September 29th. AT NATRA - NATRA held its annual event at the Marriott Hotel in New Orleans, August 8 thru the 12th.. Of course, the highlight of the event is the Golden Mike Awards Show. It was held Saturday (11th) evening. The Ballroom capacity crowd was treated to an enjoyable evening as the ceremonies un- folded. The event was hosted by E. Rodney Jones who puts plenty of zip into the works. He is together! D. J.'s, record execs and industry personnel from throughout the country gathered at the Marriott for this event and most every- one will agree it was a swinging affair, without incident or trouble, and despite elevator delays the affair went smoothly. The hospitality suites kept things hummin' with plenty of music including the new product to be released shortly. And, you can believe it, Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes will be filling the air- waves very shortly. Judging from the reaction when hearing the cut in the Columbia suite, it can't miss. I, also, wish to take this opportunity to express my sincerest thank you to all of you for the fine reception accorded me at my first NATRA event. Brown will be situated at the UA offices in New York City and will cover the key areas of Boston, Baltimore and Washington, as well as the state of Virginia. To Honor Don Covay CHICAGO - Mercury recording art- ist Don Covay, born and raised in Washington, D. C., will be presented with the key to his home town in special ceremonies Aug. 24. Covay's initial experiences in music came while growing up in Washington. Covay, the writer of several mil- lion sellers throughout the years, is well on the way to his first gold rec- ord with "I Was Checkin' out, She Was Checkin' in," currently riding high on both (CB Top 100 #30 bullet & RB e5 bullet) the pop and soul charts. CashBox Radio-TV News Report ATI Expands To TV Music NEW YORK - American Talent In- ternational is expanding its involve- ment in the area of television by signing an agreement with Hanna - Barbera Productions to produce the music for their new animated televi- sion series, "Butch Cassidy." The an- nouncement was made by Buddy Ep- stein, executive head of ATI's west coast office, who completed the nego- tiations with Hanna -Barbera. ATI will furnish the music for the new series which will be performed by a four -member group to be known as The Sundance Kids featuring Butch Cassidy. Buddy Buie, writer and producer of such hits for the Classics IV as "Stormy" and "Traces," will produce the music for the show as well as producing the group for MGM Records. The "Butch Cassidy" series will air on Saturday mornings at 10 on NBC starting in the fall. TALENT ON TV In Concert, ABC (August 31) - Al Green, Taj Mahal, Dr. Hook, Eric Weissberg and the Maha- vishnu Orchestra are featured per- formers in this Wide World of En- tertainment re -broadcast. Action '73, ABC (September 1) - The New Birth and Rick Spring- field are Dick Clark's guests along with featured regulars Bo Donald- son and The Heywoods. Midnight Special, NBC (Septem- ber 8) - The beginning of the Fall season for the "Special" fea- tures Mac Davis as host with his guests Edgar Winter, Harold Mel- vin and The Blue Notes, Mark -Al- mond, Chuck Berry and Ravi Shankar. KQV Air -Staff To M.D. Telethon PITTSBURGH - The annual Jerry Lewis Telethon, benefitting the Mus- cular Dystrophy Foundation, and tel- evised Sunday and Monday, Septem- ber 2-3, Labor Day weekend, will in- corporate the talents of the KQV Ra- dio personalities. The Telethon will be broadcast on WIIC-TV, Channel 11. Beginning at 6:00 p.m. Sunday, September 2, and continuing until 6:00 p.m. Monday, September 3, each of the KQV on -air personalities' shows will be aired from the Channel 11 studios, while they are simultaneously being seeen on television. Last year, through the cooperation of the KQV personalities, the local chapter of the Muscular Dystrophy Foundation raised over $70,000 on the Jerry Lewis Telethon. Dawn Taping Laugh -In Fall Opener HOLLYWOOD - Dawn Featuring Tony Orlando, currently on the na- tional record charts with "Say, Has Anybody Seen My Sweet Gypsy Rose," has been set to guest on the Dick Clark Presents 'Rock & Roll Years' NEW YORK - Chuck Berry, Fabi- an, The Drifters, Marty Robbins, Lesley Gore, Chubby Checker, James Brown, and Donovan will be part of a new ABC Television Network spe- cial, "Dick Clark Presents the Rock & Roll Years," airing on Thursday, Sept. 27 (8:00-9:00 p.m., EDT). The musical special was announced by Edwin T. Vane, vice president and national program director for ABC Entertainment. Dick Clark hosts a history of the rock & roll years live, on film, and on tape, with stars who represent the many elements which combined to create this musical phenomenon. It all began with the music of peo- ple like Chuck Berry and The Drifters, and went on to include country -western influences from Brenda Lee and Carl Perkins. The rock & roll "Idols" like Fabian and Bobby Vee led to dance crazes like Chubby Checker doing the Twist. James Brown and The Supremes rep- resent the soul side of rock & roll, while Gerry & the Pacemakers, and Chad & Jeremy, were among the stars in the important British rock invasion. Finally, the music reached a calmer stage with the lyrical love and peace themes of Three Dog Night and Donovan. Presented before a live audience at the Santa Monica Civic Auditorium, "Dick Clark Presents the Rock & Roll Years" will recreate the feeling and the atmosphere which produced the music that spanned two decades. The special is produced by Bill Lee, with Mark Warren as director, for Dick Clark Teleshows, with Dick Clark as executive producer. cashbox' album reviews DELIVER THE WORD-War-United Artists- UA LA128 F To say. that War has sophisticated since their last fine album, would be understating matters somewhat in reference to this collec- tion. What the group "Delivers" here is not only the "Word", but seven perfectly con- ceived tracks of music as well. Included is the group's current single smash, "Gypsy Man" along with a super jazz oriented instrumental, "H2 Overture", and the brilliant title track. This disk will undoubtedly be the group's most successful to date due to their current popu- larity but judging this LP on merit alone will make it an absolute smash. A very special "Delivery". RAINBOW-Neil Diamond-MCA-2103 Talking about gold at the end of the rain- bow, this collection's got it all! Although there's nary a Diamond composition to be found, what is included here are eleven previ- ously released tracks. A veritable "Best of Neil Diamond" that every Diamond fanatic will de- light over. Included are the performer's per- fect representations of such pop classics as "Everybody's Talkin' ", "Until It's Time For You To Go", "Suzanne" and "He Ain't Heavy, He's My Brother", each guaranteed to further increase the artist's popularity. Definitely a "diamond -studded rainbow". JONATHAN LIVINGSTON SEAGULL-Richard Harris-Dunhill-DSD 50160 It has long been accepted fact that Richard Harris is one of the finest actors of our time. The attraction of the best selling book on which this recording is based along with Har- ris' magnificient voice makes this recording one of the most poignant spoken word re- cordings to come about in years. The accompa- nying orchestration, composed, arranged and conducted by Terry James, is soft and haunting, reaching crescendo at particularly dramatic points and perfectly accentuates the immaculate vocal performance. All that needs to be said is that if you liked the book, you'll love this recording. AUSTIN, TEXAS-Johnny Winter-United Art- ists-UA LA 139 F When you're talking Johnny Winter, you know you're talking Texas blues, so what bet- ter way to examine the artist's talents than to take a trip back to 1968 and hear what he was doing while paying some dues. This col- lection is just that and is a great nostalgic anthology of the elder performing Winter's ear- ly days. Included here is some extra tasty blues, spicy rock and solid hard driving rock - blues, guaranteed to get anyone up and danc- ing. Listen especially to "Black Cat Bone", "Rollin' and Tumblin' " and "Help Me" for a real taste of Johnny Winter, and Texas blues. MOBIUS STRIP-Delaney Bramlett- Columbia-KC 32420 The break up of Delaney and Bonnie Bram- lett was a blow to their many fans and follow- ers, but as they say, from all bad there comes good. What we now have is two solid individu- al performers releasing fine collections as solo artists. Bonnie's release a couple of months back was super fine and so is this Delaney debut. In compiling mostly rock and blues material, the artist immediately demonstrates, via "Are You A Beatle Or A Rolling Stone" that he is as capable a performer on his own as he ever has been. No guess on what "Mobius Strip" is, but the music sure is good. ELECTRA GLIDE IN BLUE-Original Soundtrack-United Artists-UA LA062H It's difficult to remember exactly when pop motion picture soundtracks first became an integral part of film making, but that really doesn't matter. What does matter here is that this soundtrack, from what will undoubtedly be the most important film of 1973, carries with it that same intense impact as the film itself. Included here is the stunning "Tell Me" (the highly emotional closing song) as well as important dialogue from the film and the rest of the film's music that so perfectly typifies the entire work. A monumental achievement for James Guerico, both cinematically and mu- sically. 'I;F 1.37 îsl oSi'IXi@k?FIös3ºß -F NEWCOMER PICKS LOS COCHINOS @#!!*-Cheech & Chong- Ode-SP 77019 The two comedic maniacs are back with yet another mind blowing comedy experience that will have any listener rolling in the aisles. Once again, the humor is as unorthodox as can possibly be and covers a range of subjects from dope to basketball. The single release from this disk is the totally outrageous "Bas- ketball Jones (Featuring Tyrone Shoelaces)" which features George Harrison, Carole King, Billy Preston and others on musical back up. Although it's often wondered exactly when these two were released from the asylum (and if the cure actually took), the fact remains that the comedy is still sick, sick, sick. 3 PLUS 3-The Isley Brothers-T-Neck-KZ 32453 The extra three are the latest Isleys to join the band and welcome additions they are in- deed. This latest collection is without a doubt their strongest ever and should be met with an overwhelmingly great response from the public. Featured is their fast rising single, "That Lady", but the true meat and potatoes of this grouping is in the group's covers of "Listen To The Music", "Summer Breeze" and "Don't Let Me Be Lonely Tonight". The ar- rangements are perfect and quite attractive, in a very heavy r&b way. No addition has ever totalled such perfection. THE EARL SCRUGGS REVUE-Columbia-KC 32426 Now that Earl's on the express track with his sons, Randy, Gary and Steve and working with the likes of Jody Maphis and Josh Graves, his career and popularity are both stronger than ever. The material performed by the conglamorate. Revue is country orien- tated, but pop powerful as well. With Gary on lead vocals, sounding like an early Roger McGuinn, the group delightfully performs top flight material such as "Some Of Shelly's Blues", "Down In The Flood", "Salty Dog Blues" and "Tears". The prediction here is that this revue will be a giant success and the beginning of yet another Scruggs era. FOOD OF LOVE-Yvonne Elliman-MCA-356 It's not the green jello on the cover either. It's the music contained within this absolutely dynamic collection by the lady that should have been a "Superstar" in her own right some time ago that's the meal for the mind and ears. In covering hard rocking, cool cooking and soft soul searching material, Yvonne dem- onstrates her full potential and is constantly entertaining as a result. "I Can't Explain", the Peter Townshend rocker, receives a spirited treatment as never before and stands out as the best single possibility, but also listen closely to "Casserole Me Over", "Hawaii" and "Sunshine". Ms. Elliman seems ready to lose her "Superstar" label and become one on her own. SOUNDTRACK PICKS prr:k M1M4 F SMOKE DREAMS-The Captain Matchbox Whoopee Band-ESP-3009 Now here's one that not only comes from "down under" (Australia), but from "way out" as well. This somewhat weird conglomeration of Aussies performs their music a la Dan Hicks and His Hot Licks, but they add an extra spice of "strange" to make this disk a totally delight- ful, high camp experience. Tracks such as "My Canary Has Circles Under His Eyes", "That Cat Is High", "I Can't Dance (I Got Ants In My Pants)" and "Nagasaki" are tops in en- tertainment value and should attract faithful followers of camp and folly upon first listen. Don't sell this one short, it grows on you (but is it contagious??). DILLINGER-Original Soundtrack-MCA-360 The skillfully executed film account of the life and times of "Public Enemy #1", John Dillinger, carries with it a musical score equally as dramatic and entertaining, in the form of this latest release with music by Barry DeVor- zon. In perfectly capturing the period, De- Vorzon has chosen, and arranged, material that will keep the memory of the film long af- ter it is gone. Listening to such nostalgic pieces as "We're In The Money", "Honey" and "It's Easy To Remember" is a truly de- lightful experience. Tack on the "Theme From Dillinger" for a topper. Great movie, great music. 22 Cash Box - September 1, 1973 www.americanradiohistory.com

Tour, LP Due From Coryell NEW YORK - Vanguard recording artist, Larry Coryell has formed a new band which debuted Aug. 10 at My Father's Place in Roslyn, Long Island. The personnel of the new group includes Randy Brecker, elec- tric trumpet, formerly with Dreams and Deodato; Mike Mandel, key- boards, who has played with Coryell for the past three years; Alphonse Mouzon, drums, formerly with Weather Report and McCoy Tyner; and Danny Trifan, bass, who was last with Buzzy Linhardt. Currently recording in Vanguard studios, Larry and the band will ap- pear at the Morgan Mechanic Theater in Baltimore Aug. 21 followed by a European tour in September. After returning from Europe, they will travel to Japan for appearances there. Vanguard plans to release the band's first album in the fall. Levine/Brown Pen Dee's Return NEW YORK - Joey Dee of Joey Dee and the Starlighters and "Peppermint Twist" fame has returned to the rec- ord scene via the Sunburst label. His new record is "Wasn't It A Heavy Summer," written by Irwin Levine and Larry Brown, and produced by Steve Metz and Norman Bergen. Ms. Churchill's Book To Musical Via Stanton/Badale NEW YORK - Publishers Andy Badele and Frank Stanton have ac- quired from British book publisher Leslie Frewin the production rights to "The Boy Who Made Magic" writ- ten by Sarah Churchill, daughter of the late Sir Winston Churchill. Miss Churchill will star in the mu- sical which is planned. The adaptation is being handled by writer James Lig- gat with music by Andy Badale and lyrics by Frank Stanton and Murray Sernos. MGM Plans Jet Assist For Artists NEW YORK - An evening of "danc- ing on the moon," a tri -city event involving a chartered luxury jet, one of the world's largest hangars, cham- pagne -rigged fun -busses, "Peanuts" creator Charles M. Schulz, possibly an astronaut or two, and a small coterie of music world personalities, has been assembled by MGM Records to hail the debut of composer -performer and new act Judi Pulver. Judi entertains on Monday, Aug. 27, but not before one of the year's most elaborate promo ventures is launched. It begins in Los Angeles, settles briefly in Oakland, peaks in San Francisco, and plays to immediate im- pact on a nationwide basis, according to the label's vice president of mar- keting, Stan Moress. Special guests will board the "Star - ship I," a luxury -appointed, private Boeing 720-22, at an early evening hour on August 27. They'll meet in the grand salon and clubroom en route to the World Airways private terminal in Oakland. Janna Feliciano Will Represent Other Artists LOS ANGELES - Janna Feliciano, who for the past 18 months has been actively managing the career of her husband, RCA recording artist Jose Feliciano, has formed Mother Music Management. In addition to continu- ing to guide Jose Feliciano's career, Mother Music will manage established individual and group music acts as well as a small number of emerging talents. Mother Music Management will headquarter in the Feliciano Enter- prises complex, 415 North Tustin Avenue, Orange, California (714) 639-6420. Staff and client announce- ments are expected to be made within the next two weeks. Led Zep Heist: $10 G Reward Offered For Info NEW YORK - Entertainment Over- seas Ltd. is offering $10,000 reward for information resulting in the recovery of money taken from a safe deposit box at the Drake Hotel on July 29, representing proceeds of Led Zeppelin's Madison Square Garden Concerts. Persons having such information should call (212) P1-2-1330 and ask for Box 208. $180,000 in cash was discovered missing from the safe deposit box July 29 shortly before Led Zeppelin's final concert of their 1973 American tour. BMI's Cramer Lectures At New School NEW YORK - BMI president Ed Cramer will deliver a series of lec- tures on "Copyright law for muscians and producers" at the New School for Social Research, beginning on Sept. 20. During the four sessions, Cramer will present a brief outline of copy- right law, particularly with respect to music, together with an examination of practical business problems of composers and publishers. The course covers United States and internation- al copyright. It will also examine the relationships between composers, publishers, record companies and per- forming rights organizations. The four lectures will be given on Thursdays, from 7:45 to 9:15 p.m., starting Sept. 20. T. B. Harms Company, wherein Harms will continue in the capacity of managers, on behalf of Williamson, of the score of the Rodgers and Hammerstein mu- sical "Carousel." NEW YORK - The largest single crowd ever to witness an event at the Nassau Veterans Memorial Coliseum, 16,563, saw the Beach Boys last week (19). The previous high attendance was accomplished five times this year when 16,203 music fans attended four performances of Elvis Presley, June 22-24, and the one-night stand of Newport Jazz Festival on July 8. At the time, those performances were "sell-outs," but the new higher atten- dance was made possible by the addi- tion of over 400 seats, with that num- ber expected to be over 500 within the next two weeks. The Coliseum is shoring up its seating capacity with large crowds expected to view the Nets and Island- ers basketball and hockey teams when their play begins late next month and with the larger audiences expected from a greater demand for tickets for all other events. Polydor LP's (cont'd from p. 8) al sales manager Sid Love outlined promotion, advertising and marketing strategies on new and upcoming prod- uct. Among highlights of the classical release unveiled at the convention are Berlioz' "Symphonie Fantastique," with the Boston Symphony Orchestra under Seiji Ozawa; the Mendelssohn and Tchaikovsky violin concertos, with Nathan Milstein making a DG debut and Claudio Abbado leading the Vienna Philharmonic; the Brahms pi- ano concertos, with keyboard maestro Emil Gilds and Eugen Jochum direct- ing the Berlin Philharmonic; and Bach's monumental "Saint Matthew Passion," with soloists Gundula Janowitz, Christa Ludwig, Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau and others, the chorus of the German Opera Berlin and Berlin Philharmonic under Her- bert von Karajan. Karajan and the Berlin Philharmon- ic are also represented in the new release by Grieg's "Peer Gynt Suites" and "Sigurd Jorsalfar"; and orches- tral renderings of chamber works by Albinoni, Pachelbel, Boccherini and Respighi. Conductor Karl Boehm, an- other DG stalwart, leads the Vienna Philharmonic in Haydn's Symphonies 88 and 89, and the Berlin Philharmon- ic in Mozart's Symphonies 25, 26 and 27. In the solo piano repertoire, Wil- helm Kempff is heard in Schumann's "Kinderscenen" and G minor Sonata, and Roberto Szidon in Liszt's Hun- garian Rhapsodies and "Rhapsodie Espagnole." Finally, pianist Gerald Moore accompanies Schubert special- ists Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau and Janet Baker in a program of Schubert duets; and the LaSalle Quartet per- forms Beethoven's 13th Quartet and "Grosse Fuge." The September release, also covered in depth at the convention, is entirely devoted to a series of deluxe boxed sets, specifically geared to DG's 75th - year celebration. These specially priced, limited Anniversary Editions, available only through the end of the year, comprise the Haydn "London" Symphonies, with Eugen Jochum con- ducting the London Philharmonic; the complete Schubert Symphonies, with the Berlin Philharmonic under Karl Boehm; the Mendelssohn Symphon- ies, Herbert von Karajan directing the Berlin Philharmonic; the Dvorak Symphonies, Rafael Kubelik leading the Berlin Philharmonic; and the Si- belius Symphonies, with the Helsinki Radio Symphony under Okko Kamu and Berlin Philharmonic under Kara- jan. Later fall highlights will include the Mozart "Jupiter" and Schubert "Un- finished Symphonies, performed by the Boston Symphony under Eugen Jochum; pianist Maurizio Pollini's rendering of Schumann's C major Fantasy and F sharp minor Sonata; the Mozart "Coronation" Mass, Missa Brevis and Ave Verum, with Rafael Kubelik leading the Bavarian Radio Symphony; Lehar's "Merry Widow," Karajan and the Berlin Philharmonic; Handel's "Messiah," with the London Philharmonic under Karl Richter; Pfitzner's contemporary opera "Pales- trina," in its first recording with Kubelik and the Bavarian Radio Sym- phony; and on Archive, Handel's "Saul," Charles Mackerras conducting the English Chamber Orchestra. Advertising and marketing plans, as outlined at the convention by Dumont and Love, will also follow up on last spring's Metropolitan Opera recording of "Carmen," with Marilyn Horne, James McCracken and conduc- tor Leonard Bernstein; Seiji Ozawa's DG debut in Russo's "Three Pieces for Blues Band and Orchestra" and Bernstein's Symphonic Dances from "West Side Story," as well as three orchestral versions of "Romeo and Juliet"; and recent outings on the la- bel by pianist/conductor Daniel Barenboim and pianists Emil Gilels, Maurizio Pollini and Arturo Benedet- ti Michelangeli. AFM Members OK Label Pact NEW YORK, NEW YORK - Ameri- can Federation of Musicians Pres- ident Hal Davis today announced ap- proval by affected members of the AFM of a 27 -month contract between the 320,000 -member union and the phonograph record industry. Tenta- tive agreement between negotiators for the industry and the Federation was announced on July 23, after which those AFM members who earned $1,000 or more from recording during the calendar year 1972 were polled by secret -ballot. The result of the mail ballot was 907 in favor of acceptance, 156 opposed. Union nego- tiators had recommended acceptance of the pact, which is retroactive to Aug. 1, 1973. Davis noted that "In the symphonic field, an area where during the past several years we have been experi- encing sharp decreases in employment opportunities, agreement was reached on not only a substantial wage in- crease, but also on the availability of a four hour session and on a reduc- tion in the amount of product that can be taken from a session. It is our firm hope," he said, "and this is shared by symphonic players and by management representatives attend- ing the negotiations, that these changes will result in increased re- cording activity for U.S. and Canadian symphonic players." Davis noted that in the area of non -symphonic recordings, "we suc- cessfully obtained scale increases which in our judgement will not only benefit our players financially but will not dilute the number of job op- portunities currently available to mu- sicians working in this industry." He said that a most significant agreement was reached to clarify the language of the Special Payments and Music Performance Trust Funds, dealing with employer contributions to those funds. "This will eliminate many disputes and expedite the flow of money to the funds," he said. Contract highlights include: Scale wages: Non -symphonic: For a three-hour session, $95, going to $100 effective September 15, 1974. (The old rate was $90.) Special Session (11 hours): $63; rising to $66 on September 15, 1974. (Old rate was $60..) Special Canadian rate: $79; $83 in September of 1974. (Old rate, $75.) Symphonic: For three hour session, $101; going to $106 on September 15, 1974. (Old rate was $95.) Entirely new is provision for a four hour ses- sion, which will pay $134.67, and which will be increased to $141.33 effective September 15, 1974. Schoenbaum's opening remarks introduced an elabo- rate audio-visual presentation of new Polydor product, as well as that of Polydor-distributed labels Spring, People and Silver Blue, and Polydor's classical labels Deutsche Grammo- phon and Archive. give employers greater flexibility in programing recording sessions and, it is hoped, enable more symphony or- chestras in the U.S. and Canada to record. Local Health and Welfare contribu- tion has been raised to $3 (from $2) for each original service. Because of the difficulty of many recording musi- cians qualifying for local health and welfare programs, the union's effort in negotiations was to achieve these substantial increases so that many more members will be able to partici- pate in these important local plans," Davis said. Of particular importance to re- cording musicians, according to Davis, are provisions assuring more prompt and more accurate remittance of wage payments. These are reflected in stric- ter late payment penalties and also by advance notice of sessions. Additional provisions governing cartage, rest periods, doubling, premi- um rates were among other improve- ments obtained. Arrangers, orchestrators and copy- ists also won wage scale increases of 5% (with an additional 5% increase on September 15. 1974). Other Events Extensive radio, TV and press cov- erage is anticipated. Symphony or- chestras across the U.S. are already planning special Gershwin tributes. One of these, featuring the Mormon Tabernacle Youth Chorus & Sympho- ny was televised last week on WNET. In addition, there will be numerous store displays in the metropolitan area. Currently, there is a Gershwin show that is touring the Northeast area. Entitled "The Gershwin Years," it features all Gershwin material cel- ebrating the 75th birthday with such stars as Helen Gallagher and Barbara Cook. The U.S. Postal Service has already saluted Gershwin with its Gershwin commemorative stamp issued earlier this year featuring the head of Gersh- win against a montage of figures from "Porgy and Bess." Internationally, many events are in the works. Chappell -London has is- sued a biographical brochure for dis- tribution abroad and are coordinating radio/TV and press events. The BBC is planning a Gershwin special. Chap- pell -Germany has arranged for every German broadcasting station to do a special Gershwin program in Sept. For instance the RIAS in Berlin is preparing a 90 minute program. Oth- er branches such as those in Holland and Paris are also deeply involved in the worldwide celebration. Weiser Comment Norm Weiser, president of Chap- pell, noted that with the assistance of the worldwide Polygram Group "we are certain that people in every civi- lized country in the world will be re -exposed to the wonderful music created by the Gershwins." Abroad, Meyerstein-Maigret, pres- ident of Polygram S.A., is coordinat- ing worldwide publishing efforts from his headquarters in Paris. In the U.S., Ed Silvers, president of Warner Bros. Music, Sol Reimer and Henry Marks are working with Chap- pell on the 75th anniversary cam- paign.
