CBS Acts Launch Euro Tour Capitol Sept. Album Release w/ Radio Veronica Promotion HOLLAND - Top CBS International American artists, Dr. Hook & The Medicine Show, Albert Hammond and Redbone will kick off their fall Euro- pean tours with a major CBS Interna- tional/Radio Veronica (Holland) co- operative promo drive. The first per- sonal appearances by these artists in Europe this fall are to be at Club Veronica, an important new rock room which is owned and operated by Radio Veronica. Also set to appear during this special grand opening fes- tival are CBS U.K. act Colin Blun- stone, CBS France's Titanic and CBS Holland's The Buffoons and Albert West. In conjunction with Club Veronica's opening promotion and the artists' European tours, CBS Holland has created a one -of -a -kind LP which features all of the groups participat- ing in the festival. The album, enti- tled "Veronica -CBS Pop Festival," has already shipped more than 100,- 000 copies in Holland alone. Addi- tionally, a heavy poster campaign has been created and extensive radio Motown's Big Campaign On Gaye's New LP HOLLYWOOD - Motown Records is preparing a big marketing campaign to launch the new Marvin Gaye album "Let's Get It On," according to Phil Jones, director of sales, Motown Rec- ords. Except for the soundtrack album "Trouble Man," this is Gaye's first album since the release of "What's Going On" in 1971. Motown sales execs feel that "Let's Get It On," a concept album dealing with the emo- tions of a love affair, has a broader range of appeal than anything pre- viouly recorded by the artist. There- fore, the company's public relations/ advertising/merchandising thrust has been aimed at reaching a much greater range of consumers. The album is scheduled to ship this week as the single preceding it is number one on the charts. One of the largest -selling singles in Motown history, "Let's Get It On" went gold within six weeks of release. National Consumer Advertising In addition to radio spots adver- tising the album, Motown will place its first wave of advertising in na- tional publications such as the Na- tional Lampoon, Time (college edi- tion), Essence, Jet, and Rolling Stone, and in important local publications such as the Los Angeles Times Sun- day Calendar. For further local advertising, the company has created a series of ad mats in various sizes. A large bill- board on Sunset Boulevard will go up shortly after the album is released. A public relations campaign for re- views of the album will begin with the release of the record. Nearly 4,000 entertainers, sports figures and other celebrities will receive copies of it. Two posters-one 4 x 6 feet and another 22 x 33 inches will be supplied to stores and radio stations, as will "Let's Get It On" lapel buttons. Late in Sept. "The Master: The Magic of Marvin Gaye," a 90 -minute radio special documenting the record- ing career of the artist through the new album, will be made available to radio stations. The program will be co -produced by Motown and Water- mark, Inc., producers of American Top 40 and the Elvis Special. Planning for the campaign was handled by Mike Lushka, album sales manager; and Herb Wood, director of advertising. Dave Swaney's Company was retained by Motown to develop merchandising and public relations elements for the campaign. spots have been running on Radio Veronica to promote the groups' ar- rival. The groups' stay in Holland cli- maxes with their appearance at the Sportshalle in Rotterdam where they'll perform for 8,000 spectators and be televised on "Top Pops," Hol- land's most important scheduled TV special this fall. Previous CBS International coordi- nated European tours have resulted in the shaping of these artists' European careers. Albert Hammond's first tour produced sales of half a million co- pies of "It Never Rains In Southern California," and is considered an im- portant factor in the success of his current single, "Free Electric Band," now on the charts throughout Eu- rope. Hammond will introduce his third single, "Peacemaker" in Europe shortly. Redbone's prior European trip resulted in their current "Wound- ed Knee" smash there. Dr. Hook is making their first visit to Europe, following up on their earlier Europe- an success with "Sylvia's Mother" and their record currently rising on the Dutch charts, "Roland The Roadie." All tours have been closely coordi- nated between CB.S International's New York and European operations offices. Wallichs Shows 1st Profits In Four Years HOLLYWOOD - Wallichs Music & Entertainment Company, Inc., has re- ported a sales increase of 4.5% and its first profit from operations in four years for fiscal 1973, ended May 31. Net income, before extraordinary item, was $26,507, or 2 cents per share, on revenues of $8,168,085. This compares to a net loss, before ex- traordinary item, of $18,857, or a loss of 1% per share on revenues of $7,- 840,489 for the previous fiscal year. The extraordinary item for fiscal 1973 of $17,000 or 1 cent per share, resulted from a tax benefit operating loss carryover. In fiscal 1972, the company had an extraordinary item of $67,875, or 5 cents per share, from insurance benefits paid upon the death of Glenn Wallichs, a founder of the company. In announcing results, Clyde O. Wallichs, president, said sales in all departments increased with gains of 5.1% in records; 5.4% in pianos and organs and 3.4% in television and stereo. He said the gain in record sales was achieved in the second half when a switch from reliance on jobbers to direct buying improved selection. Among other factors cited for con- tributing to the company's up swing in sales and return to profit were overhead reductions, reorganization of the stores and a better balanced advertising program. Pirate Action (Cont'd from p. 7) selves unjustly at plaintiff's expense. The appropriating of the per- formances recorded by plaintiff and selling them in competition with plaintiff constitutes unfair competi- tion in North Carolina. Such unfair competition entitles plaintiff to recov- er damages and it is subject to in- junctive restraint," the Court de- clared. The Court also cited the U. S. Su- preme Court decision in Goldstein v. California which, it noted, found that a statute "which bars unauthorized copying of sound recordings (is) a valid exercise of the powers of the state." Rejecting the claim that the plaintiff record companies were as- serting a monopoly in violation of the State constitution, the Court observed that "plaintiff is simply trying to pre- vent defendants from stealing its property. Defendants are not restrict- ed from securing their own per- formers, recording these per- formances, and selling their own rec- ords or tapes in fair competition with the plaintiff." As to the defendants' claim that the sale by a record company of an album with a number of different composi- tions constitutes a tie-in sale, the Court declared: "Upon the basis of the undisputed facts, the conduct of plaintiff in marketing its products has not been shown to be improper or contrary to public policy." Finally, on the question of the re- fusal by legitimate record companies to license their material to pirates, the Court held that "the evidence shows that this action on the part of plaintiff was unilateral and not pur- suant to any agreement . not to deal with the defendants. In the ab- sence of conspiracy or monopoly, one may deal with whom he pleases." 22 Cash Box-September 8, 1973 www.americanradiohistory.com

ASCAP Annual War, John Cage NEW YORK - The American Soci- ety of Composers, Authors and Pub- lishers, has announced the completion of the 13th annual meetings of the Special Awards Panels. Society pres- ident, Stanley Adams, advised that $629,000 in cash awards, in addition to the normal royalty distributions, will be distributed this year to the Society's writers to offer financial en- couragement and in recognition of their important role in American mu- sic. Since the inception of this pro- gram, in 1960, the Society has dis- tributed some 6 million dollars in awards to its composer and author members. The program was devised and sums set aside to encourage and foster the contribution of ASCAP members to American music. Its pur- pose is to give recognition to those writers whose unique contribution may not be sufficiently rewarded through normal earned royalties. In volunteering to allocate a share of their earnings in this way, the mem- bers of the Society give tangible evi- dence of their continuing support of contemporary music. The awards recipients represent the complete spectrum in contemporary composition. Among them are such writers of international renown as Gian -Carlo Menotti whose Spoleto festival draws thousands of music lovers every year, Broadway figures Warren Casey and Jim Jacobs with the longest running musical "Grease" and the "Purlie" team, Gary Geld and Peter Udell, who have a new show coming up this season "All The Com- forts Of Home"; John Gage, a semi- nal figure in American music; Nash- ville country writer Buzz Cason; Joe Raposo, the chief writer for Sesame Street; rock groups such as "War," "Steeley Dan" and the "J. Geils Band"; and Richard Feliciano, pioneer in new religious liturgies. Young ASCAP writers are carry- ing on the tradition of such early members as Jerome Kern and Victor Herbert with contributions to the On and Off Broadway Theatre. Steven Schwartz has two shows running "Pippin" and "Godspell" (now also a movie), co -written with Michael Te- belak. Paul Jacobs and Christopher Guest's "Lemmings" continues at the Village Gate and Richard Weinstock, whose show "Magic Show Of Dr. Magico" received an Obie nomina- tion, is a regular contributor to such established Off Broadway Theatres as Where The Music and Entertainment People Meet To See and Be Seen in Hollywood it's frwfoqis IDEAL FACILITIES FOR ARTIST'S PROMOTION PARTIES CALL YOUR HOST TONY RICCIO 1523 CAHUENGA 466-3441 Awards Due; Among Winners La Mama and the WPA Theatre. Al Carmi::es is again represented with his new show, "The Faggot," at the Truck and Warehouse Theatre. Obie Award winning playwright Rochelle Owens, as well as Barbara Bonfigli and Cathy MacDonald, who are providing the music for the Lincoln Center's "A Street Car Named De- sire," are welcome new members to the Society who promise a bright future for Broadway Theatre. Among the other writers of pop music receiving awards for their con- tinuing contributions to America's musical traditions are: soul writer Jerry Butler; rising new star Chi Coltrane; jazz giant Ornette Cole- man; "Oscar" winner Al Kasha; country star Webb Pierce. Also among those recognized for their work were such other well known pop writers as Herb Alpert, Joan Baez, Richard Carpenter, Vaughn Horton, Randy Newman and Phil Ochs. The Popular Awards Panel consists of T. Dot 17474 Additional Promotions Announced At Wurlitzer Sales; Vaughn and Hager To Tonawanda In Key Phonograph Roles VAUGHN HAGER NORTH TONAWANDA - Two additional appointments to the Wur- litzer Company's North Tonawanda Division sales staff were announced by Dick Williams, manager of do- mestic sales -phonographs. The pro- motion of Larry Vaughn to the po- sition of sales manager for Wur- litzer Distributing Corporation and the transfer to the North Tonawanda Division of Larry Hager, operations manager for the eight campany- owned branches, come as a result of Wurlitzer's recent re -alignment of sales managerial responsibilities. The changes become effective September 1 when the responsibility for Wur- litzer Distributing Corporation offi- cially returns to North Tonawanda from the DeKalb, Illinois Division. The appointment of Vaughn as Wurlitzer Distributing Corporation sales manager follows the opening of a new Wurlitzer distributorship in San Francisco, announced last week by North Tonawanda division manager Amile Addy. As a result of an agreement with Bally Distributing Corporation, Wurlitzer will be rep- resented in San Francisco by Ad- vance Automatic Sales Co., Inc., Cal- ifornia Corporation. Vaughn was manager of the Wurlitzer Distribut- ing Corporation branch formerly lo- cated at 1315 -16th Street. Vaughn brings to the North Tona- wanda Division twenty-three years of experience in the coin machine in- dustry. He has been involved in every phase of vending operation including work as a routeman, serviceman, route supervisor, office manager and distributorship manager. Vaughn joined Wurlitzer Distributing Cor- poration as a sales representative in Nashville and has since served as manager of the Atlanta and San Francisco branches. His record as an administrator of branch offices has been outstanding, Addy stated. Larry Hager has been operations manager for Wurlitzer Distributing Corporation for the past eighteen months and will continue in that capacity, working out of North Tonawanda. His transfer will enable him to assist Williams on the same first-hand basis as in the past. Hager is chiefly responsible for coordinating all Wurlitzer Distributing Corpora- tion business including sales training, office training and financial analysis. Both Vaughn and Hager are ex- pected to move into the North Tona- wanda, New York area within the month. Their transfers are expected to bolster the increasing sales activity of the North Tonawanda Division. Wurlitzer spokesmen indicate that public and operator acceptance of the Americana phonograph and nos- talgic 1050 Jukebox has prompted one of the company's best sales years in recent history. Lynd Pickwick Gains In Fiscal Qtr NEW YORK - Amos Heilicher, president of Pickwick International, Inc., stated at the company's annual meet here last week that fiscal 1974 first quarter operations ended July 31, achieved new record results. This marks the 81st consecutive compara- tive quarter in which sales and earn- ings exceeded the previous year's quarter. During the first quarter, sales rose 25% to $33,630,912 from $27,019,180 and net income rose 19% to $1,235,- 804 from $1,041,873 in fiscal 1973. Earnings per share for the quarter ended July 31, rose to $0.29 from $0.25, an increase of 16% from the previous fiscal quarter ended July 31, 1972. A 4% stock dividend was de- clared for shareholders of record on Oct. 1, payable Oct. 31. In commenting on these figures, Heilicher stated "We are gratified with the results despite the increased cost of borrowed funds and the fact that this period is traditionally the smallest of the year. It remains our determination to decrease the effect of increasing costs by trimming in- ventories and other operations which can be streamlined. "Our strategy in adding retail out- lets and strategic regional warehous- ing units, we believe, continue to contribute sales and profit growth to our operations. Our international participation via our English and Canadian companies are also great sources of satisfaction in terms of current contributions and future po- tential. "The new product of our Proprie- tary Records Division and its innova- tive record packages and ideas should continue to add its strength to our operations for the year. "On June 25, 1973, Pickwick con- cluded its acquisition of Keel Manu- facturing Corp., a record pressing plant in Hauppauge, Long Island and on July 2, 1973, we acquired certain record pressing facilities of True Sound Manufacturing Corp., a divi- sion of A.B.C. Records. Both of these were reported to you previously. It is our expectation that after the current short integration period, these facili- ties will make their contribution to sales and profit. UA's DeMann: 'Ringmaster' For Label's 'Super Circus' HOLLYWOOD - The undisputed highlight of the recently concluded United Artists/UDC confab was the multi -media extravaganza billed as the UA Super Sales Circus, presented under the aegis of the label's creative merchandising director, Freddy De - Mann, during one of the morning ses- sions. If, in his own words, DeMann set out to remake the usual product presentation into "something different and exciting," the consensus was that he certainly achieved his goal. 2 Months Planning DeMann's "circus" was over two months in the planning and called for a cast of 50 with the support of a crew of up to 60 people. The creative team for the project was the staff of Chiaramonte Films of Hollywood, headed by Andy Chiaramonte. Said DeMann, "I knew what I wanted basi- cally and was interviewing a number of firms, as well as media agencies, and Chiaramonte emerged as the most unique and innovative in their ap- proach. They also impressed me with their feel for music." As for the budget, DeMann pointed out that it came within the amount annually set aside for such projects, but pressed for figures, he would say no more than that "while it cost something like $600,000 to produce 'Mame' on Broadway, we didn't spend anything like that." Initial List Over 1000 For NARAS 'Hall' NEW YORK - Well over one thou- sand initial nominations to the new- ly-organiz&I NARAS Hall of Fame have poured into the national offices of the record academy in response to recent requests issued to members for their recommendations of outstand- ing recordings released before the 1958 inception of the Grammy Awards. The list covers as broad a musical spectrum as that of some of the NARAS members who have sub- mitted their lits, such as Leopold Stokowski, Guy Lombardo, Johnny Mathis, Nelson Riddle, Laurindo Al- meida, George Beverly Shea, Percy Faith, Pee Wee King, Teddi King, Meredith Wilson, John Scott Trot- ter, Cy Coleman, David Rose, John Green, Sam Donahue and Cliffie Stone. Included among the suggestions are recordings by such legendery mu- sical figures as Enrico Caruso, Ar- turo Toscanini, Paul Whiteman, Louis Armstrong, Glenn Miller, Tom- my Dorsey, Billie Holiday, John Charles Thomas, Gene Austin, Nat - "King" Cole, Judy Garland, Hank Williams, Al Jolson, Mario Lanza, Bessie Smith, Bix Beiderbecke, Jelly Roll Morton, the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, plus many more who are still active on today's recording scene. The widely varied list of Initial Nominations extends all the way back to the year 1903 when Caruso recorded his famous version of "Ves ti La Giubba," to 1905 when Byron G. Harlan introduced "School Days," and to 1907 when Billy Murray waxed "Harrigan." Ben Selvin, one of the founders and first secretary of the New York Chapter of NARAS, was cited for his 1919 recording of "Dardanella," described as the first pop million seller. Perhaps the most concentrated and dedicated of all lists came from one member who cited 43 separate selections, every one of them sung by Bing Crosby. Weston Comment The abundance of ballots and breadth of initial nominations drew this response from arranger - conductor Paul Weston, co-chairman with Frank Jones of the NARAS Hall of Fame: "I'm tremendously en- thused with the response, both as re- gards the number of members who have sent in their suggestions as well as the reaction of the industry in general to this move by NARAS-to finally bring long -overdue recogni- tion to those great recordings re- leased before there ever were any Grammy Awards." A Final Nominating committee, comprised of 30 NARAS members, elected by the Academy's National Trustees, will soon be announced, and will then select the twenty-five NARAS Hall of Fame nominations. Following this, the voting procedure will be turned over to a larger, nine- ty -man board, consisting of many of the industry's most knowledgable cit- izens, who will then select the five recordings that will become the initi- al entrants into the NARAS Hall of Fame. UA Supercircus (Cont'd from p. 9) projection screens, each served by both slide and motion picture projec- tors and a multitude of speakers. Lighting was in the hands of Joe Ganon, known to the industry for having staged the Neil Dia- mond/Greek Theatre and Alice Coop- er/" Million -D olla r Babies" produc- tions. Alternating in a circle with the four projection screens were four sets of bleechers, and in the center "ring" area a giant mock-up of an LP bear- ing the UA label. "Considering the equipment we were using," DeMann said, "we had a technical monster on our hands, and we never even had time for a dress rehearsal. Participating in the show itself were a group called the Yerkus Circus Performers, the Jeff Kutahn Dancers, and in the corrider leading to the ring, the Oily Scarf Wino Band. The script was by Chiaramonte's Randy Kirby, who also served as ringmaster. In the audience were all UA /UDC home office and field personnel, as well as representatives of a number of the company's overseas licensees, along with the press and a smattering of UA's competitors-a total of near- ly 300 people. "Personally, first and foremost, I have to thank Mike Stewart for be- lieving in a very unsafe project and having the courage and conviction to see it through to fruition," DeMann said. UA's Mike Stewart at Supercircus Ms. Harris Is Atlantic Director A & R NEW YORK-Jerry Greenberg, se- nior vice president and general man- ager of Atlantic Records, has an- nounced the appointment of Barbara Harris to director of artist relations. Ms. Harris, who originally joined Atlantic under the auspices of Henry Allen, vice president of promotion in 1968, has held a variety of positions from executive secretary to Jerry Greenberg in 1969 to distributor pro- motion coordinator the following year. She then joined artist relations as as- sistant director in 1972. In her new post, she will liaise to- gether with John Gibson, who is the division head of publicity and artist relations. Barbara Harris Mike Kelly To GSF Promo NEW YORK-GSF Records Inc. re- cently announced the appointment of Mike Kelly to the company's promo staff. Kelly will be doing promotion covering the South and Southeastern regions of the country. Kelly was most recently associated with Starday King where he worked with such artists as James Brown, the Manhattans, and Arthur Prysock. Joe Jones To West Coast HOLLYWOOD-Joe Jones, producer and recording artist ("You Talk Too Much"), has announced his relocation to the west coast. Associated in the past with such hits as "Chapel of Love" and "Land of 1000 Dances," Jones has come to California with the intention of "helping talented young black artists find their way through the industry." Inquiries may be ad- dressed to 11637 Prager Street, Lake- view Terrace, Calif. Anderson To RCA Reg. Post NEW YORK-Ray Anderson has been appointed regional promotion manager on the west coast by RCA Records, ac- cording to Frank Mancini, vice presi- dent of promo, to whom he will report. Anderson was most recently RCA's Los Angeles field promo rep, a post he held since June of 1970. He had previously handled promo for RCA in the Pittsburgh -Cleveland -Buffalo - Detroit regions. Before joining RCA, Anderson han- dled local promo in Pittsburgh for Hamburg Brothers Distribution, and before that he functioned in the same capacity for Standard Distributors in the same city. Wilkowski Dave Mani To Capitol Pubs HOLLYWOOD-Dave Mani has been appointed east coast professional man- ager for Beechwood Music Corpora- tion (BMI) and Glenwood Music Corp. DiMaria Heads GRC Sound Studio ATLANTA-Michael Thevis, presi- dent of the General Recording Cor- poration (GRC), announces Tony Di - Maria has been appointed to the po- sition of manager of the Sound Pit recording studio. DiMaria was most recently execu- tive administrator and general man- ager of Ter -Mar Recording studio, a division of Chess Records located in Chicago. During his affiliation with Ter -Mar he handled such recording artists as Chuck Berry, Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf and The Dells. Before joining Ter -Mar, DiMaria worked as producer, arranger and composer in a studio administrator capacity for Bay Studios in Toronto, Canada where he handled Anne Mur- ray's recording of "Snow Bird" and worked with David Clayton Thomas. As new manager of the Sound Pit studio, a $2 -million recording opera- tion, DiMaria will be coordinating all sessions for the artists and groups signed to the General Recording Cor- poration's two labels: GRC (contem- porary) and AWARE (r&b). In addi- tion he will oversee all custom label work recorded and/or mixed at the "Pit" by outside individuals or inde- pendent firms. Already the 10 -month old studio has been used for mixing and record- ing by such noteables as B. B. King, Tommy Roe, B. J. Thomas, The Plat- ters and Joe South. 45'er 'Edits' President On Watergate NEW YORK - SRI, a division of Syntonic Research, Inc., a New York City firm specializing in acoustical research, has released a deliberately edited recording based on President Nixon's Aug. 15 speech on Water- gate. "To prove the contention that re- cording tape can be made to do almost anything in the hands of a precise tape editor," SRI has changed the speech into a confession. The other side of the recording con- tains the sentences from the original speech used for the editing. "The tape is not meant to be an attack on the Presidency but merely an example of what can be done with tape recordings," asserts I. S. Teibel, president of SRI and editor of the tape. "The 'Nixon Tapes' that every- one is so concerned about are proba- bly a snap to alter, and so much time has gone by since the matter was brought up that, if editing was in- tended, it probably has already been done. This editing would be almost impossible to detect by almost all audible or electronic means," Teibel adds. "Our tape is not an ultimate edit- ing job. There are intentional flaws and a certain amount of tape echo added, so that there will not be con- fusion with President Nixon's own official statements. If it had been our intention to truly fake the speech, it could have been done, primarily through digitalizing of the informa- tion. Such an editing job would be totally undectable, even with the use of voice spectograms or oscillogra- phic tracings. "To further protect the rights of the President, we specifically prohibit the use of our recording by broadcast- ing companies and state on the disk itself that it may only be used for private listening in the home." "We have also made it quite clear on the packaging of the recording that this is an altered tape and not an actual utterance of the President," states Teibel. The company feelsthat the public should be made aware of the danger of believing what one hears on a tape recording and has made the recording available to the public so that a per- son can hear with his own ears, the potential of edited tape. The recording is available on a 7" 45 rpm pressing which can be ob- tained by mail order. Cost is $2.00 plus 500 handling and 7% sales tax to New York State residents. Mail orders should be sent to: SRI, 623 Fifth Avenue, New York, N.Y. 10022. Howard Bloom Heads Famous PR Section NEW YORK --Howard Bloom-for- mer editor of Circus Magazine-has been named director of press and artist relations at Famous Music Corp., and has begun to organize a new public relations department for the firm. The department, located in Famous Music's New York headquarters, will prepare bios, press kits and press re- leases. It will also service the needs of writers, editors and television pro- ducers and will develop a clear image for each of Famous Music's artists. Famous' vice president of market- ing Andy Miele said, "We are rapidly acquiring new labels and need a vig- orous public relations arm. Howard is the perfect person to give us one." From 1968 to 1971, Bloom headed Cloud Studio, Inc., a commercial graphics firm which art -directed the National Lampoon created films for NBC-TV, and produced posters for ABC's seven FM stations. In 1971 he took over as editor of the full color rock monthly Circus Magazine. 10 Cash Box - September 15, 1973

Uttal Yetnikoff On CBS Intl (Cont'd from p. 7) here? Yetnikoff questions whether the same 400% growth can be accom- plished in the next five years. But one gets the feeling he will be trying. His primary goal is to develop interna- tional acts that will have impact on the American market as well as the rest of the world. Mott the Hoople and Argent are two UK entities that are enjoying heavy success in the U.S. But he wants to see a flow simi- lar to the flow of American acts that break big abroad. "We are enjoying great interna- tional success with Albert Ham- mond," said Yetnikoff, "and his 'Free Electric Band' cut is being more strongly accepted by people abroad than it was in the states." There will also be a big world-wide push on behalf of a new CBS find, David Es- sex, who is up at the top of the charts in England with "Rock On." Essex appears in the Ringo Starr film "That'll Be The Day." The disk will be out soon in America. Other areas Yetnikoff is acting in to accomplish further growth include the publishing arena. "Our April Mu- sic company is now one of the world's foremost publishing companies and we are going to expand in that area thru acquisitions and continued de- velopment of our own artists and writers." Yetnikoff estimates that be- tween five and ten percent of CBS Int'l's income is derived from publish- ing. The company will also expand its pressing facilities in the UK. In addi- tion to England, CBS now has press- ing facilities in Holland to cover Ger- many and France; presses singles in Germany; has a joint pressing oper- ation in Italy and presses in Spain and Israel as well. "We will also be tailoring product from America to the tastes of each local market," Yetnikoff continued. CBS Int'l issued two Andy Williams ABC/Dunhill (Cont'd from p. 9) stressed the enormous diversity and range of ABC product and showed them we were giving them more to sell and to play than they had expect- ed. "Basically, we asked them think music instead of categories." In addition to the get -acquainted functions at the Century Plaza Hotel, ABC/Dunhill staffers saw to it that out-of-towners, at least, familiarized themselves with the label's home office and studio facilities on Beverly Boulevard in Los Angeles, including the two new studios currently under construction. Double decker buses were used for transport across town. cuts of "Love Story" in Japan, one in English and one with Andy dubbing in a lead vocal in Japanese. Both versions sold equally, almost to the record. However, his Spanish record- ing of the "Godfather" theme was the only version that sold in Spain. He also indicated that his people will work on American records that are not necessarily released in Ameri- ca as singles but are potentially strong abroad. He pointed to the suc- cess the company had in Europe with Chicago's "I'm A Man" before it was released in the U.S.; and Andy Williams' "Home Loving Man" which was a smash in England and was never issued in the States. He also pointed to the jazz acts such as Miles Davis, Weather Report and Chase who enjoy great success abroad. With regard to the establishment of a CBS label in the Soviet Union, Yet- nikoff would not comment further. Such a move would mean the first entry by a U.S. label on Soviet soil, although Soviet -made recordings are available in the U.S. through various arrangements. EMI, Elektra/Asylum (Cont'd f.om p. 9) The Elektra catalog includes re- leases by such major artists, as Carly Simon, Judy Collins, The Doors, Har- ry Chapin, Bread, David Gates, Ian Matthews and Mickey Newbury. EMI will be taking over arrangements for the next release of album product for Elektra, (due Oct. 19). which includes releases from Ian Matthews, David Gates, Court Pickett, Dennis Coulson and Dennis Linde. An October cam- paign will include a special sampler featuring these artists. The EMI-Elektra/Asylum agree- ment comes within two weeks of the announcement from Warner Commu- nications, Inc., New York, that the Asylum label was merged with the Elektra operation to form a new com- pany to be called Elektra/Asylum/ Nonesuch Records. At the same time, it was announced that David Geffen, who had started the Asylum label in 1971, would be chairman of Elektra/Asylum/Nonesuch Records. Mel Posner is president of the combined company. As part of the new agreement between EMI Records and Elektra/Asylum, EMI relinquishes its rights to the Asylum label outside the U.K. to WEA, so that WEA affiliated companies and licensees will be dis- tributing all new Asylum releases. The Asylum roster of artists in- cludes: Eagles, Joni Mitchell, Jackson Browne, Jo Jo Gunne, Linda Ron- stadt, David Blue, J. D. Souther. - ... Here New York branch manager Lou Sebok (back to camera) prepares his sales team, decked out as Nathan's countermen, for the meeting and greeting ahead. (Cont'd from p. 7) publicity and promotion. It takes a long time and it requires on -the -road and on -tour support. "We now involve ourselves in every aspect of our artist's career. We work closely with managers and with book- ing agencies to develop and promote the talents of artists we sign. Young artists like Barry Manilow and Melis- sa Manchester are perfect examples. They work all the time and it is our purpose to maximize that exposure through advertising, publicity and promotion." "A group like Brownsville Station, which is constantly working, appear- ing with increasingly more important acts and getting great reviews will ultimately break through and we are helping to add to the impact of each appearance through our efforts. 'Tex- as', currently on tour with Three Dog Night, is another young group whose musicianship and professionalism build a growing following with every performance. Close P.A. Ties "We work as closely with the itineraries of these artists as we do with the distribution pattern of a new release. We take radio spots and sup- port the artist with print advertising and publicity. With nine regional pro- mo men and four regional salesmen, we are always in a position to sup- port a personal appearance with a Bell Records representative in the area. We arrange window displays, provide for direct back-up to disk jockeys, distributors and dealers and support the appearance through our entire marketing apparatus. This has now become a major responsibility of both our press and advertising de- partments. Coordination in a program like this is crucial. "We have always been careful to `manage' our growth by devoting to- tal effort to a given goal, establishing systems and expertise in one area and then going on to the next. We build on experience, translate techniques, and make a concerted effort to utilize all our facilities through highly effec- tive channels of communication. We are now directing these efforts into careers as well as into product." GRC (Cont'd from p. 10) onds, thus avoiding the moisten -seal process. GRC has already used the one -color jacket design for the first four of its single releases; Loleatta Holloway, Ripple, Marlys Roe and Sammy Johns. As a close follow-up, the firm is now printing full -color mailers for the future single releases including Heartwood's disk, "Rain." Denise Owen's single "Apples Don't Fall Far From The Trees," and the newly re- leased single 'Stop This Merry Go Round" by John Edwards as well as the upcoming new single to be re- leased September 24 by Ginger Boat- wright on the GRC label. "All the printing and artwork and production is handled locally by an Atlanta firm," Wilburn commented, "thus saving GRC a tremendous amount of working time as well as shipping costs and handling expen- ses." In addition to the 45 rpm mailer, GRC, under Wilburn's direction, has designed a new programming guide format for all GRC/AWARE product 1p's. This new style, stripped across the lower portion of the album, will enable the music and program direc- tors to quickly spot songs, titles, pro- ducer's names and publishing in- formation. This LP programming guide data will be available on GRC's multiple album product which released last week. According to Wilburn, "GRC is the only company I know of that is using the single mailing jacket cover as well as the programming guide format on both 1p's and singles." Wilburn also pointed out that GRC plans to patent the single mailer cov- er this year. Little Rodney (Cont'd from p. 7) play and heavy sales in the seven major Western markets in which the TV spots are being shown. What was not expected is the spontaneous na- tional pickup on the single. "In a very real sense, however," Biegel commented, "this is exactly what happens with Rodney on every level. He is one of those fantastic personalities that come into show business once in a generation and are just irresistible. No child performer has had that quality developed to such an extent since Shirley Temple. "Based on his forthcoming motion picture (Rodney starts filming Stagolee' next month), his appear- ance on the Tonight Show and the way he has handled himself at press parties, interviews and when he's in- troduced to large groups, there is simply no area of entertainment he can't handle." John Annarino, vice president of Doyle Dane Bernbach, the agency that makes Rodney's commercials, says "He is the greatest personality to emerge for us. We have inter- viewed people in areas where the commercials are shown and find that 90% can identify Rodney. That's con- siderably better than double normal recall." Dorothy Day Otis, Rodney's agent observed,"I have never seen anything like this. So many people want him it's a question of picking out what's best for Rodney. He could work 48 hours a day and still not fill all the requests coming in." How is Bell's pint sized superstar taking all this? Obviously a practical young man, he carries a rubber stamp with his name written on it to satisfy autograph hunters who now mob him wherever he goes. To quote a hit song written long before little Rodney ever saw his first microphone, "He signs his checks with x's but they cash 'em just the same." Rodney Allen Rippy Croce (Cont'd from p. 7) Croce, who flavored his songs with the life of the open road, first burst into national prominence in 1972 with his million -selling single, "Don't Mess Around with Jim," later the title of a best-selling LP. Croce, whose current single, "I Got A Name," is on the charts for the first time this week, just received gold certification for his previous hit "Bad, Bad Leroy Brown," according to the RIAA and is about to receive a sim- ilar award for his LP "Life And Times." Elliot Abbott, Croce's personal manager flew immediately to Natchi- toches to make funeral arrangements. The singer is survived by his wife, Enid, and their two year old son Adrian James. Chrysalis (Cont'd from p. 7) though they are an English company they are still very much interested in finding American acts. Ellis doesn't envision more than a dozen LP re- leases per year. Camillo, formerly with the Wes Farrell Organization, is the producer/ arranger of 23 hit singles including Freda Payne's `Banc] Of Gold," and several major hits by Gladys Knight & The Pips including their current chart rider "Midnight Train To Geor- gia. He has completed the musical score for the feature film "Welcome To Arrow Beach" starring Laurence Harvey and has begun work on a second feature film score for Brute Productions. In the commercial area, Camillo has composed and arranged successful themes for such leading clients as Clairol, Schick, Fritos and Lancers Wine. Bob Sanders, guest performer re- cently on the NBC `Today Show" and first recording artist to inaugurate the ITT Sheraton Hotels' showcase entertainment program, has also joined the creative staff at Trapeze. 26 Cash Box - September 29, 1973 www.americanradiohistory.com

SI The Philadelphia Blitz. This is the kick-off to a tremendous new advertising and promotional campaign for Philadelphia International Records. With such outstanding artists as Billy Paul,.. The O'Jays, Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes, and The Three Degrees, an all-inclusive media and store dealer campaign has been devised. The in-store kit includes a four-color mobile, a counter display unit, free catalogs, and divider KZ :3 .106 cards with photographs of Billy Paul, The O'Jays, and Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes. There will be a complete schedule of R&B and Top -40 radio spots. And one of the most pervasive print campaigns ever conceived. Finally, there'll soon be a special album called "The Sound of Philadelphia'737 It features all the big hits from Billy Paul, The O'Jays, The Ebonys, Harold Melvin, MFSB, and the Intruders. KZ 321)9

No New Additions WHB-KANSAS CITY Photograph-Ringo Starr-Apple Rocky Mountain Way-Joe Walsh-Dunhill Yes We Can Can-Pointer Sisters-Blue Thumb I Won't Last A Day Without You-Maureen McGovern -20th Century Top Of The World-Carpenters-A&M James, Puente Bands, At UJA Fete For Levy NEW YORK - The guests at the Eighth Annual UJA Music Division Dinner Dance will be entertained for dancing throughout the evening by both the 17 -piece Harry James Big Band and the 15 man aggregation of Tito Puente and his Latin rhythms. Rather than individual soloists or groups performing and necessitating total audience attention, the presence of two top bands will afford the peo- ple of the industry an opportunity to meet, mingle and exchange social and shop talk for the duration of the black tie affair which this year hon- ors Roulette Records president Mor- ris Levy as "man of the year." This year's dinner, being held Oct. 27, at the New York Hilton Hotel, will be attended by many record company founders and industry pioneers. Cash Box/R&B News Report Keeping Up With The Joneses Phonogram artists the Joneses visited the New York offices of Phonogram, Inc. recently to discuss the release of the group's first Mercury single, "Baby, Don't Do It." Sales of the single have been bolstered by the group's extensive touring activity. Pictured are (from left): Glenn Dorsey, business manager, non -performing member of the Joneses, and writer of the single; Bobby Noble; Charles Fach, vice president/A&R at Phonogram; Reggie Noble; and Sam White. Group member Sy Brooks was not present. `A Decade of Jazz' From Blue Note HOLLYWOOD - Blue Note Records is currently shipping three "A Decade of Jazz" double LP sets encompass- ing the years 1939 through 1969. The reissue, prompted by innumerable re- quests from jazz devotees and histo- rians, contains in three albums a sig- nificant cross-section of the great recordings released by the blue Note label during this period. Volume I of "A Decade of Jazz," covering 1939-49, runs from the "boogie woogie" of Albert Ammons and Meade "Lux" Lewis to legendary greats like Sidney Bechet and Bunk Johnson and experimentalists of that period like Thelonious Monk. Volume II (1949-59) contains ma- jor performances by Bud Powell, Thelonious Monk, Milt Jackson, Jay Jay Johnson, Clifford Brown, Miles Davis, Horace Silver, Jimmy Smith, Sonny Clark, John Coltrane, Sonny Rollins, Art Blakey and Lou Donald- son.Volume III (1959-69) offers tracks by Jimmy Smith, Ike Quebec, Kenny Burrell, Donald Byrd, Lee Morgan, Eric Dolphy, Horace Silver, Stanley Turrentine, Ornette Coleman, and Lon Donaldson. Blue Note, the jazz division of United Artists Records, is offering complete backing to the three pack- ages via advertising, display material and an all-out promotional cam- paign. Thrasher, 20th Cent. Regional R&B Dir. HOLLYWOOD - Norman Thrasher has been appointed r&b southern regional promotion director for 20th Century Records, reporting to label's Hosea Wilson. "We're delighted to have Norman join the team full time," Russ Regan, president, said. "As an independent promotion man, he has already proven himself extremely valuable to us." UJIMA New R & B Band On Epic NEW YORK - Ujima, a seven man progressive R&B band has been signed to Epic Records, it was an- nounced by Don Ellis, Director of A&R for the label. The group, which hails from Richmond, Virginia, has completed their first single, "Hip To Your Ways," which is shipping immediately. The single was cut at Alpha Audio in Richmond with co - producers Nick Colleran and Eric Johnson (who is also the group's manager) and supervised by Torn Werman, Associate Director of A&R for Epic Records. Ujima is currently in the studio recording their first al- bum. Getz & Jamal Open Jimmy's Jazz Season NEW YORK - Stan Getz and Ah- mad Jamal and their groups kick off the fall jazz season at Jimmy's down- stairs 52nd Street Room, from Sep- tember 27th to October 6th, it is an- nounced by Jimmy's owners Sid Da- vidoff and Dick Aurelio and impre- sario Willard Alexander. Getz, ac- claimed as one of the jazz world's premier tenor sax men since the for- ties when he was a teenage prodigy playing with the great bands of Stan Kenton, Jimmy Dorsey and Benny Goodman, went on to win more crit- ics' and readers' polls than any other saxophone player. He has won the Playboy Jazz and Pop Poll 16 times and the Down Beat Poll 17 times. Benny Goodman has praised him as the finest tenor saxophonist of all time. Getz records for Columbia. Party Time Motown Records president Ewart Abner (left), co -hosting a party for the Jackson 5 at their Encion, Calif., home, chats with Metromedia/KTTV newscaster Ken Jones and Cash Box publisher and president, George Al- bert. Party was the second annual affair thrown by the J-5 as a special thanks -to -the -industry event. R 1.4 B INGREDIENTS-Renee Records who had an excellent release with "Follow The Wind" by the Midnight Movers Unitd. have formed a produc- tion company, Dimpaco Productions, for the purpose of developing new record- ing artists. The first production Inder the new banner "Party-With Every Muscle In Your Body" by Midnight Movers Unitd. is now on the Buddah label . . Michael Masser, who co -wrote Diana Ross' "Touch Me In The Morning," and also co -produced the record, has just completed production on a new Thelma Houston album for Motown . . . Rochell Anderson's single, "Know What You're Doin'," which was a regional seller on the Soul Potion label, has been purchased by Sunburst Records for national distribution . . .. That Soul Power label artist, Tommie Young with a hit single 'Do You Still Feel The Same Way" is now available in LP form with the single hit as the big draw . . . B. B. King will receive an honorary doctorate of humanities degree from Mississippi's Tougaloo College, Sept. 30th, during the famed 104 -year -old black college's annual Founder's Day observance, thus making him the first blues musician ever to receive an honorary doctorate for his contirbution to the world of music . . . Continuing is R & B expansion through Aware (GRC) Records, a new single by Deep Velvet, "Hanna Mae" is now being shipped .. . Also from the GRC front, Jake Jordan has been appointed Southeastern R & B markeing manager and Chester Simmons is also handling independent promotion for the Aware and GRC labels. Simmons will be handling product in the North and South Carolina areas . . . Alexander The Great, located at 216 West 46th Street (NYC) is the latest and newest Disco in the Manhattan area. And, it is elegant, to say the least. There is singles night, live latin and disco on alternate nights of the week. Worth a trip to see. Also, a great spot for acts to work. Rex and Carlos are the hosts. All functions begin at 10 p.m. The Cocktail lounge, of course, opens at 3 p.m. . . . Grambling College and Morgan State held their 3rd annual football duel at Yankee Stadium which was again won by Grambling. Over 60,000 blacks were in attendance. The Grambling Band did their thing during half time. It was a total black experience and totally enjoyable. Aretha Franklin delivered a rousing version of "Respect" during the half intermission with the Grambling Band backing her up. The first lady of soul got a standing ovation as she left the field . . . The Ambassador of the Republic of Niger and the Board of Trustees of Africare hosted in a reception honoring Roberta Flack. TV press and industry personnel were on hand to learn of the forthcoming Roberta Afro tour which will include Stevie Wonder and the Jackson Five. The concert tour will be filmed. Plans are in the making to release the filmed concert in this country.. The proceeds to be used to help black thru Africare. Roberta feels that blacks should reach out to help blacks regardless what nation they are living in. JAZZLINES--Gato Barbieri, saxaphonist and composer of the "Last Tango ir, Paris" soundtrack has signed with ABC/Impulse label. His debut album, using musicians from his native Argentina and elsewhere in Latin America, figures prominently in ABC/Dunhill's designation at "Impulse Month." Don Drossell October 'Phila. Intl Sound' Month NEW YORK - October has been designated "Philadelphia Internation- al Month" to herald new album re- leases by such Superstars as Billy Paul, The O'Jays, Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes, and The Three De- grees. During October, Philadelphia In- ternational, the Columbia Custom Label headed by Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff, will release the following Lp's: "War Of The Gods," by Billy Paul of "Me And Mrs. Jones" fame; "Ship Ahoy," by the O'Jays, whose singles, "Love Train" and "Back Stabbers" have each sold more than two million copies; the newest album release by the Three Degrees, which is entitled "The Three Degrees"; and "Black & Blue Featuring 'The Love I Lost,'" by Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes. In addition, the label will be cel- ebrating its success and saluting its artists with an album entitled "The Sound of Philadelphia, '73." Specially priced at $4.98, this Lp features some of the past year's biggest selling Philadelphia International singles, including Billy Paul's "Me and Mrs. Jones;" The O'Jays' "Love Train;" "If You Don't Know Me By Now" by Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes; "It's Forever," by The Ebonys; and "Family Affair" by MFSB. In addition, two recently released albums will be spotlighted-the debut Lp by the group Spiritual Concept, and the album "Yellow Sunshine" on the Gamble label. "Philadelphia International Month" will be supported by massive promotion and marketing drives de- signed to call maximum attention to the new product, as well as the la- bel's catalog items. Ads will be featured in many prominent Black periodicals including Soul, Jet, Soul Sounds and Essence. There will also be a heavy emphasis on outdoor bill- board advertising in Black communi- ties, and multi -product time buys are being scheduled for bath Black and Top 40 radio stations. Jim Tyrrell, Director of National Sales, Epic & Columbia Custom La- bels, said, "We are happy to be able to launch a program which will en- tail a major involvement of our com- pany with the entire retail structure, in the United States, both black and white. An incentive program is being offered that will be equitable to both large and small retail dealers, with all receiving their share of merchan- dising materials. Billy Paul, the O'Jays and Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes took the country by storm earlier this year, and we are confident that their second Lp's featured in 'The Sound Of Philadel- phia' Month will consolidate their position as major recording stars." The label has assembled a "Sound Of Philadelphia Kit" for in-store dis- play. It features a mobile display unit depicting eleven albums in four colors; a counter take -one bin which includes free folders containing pho- tos and information about the Phila- delphia International catalog; and di- vider cards to facilitate customer findng of the label's product. Ron Alexenburg, Vice President, Epic & Columbia Custom Labels, said: "In the past two years one of the most exciting things that we have been involved in has been the emer- gence of the Gamble and Huff labels- Philadelphia International and Gam- ble. During these two years, Gamble and Huff have built a strong artist roster and upon completion of the new albums we wanted to emphasize to everyone that this product has re- ceived the acceptance of not only the blacks, but whites as well and are giving special attention to their sound during the month of October. We are proud to be able to distribute the Gamble and Huff artistry, as well as the artists they produce." Commenting on the upcoming month of activity, Kenny Gamble said: "Our thanks and appreciation we give to Columbia/Epic Records for helping us expose 'The Sound Of Philadelphia' . . . a Message Of Love To The People." To Go After Rock PHILADELPHIA — The Philadelphia Civic Center is offering Convention Hall Auditorium to promoters for rock concerts, according to John Pier- ron, exec. dir. of the Center. The de- cision reverses a recent city decision forbidding use of the Center for hard rock. The Convention Hall Auditorium, with 11,000 seats with unobstructed view of stage events, is totally air- conditioned, and has up-to-date acous- tical and lighting systems. Some of the nation’s top soloists, groups and bands have appeared there. Inquiries about available dates and rates should be directed to James Amadie, Conventions mgr. of the Philadelphia Civic Center, phone 215- 561-5100, ext. 21-231. THE BIG THREE 1. Cash Box/R&B News Report ‘Soul Explosion’ Begins At RCA NEW YORK — RCA Records has announced the inauguration of an on going campaign geared to its R&B roster called “Soul Explosion.” The program will start with con- centration on six acts; Wilson Pick- ett; the Hues Corporation, New Birth, Main Ingredient, Jimmy Cas- tor, and Labelle. Advertising plans in support of the Soul Explosion Program will include omnibus ads in black consumer media, such as: Ebony, Essence, En- core, Soul, Soul Sounds, Jet, and the Dann Suppliment, massive radio ad- vertising, and a television time buy on Soul Train. Additionally RCA will utilize an extensive mini-billboard campaign in the Los Angeles area. The advertising schedules, in addi- tion to being used for several acts, will also spotlight individual acts within the campaign. Merchandizing support for the pro- gram will include T-shirts, stickers, posters, and tambourines. According to Andre Perry, manag- er, product merchandising, RCA Rec- ords, “The Soul Explosion will be geared to all key black accounts. All one stops and retail accounts will be serviced as part of the program. He further stated: “The program is designed so that its flexibility will allow us to keep it operable indefi- nitely. We will add new acts to the Soul Explosion as situations war- rant.” With Winley Lynn Signs NEW YORK — Gloria Lynn has signed a recording pact with Paul Winley Records. Ms. Lynn’s debut with the label will be an album to be released in the near future, according to Paul Winley, president of the com- pany. WWRL’s H. Spann Wins NATRA Honors NEW YORK — Hank Spann, D.J. and a dynamic force of WWRL, in this city, does his regular gig from 2-6 PM, Monday-Saturday. Plus a re- lentless number of personal appear- ances throughout the Metropolitan area. Most recently, Hank along with Bob Law, host of Black Dialogue and community relations director at WWRL have completed a series of benefit concerts employing top stars such as: Stevie Wonder, James Brown, The Moments, the Midnight Movers Unltd., Black Ivory, and oth- ers. Such institutions as Windgate Prep, Black Studies Department of C.C.N.Y., National Youth Movement, and others have benefited from funds raised by Hank and Bob. These con- certs will continue this fall, as plans are already in motion. Hank’s popularity in New York is a direct reflection of his hard work and love for his profession. If you’ve heard Hank’s show, you understand Natra’s presentation at that organi- zations last convention in New Or- leans. Hank was awarded Natra’s “Radio Excellence award” for Major Markets. (Hank gets mobbed by his adoring fans, and he loves it). “The Soul Server” started his career in New Orleans, Louisiana at WBOK, then to St. Louis’ KXLW and KADI—Charlotte’s WGIU, then At- lanta’s WAOK. Hank has been Num- ber 1 in all the markets he has worked and that seems to be true thus far. R&B INGREDIENTS—Things are really beginning to cook again in the R&B musical scene. Labels and artists are coming with material that is in the groove and Black stations have some smokin’ material to select in con- tinuing to serve a black community (basically single buyers) that is and continues to be enriching to the record industry. Black producers and writers, of later (from new releases that have been coming acros my desk) seem to be returning more and more to basic roots. These basic roots have and continue to be the vital creative force in the musical spectrum of today. But, this can so easily be lost. With few exceptions, most of the black artists and producers have duly paid their dues, but they, nevertheless, have been able to continue in the business because of black radio. Yes, it is true that black music is a big element on what is referred to as the pop scene, but most will have to agree that it is also because of black radio and black programming that they now enjoy top 40 success. How many of these performers would now be stand- ing where they are without the assistance of black radio? Harold Melvin (The Blue Notes) popped into the Big Apple Thursday (4th) for a small luncheon with trade and black press personnel. Harold, among many topics discussed, also said that he felt the need and necessity for returning to the roots. Harold & The Blue Notes are smokin’ with "The Love I Lost". Harold is also on the verge of announcing some dramatic new ventures. But, you can rest assured that these new ventures will retain the Harold Melvin roots and identity . . . Eddie Floyd (Stax) “Baby Lay Your Head Down" is another artist who also recently mentioned that he is returning to his roots in musical expression. Maybe musical styles and cycles are synonomous with our musical heritage, but to those of you who understand where black music is coming from, there is just no way to put down the music that is coming from the soul—white or black . . . GRC Records hosted and introduced their hot recording act ‘Ripple’ at the Martinque in Manhattan, Wednesday (3rd) and a goodly number of press and industry personnel dropped in. Ripple is a solid performing group and it was a swingin’ good time for everyone. Of course, "I Don’t Know What It Is, But It Sure Is Funky” is a cooker and the live performance comes off as well as it does on record. JAZZ LINES—Jazz Interactions, Inc. is bringing Jazz back to Broadway when it presents Clark Terry and his Big Band and the Rashied Ali Quartet in the first in a series of monthly Monday sessions sponsored by the organization at Pub Theatrical on the corner of Broadway & 51st Street. The events will take place on the last Monday of each month with the first one on Monday, October 29th at 8 p.m. Admission charge will be $3.50 for the general public and $2.50 for Jazz Interactions members who will also re- ceive a copy of a recently recorded album from a wide selection donated by the record companies. Food and beverage will be available at reasonable rates, food ranging in price from $2.50 to $3.75 and drinks from 500 to $1.75. Tickets may be obtained in advance from Ticketron, Record Shack at 274 West 125th Street, King Karol Record Store at 111 West 42nd Street, and from the Jazz Museum at 125 West 55th Street. Q0 n Drossell Push Expo 73 Gets Heavy Label And Artist Support (Rev. Jesee Jackson Speaks) E. Rodney Jones WVON P D Gets Testimonial CHICAGO -— E. Rodney Jones, pro- gram director of Radio Station WVON, Chicago, Illinois was honored at a Testimonial and Dinner on Fri- day, September 28, 1973 at the Conrad Hilton Hotel in this city. Honoring Rodney for his twenty-five years of dedicated service in the field of broad- casting, dignitaries and industry per- sonnel came from across the nation to pay tribute to Jones. Among those present were Ewart Abner, president, Motown Record Corporation, Los An- geles; A1 Bell, president, Stax Rec- ords, Inc., Memphis; William “Smokey” Robinson, songwriter and Motown recording artist, Los Ange- les; Marv Stuart, vice president, Cur- tom Records, Inc., Chicago; Willie Mitchell, president, Hi Recording Company, Memphis; Clarence Avant, Sussex Records, Los Angeles; Aider- man Tyrone Kenner, Chicago; Con- gressman Ralph Metcalfe, Chicago; Don Cornelius, Soul Train, Chicago and Los Angeles; Roy Wood, Nation- al Black Network New York; Larry Maxwell, United Artists, Los Ange- les; Howard Bedno, Bedno-Wright Associates, Chicago; Rev. Jesse Jack- son, Operation Push, Chicago; Geor- gie Woods, WDAS, Philadelphia; Ed- die O’Jay, New York; Alonzo King, Motown, Chicago and Pervis Spann, WVON, Chicago. Candido Signs With Polydor NEW YORK CITY — Jerry Schoen- baum, president of Polydor Incorpo- rated, has announced the signing of renowned master of percussion Candi- do to an exclusive recording contract. Sessions have recently been completed at New York’s A&R Studios and the LP is slated for early fall release. Pictured in the signing photo are (1. to r.) Candido, veteran arranger Chico O’Farrill, Jerry Schoenbaum, Polydor A&R director Peter Siegel and Mrs. Candido, who acts as man- ager for her husband. In over two decades on the Ameri- can scene, the Cuban-born conga vir- tuoso has performed and recorded with the greatest names in jazz, pop and latin music. Since first gaining fame with Dizzy Gillespie, who intro- duced his explosive talents to these shores, Candido has played with such musical giants as Stan Kenton, Woody Herman, Lionel Hampton, Count Basie, Art Blakey, Coleman Hawkins, Stan Getz, Sonny Rollins, Errol Garner and George Shearing— as well as such luminaries as Tony Bennett, Ray Charles, Johnny Mathis, Harry Belafonte and latin stars Ma- chito and Tito Puente, among others. Candido’s countless session dates, in addition to his own recordings, in- clude Ellen Mcllwaine’s “Honky Tonk Angel” and “We the People” and Randy Weston’s newly-released “Tan- jah” on the Polydor label. Between record dates and tour engagements throughout the world, Candido has headed up a latin band for several years at New York’s Chateau Madrid. The upcoming album draws on this wealth and variety of experience, with Candido’s congas and bongos as well as his dubbing of five other percus- sion instruments, while fronting a band of New York session pros. There was a tremendous rapport be- tween artist Candido and arranger O’Farrill, which worked very well for the album. Chico O’Farrill, who him- self boasts past affiliations with Ben- ny Goodman, Stan Kenton, Dizzy Gil- lespie, Count Basie and Machito, and even musical background involvement with the Sesame Street show, lent a hand in composition, arranging and production. CHICAGO — Following the last en- tertainment performance at Push Expo ’73, Black recording label own- ers met in caucus with the Reverend Jesse L. Jackson and key Operation Push aides to assess the level of in- dustry responsiveness to Push Expo ’73. It was concluded by these rep- resentatives that the trade publica- tions exhibited a blatant disregard for the serious, unilateral support of per- formers and label owners and their contribution to Push Expo ’73. During the five day, seven show exposition, more than 100 recording performers contributed their talent to help insure the success of an event deemed vital to Black America. Their recording labels contributed financial support through advertising subsidy and expense guarantee. The two heaviest label contributors were Stax Records and Motown, both owned and operated by Black chief executive officers. In addition, sub- stantial support was rendered by London, M.G.M., Atlantic, Chess, Janus, RCA, Impulse, Ward and Bell Record companies. In a prepared statement, Rev. Jesse L. Jackson, President of Operation Push, levied the charge of discriminating neglect against the trade publications. “Such negligence or disrespect of the largest series of concei'ts in the history of the music industry, appears to be an extension of the same atti- tude and behavior exhibited in the charting of music product that is mer- chandised to the Black community, through Black retailers and Black- oriented radio stations,” Rev. Jackson charged. Moving into the underlying threat as seen by the Black record label owners, Rev. Jackson summar- ized the economic significance of the alleged “white out” in the trade pub- lications. “We, ivho are major contributors to the Recording Industry, both as con- sumers and talents, are conspicuous by our absence from the editorial cov- erage oj the Music Industry Trade Publications, Billboard, Record World, Cash Box and others. Such negligence or disrespect of the largest semes of concerts in the his- tory of the Music Industry, appears to be an extension of the same atti- tude and behavior exhibited in the charting of music product that is marketed to the Black market, through Black retailers and Black radio stations. In the interest of economics of Black people, ive must take direct in- terest and action, for we understand, as do the trade publication editors, the increasing significance of the re- lationship between chart position and broadcast exposure for Black music on radio stations. It is very clear that unexposecl music is unsold music and unsold music means, no gold music for the Black record companies and the Black community. We feel that the objectives of the community and our organization oblige us to expose such practices for “ive must get paid for the work we've done.” Among the recording entertainers appearing at Push Expo ’73 this year were: A1 Green, The 5th Dimension, The Independents, Roberta Flack, Quincy Jones, Barry White. The Mira- cles, The Temptations, Smokey Robin- son, Edwin Starr, Jr. Walker & The Allstars, The Sisters Love, son Five, Nancy Wilson, Earth, Wind And Fire, Ahmad Jamal, James Cleve- land, Delores Barrett Campbell & Bar- rett Sisters, Inez Andrews, Albertina Walker. Rev. Clay Evans, LorePa Oliver, Jackie Verdell, Gene W iels, Gene Barge, Mondr' Ml lie Jackson and Isaac Hayes. Cash Box — October 13, 1973 31

Gets New Label NEW YORK — A new recording company, Fenoragh Records, has been established in New York City. Headed by S. L. Scher, the new label will con- centrate on the production and dis- tribution of contemporary music. Fenoragh’s production division, Lorenzo Productions, directed by pro- ducer/arranger Morty Jay, is cur- rently completing the label’s first al- bum, “Masters Gone Modern (Now and Then).” The album offers modern- istic interpretations of classical pieces by composers Tchaikovsky, Dvorak, Leoncavallo and di Capua. The pro- duction is performed by Larry O’Neill, a classically trained vocalist with a list of appearances on both opera and supper club stages. Fenoragh Records is seeking new artists & material for future releases. The company is located at 227 River- side Drive, New York, N.Y. THE BIG THREE 1. (R&B News Cont*d) Impulse Tour Coordinates Fall Release Program HOLLYWOOD — On Oct. 21 ABC/Impulse will kick off its fall na- tional tour at Carnegie Hall with a concert featuring Gato Barbieri, Keith Jarrett, and Alice Coltrane. The event is syncronized with the compa- ny’s release of 14 new LPs show- caseing Barbieri and Jarrett along with other major innovators such as John Coltrane, Pharoah Sanders, Sam Rivers, and John Klemmer. The concert tour will feature eight of the Impulse artists in a major hall /major market itinerary that in- cludes New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Detroit, Boston, and Washington, D.C. Gato Barbieri will be the headliner at all the concerts, being backed up with Keith Jarrett on the East Coast and Alice Coltrane on the West Coast. Barbieri, who has gained a sizable following since his scoring of Ber- tolucci’s ‘‘Last Tango in Paris,” will be working in an entirely new format. The Argentine saxophonist will be playing with muscians from his native South America, performing a style radically different from his style on the New York jazz scene. Impulse feels that the time is riedit for their artists’ progressive music, and the tour may reach a great por- tion of the rock concert audience and introduce them to this “new music.” R&B Additions WWRL—NEW YORK Come Go With Me—Staple Singers—Stax Come Live With Me—Ray Charles—Crossover Get Involved—George Soule—Fame Somebody’s Been Enjoying My Home—Don Covay—Mercury Doin’ What Cums Naturally—Charles Wright —Dunhill WGRT—CHICAGO Take A Closer Look—Wilson Pickett—RCA Come Go With Me—Staple Singers—-Stax You Can’t Hide Love—Creative Source Sussex Doin' What Cums Naturally—Charles Wright •—Dunhill KATZ—ST. Pictured at QBC’s West Coast offices in Holly- wood are (left to right) Warren Ste- phens, west coast head of QBC; DeeJay Jackson, Floyd Butler, Rlak- ey, Jerry Gardner, manager of The New Friends, and Harry Elston (seated). The New Friends of Distinc- tion record for RCA. The seeds for the concert series were planted this summer in Mon- treux, Switzerland, where Gato, Michael White, John Klemmer, and Sam Rivers were met enthusiastically at that city’s jazz festival. Impulse felt that, if the European acceptance for their artists could begin to ap- proach that of pop star mania, there was no reason that the same couldn’t be achieved in the U.S. Impulse is interested in some type of media crossover for its music. At Montreux the entire evening of Im- pulse music was video-taped, and the company is now exploring possibilit- ies of the tape being telecast on net- work television. As the idea for an Imoulse “In Concert” of sorts is being worked out, a kinescope of the event is also being negotiated for distribu- tion in theatrical film release. The Fall release includes albums from John Coltrane, Sun Ra, and many other “established” artists. The emphasis, however, is on the new ar- tists whom Impulse has brought to the label. Steve Backer, general manager for Impulse, is ecstatic about the new frontiers that will be explored this fall. “The -tour and the fall releases give us the opportunity to stretch out and do things with this music that haven’t been done before. ‘Lady’ Takes Int’l Awards NEW YORK — The Venice Sound Festival made an award to a motion picture Motown-Paramount’s “Lady Sings The Blues” as the best interna- tional film of the year and simultane- ously named its star Diana Ross as the best international actress of the year. Ms. Ross currently on a concert tour throughout Europe to coincide with the ooening of “Lady” there made the trip to Venice to accept both awards. She also performed an eleven minute medley from “Lady” which was televised by Eurovision to an au- dience which the festival officials esti- mated at two hundred million peo- ple. Prior to flying to Venice Ms. Ross appeared at a benefit in London for Variety Clubs International headed by Prince Philip. David Niven told Michael Roshkind vice chairman of the Board for Mo- town that he “never saw anything like Diana Ross’ performance in ‘Lady Sings The Blues’ and again at the Royal Albert Hall.” Blue Note Culls Pacific Jazz HOLLYWOOD — Blue Note Records is culling the archives of its now- defunct affiliated label Pacific Jazz and is releasing highly-in-demand vintage recordings of a pair of to- day’s hottest acts, Les McCann and the Jazz Crusaders. “Fish This Week,” the title of the Les McCann double-LP set, contains the initial successful disk per- formances by the highly-acclaimed pi- anist, dating back to the early 1960’s. The Jazz Crusaders’ two-record pack- age, “Tough Talk,” also contains ma- jor recordings from the early six- ties. Both McCann and the Jazz Crusad- ers are currently top-selling artists, with the Atlantic and Blue Thumb labels, respectively. The majority of their Pacific Jazz platters have been unavailable to the public for nearly a decade. With Blue Note long established as a dominant figure in East Coast jazz circles, and Pacific Jazz a major fac- tor on the West Coast until its de- mise, Blue Note is planning a reissue program that will encompass the best of vintage product. R&B INGREDIENTS—Shelly’s Manne-Hole, which became one of the best known jazz clubs in the world during its nearly twelve years of oper- ation, reopened at a new western Los Angeles location, 6420 Wilshire Blvd., Tuesday, Oct. 16, with Carmen McRae and the Julian “Cannonball” Adderley Quintet. The new Manne-Hole is downstairs at the Century Bank Plaza, where Tetou’s Restaurant operates during daytime hours. At 9 p.m. the cafe becomes Shelly’s, presenting the top names in jazz nightly except Mondays. Tetou’s food will be served at the Manne-Hole. Jackie and Roy will share the bill with Ms. McRae beginning Oct. 23 for one week. Drummer Shelly Manne started the original ground-level Manne-Hole in the heart of Hollywood, Nov. 2, 1960. In 1972 the club's neighbor and landlord, Wally Heider Recording, expanded its studios and found that the bandstand amplifiers fed directly onto their tapes. Neither the Manne-Hole’s attempt to book "quiet” attractions nor Heider’s soundproofing solved the problem. Shelly shopped in vain for a place to move, and at 2 a.m. on Labor Day, Sept. 4, 1972, reluctantly closed. Eor the past year, while composing scores for films, television and legitimate theater, tour- ing with his group—Manne-Kind—and recording his own albums and sound- tracks, Shelly has constantly sought the right spot to reativate his club. With Tetou’s invitation to share their spacious new establishment, Shelly’s Manne- Hole has an easily accessible, centrally located new home. . . . “The Black Woman as Reflected in B. B. King’s Blues” is the title of the paper to be de- livered by Professor Lou E. Holloway on Saturday, October 20, during the 3-day 53rd annual meeting of the Association for the Study of Afro-American Life and History to be held at the Commodore Hotel, Park Avenue at 42nd Street, New York City. The nation’s oldest and most prestigious Black organization, the Association’s meetings attract scholars from all over the country, according to program chairman Dr. Edgar Toppin, professor of history at Virginia State Col- lege, Petersburg, Va. Miss Holloway is currently on leave from Tougaloo Col- lege, Tougaloo, Miss., where she is chairman of the history department and part time professor of history at the University of Mississippi Medical Center’s School of Nursing at Jackson. Her impressive credentials also include being the first female Tallman professor at Bowdoin College, Brunswick, Me. She is currently visiting lecturer in history at William College, Williamstown, Mass., where she is developing a course entitled “B. B. King, Blues and Black Heri- tage.” . . . Bill Withers and Bill Cosby have been signed to headline Nov. 15-18 at the Circle Theater in San Carlos, Calif. Marquee Productions is producing the show. This will be the final concert of the year for Withers, who is working on material for his next Sussex Records album. For Cosby, the Circle Star date will be his last U.S. show before heading to England for a London Palladium engagement, set by Chrysalis Talent Agency of that city. JAZZ LINES—Jazz party at the Waldorf, on October 21 from 1 to 11 p.m. Time Of Your Life, Inc., in association with the N.Y. Jazz Museum, will present the jazz event of the year at the Waldorf Astoria Hotel in New York City. It will feature about 20 of today’s greatest jazz artists including Teddy Wilson, Tyree Glenn, Clark Terry, Budd Johnson, Urbie Green, Bobby Rosengarden, Zoot Sims, Milt Hinton, Joe Newman, Johnny Mince, Buddy Tate, Don Elliot, Lou Stein, Bucky Pizzerelli, Dick Hyman, Pee Wee Erwin, and others. It will be a private party atmosphere and the music will run non-stop. Table service will be available for purchase of the hot buffet and beverages. There are a limited number of reservations available. All tickets are $35 per person. It is expected that this will become an annual event in New York. For more information con- tact the N.Y. Jazz Museum, 125 West 55th Street, N.Y.C.; (212) 765-2150 or Time Of Your Life, Inc. at (212) 249-4500. Don Drossell coming soon O LUTHER INGRAM?
