LaBelle Set Two At Town Hall NEW YORK — RCA recording art- ist LABELLE—composed of Patti LaBelle, Nona Hendryx and Sarah Dash—are set to headline two shows at TOWN HALL on Saturday November 3rd at 8:30 p.m. and Mid- night. This is their second NY ap- pearance in their own concert—the first was the very successful debut at Carnegie Hall in May. As before, they will be the only artists appear- ing and will perform a special 2-hr. concert of some old, but mostly brand-new material drawn from their new RCA album “Pressure Cookin’ ”. R&B INGREDIENTS—Fans and blues afficionados, who did man- j age to catch Willie Dixon during a limited engagement recently at Kenny’s Castaways in Manhattan, certainly did not go away disappointed in having had the opportunity to catch this legendary bluesman. The artists who have per- formed his material reads not unlike that of a who's who. “Spoonful,” “Back Door Man,” “Bring It On Home” and “I Can't Quit You Baby” are some of the scores of tunes from this master storyteller. Willie, a native of Vicksburg, took up permanent residence in Chicago when he was 17. His first big selling tune was, “Signfying Monkey” and then in the early 50’s Muddy Waters brought home “I’m Your Hooche Cooche Man." Willie Dixon was in on the early Chuck Berry and Bo Diddley sessions. The Rolling Stones recorded “The Little Red Rooster” which was originally written for bluesman Howlin’ Wolf. Willie still handles the standup bass with perfection. Whether it’s down home shuffle, slow walkin’ or struttin’, Willie and his back up band put it together. "Soul Wrinkles” a new tune is outstanding. "Willie Dixon—Catalyst” is available on Ovation Records. . . . Pop jazz organist Seleno Clarke goes into Buddy’s Supper Club at 1812 Rhode Island Ave., N.E. in Wash., D.C., Friday the 26th of Oct. James Stemley is owner host of the popular spot. Seleno is now completing new LP product. . . . “In order to be a real blues singer—speaking from my own experience—you have to go through some of the things that you sing about,” says Bobby ‘Blue’ Bland. The ABC-Dunhill Records veteran, who plays Nov. 7-11 at the Whisky a Go Go in Hollywood with the Dixie Hummingbirds, has had over 30 single records on the music magazine charts, and more than that on the Harlem, race, r&b and soul charts. His current single, “This Time I’m Gone For Good” is #32 bulleted on CB R&B chart. His name is a legend, even to those who have never heard him sing, and he is considered one of the greatest pop-blues singers of our times. "It’s not what you say,” Bland says, “but how you say it. I try to do songs in a ballad-type way, where it won’t be strictly blues. Now what I have basically to rely on is the blues, but I educate myself through a spectrum of records, and people that I think have something to offer me. “For instance,” he admits, “I’ve always admired Tony Bennett, Perry Como and Andy Williams. This is the thing that I based my blues on, and I have quite a few of their records that I listen to, and learn from.” CHECK IT OUT DEPT.—“Do You Have The Time,” The Younghearts on 20th Cent. Also, 20th Cent, has signed Patti & The Love Lights, “Love So Strong” sounds like a winner. . . . “Let The Ceiling Talk To You” from the Dells LP is worth a listen. . . . “You’re Sweet, You’re Fine,” by Tomorrows Promise on Capitol For an absolute groove you’ll find “Charles III” by Charles Earland on Fantasy a delight. don drossell Groove Merchant Host ‘Rich’ Bash ROAR OF ’74 (Seen above, Buddy’s Band in Action)—Groove Merchant Records hosted a cocktail party and luncheon at Jimmy’s Restaurant on Tuesday, Octo- ber 9 to introduce its newly pacted Buddy Rich Band to the press, radio and New York distributors and dealers. The “Roar of ’74,” the title of Rich’s debut album for the label, served as the theme of the party which was introduced via six souped up racing cars roaring thru West 52nd Street to a screeching halt at the front door of Jimmy’s where the Rich band is appearing. Buddy Rich, a racing car enthusiast himself, then took the wheel of one of the souped up racers, much to the delight of the large lunch time crowd that had gathered in front of the restaurant. Half Note Celebrates Uptown Anni NEW YORK — For fifteen years jazz afficionados beat their way downtown to Spring and Hudson Streets to the Half Note to groove to the music of Dizzy and Mingus and Zoot and Carmen and Anita and oth- er jazz giants presented nightly by the Half Note proprietors, the Cante- rino family. Came the rock revolu- tion and jazz and jazz emporiums virtually disappeared into the never land of other declasse art forms except for diehard faithfuls, like the Half Note, which kept going even though customers now trickled in- stead of streamed in. By the late 1960’s the neighbor- hood around Spring and Hudson fell into decline, but it wasn’t until last October 19 that the Canterinos finally packed their reservations book, moved uptown to 149 West 54th Street (the building was once Texas Guinan’s carriage house). Not only did the regulars find the new Half Note but so did a new and younger crop of fans. And it looks like the beat will go on. Coincidental with the Half Note’s move uptown, jazz began its big comeback all over town (even Horn & Hardardth’s doing it) and people are once again coming out to dig the sounds of Dizzy and Zoot not to mention the Modern Jazz Quartet, another jazz establishment celebra- ting some 21 years of togetherness — which is currently playing’ a two week engagement at he H Note through October 27. Cash Box — October 27, 1973 37

Foster will produce the trumpet player, whose hits include “Java,” “Cotton Candy” and many more. Currently recording for Monument are such artists as saxophonist Boots Randolph, Nashville studio veteran Lloyd Green and award-winning har- monica player Charlie McCoy. Hirt, who will remain based in New Orleans, is scheduled for at least two albums and two singles a year on Monument. “We have always been selective about the artists signed to Monument Records, and with Al Hirt there’s no doubt that we now have one of the all-time greatest. Both as a musician and as an entertainer, Al Hirt is tops in his field. I look forward to our association,” said Foster. Dolls To Make Waldorf Date CHICAGO — To spotlight the New York Dolls’ appearance Oct. 31, Hal- lowe’en Night, at the Grand Ballroom of the Waldorf Astoria in New York, Phonogram, Inc. has launched a cam- paign promoting the appearance. Special print and radio advertising is already running to promote the date, with two hundred special pos- ters being distributed to New York retail stores in conjunction with a giveaway contest for tickets. One pair of tickets will be given away to each of ten contest winners. There will also be a similar contest on WNEW-FM. A six-foot square of the album cover has been made as a backdrop for the stage and will be used while the Dolls perform. At this point, the New York Dolls will be the only act appearing at the show. The appearance at the Waldorf will mark the end of a three month cross country tour the Dolls have completed. THE BIG THREE 1. LET ME SERENADE YOU—3 DOG NIGHT—DUNHILL 2. RINGO—Ringo Starr—Apple—SWAL 3413 Ringo continues to develop his own identity in this fascinating Richard Perry produced LP which features the sensational hit single "Pho- tograph.” The artistry on this album is the most unique in the history of pop music. All of the ex-Beatles, The Band, Marc Bolan, David Bromberg, Nicky Hopkins, Billy Preston, Steve Cropper, and a host of the finest studio men in the world combine to make each track a mas- terpiece. John Lennon’s “I’m The Greatest” is a gem as is Randy Newman’s “Hold On.” In fact, every cut on the LP is distinguished by the individual genius of Ringo and the collec- tive talents of his friends. FULL SAIL—Loggins & Messina—Columbia KC 32540 Kenny and Jim’s new LP is, as the cover indicates, a step into paradise. Led by their current hit, ‘‘My Music,” the album is an exer- cise in the brilliant collaboration of two men with the four musicians who work with them. Jim’s “You Need A Man” is one of the finest songs the group has ever done, featuring a funky backbeat and Jim’s distinctive guitar highlights. “Lahaina” sets the stage for the show which is full, rich, and atmospheric as only the duo can render it. “Coming To You,” “Sailin’ The Wind,” and "Pathway To Glory” are splendid and give notice that the long wait for this record was worth it. BOWIE PINUPS—David Bowie—RCA APL1- 0291 A collection of some of the finest esoteric and popular songs from Britain’s mid-1960 period are the substance of David’s explosive new LP which reaches out and grabs you from the power of "Rosalyn” (Pretty Things) and “I Can’t Explain” (The Who), to Bert Berns’ la- ment, “Here Comes The Night.” Bowie has always been a master stylist, and this LP rein- forces his reputation. With powerful drummer Aynsley Dunbar lending thumping support to Mick Ronson’s ethereal guitar, Dave has a strong band with which to render this excellent selection of old hits. “See Emily Play” and "Friday on My Mind” are our favorites. SONNY & CHER LIVE IN LAS VEGAS VOL. 2—MCA MCA2-8004 More of the familiar distinguishing talent which has made the renown duo one of the most popular acts in show business is in full and dazzling evidence on this special two rec- ord set recorded live at The Sahara Hotel, in Las Vegas. Featuring many of their greatest hits, including “I Got You Babe,” “Bang Bang (My Baby Shot Me Down),” “Gypsys, Tramps, & Thieves,” and “All I Ever Need Is You,” the album sparkles with comedic interludes that add spice to the fine music. Particularly mov- ing are the couple’s version of Leon Russell’s "Superstar” and the Sonny Bono classic, “You’d Better Sit Down Kids.” SHIP AHOY—The O’Jays—Philadelphia Inter- national KZ 32408 Always moving with the relentless beat that keeps the city of brotherly love jumping contin- uously, the fabulous O’Jays have another great LP to be proud of with this collection of fine and foxy tunes. Led by the strong candidate for their next single, “Put Your Hands Togeth- er,” this album is an extraordinary sampling from the trio that gave the “Love Train” its steam. The title track is an exercise in beauty, one of the most soulful ballads we’ve ever heard with excellent sound effects accenting the effort smartly. The fine Gamble-Huff pro- duction team is very much in evidence on the LP. We like “For The Love Of Money.” FOCUS LIVE AT THE RAINBOW—Focus—Sire SAS-7408 One of the most amazing musical pheno- mena of the decade, Focus became a part of the lives of millions with their huge hit “Hocus Pocus” which highlights this magnificent live recording. Produced by Mike Vernon at Lon- don's Rainbow Theatre, the album displays all the virtuosity that has made the quartet such a favorite. Thij Van Leer's hauntingly beautiful “Focus III” is a study in masterful dynamics, and “Answers? Questions! Questions? An- swers!” sparkles with the consummate guitar artistry of Jan Akkerman, who recently was voted best guitarist by Melody Maker. “Erup- tion” and “Focus II” are mind blowing. COMIC BOOK HEROES—Rick Springfield— Columbia KC 32704 Australian singer/composer/musician Rick has a great debut LP on Columbia that’s load- ed with his particular genius for rockin’ and rollin’ complimented by his deft ballads. High- lighted by the single “Believe In Me,” this collection of eleven original compositions pro- duced by Robie Porter ranges from the heavy rocker “I’m Your Superman” to the polished and full “Weep No More.” “Misty Water Wom- an” and “The Liar” are splendid examples of Rick’s songwriting virtuosity as each reflects several contiguous textures that are rough and refined alternately. This LP is well worth get- ting into. ATTEMPTED MUSTACHE—Loudon Wainwright III—Columbia KC 32710 More of Loudon’s own inimitable wit shines on this new LP featuring the single “Down Drinking At The Bar” and a host of raucous lyric lines that weave in and out of the music like so many golden threads. “A.M. World” is a funky tune highlighted by a smokin' guitar riff and “Bell Bottom Pants” (which Loudon dedi- cates to the U.S. Navy) is one of the funniest satires on a trend we’ve ever heard. “Liza” is a tongue-in-check poem dedicated to Ms. Minelli and “I Am The Way” is an irreverent spoof on the Jesus craze. “Clockwork Chartreuse” and “Dilated To Meet You” put the finishing touches to this funny LP. THE PARTRIDGE FAMILY BULLETIN BOARD— Partridge Family—Bell Bell 1137 Televisions have long been tuned into this delightful musical family and record players around the world have played their joyful mu- sic for years, and this new LP promises to keep those machines running for a long time to come. “Money Money” is a strong uptempo rocker and “Roller Coaster’’ is surprisingly funky and moves steadily with David Cassidy’s lead vocals superbly accented by Shirley Jones’ multitracked harmonies. "Lookin’ For A Good Time” is a great pop tune with a catchy melody and Cassidy does a beautiful job on The Goffin-King 60’s hit "Oh, No, Not My Baby.” BLACK & BLUE—Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes—Philadelphia International KZ 32407 The fabulous quartet has everything to be proud of on their latest LP featuring the soul- ful single “The Love I Lest.” interestingly, the group opens this Gamble-Huff produced album with the atypical "Cabaret,” but manages to give a very creditable performance. In* fact, performance may be the key word for this versatile vocal group because each tune owes its brilliance to the dedicated hard work of every member of the team. “It Ail Depends On You” is a sweet and sexy ballad complimenting the powerful rhythms of “Is There A Place For Me” and "Satisfaction Guaranteed (Or Take Your Love Back),” perfectly. TATTOO—Rory Gallagher—Polydor PD 5539 Rockin’ Rory has never been any better as you’ll quickly discover from a single listen to his new LP. Every cut is on fire from the heat Rory makes when he brushes those steel picks against his guitar strings. “Who's That Corn- in' ” has to be one of the finest slide guitar rockers we’ve ever heard and "Sleep On A Clothes-Line” is a rock'n’roll beauty in a class by itself. Rory's incredible slide technique is also featured on “20:20 Vision” and his vocals cut through the avalanche of sound like a hot knife through butter. Putting as much into this LP as he does in live concert, Rory has cap- tured the tiger by the tail. Cash Box — November 3, 1973

IV November 9th At MSG NEW YORK — On Friday, Novem- ber 9 at 9 PM, Richard Nader and Madison Square Garden Productions will present Latin Music Festival IV. Featuring Latin Jazz, Rock and Soul, the festival will headline outstanding talent representing Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic as well as New York “Salsa” stars. Puerto Rican songstress Lucecita, Eddie Palmieri, Willie Colon, Domin- ican Republic artists Joseito Mateo and Alberto Beltran and their orches- tras, Pellin Rodriquez and La Selecta are feature artists with special guest star, multi million seller Perez Prado and his 17 piece orchestra, who is flying in direct from Mexico for his first New York appearance in 10 years. Eight New Jewel Distributorships SHREVEPORT — Stan Lewis, pres- ident of Jewel Record Company, an- nounces the appointment of eight new distributorships. Apex Martin Distributors, Hillside, N.J., Seaboard Distributors, E. Hartford, Conn., Ac- tion Music, Cleveland, Ohio, Music City Distributors, Nashville, Tenn., Sixtoe Distributors, Oak Park, Mich., Tone Distributors, Hialeah, Florida, Reocrd Service, Houston, Texas, Chips Distributors, Philadelphia, Pa. They have abeen appointed the dis- tributors for Jewel, Paula, Ronn, and Soul-Power labels. Master of ceremonies duties will be shared by local disc jockeys, Paquito Navarro, WHOM-AM: Joe Gaines, WEVD-AM; Polito Vega, WPNX-AM and Dick (Ricardo) Sugar, WHBI- FM. Joe, Lester, George and Willie. R&B INGREDIENTS—Paramount Pictures is conducting a nation- wide search for a new black actor for the forthcoming movie project, “Lead- belly.” Director Gordon Parks, Sr., says that production is projected to begin on locations in Louisiana and Texas in March, 1974, on a 10-week shooting schedule, covering about 20 years of Leadbelly’s life. Parks says that the film will say something important to a lot of people, also letting them know what a black man went through in that particular time in history. “Take This Ham- mer,” “Silver City Bound” and “Kisses Sweeter Than Wine” are some of the Leadbelly tunes to be included in the film. Parks says that Richard Roundtree (Shaft) was discovered through open call. Black actors between 25 and 35 may send photos to: Otto & Windsor, Paramount Pictures, #1 Gulf & Western Plaza, 37th Floor, New York, NY 10023. Good Gracious Lord, you actors out there get busy . . . The Spaniels, one of the prominent groups of the '50’s, are soon to be heard from. Henry Farag, president of Canterbury Records an- nounced the signing of the group. They have just finished cutting their first single to be released shortly . . . John Edwards (Aware) “Stop This Merry Go Round” single, beginning to happen; has also been in the GRC studios in At- lanta working on his first LP for the R&B Aware label ... I had the opportun- ity to meet Charles Bevel, who stopped in at the CB offices to say hello. Charles is on the A&M label with his first LP, “Meet Mississippi Charles.” He is another alumnus of the Jerry Butler Workshop in Chicago. That workshop is becoming a significant force on the musical scene. Charles joined the work- shop in October '12 and is fully released with his own material on A&M. Con- grats to him! Also to the others, such as, Terry Callier another talented writer . . . The Crusaders wind their ’73 touring season with a Nov. 8-10 stand at the new Roxy Theater in Hollywood . . . The Independents—Chuck, Helen, Eric, Maurice—also the title of their new LP, have a new single, “It’s All Over” starting to cook. The PR firm, Richard Gersh Associates, is now handling the Independents PR. don drossell Black Caucus Dinner DURING A BREAK IN THE ACTION—At the recently held Black Caucus Dinner in Washington, D.C., (Shown L. to R.) Ruth Bowen, president of Queens Booking Corp.; Aretha Franklin, Queen of Soul; Rev. Jesse Jackson; unidentified woman and Mrs. Cecil Franklin let photog catch group rapping with Aretha. Rufus On Stax MEMPHIS — Stax artist Rufus Thomas recently re-signed an exclu- sive long term artist contract with the Stax Organization. Thomas’ latest single “I Know You Don’t Love Me No More” is from his forthcoming lp “Crown Prince Of Dance.” Atlantic Signs Oscar Toney, Sr. NEW YORK — Henry Allen, Atlan- tic’s vice president of promotion, an- nounced that singer Oscar Toney, Jr. has signed with Atlantic Records. Atlantic will be releasing a single by Toney, “Everything I Own,” which was a smash for Bread last year. It was recorded in England and Allen indicated that there is enough mate- rial from that session to make an album. Toney, a vocalist known for his ballads, is popular in the South. “Your Precious Love,” “Dark End Of The Street,” and “Down In Texas” were a few of his hits. ABC Sets Promo For Bobby Bland BOSTON — When Bobby Bland opened at Paul’s Mall in Boston on Oct. 8, ABC/Dunhill Records pro- moted the event for all press and radio personnel of the area. Bland’s new album, “His California Album,” had begun to take off in the Boston area, and his opening night set was broadcast “live” on WBCN-FM to reach the widest possible audience during his week in the city. From the Boston area, Bland has moved to New York City and a week at Max’s Kansas City. Again ABC/Dunhill invited press and radio. Bland follows the east coast en- gagements with bookings in Califor- nia at Ruthie’s Inn in San Francisco and the Whisky in Hollywood. Ac- cording to Marv Heifer, vice pres- ident at ABC in chai’ge of artist rela- tions, “the Whisky date will be a very big affair. Bland’s name ranks in the Pantheon of blues singers, his influence on today’s pop singers is phenomenal. The time is right for Bobby Bland—he’s going to get the recognition he’s deserved for many years now.” Bland’s single release from al- bum is “This Time I’m ( Good.” Cash Box — November 3, 1973 37

NEW YORK — Metromedia Records president Jack Wiedenmann has an- nounced that special release arrange- ments have been completed with RCA Ltd., London, England, for distribu- tion of the soundtrack album of “Catch My Soul” featuring Richie Havens and Tony Joe White. Negotiations for the release of the album were handled by Metromedia’s international representatives, TARA International and its president Dick Broderick. The soundtrack album will also get simultaneous release through GRT, in Canada, to insure full sales capitaliza- tion on the advertising and promotion of the movie. Event Records For ‘Pepper Box’ NEW YORK — Polydor distributed Event Records has announced the ac- quisition of the record “Pepper Box” by the Peppers from the European company Sirocco Records. The single, currently the number one record in France and Belgium had triggered a world wide bidding spree as a result of its success in Europe and after negotiations, Event bagged the master for the U.S. market and is already in the process of rush releasing it. In their new LP, “The Dells,” Davis has taken a com- plete change of direction and concept with the group. All the material was written especially for them, many tracks are longer and more complex than anything else the Dells have done before and different vocal com- binations within the group were util- ized. Together for twenty years, mak- ing them one of the longest-running popular groups, the Dells have reached a new creative plateau with their current album. With many hits to its credit, Don Davis’ Detroit-based Groovesville Productions has struck gold twice with the Dramatics (“What You See Is What You Get” and “In The Rain”) and with Johnnie Taylor (“Who’s Making Love” and “I Believe In You”). Booked for concert dates at the stadium include Three Dog Night along with Stevie Wonder and possibly Humble Pie . . . The NY chapter of FORE held a special seminar at the City Squire, Manhattan, Oct. 31st. Key speakers at the FORE meeting included Bo Frazier, vp at Perception-Today Record Co., Jan S. Mirsky, treasurer of GSF Productions Inc., and Ron LeGalt, controller of Polydor Inc. The major topics, of course, were on the subjects of financing and operating independent labels and the methods of obtaining financing for starting a label. FORE members were on hand including several key personnel from many areas of the record industry. It was also brought out by the panel members that there is definitely a vinyl shortage that will effect the manufacturing costs of records. It appears that the costs will have to be absorbed or passed on to the consumer. It was also brought out that computerized systems are in vogue for the major operations. One would tend to think that it is impossible to run a company without a computer. On the other hand, companys such as Perception manage reasonally well. Money management, corporate accounting and management accounting were the topics discussed. It was also brought out that the day of the single may have had its day, but one need look only at the impact of a Marvin Gaye, who did well over 2 million in single sales, so there is much that has to be considered before that single can be written off. It is true that an LP has a powerful influence on the profit side of things. But, it is still the single in combination with a forthcoming LP that can make an act profitable; it will enable an independent label to continue to be an influence on the musical scene. Shut off this single activity and you may have snuffed out the creative artist; and possibly some of you may have forgotten that it is still this creative artist, writer, or producer who contributes to the livelihood of any company. It is therefore possible, that many blacks have been washed into the computer age. When it comes right down to basics, it is still roots! The roots are where it’s at, and I still don't see where that is going to change. It is far too easy to walk in the gray. Black is black and white is certainly tuned to black radio. There are those who say that music is universal, but I defy anyone to tell me that a Rolls Royce is of the same structure as a Chev- rolet. Right now I’ll take the grey, many blacks are thinking, so it seems. Black radio has been instrumental in promulgating and promoting new artists as well as maintaining established black artists for many years. The time has come for re-establishing those goals. Lets face it, black radio with 90% less wattage power can outsell many of the so-called top 40 stations. So, the company that chooses it’s goals and aims carefully will survive!!! The release has been titled “The Name Game” as a means of em- phasizing the strength of the artists included in the release. The sevenart- ists represented have jointly com- piled a record of having records on the charts for over 800 weeks. The conceptual marketing approach is also an effective means of emphasiz- ing the value of quality reissues by name artists in the retail market- place. NEW YORK — Vittorio Benedetto and Jimmy Ienner of C.A.M. have an- nounced that the musical score com- posed by Jacques Brel- for the soon- to-be released feature film “L’Emme- deur,” (The Pain In The Neck) has been produced and published by C.A.M. The music was produced in France. In addition, C.A.M. feature film ac- tivity includes a number of scores produced and published for motion pictures which will be released here soon. George DeLerue composed the music for “How To Destroy The Rep- utation of The Most Celebrated Secret Agent In The World” for C.A.M.; Ar- mando Trovajoli has composed the score for “Paolo II Caldo”; Peguri has written the music for “The Seven Nuns of Kansas City” and for “Silk Worm” starring George Hilton; Stel- vio Cipriani, composer of the music for “The Anonymous Venetian” has turned his talents to the film “The Last Trip.” The C.A.M. score for “Teenager” was composed by G. Ardison, and the C.A.M. score for “Free My Love” was written by Mor- ricone. Imhoff Named AMF Int’l. Rep. NEW YORK — Hal Davis, president of the American Federation of Musi- cians (AFL-CIO, CLC) has appointed Harold “Hal” Imhoff as an interna- tional representative to fill the vacan- cy created by the recent death of Al- bert Aan. Imhoff’s territory will be the same as that of the late Aan; the Southeastern and Atlantic seaboard states. Imhoff, who will work out of Ft. Myers, Florida, has had many years of union experience. He has been an AFM delegate to the union’s national convention since 1968. He first joined the Federation in 1943. Imhoff began studying piano at age seven, and later studied bass viol, the- ory, harmony and composition dur- ing his college days. He has played with many orchestras, including those under the direction of Ray Herrara and Pee Wee Hunt. Cash Box — November 17, 1973

R&B News Report AL GREEN CONQUERS NEW YORK—A1 Green came to New York City and conquered all. Green spent a full week headlining at Harlem’s prestigious Apollo Theatre and every show drew SRO houses. In fact, Robert Schiffman, the owner-General Manager of the Apollo, said, “A1 Green set the all-time Apollo box office record during his appearance here during November 2 to 8.” During this week, A1 performed an incredible 17 shows at the Apollo—all of which included debut live performances of his new single, “Livin’ For You” and on the last night he was surprised onstage by a presentation of a plaque and photos awarded to him for his service to Harlem community youth. It seems the Hi/London Records artist had on past visits to New York slipped away to counsel underprivileged youth of the area, without even letting his management know. AI considers the Apollo his home and the fans welcomed him. For that matter, during the hectic week at the Apollo which included visits to all local radio stations with London promoiotn people, Al found time to continue his humanitarian ventures with a full-blown concert at the dockside Federal House of Detention in lower Manhattan before an enraptured, boogy- ing-in-their-seats audience of 250 inmates (see photo). And for this concert, no expense or effort was spared, as Al brought along his entire band and per- formed a complete, specially programmed set for the institution’s inmates. The delighted and appreciative audience presented Al with a hand-painted card that promised “Peace in the star, Love in the grass” and a book of poems. Green humbly thanked the inmates and afterwards noted that the reason for the concert was simply, “They’re locked up and can’t get out, but I can get in.” ‘Pepper Box’ Hit In France Goes To Event Records NEW YORK CITY — Polydor dis- tributed Event Records announces the acquisition of the record “Pepper Box” by the Peppers from the Euro- pean company Sirocco Records. The single, currently the number one rec- ord in France and Belgium had trig- gered a world wide bidding spree as a result of its success in Europe and after an intensive negotiating ses- sion, Event bagged the master for the U.S. market and is already in the process of rush releasing it. NEW YORK — Garland Greene has just signed a long term recording contract with Spring Records, as shown above with label principals Roy and Julie Rifkind. Greene has been constantly represented on the charts, and has had a million selling disc with Jealous Kind of Fellow. He Didn’t Know (He Kept on Talk- ing), Greene’s new single for Spring ships this week, while the artist is in the studio completing tracks for an album with producer Brad Shapiro. The album is expected to be ready for release after the first of the year. Spring Records are distributed by Polydor Incorporated. Johnnie Taylor Dallas ‘Homecoming’ DALLAS — “Johnnie Comes Singing Home” will be the theme of a five-day homecoming here for Stax recording artist Johnnie Taylor, who is giving Dallas a concert and a series of other appearances to thank his home com- munity for their support. Beginning Nov. 14, Taylor will lead a band of musicians into Dallas, wind- ing in a concert on Nov. 18 at the Dallas Memorial Auditorium. Appearing with Taylor will be the Rev. Jesse Jackson and Stax star Rufus Thomas, with artists Millie Jackson, the Ovations and Syl John- son booked into the special concert. Civic festivities will fill the several days leading up to the concert. Tay- lor will perform much of the music from his Stax album “Taylored in Silk.” Magic From Marlena The _ occasion was the sensational opening at L.A.’s Lighthouse, west coast jazz mecca, by Blue Note’s sul- try songstress, Marlena Shaw. Shown congratulating Marlena after her performance is Michael Stewart, President of United Artists Records. Interestingly enough, one of those who is taking an active role in the Memphis celebration is Diane Crump, grand- daughter of the well-known political figure who was known as “Boss” Crump. Don Drossell Ashford & Simpson On Concert Swing NEW YORK — Composing, produc- ing and performing team Nickolas Ashford & Valerie Simpson have just begun a cross-country mini-tour of the major market cities to introduce themselves to the concert audience as a duo, and to meet radio and press in each city to discuss “Gimme Some- thing Real,” their debut LP for War- ner Bros. Records, and their just re- leased single “(I’d Know You) Any- where.” Already well-known for their writ- ing and production of such r&b hits as “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough,” “Let’s Go Get Stoned,” “You’re all I Need to Get By” and “Ain’t Nothing Like the Real Thing,” Ashford & Simpson are making their performing debut with this tour. Responses to the first stop, the Troubadour in Los An- geles, are indicated by a review in the Hollywood Reporter saying “Ashford & Simpson brought down the house when they opened Tuesday. The Trou- badour was trembling with vibrations of life, moans and cries of apprecia- tion.” Other stops on the Ashford & Simpson tour include Alice Tully Hall in New York (November 11th) the Ford Auditorium in Detroit on November 16th the Cellar Door in the Bijou Theatre in Philadelphia on November 26 & 27, the Saunders The- Washington, D.C. on November 19th, atre in Boston on December 1, and the Happy Medium in Chicago on De- cember 3rd and 4th. Gospel Acts Need Showbiz Help NEW YORK CITY — The majority of gospel singers will never graduate into the big money unless they get organized and let others handle their business affairs, predicted one of Broadway’s top booking agents. Herb Moon, who handles the gospel department of Queen Booking Corp., said that these groups will have to stop booking themselves in whistle stop engagements that sometimes don’t gross $200.00. He credited the success of James Cleveland, rated the foremost male gospel singer in the nation, to his professionalism. His one night tours start at $2500 and often he walks awav from a concert with as much as $7500. “There are a few such as Cleveland, Inez Andrews, Mighty Clouds of Joy, Soul Stirrers and Shirley Caesar, “said Moon,” who have signed con- tracts with our agency. And they are amazed at the profitable engagements we secure for them in comparison to what they once earned.” While most groups and singers in the gospel field have restricted them- selves to dates in small churches and lodge halls that seat 200 and 300 per- sons, Moon books QBC’s clients into large concert halls, auditoriums and on college campuses. With crowds of as much as 8000 that can be ac- comodated in these places, he points out that the artist can walk away with a larger share of the boxoffice. He laments the fact that these groups are poorly educated into the methods of show business by not hav- ing personal managers, accountants and business advisers as do bigtime pop artists such as Sammy Davis, Aretha Franklin, Curtis Mayfield or Gladys Knight and the Pips. “It’s a proven fact,” said Moon, “that performers can’t work all night and then arise at daybreak to talk facts and figures with shrewd and sharp business men. They need such advisers to advance their interests.” To bolster his arguments he said that the late Clara Ward and Mahalia Jackson struggled for pennies until they retained professionals to guide their careers which brought them lu- crative TV, record and theatre ap- pearances. The late Sam Cooke and Aretha Franklin, said Moon, both were products of the gospel world and amassed a fortune when they placed their business affairs in the hands of competent persons. 28 Cash Box — November 24, 1973

NEW YORK — Lewis Merenstein, has been named the company’s gener- al manager and director of A&R, ac- cording to Art Kass, president of The Buddah Group. In his position, Mer- enstein will also continue to direct Buddah’s marketing and creative serv- ices divisions and will report direct- ly to Kass. Merenstein joined The Buddah Group last March as vice president and director of marketing and creative services. Since that time, the company has been awarded five gold albums, with Merenstein coordinat- ing Buddah’s entrance into the field of television advertising. Stated Kass, “This performance, in a mere seven months, speaks for itself. We are tremendously enthusiastic about Merenstein’s activities in the compa- ny, and we are looking forward to an expanded utilization of the artistic side of his talents with his new re- sponsibilities in A&R.” Merenstein, producer of Van Mor- rison’s “Moondance” and “Astral Weeks” albums, entered the industry as a free-lance engineer, working with the top names in jazz, among them Thelonius Monk, Dizzy Gilles- pie, Art Farmer, Cecil Taylor and Lee Morgan. At the height of his engineering career, he was invited to join a major record manufacturing and plastics firm as vice president. Merenstein traveled the country, working in marketing at the crucial period when rack jobbers and new forms of dis- tribution were coming into effect. During that time he also worked with leading chains like J. C. Penney, Kor- vettes and Sears. In addition to Van Morrison, Mer- enstein has produced albums by Miri- am Makeba, Mama Cass, John Cale, Spencer Davis, Barry Goldberg, the Association, and also a young artist on the Buddah label, Michael Wen- droff. It was during the production of Wendroff’s album that he was invited to join the company. Merenstein Linsky Opens Indie Sales, Mkting Firm Herbert A. Linsky Associates has been formed by the vet recording exec. The firm will specialize in the sales and marketing of specific album product. Linsky had previously been with both the Columbia and RCA labels in various capacities of merchandising and marketing. He was associated with Columbia’s Harmony RCA’s Camden budget labels. Linsky stated, “Our industry has changed, and our methods of mass merchandising have to change ac- cordingly.” “This is an exciting chal- lenge for me and I look forward to establishing new sales dimensions through longtime relationships.” It was also announced that Herbert A. Linsky Assoc, has been appointed the exclusive representative of special promotional product for K-Tel Inter- national, Inc., a leader in TV record merchandising. Linsky’s address is 250 West 57th St., New York, N.Y., phone number is: (212) 582-2594. i Paramount Expands A&R Dept NEW YORK — Chuck Gregory, vice president of A&R for Famous Music and the Paramount label, has an- nounced a major expansion of his department. Says Gregory, “A&R is no longer going to end its responsi- bility when it signs an act. We’re going to help those acts get ready for the marketplace.” As a first step, Gregory has named Michael Barbiero A&R assistant and Michael Leon director of artist de- velopment for Paramount Rec- ords. Barbiero studied synthesizer with Roger Hannay at the University of North Carolina, then became an assistant recording engineer at Media Sound Studio, where he worked on sessions with Buzzy Feiton, Buzzy Linhart, and Alan Douglas’ Last Poets. Barbiero will screen all new pro- duct submitted to Paramount, help Leon, Barbiero Philbin To Col. Int’l Pop Ed. NEW YORK — Bunny Freidus, di- rector for U.S. popular product, CBS International Division, has named Peter Jay Philbin as international editor for U.S. popular product. Philbin has been a rock journalist the past three years, having his arti- cles appear in “Melody Maker”, “Cir- cus”, “L.A. Free Press”, “Chicago Sun Times”, “Phonograph Record Magazine”, and other publications. Philbin will be responsible for the preparation of a weekly international news device. His appointment is ef- fective immediately. Davis Exits Summit CHICAGO — Harold Davis, after 12 years at Summit Dist. in Skokie, 111., has announced his resignation. He was vice-president and sales manager for the firm. He will shortly announce his new plans. make the final decision about which product is accepted, and be responsi- ble for quality control. “The result,” says Gregory, “is that we’ll be able to give faster answers to people sending us tapes and demos.” Leon, who takes over the newly- created position of director of artist development for Paramount Records, comes from Bell Records, where he was marketing administrator. Leon will strengthen communication with the artists and their managers, coor- dinate tours, and will act as liaison with Famous Music’s promotion, pub- licity and marketing personnel. Concludes Gregory, “With the changes in our department, we will do far more than just signing new ar- tists. Through a program of follow through, we will develop those artists in the early and most Jo Bergman To Warner's A&R Warner Bros. Records’ director of artist relations, Bob Regehr, has an- nounced the appointment of Jo Berg- man to the post of director of special projects for Warners’ Artist Rela- tions Department. Ms. Bergman, former tour orga- nizer, and logistics engineer for the Rolling Stones, will make her head- quarters in Warners’ New York of- fices and report directly to Bob Regehr in Burbank. An American who has lived in Lon- don most of her life, Ms. Bergman broke into the music business in 1963 when she landed a job with Tony Bar- row, then press officer to Brian Ep- stein and his fledgling group, The Beatles. When the organization grew too unwieldy, Jo left for jobs as an in- dependent publicist—first in Paris, then back in London—working for Marianne Faithful, The Animals, The Byrds, Georgie Fame, CBS Records, and various boutiques and theatre people on the scene in ’65 and ’66. A year in California working with d.j. Tom Donahue, Harper’s Bizarre, Kama Sutra Records and radio sta- tion KRLA. ended when a phone call from Mick Jagger asked her to “come back and run the office,” a task that Jo performed for AV2 years. Follow- ing the completion of the Stones’ 1972 American tour, Jo went to work for filmmaker Sandy Lieberson. Interland Named To London FM Promo Esther Edwards New Bank Dir. DETROIT — - Senior vice-president and corporate secretary of Motown Industries, Esther G. Edwards, has been elected to the board of directors of the Bank of the Commonwealth. One of the few women bank direc- tors in the nation, Ms. Edwards re- cently became the first woman to be elected to the board of directors of the Greater Detroit Chamber of Com- merce. She is sister of Berry Gordy Jr. who founded Motown Record Corpora- tion and Motown Industries, the larg- est black-owned company in the na- tion among manufacturing, service or retailing firms. She is married to Michigan State Representative George H. Edwards. Sheperd Exits Starday-King NEW YORK — Mike Sheperd has left his post as general manager of Starday-King Records. Sheperd said he can be reached at (615) 824-1784. NEW YORK — Brian Interland has been appointed director of FM pro- motion for London Records, it has been announced by Sy Warner, Lon- don’s director of promotion and sin- gle sales. Interland, in the business for 13 years, has been serving as east coast regional promotion representative for the past year. In his new position, Interland will be involved with FM stations across the country along with special proj- ects for FM progressive promotion. He will be working in coordination with college program administrator Ray Caviano on London’s college pro- motion program. Interland will be re- sponsible to Dave Marshall, promo manager for London Records, for all facets of his new position. Interland Grady Phonodisc Operations Veep NEW YORK — Bill Farr, president of Phonodisc Inc., has announced the appointment of William F. Grady to vice president of Operations at the distributorship. Mr. Farr commented, “It’s particu- larly good news for Phonodisc that Bill Grady’s joining our executive staff in a capacity in which he’s proved himself an industry leader. His knowledge and experience in dis- tribution and fulfillment will bring added strength to our team of skilled record professionals.” Until his Phonodisc appointment, Grady was head of fulfillment and manufacturing for the Longines and Capitol Record Clubs. In the past, he has served as vice president of manu- facturing for Columbia Records and later held similar posts at MCA and Famous Music. Grady Garfield To Blue Thumb BEVERLY HILLS — Sal Licata, president of Blue Thumb Records, has appointed Bruce E. Garfield to the newly created position of director of artist relations. Garfield’s primary responsibilities will lie in the areas of artist develop- ment and inter-industry communica- tion. He will be in constant contact with all the label’s artists and will travel into all markets to help co- ordinate artist tours. A six-year veteran of the music industry, Garfield brings to Blue Thumb an extensive background in talent development. Prior to joining Blue Thumb, he was director of Chisa Record Productions. W-E-A Adds To Home Office Staff Unit HOLLYWOOD — Joel Friedman, president of WEA, has added Stan Harris and Joe Mason to the firm’s home office staff. Harris will serve as staff assistant to Henry Droz, vice president in charge of sales, and to Friedman, op- erating out of the company’s home office. Harris formerly was exec vice president of AKAI, Ltd., manufactur- ers and distributors of audio high fi- delity equipment. He joins WEA with a background of some 20 years experi- ence in the marketing of audio equip- ment. Mason will serve as assistant credit manager to Tom Romano, the com- pany’s national credit manager. Mason recently was with MGM Records and has a record of life-long experience in credit management. 10 Cash Box — December 1, 1973

Motown Sets Movie Music Co. For Its Own & Indie Efforts Holiday Sales Off To Solid Start Retailers Report In Key Markets Rob Cohen Unit Chief HOLLYWOOD — Rob Cohen, Mo- town Production’s creative veep, ex- clusively told Cash Box last week that plans are underway to establish yet another division to the ever burgeoning entertainment conglom- erate. The new department is tentatively referred to by Cohen as Motown’s “movie music company” which will handle the scoring to Motown’s own film properties as well as making its services available to independent pro- ductions. Motown’s movie music com- pany is presently under the aegis of Cohen and Suzanne Depasse. Cohen stressed the importance of this new division by saying “Up until now most film producers have only had a small kernel of movie com- posers to turn to.” He opined that movie music has not appreciably changed since the piano played behind Chaplin but feels that Motown’s growing participation in this field will initiate “a whole new concept of thematic music in movies.” This initiative will make accessible FRONT COVER: Four years ago the name J. Geils might not have rang a bell, but ex- ecutive vice president of Atlantic Rec- ords, Jerry Wexler, signed the Boston rock group in early 1970, and ever since then the hard rockin’ sextet has been ringing the bells of rock fans from Beantown to London, from the Golden Gate to Miami Beach. In fact, they’re as popular right now as any band in America. The group’s latest album, “Ladies Invited”, is selling at a golden pace, and their previous album “Bloodshot” earned the bad boys from Boston their first RIAA certified gold LP. Singer Peter Wolf and keyboard dynamo Seth Justman write most of the band’s material which J. Geils, Stephen Bladd, Danny Klein, and Magic Dick help turn into musical meteor show- ers. Constantly in demand for live per- sonal appearances, the group last week packed Madison Square Garden when they played their first date there as headliners. Cohen point- ed out how this department will provide a new outlet for many of the label’s writers, some of which only get one side released a year. “Now,” says Cohen, “these artists will have new challenges, new deadlines, and will be occupied in film projects which could require 'as much as three months of creative work.” In addi- tion, this new scoring entity will fur- nish the Motown label with soundtrack LP’s as well as singles of “title songs.” Motown has already achieved tremendous success with the few soundtracks it’s released to date including “Lady Sings The Blues,” “Trouble Man,” and “The Mack.” In negotiation are deals whereby Mo- town’s movie music arm will supply all of the scores for at least two outside production outfits. First project The first in-house soundtrack to come out of all of this could be Mo- town’s next projected Diana Ross film vehicle, Bob Merrill’s “Mahogany.” Although written by one of Broad- way’s most accomplished lyricists (“Funny Girl,” “Sugar”) this is not a musical. However Cohen has 'asked Merrill to think about where in the treatment a few songs could be feasibly worked in. Harbach, Weill, Golden Members Of Theatre Hall NEW YORK — Three additions to the Theatre Hall of Fame are the late lyricist Otto Harbach, composer Kurt Weill and composer-lyricist John Golden, according to Drama Desk president Henry Hewes. Membership in the Hall, housed in the Uris The- atre on Broadway, is based on at least five major Broadway credits in the course of a theatre career of no less than 25 years. NEW YORK — Retail sales over the Thanksgiving Day weekend generally initiated a strong start in Holiday sales in some key markets, according to a survey conducted by Cash Box. The Record Hunter reported excel- lent sales figures for the holiday weekend. It reported a 25% to 30% increase over normal sales. Pop and classical music were the dominant trends, and the particularly hot LP’s were; “Jonathon Livingston Seagull” by Neil Diamond, “Shirley Bassey Live At Carnegie Hall,” “Ringo,” Traffic’s “On The Road,” Phillips “Brandenber Concerto,” “William Tell Overture,” and “Turndot.” May’s reported good sales with a significant increase over normal weekends. The rhythm & blues cate- gory predominted with Marvin Gaye, Stevie Wonder, Barry White, and Gladys Knight & The Pips leading the category. Korvette’s reported “excellent” sales figures with a significant in- crease over normal sales. Pop pre- dominated with the Stones, Lennon. Ringo, and Harrison, doing very well and r&b wise Harold Melvin and The Blue Notes, and Gladys Knight and The Pips brought sales up. Alexander’s reported good sales figures with a better than average increase over a normal weekend. The r&b category prevailed with Love Unlimited, Barry White, Marvin Gaye and Stevie Wonder as leaders. Pop sales were good also with Ringo, Lennon, and Loggins & Messina pre- vailing. and Cafe Americana Music (BMI). Reach Agreement On NY Times Music Buy Of Metromedia NEW YORK — An agreement in principle has been reached for the sale of the assets of the music pub- lishing companies of Metromedia, Inc. to The New York Times Music Corp. The purchase agreement, which is subject to approval by The New York Times board of directors, was an- nounced by John W. Kluge, president and chairman of the board of Me- tromedia, and Sydney Gruson, execu- tive vice president of The New York Times Co. The purchase price was not disclosed. The acquisition would be the Times’ music publishing division’s first major acquisition of an existing catalog. Metromedia’s music publishing companies hold copyrights on a num- ber of Broadway musical shows such as “Cabaret,” “Fiddler on the Roof,” “Follies,” “Fiorello!” and “Godspell” and many other scores. The Times Company recently en- tered the music publishing business when it formed The New York Times Music Corp. last Sept. Sam Goody’s reported sales were good, and better than average. Classi- cal, rock, and jazz all did very well with no particular LP’s cited. King Karol reported sales were moderate to good with no real in- crease over a normal weekend. Pop wise the new Emerson, Lake & Pal- mer, and Alice Kooper’s “Muscle of Love” did particularly well. Gimbel’s reported good figures with no real increase over a normal week- end. Rhythm & Blues and pop were the big sellers, and the big artists were Love Unlimited, Barry White, and Elton John. Major retailers throughout the west coast reported increases in sales over the Thanksgiving holiday. One major chain recorded an increase sales percentage of 40%, with LP’s account- ing for the major portion of the surge in volume. Sales reports from the midwest, south varied from “very good” to “very slow,” the latter due in some measure to the fact that some stores did not open on Saturday or opened doors in the afternoon. Pirate Hearing NEW YORK — In what is believed to be unprecedented in a piracy hearing, two artists, Paul Simon and Tammy Wynette, gave testimony last week in an action Wisconsin Civil Circuit Court against four defendants ac- cused of unauthorized duplication, in- cluding E-C Tape Service. Miss Wynette said she was “in- sulted” that her gospel sons were being advertised by pirates in “skin” magazines. Simon, like Miss Wynette a Columbia artist, was “incensed” over the coupling of his performances with others on pirated goods. Nine labels have brought suit against the defendants, which also in- clude Economic Consultants, David L. Heilman, James Kapsa, David M. Gor- sky, all doing business in Wisconsin. In addition, the American Feder- ation of Television & Radio Artists filed an affidavit in support of an injunction against the defendants, cit- ing “the grave harm and injustice being done (to all) vocal performers and artists by the manufacture, dis- tribution and sale of unauthorized du- plications.” A&R Execs Exit RCA On Coast HOLLYWOOD — Four A&R execs at RCA Records in Hollywood have resigned from their posts. They in- clude Don Burkhimer, vp of west coast A&R; Joe Reisman, A&R pro- ducer; David Blume, A&R producer; and Don Grierson, AR coordinator. In addition it’s understood that Gre- lun Landon, vet manager of west coast pi-ess and information at the label, has been named acting manager of west coast operations, reporting directly to Gil Beltran, the label’s vp and general manger. Remaining in A&R on the west coast is David Ker- shenbaum. PLATINUM FOR A TRIO—Warner Bros. Records’ president Joe Smith, left, and board chairman Mo Ostin hold two of four platinum LPs presented re- cently to Mary Travers, who sits between the two execs holding the remain- ing two RIAA-certified million unit sellers. The four platinum awards were for Peter, Paul and Mary’s “In Concert’’, “In The Wind”, “Moving”, and “Album 1700” LPs. All members of the trio have since been concentrating on solo albums for the label. Mary Travers’ latest LP is “All My Choices”. Bassey Leads UA Quad Pack HOLLYWOOD — United Artists Records and its jazz division, Blue Note Records, have scheduled s.ix Quad cartridge tapes for release in January. Included are Shirley Bassey’s hit “Never, Never, Never.” “Killing Me Softly” from Ferrante & Teicher, “Space Ritual, Alive in Liverpool and London” by Hawkwind, currently in the midst of a highly successful North American tour, and “John Barleycorn Must Die,” a contempo- rary music standard from Traffic, all via United Artists. Blue Note’s Quad representation showcases Donald Byrd with his “Street Lady” set and Lou Donaldson with “Sassy Soul Strut.” Detroit Gets ‘Power House’ DETROIT — The Power House, a new record company, has been estab- lished in Detroit. Headed by Patrick Meehan and Johnny Powers, the new firm will concentrate on production, manufacturing, leasing and publish- ing of pop, r&b, and country music. The production division of the company has developed a roster in- cluding King Diamond, Jackie Ervin, Carl James, Deacon Jones, and Cana- dian acts Ronnie Fray and Joe. The Power House has three staff writer/producers, Roger Bass, who is also head of a&r, Fiery Bursey, and Don Boileau. Other writers are Joe Konas, Tommy Ingram, and David Easley. The Power House is seeking addi- tional artists, writers, and producers. The company is located at 19804 Van Dyke, Detroit, Mich. 48234. TONY ORLANDO & DAWN RING FOR BELL—Bell Records president, Larry Uttal, was presented with a special plaque from Direction Plus, the filmmakers whose promotional film on Tony Orlando & Dawn performing their million-selling hit “Say, Has Anybody Seen My Sweet Gypsy Rose?” recently won a bronze award at the 16th annual International Film & TV Festival in competition with entries from all over the world. Made for Poly- dor, Bell’s foreign licensee for part of the world, as a tool to aid foreign pro- motion, the film was produced for Bell Records by Gloria Sondheim, who handles PR and foreign liaison, and directed by Bill Aucoin and co-produced by Joyce Biawitz for Direction Plus. Seen above (1. to r.) are: Bill Aucoin, Gloria Sondheim, Larry Uttal and Joyce Biawitz. Avco To Bow 1st 74 LP’s Via Person To Person Dist. Meets Avco Records is planning to crisscross the country in a “person to person” schedule of meetings with its distributors and distributor personnel to launch the label’s first LP release program for 1974. The meeting will be highlighted by a product presenta- tion and an outline of the marketing campaign that will support the new product. Bud Katzel, general manager of the label explained that the company had originally made plans to hold two or three regional meetings to include a number of distributors at one time. It was decided, however, that because of the product being introduced and the circumstances in the market place as it exists today, there was a need for direct face to face meetings with individual dis- tributors and their sales and promo- tion staffs. The Avco distributor meetings will also include rap ses- sions dealing with specific problems as they relate to current industry trends and practices. As the company readies for the new year its group The Stylistics are high on the charts with both their BMI Hosts Soviet Comps. NEW YORK — BMI (Broadcast Mu- sic, Inc.) provided a tour of its New York offices for Andrei Eshpai, Rus- sian composer and secretary of the U.S.S.R. Composers Union and Karen Khachaturian, composer-conductor and musical director of the All-Union Bureau for the Propagation of Sovi- et Music. The visit, in response to a State Dept, request, was followed by a luncheon at the Park Lane Hotel, hosted by BMI president Edward M. Cramer. Among the guests was BMI com- poser and musical consultant Ulysses Kay, who is professor of music at New York’s Lehman College. Dr. Kay exchanged impressions with the two composers of his trip to Russia in 1958. At that time he was one of a group of BMI composers who toured Russia under State Department aus- pices as part of international cultural exchange, the first American com- posers to do so. Other BMI composers present in- cluded Robert Helps of Princeton University and Manhattan School of Music; Otto Luening, composer- emeritus, Columbia University and Francis Thome of the Lenox Art Center, and conductor Igor Buketoff, Ms. Grace Belt and Ms. Elaine Hei- fetz of the U.S. Department of State. single “Rockin’ Roll Baby” and al- bum of the same title. Also, the label has The Softones and their single “The First Day” as well as their de- but album. The distributor tour will run through most of the month of De- cember and will cover most of the country including such key markets as New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Chicago, Memphis, Miami, Atlanta, St. Louis, Hartford, Cleve- land, Detroit, Baltimore, Washington and Philadelphia. Spearheading the person to person meetings and carrying the Avco story for the launcing of this cam- paign will be Hugo & Luigi v.p. and chief operating officers and Bud Katzel. Stars For Israel At Friars Conf. NEW YORK — The United States Stars for Israel, a morale building airlift of entertainers to Israel, begun on a crisis basis immediately after the outbreak of the Yom Kippur War, will become a permanent pro- gram, because of the unrest in the Middle-East. The announcement was made at a press conference Fri., Nov. 30, 1973 at the Friars Club. Mayor John V. Lindsay, honorary chairman of the program, accepted a check from realtor George Mehlman who represents a group of personal friends who have raised a special fund for this project. The following stars who have already returned from entertaining the troops and veterans in Israel were introduced and honored: Aliza Kashi, The Barry Sisters, Allan Jones and Geula Gill. Alan King, Roberta Peters and Elly Stone, also present at the conference, are among a group of entertainers including Hazel Scott who will be going to Israel in Dec./Jan. David Rivlin, Consul General of Is- rael, expressed his thanks to the U.S. stars who have gone to Israel to entertain the troops. Alan King, hon- orary co-chairman of the project, spoke about the great number of stars who have volunteered their tal- ents to entertain the disabled in Isra- el. In addition, Azaria Rapoport, Cul- tural and Press attache of the Israeli Consulate in New York, leaders of the United Jewish Appeal of Greater New York, and members of the advi- sory committee for the project in- cluding Phil Schapiro, Jackie Bright, and Joey Adams, were on hand for the presentation. Cash Box/R&B News Report ABC/Dunhill recording artist Bobby “Blue” Bland takes a break from au- tograph signing to chat with his band- leader, Mel Jackson. Bland was ap- pearing as a featured artist at the Lechmere Sight and Sound Show last month in Boston. Along with Bland at the show was Mel Brown (not pic- tured), Bland’s lead guitarist and an artist on the ABC/Impulse label. Columbia Purchases Gloria Taylor Master NEW YORK — Columbia Records has purchased the master by Gloria Taylor of “Deep Inside Of You,” originally released on the Selector Sound label out of Toledo, Ohio. Bill Craig, regional manager of promotion for the Columbia Records Branch in Detroit, heard the song, noted it was breaking wide open in the Detroit area, and brought it to the attention of the National R&B Promotion Department at Columbia in New York Miss Taylor, 24, is no stranger to hit records, having had her first mil- lion seller, “You’ve Got To Pay The Price,” on the Silver Fox label, in 1970. She also had two chart records on Mercury, “Don’t Want To Be A Girl That Cries,” which made the na- tional Pop Charts, and “Grounded,” which did well on the national R&B charts. Columbia will be releasing “Deep Inside Of You” immediately. UA Appoints Abbott Nat’l R&B Director HOLLYWOOD — United Artists Records has appointed Mike Abbott to the newly-created position of na- tional director of r&b promotion. He will be situated at the UA Records offices in New York. Abbott is a veteran of the enter- tainment business. Most recently his Abbott Records label was distributed by United Artists. He also headed the record department of the agency, General Artists Corp., and supervised the r&b promotional activities of MGM Records and Capitol Records. MIKE ABBOTT Pointer’s Going Jazz HOLLYWOOD — The Pointer Sis- ters’ next album will be a jazz- oriented record, according to pro- ducer David Rubinson. The girls rec- ord on Blue Thumb, which has just released their new single, “Wang Dang Doodle.” Among the tunes on their second album will be Thelonius Monk’s “Straight, No Chaser,” Neal Hefti’s “Little Pony,” Horace Henderson’s “Charleston Alley,” the Miles- Coltrane version of “Round Mid- night,” featuring Bonnie Pointer, and the Massey Hall version of “Salt Peanuts,” with June Pointer singing the Dizzy Gillespie solo. ALL THAT’S JAZZ Mammoth All-Star NEW YORK — The Gene ICrupa Fund for Retarded Children will ben- efit from the proceeds of a mammoth all-star jazz and big hand concert to be presented at Radio City Music Hall by Art Trefferson of Steady Records and Peter Mallon of Counterpoint Concerts, Inc. The event, scheduled for January 17, 1974, will be taped for a TV special and release as a two-record LP package on Treffer- son’s Steady Records via Columbia House. Governor Nelson A. Rockefeller is serving as Honorary Chairman and Lionel Hampton is Chairman of the concert with a great array of top names in music lined up to perform. All profits from the concert, TV show and album package will go to the retarded children’s fund recently es- tablished in the name of the late Kru- pa who died early this Fall following a life-time of activity in jazz and a deep concern for the plight of retard- ed youth. Ed Bland Produces Sunday Concerts NEW YORK — Ed Bland, producer, presents Blues /Jazz and Gospel on Sunday afternoons at 3 p.m. at BAM, The Brooklyn Academy of Music, 30 Lafayette Avenue, Brooklyn, New York 11217. The seven-member all woman Emma Creamer Gospel Singers will appear Sunday, December 16. Janu- ary attractions are Odetta on Janu- ary 13 and the Elvin Jones quintet on January 27. Big Mama Thornton and Screaming Jay Hawkins are Febru- ary attractions. Benefit Concert Reading like a who’s who of jazz and big band music, the talent roster includes: Benny Goodman, Harry James, Pearl Bailey, Billy Eckstein, Roy Eldridge, Anita O’Day, Helen Ward, Louis Bellson, Stan Getz, Max Kaminsky, Zoot Sims and Jo Jones. Also, Ray McKinley, Tony Mottola, Doc Goldberg, Eddie Shu, Tyree Glen, Mel Lewis, Lenny Hambro, Max Roach, Joe Morello, Grady Tate, Son- ny Igor and Bobby Rosengarden aiong with Sy Oliver, Lee Castle, Charlie Ventura, Gerry _ Mulligan, Johnny Desmond, Buddy Rich, Lionel Hampton, Teddy Wilson and radio personality William B. Williams. Trefferson stated that sponsor com- mitments for the TV show have been received and negotiations are under- way to clear network time for viewing. B.B. King Forms Blues Society NEW YORK—B. B. King this week announced the formation of an inter- national society for the appreciation of the blues with himself as chairman of the advisory board. The new organization has among its goals and purposes to place the blues in its proper historical perspec- tive, to give recognition and appreci- ation to blues artists, to develop new blues audiences, to promote a series of blues concerts, to research and col- lect blues data, to maintain continu- ous communication with blues musi- cians and persons interested in the blues, to share materials and informa- tion with individuals and organiza- tions and to establish a blues muse- um. Canada The Mercey Brothers, Ray, Lloyd and Larry, have opened their new six- teen and eight track studio in Elmira, Ontario. The successful RCA record- ing group, who has walked off with RPM Juno Awards (1966, 1969, 1970, 1971, 1972) at Country Group of The Year, built the studio, primarily for its own use. Pressure from artists and groups locally as well as from Toronto and Western Canada as well as from the Atlantic Provinces would indicate the trio is in the recording studio business whether they want to be or not. An open house (8) attract- ed industry people from any areas of Ontario. Engineer for the new setup is Ernie Lyons, a young technocrat who earned his lumps through several studios in Toronto. CKCK’s Johnny Sandison is still hard at work even though he has just celebrated his twentieth year as “morning mayor”- of the popular Regina Radio station. Most of the town turned out for the big day in- cluding the Mayor who proclaimed Nov. 14 as “Johnny Sandison Day.” Gary & Dave, an Axe recording unit that broke into international fame with “Could You Ever Love Me Again” will have their song covered by twelve year old Michel Lesage. The French translation which comes out “Reste Encore Aupres De Moi” is by Jacqui Amar. Greg Hambleton, owner and producer at Axe, completed the vocal tracks at Studio Six and Tempo Studios in Montreal with final mixing at Toronto Sound in Toronto. Lorence Hud and his manager Paul Chesborough have decided to call it quits. The split is reported to have been amicable. Hud is currently showing chart strength with his new A&M deck, “Guilty Of Rock & Roll,” taken from his album, “Dancin’ In My Head.” The session was produced in Nashville by Norbert Putnam. The big chart news from A&M is Keith Hampshire with “Big Time Opera- tor.” The single is very close to cracking the top of Canadian charts. A&M’s promo people are giving this one the final heave-ho to take it over the top. Terry Jacks and his wife Susan are doing it to the charts and this time with their own label— Gold Fish. Ter- ry’s got “Seasons In The Sun,” while his wife has “I Thought Of You Again.” The Stampeders are running away with charts. Their single, “Running Wild” has made strong moves up the chart but their album, “From The Fire” has become the top selling album at Quality Records. Maria Muldaur is receiving a break with her single, “Midnight In The Oasis” as well as the album under her own name. CHUM-FM jumped on the single first and WEA have now given an extra push which seems to be showing signs of breaking across Canada. WEA very busy right now with Alice Cooper, Mothers Of Inven- tion, Emerson Lake & Palmer and Grateful Dead. The company publishes the music of Jan Rado’s “Poppa’s side of the bed”, which is doing well in the USA. Jean Kluger is very active on the Belgian market. Both a Christmas single and LP by Will Tura have been released. Further there are new sin- gles and LP’s by top Flemish art- ists such as John Terra and Marva. Polydor has a big hit with The Hollies’ “The day that Curly Billy”. Still very successful in Belgium is David Cassidy. His young female fans are delighted with his new LP “Dreams are nuthin’ more than wishes”. Tnelco rush-released the British number 1 hit “My coo ca choo” by Alvin Stardust. Alvin was in Belgium for TV-shots. “My coo ca choo” was released on Ariola. Fonior released the new Gilbert O’Sullivan record “Why oh why oh why”. Since the film “Lady sings the blues” starring Diana Ross will be seen in Belgium, there are many re- quests for original recordings of Billie Holiday. On the Black Elephant label Fonior released three LP’s “Broadcast performances”. CBS-Artone reports that The Philly Sound got to Holland and Bel- gium. On Dec. 15 in Antwerp and on Dec. 18 in Amsterdam there is a performance with Billy Paul, The O’Jays, The Intruders. On that oc- casion new LP’s by Spiritual Con- cept, The Three Degrees, Harold Mel- vin & The Blue Notes, Billy Paul, Yellow Sunshine, The O’Jays and The Intruders have been released. Very popular throughout Europe is the Dutch singer Albert West. Lie spe- cializes in re-recording older Ameri- can hits. His new single hit is the old Paul Anka standard “Put your head on my shoulder”. Albert recorded an album with new version of among others “When”—“Send me the pil- low”—“Ginny come lately”—“Are you sure”—“Roses are red” “Sheilo”—-“Tell Laura I love her” “A lonely boy”;—“Oh Carol”—“Sealed with a kiss”—“I’m gonna knock on your door”. Japan Radio Pop Awards Listed Carpenters: Best Single, LP TOKYO —- The hit research commit- tees of all of Japan’s civil radio com- panies (34 in all) have chosen the winners of the annual pop music awards. All records released between Dec., 1972 and Nov., 1973 were eligi- ble for selection. At the award ceremonies held at the Hotel-New-Japan, Dec. 4, prizes were pesented to the Carpenters for best single (“Yesterday Once More”) and best album (“Nov/ And Then,” both released by A&M/King); Michel Polnareff for top male vocalist (on Epic/CBS-Sony) ; Roberta Flack for top female vocalist (on Atlantic/War- ner-Pioneer) ; the Carpenters for best vocal group (on A&M/King); Albert Hammond for top new male vocalist (on Epic/CBS-Sony); Suzi Quatro for top new female vocalist (on Odeon/- Toshiba-EMI) ; Raspberries (on Capi- CBS Int’l Gets Rights To Ian Hit NEW YORK — CBS International Music Publishing has obtained Sub- publishing rights for most of the world to the recent Roberta Flack single, “Jessie,” have been bought by CBS international Music Publishing. Written by Janis Ian, the song fol- lows Ms. Flack’s recent hit, “Killing Me Softly,” which was also sub- pubfished in parts of the world by CBS International. CBS also reports that Charles Aznavour has written lyrics to “Jessie” for release in France and that local cover versions of the song are being prepared by CBS Int’l affiliates around the world. Mexican Execs Meet w / Mogul NEW YORK — Currently visiting New York is Mario Freidberg, music publisher and recording entrepreneur here for discussions with his associ- ate, Ivan Mogull, and his attorney, Michael Gusik, as well as Mario Wil- son of Discos Capitol, and Sergio Licon of Musart Records. tol/Toshiba-EMI) and Stories (on Kama Sutra/Columbia) for best new group; Paul McCartney & Wings for best movie title song, “Live And Let Die” ( Apple/Toshiba-EMI) ; and Deo- dato for best instrumental, “Also Sprach Zarathustra” (on CTI/King). Nippon Columbia To Re-Structure TOKYO — Nippon Columbia Co. held its regular shareholder conference for the 120th term, Nov. 29, at the firm’s head office in Tokyo to settle the period’s accounts. Takami Shobochi, president of the company, said at the meeting, “Thanks to the efforts of all company members and dealers, the company’s debt has been reduced to 500,000,000 yen ($1,780,000). We will strive to eliminate this debt entirely in the next term. Japan’s record industry is now in a difficult situation due to the critical shortage of PVC resin. So we are appealing to the Japanese gov- ernment along with our competitors to regulate our supply g-radually. In line with industry trends, we have decided to reconstruct our operation as soon as feasibly possible.” Garrett-Kapps To Produce The Cats AMSTERDAM — Dutch band the Cats, will be recording their next al- bum in Los Angeles, Jan. 1974, to be produced by the Snuff Garrett-Al Kapps team. The Cats, a Bovema Holland act, have been together for 10 years and during the last 12 months hit the charts all over Europe, Japan, Malaya, New Zealand, and Israel. In Holland alone the Cats have 15 gold singles and 8 golden albums. Their single “Let’s dance” sold over 2 mil- lion copies in Europe. Garrett-Kapps are to record an al- bum including 6 older Cats titles to be re-arranged and re-produced and also to include 4 or 6 original songs from American composers. In the U.S. the Cats are represented by Fantasy Rec- ords. The album is projected to be the break-through for the Cats in the U.S. and U.K., as well as celebrate the group’s tenth anniversary. Dolls Score In Euro Markets CHICAGO — The New York Dolls have just returned from a sold out three week tour of Europe, highlight- ed by a near-riot at the Olympia in Paris with mob scenes at the Para- disio in Amsterdam and Biba’s in London. The two shows at Biba’s sold out within 24 hours of ticket availa- bility, and marked the first rock con- certs ever presented in that venue. The tour was spearheaded by Irwin Steinberg, president of Phonogram, Inc., and David Hofstede, manager of pop artist promo for Phonogram. In- ternational, in conjunction with Doll- house, Inc., representatives Marty Thau, Steve Leber, and David Krebs. The actual dates were set by Doll- house Inc. and MAM Agency rep- resentatives Lindsey Brown. LP Success The New York Dolls have generat- ed much interest overseas, evidenced DOLLS by the fact that their debut album was the number one import record before European release, according to Virgin Records import charts. Major cover stories in Melody Maker, Sounds, and Disc magazines in En- gland heraled the group’s arrival. A press conference at Blake’s Hotel greeted the Dolls on their first day in London. This tour was the second En- glish trek for the Dolls, but their first of the continent. Their debut album, “New York Dolls,” was released prior to the group’s arrival in England and the continent. During the tour there were several major radio and television appear- ances, including a live broadcast on Radio Luxemburg beamed throughout Europe, a one hour TV special on French Bataclon, plus national televi- sion appearances in Germany, En- gland, Holland and Belgium. The Dolls also made a special appearance at the Star Club in Hamburg for the German press, radio, and television people. “The expansion of the New York Dolls audience was very gratifying to Dollhouse Inc.,” stated Thau. “The tour was a success with the audiences and the European press giving the Dolls near-unanimous rave reviews.” The year’s end marks the six-month anniversary of the Dolls as recording artists. Their first LP was released in Aug. to coincide with the start of a three month, cross-country tour of the U.S. climaxed by their much- publicized special Halloween con- cert/party at the Waldorf Astoria in New York. Cash Box/R&B News Report E & B INGREDIENTS—"That's The Sound That Lonely Makes” is the new single from the Tavares LP on Capitol. But, for an LP cut that is really sayin’ something, check out, “Hello Little Girl” . . . Also, the correct title of the Kool & The Gang LP cut that is getting lotsa play action is, "Hollywood Swinging” . . . Concerning Kool & The Gang, Henry Nash at Queens Booking Corp. says that the Gang, Millie Jackson and RCA’s New Birth are getting priority attention for '74. Nash says these three acts are heading in new directions as far as book- ings, etc. . . . Now that the Holiday season is over, and many among us are slowly recovering from being a little tore up, it’s again time to get down to the business at hand. ‘Tis true that '73 was one heluva year. Despite all the '73 problems, black artists continued to make headway in many areas, including album and single sales. And, proper credit has to be given to those dedicated cats male and female in black radio who have struggled and survived thus far in serving blacks in their respective communities. Planting the seed that serves the need is what black radio is about. It is the dedication of such people as: E. Rodney Jones, Jerry Bolding, Al Gee and Johnny Jones, to mention a few, who have, through the years, kept many talented black artists alive. They have also laid the groundwork for the future Frankie Crockers. Unfortunately, many blacks who are qualified are often not given the opportunities to succeed (or fail) nevertheless, qualified blacks (and this goes for any qualified individ- ual) should be entitled to prove that they can indeed serve the needs of the community. After all, isn’t it the aware disc jockey who knows the street who works the record hops and does his thing at the discos—isn’t this the guy or gal who knows what is happening. There are many who really care. Those who are for real really care. Would it make sense to have Golda Meir running for Mayor of Cairo? . . . Sparkie Martin (Avco promo) held a swinging New Years Eve party. The party apartment was a total sea of grovin’ dancers because Sparkie kept the music in the groove. Main Ingredient dropped in after their Apollo stint. G. Fitz-Bartley and Rod Bristow dropped in. The affair broke up at dawn. As usual, it was a Sparkie (Sparkling Event) . . . The NATRA convention will be held at the Century Plaza in Los Angeles the third weekend in August. Start making your plans now. This convention should be one of the most significant of all. It takes your support. You now have sufficient time to make plans and to eliminate objections (if you’re from the East Coast) about the length of the trip. Details will be forthcoming . . .
