Originally produced by Manfred Eich- er for the West German ECM label, these Ip’s have already received rave reviews in the European and Ameri- can press. Chick Corea’s “Piano Improvisa- tions Volume One” (ECM//Polydor 1014) consists of “fragile, mesmer- ising, utterly beautiful” solo piano performances according to England’s Melody Maker. MM went on to call Piano Improvisations “one of the most sensitive, delicate, inventive solo piano albums ever made.” Down Beat gave the album five stars, its highest rating. Record World named “Piano Improvisations” “the best jazz record of 1971” despite the fact that it was then unavailable in this country. Even the grand piano, furnished by ECM for the recording, received a rave: Canada’s Coda magazine said, “the quality of the instrument impresses with the release of every note, imbues each chord with caloric richness, re- sponds to the slightest suggestion of movement.” Vibraphonist Gary Burton has been a trend-setter, a poll-winner, and a best-selling recording artist since his memorable first quartet introduced guitarist Larry Coryell and triggered the jazz /rock fusion movement of the sixties. Burton’s “The New Quartet” (ECM/Polydor 1030) is an astounding tour-de-force by four incomparable young musicians. Abraham Laboriel breaks new ground on the electric bass; Melody Maker emphasizes that “Laboriel sounds like a major artist in the making—throughout the album there’s almost a wall-of-sound rhythm section with astonishing bass work dominating the pace and, indeed, the energy of the music.” Guitarist Michael Goodrick is subtly melodic and inventive, and drummer Harry Blazer bridges the gap between rock and jazz rhythms with ease. Original compositions by Chick Corea, Keith Jarrett, and Carla Bley also con- tribute to the importance of this ex- ceptional Ip. As Melody Maker said, it’s “the best Gary Burton album in a long while.” Robin Kenyatta’s “Girl From Mar- tinique” (ECM/Polydor 1008) features “a superb and unique reedman” (Down Beat) performing a program of bright, lively originals, supported by a gifted Euro-American rhythm section. Kenyatta’s recent jazz/reggae “crossover” and his popular version of “Last Tango in Paris” have won him many new fans, who will be de- lighted with his lyrical, personally- inflected alto and flute improvisations on “Girl From Martinique. The title tune combines singing flute solos with Wolfgang Dauner’s futuristic electric keyboards; “Thank You Jesus” is a stirring, unaccompanied alto solo in a spiritual vein. American drummer Fred Braceful and Norwegian bass virtuoso Arild Andersen complete the rhythm section. “Ruta and Daitya” (ECM/Polydor 1021) is an album of duets by pianist Keith Jarrett and percussionist Jack DeJohnette, who first played together in Charles Lloyd’s original quartet and were later reunited in the Miles Davis group featured on “Bitches Brew” and “Live at the Fillmore.” With Jarrett, described in Rolling Stone as “the most important new keyboard stylist in jazz since McCoy Turner and Bill Evans,” doubling on electric piano, organ, and flute, and DeJohnette—“the master of poly- rhythmic funk”—playing percussion instruments from around the world, “Ruta and Daitya” achieves an im- Dr. Martin Luther King, (Major Events ATLANTA — The largest and most significant celebrations ever of the Birthday Anniversary of the late Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. are being planned across the nation for January 15. It will be the sixth consecutive year in which millions of persons from all walks of life will observe “Martin Luther King Day” in tribute to the life and work of the slain human rights leader. In his home city of Atlanta, gala Benefit Concert for The Martin Luth- er King, Jr. Center for Social Change will be followed by an Ecumenical Service, a Celebration March and mass Community Rally. In Los Ange- les, another star-studded benefit will be held, while a special observance can be seen nationwide on CBS televi- sion’s broadcast of the National Bas- ketball Association All-Star game from Seattle. Community groups in Washington, D C., will be pressing Congress to make Dr. King’s birthday an official national holiday. In New York City, the Council of Churches and the King Center will sponsor ac- tivities in support of local human rights organizations. And so it goes across America. While the national holiday legisla- tion is pending in Congress, masses of people everywhere already person- ally declare the date to be their own to honor one of history’s greatest leaders. The result has been, in each year since Dr. King’s assassination. A Nation In Tribute Across the nation on January 15, people and their communities will ob- serve the Birthday Anniversary in many ways. Montgo- mery to Memphis.” Hundreds of schools, community groups, churches and television stations have shown this authenic account of Dr. King’s life and the Movement he led. HOLLYWOOD: TONY ORLANDO—CHASING PHONIES FROM THE BOOM—BOOM ROOM Almost 13 years ago, Cash Box described Tony Orlando as “one of the hottest young finds of 1961.” Tony’s records, “Halfway to Paradise” and “Bless You” were high on the charts, in th.e company of songs by such superstars as the Jive Five, Chubby Checker and Rick and the Keens. But hit records and superstars tend to be very transient phenomena in an industry that uses the term "ancient history” to denote anything that may have happened more than five years ago. Tony Orlando remained in the music business, though, not as a performer but in publishing. Eventually, he became a vice president of CBS’ Blackwood Music, working with artists like James Taylor, Taj Mahal and Blood Sweat and Tears. It was a good job, and Tony might have remained there if two producer friends, Hank Medress and Dave Appel! had not come to him one day with a song titled “Candida.” “The whole thing was an accident,” said Tony. “They came to me asking what label I thought this track would be good for, never talking to me as the potential singer. I told them, Bell Records, because it was a single, a studio thing. Bell was the best singles-oriented company in the business at that time, and that seemed to be the best label to go to.” Medress took “Candida” to Bell Records’ president Larry Uttall, who bought it, but didn’t like the lead vocal that had been initially recorded. “So Hank came back to my office and said ‘considering that you used to cut with Carole King, and basically all the sounds that you used to cut were Drifters—kind of records—well, this is a very Drifterish-kind of song; would you mind doing a lead voice on it?” I said, “Yes, I would mind,” because I was working for Columbia Records and Bell was a competitor. I felt it would be a conflict of interest.” As it turned out, CBS didn’t object; Tony was persuaded to record “Candida” Records added backing voices by Telma Hopkins and Joyce Vincent, two singers that had worked extensively with Issac Hayes and many others. The company NEW YORK—BILLY PRESTON—THE CIRCLE REMAINS UNBROKEN One of the more remarkable coincidences in the rock business occurred when master composer/keyboard genius, Billy Preston wrote and recorded what was to become his second gold single which asked the musical question “Will It Go Round In Circles?” This in a sense has been prophetic for Billy because success has had him travelling the globe in circles, and the dizzying merry-go-round seems to have no intention of stopping to give him a rest. “I enjoy working," says Billy languidly lounging on his hotel room sofa, “and I get off on the enthusiasm of the audiences everywhere I play. That’s what gave me the idea for my second album title, “Music Is My Life.” For me, there’s no such thing as spare time or even vacation for that matter. I spend all my time writing or playing. In fact, last time the band and I took a holiday, we started getting edgy after a few days and before we knew it, we were back in the studio layin’ down tracks. I’m just not happy unless I’m working.” Knowing this would make it very easy for Billy’s personal physician to prescribe a cure for depression. But that condition hardly seems a likely possibili- ty when you take a look at where the artist has been and the company he’s been keeping. Starting in Sept., ’73, Billy toured Europe with the Stones, opening for them with his own band and then, after a respite of a half-hour, returning to play keyboard with Mick and co. “All the dates were enjoyable,” muses Billy, reflect- ing back on the intensity of the Stones’ tour, but I think the gigs in Wembley may have been the best. It’s kind of hard to tell in most places because all you can see are the first few rows, and you can usually assume that those people are the real die-hard fans who waited in line for hours to get tickets.” Billy did all the keyboard work for the Stones on the tour and impressed them enough to elicit some interesting responses. “For openers,” says Billy, “it was a family kind of tour. Everybody hung out together. In Hamburg, Mick Taylor (guitarist with the Stones) did my whole show with me without making a mistake and kept coming back to play throughout the rest of the tour. During the whole Tony Orlando And Dawn Billy Preston arbitrarily dubbed the group “Dawn” and released it. “Three months later,” related Tony, “I pick up the Gavin sheet and I see ’Smash of the Week—Candida, by Dawn.' Now you have to understand that I didn’t even know what the name of the group was. So when I picked up the sheet, I thought that maybe I had published the song, because the title was familiar. I called my secretary and said ‘look through the catalog and see if we have this song.’ She didn’t find it and I thought that I was mistaken— I mean, I had completely forgotten that I had cut that track. The first time I sang it and the last time I saw it was in the studio, that one time. Later, I got a call from Hank and he says “We got a smash.” I said ‘we do? with what?’ and he said ‘with that record that we cut.’ Then I put it all together—“Candida,” Gavin, Dawn, right, we got a smash.” “But I still wasn’t about to quit my job, because I’ve seen hit records come and go. I wasn’t about to get out of a position that I’d worked very hard to get to.” Tony did agree, however, to make a follow-up record, “Knock Three Times,” for which Telma Hopkins, Joyce Vincent and the name Dawn were again used. “Knock Three Times” sold six million copies world-wide, leaving Bell Records in the unusual position of having two straight number one singles and no artist signed to the label. With a little more persuasion, Bell signed Tony Orlando, Joyce Vincent and Telma Hopkins, retained the name Dawn, and set out to begin promotional tours, etc. “To my surprise,” said Tony, we had a problem, You see, there was a nine month period between the time that “Candida” first made it and I was signed to Bell. In the meantime, a lot of small-time booking agencies had invented bogus Dawns. They knew from reading the trades that I was still with Blackwood Music, that I wasn’t on the road performing as Dawn or anything else. They knew that if they booked a group called Dawn into the boom-boom room somewhere, nobody was going to know the difference. Nobody had ever seen a picture of Dawn and we were by no means famous, facially. Now you can’t copywrite a name—anybody can appear as Dawn, legally. The only thing that you can stop them from doing is claiming that they had recorded those songs.” “At one point, there were 14 phony Dawns playing gigs around the world and we couldn’t work. The booking agencies would say 'why should we want to book the real group at five thousand dollars a night when we can get a phony group for five hundred?’ Very, very vicious—and I began to get pissed off. The two most precious things to ail of us in this business are our reputation and our signature; and those groups were wrecking my reputation., At that point, I decided to commit myself to Dawn 100 percent, and I worked at a total loss, just trying to build up a good name as a performing act. It was a matter of (Cont’d on p. 37) time we were on the road, both Mick Taylor and Mick Jagger got together with me to jam and we collaborated on a lot of stuff.” Exactly what ‘stuff’ Billy is referring to will be revealed when he finishes and releases his fourth LP on A&M Records. “It’s going to be full of rock and soul cuts and both Taylor and Jagger are going to play on it,” says Billy, knowing that this little bit of help will obviously be an enormous plus for the entire project. "There’ll be a lot of potential singles off the new album,” smiles Billy, “maybe even a song called ‘Creature Feature.’ All together, I guess we will put out about ten new tunes.” Naturally Billy's not going to walk into the studio cold, having just come off an American tour which took him to places like Chicago, Providence, Pittsburgh, and Detroit. But then again, we told you Billy isn’t comfortable being idle. “Actual- ly,” he says, “we cut this tour short so we could spend a week in Munich finishing up the Stones’ next album. Turn about being fair play, it’s only natural that Jagger would offer his services as a rhythm guitarist on Billy’s next LP with Taylor spicing up the project with his unique lead guitar work. One thing is certain, Billy Preston will always be able to count on the world’s finest musicians to lend him a helping hand because he has never said no to a friend in need. On his recent A&M LP, for instance, he augmented his expansive sound by utilizing the talents of two other fine keyboard artists, Kenneth Lupper and Manuel Kellough, as well as David T. Walker on drums and Dennis Coates on bass. Billy did his own guitar work for the album entitled, “Everybody Likes Some Kind Of Music.” But perhaps the true essence of Billy Preston is his stage act and his own modest accounts of European reaction to his material gives a good impression of what he’s really like. "We started each set with “Daytripper,” whcih was an immediate bridge for them (European audiences), and then did “Will It Go Round In Circles?”, “Space Race,” “Everybody Likes Some Kind of Music,” and closed with “Outta Space.” Probably the song that drew the most response in terms of audience participation was “The Bus Is Cornin'.” On that one, people from about fifty rows back came running up to the stage and started carryin’ on like there was no tomorrow.” With all this happening on stage, it’s hard to believe Billy has time for the studio, let alone other projects, but within a span of two months he will have appeared on four major TV shows, “American Bandstand,” "Midnight Special,” “Soul Train,” and “New Year’s Rockin’ Eve ’74.” In the process are negotiations with Don Kirshner for an appearance on “Rock Concert” and plans for a Spring tour. Billy Preston is definitely a man on the move. Is he going round in circles? You bet, in ever higher spirals that are making his name as popular as his music, and that’s saying something, david budge. 30 Cash Box — January 12, 1974

HOLLYWOOD — - J * Croce’s “Bad, Bad Leroy Brown,” Roberta Flack’s “Killing Me Sorely With His Song,” Charlie’ Rich’s "Behind Closed Car y Simon’s “You’re So Vain” and Stevie Wonder’s “You Are the Sunshine Of M; l ife” have been voted ; his year’s Grammy Awards Record of the Year honors. According to results announced last Week by the National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences, whose members’ votes select the nominees Mom SIS and winners of the recording field’s most coveted awards, Wonder and Rich, along with the Misses Flack, Simon and Bette Midler, top the list of nominees in the pop field for ma- jor honors in the 16th annual Gram- my competition, while Leonard Bern- stein and Arthur Rubinstein stand out in the classical field. The Misses Flack and Midler, along with Rich and Wonder, join Paul Si- mon (no relation to Carly) as nomi- nees for the Album of ^the Year award, respectively for “Killing Me Softly,” “The Divine Miss M.,” “Be- hind Closed Doors,” “Innervisions” and “There Goes Rhymin’ Simon.” Wonder Leads Nominees Wonder has garnered the most nom- inations—six in all—four as per- former and two as composer. His “You Are the Sunshine Of My Life” was picked as Song of the Year, as were Ms. Simon’s “You’re So Vain” and “Behind Closed Doors,” “Killing Me Softly With His Song” and “Tie a Yellow Ribbon ’Round the Ole Oak Tree.” Ms. Midler was also nominated as Best New Artist of the Year along with Emir Deodato, Maureen McGov- ern, Marie Osmond and Barry White. She and the Misses Flack and Simon share the Best Female Pop Per- formance nominations with Anne Murray and Diana Ross; Croce, Paul Simon" and Wonder, plus Perry Como and Elton John, are finalists in the Best Male Pop Performance category, while Rich has also been nominated m the Country field in which Kris Kris- tofferson was voted a finalist as per- former and composer in three differ- ent categories. Classical Nominees Among classical artists, Bernstein has been nominated four times and Rubinstein thrice, including one each for Classical Album of the Year, the former for his conducting of Bizet’s “Carmen,” the latter for his piano performance of Rachmaninoff’s “Con- certo No. 2 in C Minor,” on which he is accompanied by the Philadelphia Orchestra conducted by Eugene Or- mandy. Ormandy is one of the four- teen classical artists receiving more than one nomination. Others are Vladimir Ashkenazy, Janet Baker, Pierre Boulez, Julian Bream. Lorin Maazel, Seiji Ozawa, Andre Previn, Leontyne Price, Gunther Schuller, Georg Solti and Herbert von Kara- jan. In addition, many of the ton nomi- nated recordings have been cited for engineering, arraneing, producing and other craft awards among the 46 Grammy categories that also include jazz, rhythm and blues, gospel, sacred, children’s, comedy, ethnic and spoken word performances along with numerous composing awards. This week, voting members of the Academy will be receiving their bal- lots, which will be tabulated by the independent accounting firm of Haskins and Sells. Winners will be announced on the evening of Satur- day, March 2nd, during the Academy’s annual television special, “The Gram- my Awards Show,” telecast live over the entire CBS network. The Awards show is telecast live from the In Concert Theatre in Holly- wood, and will honor the artists and music that are voted best in the fields of Pop/Rock, Soul and Country by a public opinion poll. Dick Clark is ex- ecutive producer with Bill Lee pro- ducing. John Moffitt will direct; Ray Klausen has been set as art director and designer of the award. In announcing the hosts, Clark noted, “It seems appropriate that three distinguished members of the musid community should represent the three major areas of contem- porary music interest.” Roger Miller, will be the represen- tative for the Country category. Today at age 37, he has written well over 300 songs, including New Technique To Launch 5 TV Specials NEW YORK — Producer Yuri Za- bran will launch a new broadcasting technique combining TV and stereo sound via five one hour TV specials. The new electronic process provides high quality 2 channel stereo to any local FM station in association with a live or taped network TV broadcast. The new technique does away with the necessity of individual audio tapes as utilized currently with ABC’s “In Concert,” and also precludes the pos- sibility of the FM sound being out of sync with the picture. Zabran will shortly announce the content of the five specials each to be aired at the rate of one a month with a target date the latter part of this year. The twenty-eight year old producer is also syndicating the forthcoming quadra- phonic rock series, “Weekend Rock” over approximately 150 FM stereo outlets. What started as a million and a half dollar “showplace” recording studio called The Sound Pit in At- lanta, has since burdgeoned into one of the biggest new independent rec- ord companies in the country, as General Recording Corp. GRC Records, under the aegis of Michael Thevis, has proven a launch- ing pad for many new acts during its first year of operation boasting $150,000 budgets on heretofore un- known talents, like Ripple. The re- sult, reported Thevis, is that out of the 12 initial singles released last year, 10 of them made the charts and/or received considerable airplay. Thevis indicated that this kind of momentum is the reason for his com- pany’s decision to open New York and London offices in addition to those Schmitzerle Is WB Exec Dir Of Label Mgmt BURBANK — Warner Bros. Records, Inc. has announced the promotion of Don Schmitzerle to the new position of executive director of label manage- ment. Schmitzerle will be involved with all artists and managers recording for Warner/Reprise and affiliated labels, introducing new artists to the work- ings of the company and providing these artists (as well as already well- established artists) with a continuity of contact through their careers with the company. Just as importantly, equal stress will be placed by Schm- itzerle and his department on imple- menting the goals of the artists them- selves. In making the announcement Mo Ostin, chairman of Warner Bros. Rec- ords, said, “Don Schmitzerle’s experi- ence as general manager of Reprise Records has proved a boon not only to the company, but also to all of the artists with whom he has been associ- ated. He, as well as general manager David Herscher, will now be able to extend the same kind of effective om- budsman role to all of our artists.” The label said that Schmitzerle’s promo is a further step in Warner Brothers’ emphasis upon service to its artists. “We have always felt,” Ostin commented, “that one of the major things setting Warners apart from other companies is that our artists are able to come to us with their hopes and their complaints, and get a sympathetic hearing and fast action. This will increasingly be the role of Don Schmitzerle.” Schmitzerle joined Warner Bros. Records in 1965 as a local promo man in Detroit, and has risen steadily through the company from that time. In his new position, Schmitzerle will report directly to Ostin and Joe Smith, president of Warner Bros. Records. Schmitzerle 3 %w»> $ & ’A *3S~2 I dy in Atlanta, Nashville, and L.A. GRC’s actual record production had been slightly delayed due to a. serious motor. :ident Thevis suffered a few months ago. On cratches at Cash Box Hollywood offices last week, he let on that his accident had been so critical that doctors told him he’d er walk again. However, unabated optimism has enabled him to dispel the doctor’s prognosis, to recuperate, and now to ready 12 singles and five albums for Feb. release. This is about as much product released by GRC dur- ing its entire first year of activity. Fields, Jeffries To Label Other expansions include the ap- pointments of Oscar Fields and Jim Jeffries to the marketing divisions of the Atlanta based entertainment con- glomerate. Fields has been named vp of marketing responsible for rec- ord sales of product on GRC and its AWARE labels. Jeffries has become national marketing manager. He will coordinate the company’s record pro- motion. Prior to this, both Fields and Jeffries had been affiliated with Bell Records. They join GRC’s growing roster of executives which include Buz Wil- burn, president of their distribution corporation; Bobby Weiss, interna- tional licensing consultant, and Dee Ervin, who heads up the West Coast offices. Thevis will be announcing shortly the names of those set to run his Nashville, New York, and Lon- don offices. Film/ Artist Ties It was learned that many of the artists signed to the GRC labels will also be applying their talents to Thevis’ Modem Films. That latter comnany has just finished “Poor Pret- ty Eddie,” starring Leslie Uggams, Shelley Winters, and Michael Christ- ian. The film and a soundtrack (con- sisting of songs sung and written by GRC acts) will be released this spring. Leslie Uggams will sing the title song. Joe Hinton, another artist signed to the record division, has com- pleted a song for Modem Film’s “Hannah Mae,” and may also get a chance to star in it. Thevis plans on making this as a television movie of the week which would spin off into a series based on black history. Fields, Jeffries Grammy Corrections HOLLYWOOD — Following are cor- rections by the Record Academy (NARAS) to the list of Grammy Award nominations announced last week. In the category Best Engineered Recording, Non-Classical, the nomi- nated engineers for Stevie Wonder’s album, “Innervisions,” are Robert Margouleff and Malcolm Cecil. In the category Best Instrumental Composition, the composers nomi- nated for “Hocus Pocus” are Jan Akkerman and Thijs Van Leer. Winners will be announced on Sat., Mar. 2, as part of the Annual Gram- my Awards telecast to be aired by CBS -TV with Andy Williams hosting. Dual Mgmt At Cohn, Mattis To Key Posts NEW YORK — Elliot Goldman, ad- ministrative vice president at CBS Records, has announced two appoint- ments at April/Blackwood, CBS Rec- ords’ publishing wing. Marvin Cohn has been appointed to the position of vice president of Administration and Marvin Mattis has been named vice president of creative affairs for April/Blackwood. These appoint- ments create a dual management structure for the publishing company which will now have a major exec based in New York (Cohn) and in Mattis, Cohn Alvini, Levine Named UA Chiefs Of Mkting, Promo HOLLYWOOD—Mike Ifipton, senior vice president of United Artists Rec- ords, has announced the appointments of Dan Alvino and Eddie Levine as director of marketing and national promo director, respectively. Levine was most recently director of sales and promo for Blue Note, the jazz division of United Artists. He had served as national promotion director of UA several years ago. Alvino has been with United Art- ists for eight years, beginning as a local promo man in Miami, later be- coming branch manager in that office and then moving on to become branch manager in Atlanta. He was then to become general manager of Sunset Records and was one of the original sales managers in Los Angeles when that program was instituted. He later became vice president and general manager of UDC in Los Angeles. Reporting to Alvino will be east- ern marketing director Dave Skol- nick, who has been with the company seven years, southwest and midwest marketing director Jack Mesler, with UA for eight years, and west coast marketing director Charlie Bratnober, associated with the company for five years. It was also announced that Jack Hakim has been named West Coast Promotion Director. Jere Hausfater will continue to oversee Blue Note Records and will be assistant to Le- vine. Alvini, Levine Meisel Indie Co. NEW YORK—Lenny Meisel, vet pro- mo figure, has opened an indie promo firm, located here at 311 W. 43rd St. c/o Raydell Publications; telephone (212) 586-5370. "Meisel was formerly national LP promo director at Lon- don, and, more recently, director of New York promo for Polydor. April/Blackwood Los Angeles (Mattis). The two men will be working closely together providing each coast with both creative and administrative leader- ship. Goldman Comments In commenting on the new dual management of April/Blackwood, Goldman said: “The dual management concept has been adopted because of the enormous growth enjoyed by April/Blackwood during the past year, an increase in both revenues and profits of over 100%. Mattis and Cohn will give us the strong management team needed to sustain and accelerate the company’s continuing growth.” Cohn will be responsible for the over- all business and administrative direc- tion including negotiation and appro- val of specific business terms for ac- quiring new songwriters, copyrights and catalogues, the negotiation of mechanical and performance royalties and coordination of the music print activities of the company. He will also be responsible for the develop- ment and monitoring of Aoril/Black- wood’s financial affairs. He will re- port directly to Goldman. Cohn joined CBS in 1965 as a financial analyst and was made direc- tor of A&R administration in 1969. He later added greater responsibilities to his job and became director of A&R administration and music pub- lishing. He has been instrumental in the recent reorganization of the A&R administratioon department, and is responsible for its overall efficiency on behalf of Columbia, Epic and the Columbia Custom Labels. Marvin Mattis will provide overall creative leadership for the music pub- lishing company, including direct re- sponsibility for and approval of the signing of new songwriters, the ac- quisition of new copyrights and cata- loges and the development of the songwriting careers of those writers currently signed to April/Blackwood. Mattis will be also be responsible for directing the professional staff of the publishing companies to obtain max- imum exposure for April/Blackwood’s copyrights. He will report directly to Goldman. Mattis joined CBS after 10 years of experience in the music publishing business. He has worked for six years with Screen Gems-Columbia Music, where he held the position of General Professional Manager. While at Screen Gems, Mattis worked closely with the well-known songwriters Car- ole King, Gerry Goffin, David Gates, Barry Mann, Cynthia Weil, and Mac Davis. Recently, Mattis was general professional manager with Robbins Music. He is familar with many as- pects of music publishing, with a heavy concentration on casting and songwriter evaluations. CTI/Kudu Debuts Three New LP’s NEW YORK — CTI/KUDU Records has announced the release of three new albums, Ron Carter’s “All Blues” Joe Farrell’s “Penny Arcade” and Johnny Hammond’s “Higher Ground.” “All Blues” is Carter’s second al- bum as a solo artist for the label. He has composed four original selections for the LP, “A Feeling,” “Light Blue,” “117 Special,” and “Rufus.” Two more cuts, “Will You Still Be Mine,” and Miles Davis’ title composi- tion comprise the remainder of the pieces heard. Ron Carter is a recent winner of readers’ polls in two national publica- tions. “Penny Arcade” marks Joe Far- rell’s return to the studio since he was featured on the latest Santana album. Surrounding him are Herbie Hancock, Steve Gadd, Herb Bushier, Joe Beck, and Don Alias. Johnny Hammond’s ‘‘Higher Ground” was arranged and conducted by Bob James, and features many CTI/KUDU artists, among them Ron Carter, Hank Crawford, and George Benson. All three albums, were produced by Creed Taylor and are released simul- taneously in the U.S. and Canada, “All Blues” on stereo LP, 8 track and cassette; “Penny Arcade” on stereo and quad LP, 8 track and reel to reel, and stereo cassette; and “Higher Ground” on stereo and quad LP and 8 track, and stereo cassette. Tara Rushes LP On ‘Mocedades’ NEW YORK — Due to the success of Tara Records’ first release, “Eres Tu,” by Mocedades, the company is rush-releasing the group’s first LP, “Mocedades.” A 3D Package NEW YORK — Grand Fnnk Rail- road, with nine consecutive gold LP’s to their credit, will release their 10th album “Shinin’. On” in mid-March. The title will introduce an industry first in packaging concepts; a pair of 3D glasses will punch out of the cov- er for viewing of both an inserted 3D poster and the album cover itself. The actual 3D process is said to be the highest quality ever printed. The album was conceived of and designed by GFR manager Andrew Cavaliere and creative consultant Lynn Goldsmith. The graphic design on the cover was illustrated by Neal Adams. Adams recreated Batman, created the Ben Casey series, Son- O’God, Dracula, Deadman, Archie, Jughead and many other comic book heroes, and has received the drama desk award, the pioneer illustrator award, the best dramatic artist award, etc. The “Shinin’ On” concept will also appear in Grand Funk’s live per- formances as the group lights up in the dark. The group is not devulging how this will be done, but they do promise it will happen starting with the opening date of their up-coming American tour the third week in March. The tour and production in- volved with Grand Funk’s show will be the biggest in the group’s four year history. Forthcoming tour plans i < will be announced shortly. Coryell: New LP NEW YORK — Larry Coryell, Van- guard recording artist, and new band The Eleventh House will appear at the National Educational Conference in Houston, Feb. 2. The nationwide convention of college booking rep- resentatives provides the first major showcase for the recently-formed group, whose Vanguard debut album ships next month. In addition to Coryell on guitar, the Eleventh House features Randy Brecker (formerly of Blood, Sweat & Tears, and Dreams) on trumpet; Mike Mandel on keyboards and synthe- sizer; Alphonse Mouzon (Weather Report, McCoy Tyner) on drums and Danny Trifan (Buzzy Linhart) on bass. In anticipation of the NEC and release of “The Eleventh House,” Vanguard and Eleventh House man- agers Vince Cirrineione and Tom Paine have mapped out an extensive advertising, sales and publicity cam- paign. Promotional materials, includ- ing bios, photos, stickers and book covers, will accompany the new LP in mailings to the press and media. Negotiations with a major booking agency, to be announced shortly, are currently under way, with a nation- wide tour projected for early spring. Aretha Franklin, Della Reese, the Jackson Five, the Dramatics Johnny Nash and the Cashears provided en- tertainment for the seventh annual gala event. Don Cornelius, acting as emcee, in- troduced awards in a variety of cate- gories, including Recording, Televi- sion, Motion Pictures and “Special Awards.” Stevie Wonder was the recipient, of three awards, two in the recording category for Best Album and Best Producer. He was also presented with a Special Award for “Music Innova- tor of the Seventies.” Other Awards were given as follows: Recording ALBUM: “Innervisions,” Stevie Won- der; PRODUCER: Stevie Wonder, “Innvervisions”; MALE VOCAL GROUP: War; FEMALE VOCAL GROUP: Pointer Sisters; COMBINA- TION VOCAL GROUP: (Tie) Gladvs Knight & Pips, Staple Singers; FE- MALE VOCALIST: (Tie) Roberta Flack. Carter; SPECIAL ACHIEVE- MENT Award for preservation of the blues: Johnny Taylor; SPECIAL CI- TATION: Raymond St. Jacques; SPECIAL AWARD: Frank Willis. Weldon McDougall Dir. of Publicity at Phila. Int’I PHILA — Kenny Gamble, co-owner and president of Philadelphia Interna- tional Records, has announced the ap- pointment of Weldon Arthur Mc- Dougall III to the position of direc- tor, artist relations and publicity. Philadelphia International is a Columbia Records Custom Label. McDougal will be responsible to Gamble for coordinating all press and information services for all Philadel- phia International Artists. He will work closely with the Columbia publi- city department in promoting artists, and will also work with individual artists in all phases of their creative and business affairs. McDougal began his career in the music business singing with a group called The Larks in the early fifties. In 1959 he first met Kenny Gamble, a friendship which he has kept through the years. In 1963, McDougal pro- duced the hit song “Yes I’m Ready” for Barbara Mason, and had his own record production company, Haw- thorne Publishing Co., which Gamble was a part of. In 1964, McDougal began a nine-year association with Motown Records, starting out as a local promotion man in Philadelphia and rising to the position of director of artist relations and special proj- ects. R & B INGREDIENTS— Bill Haywood (he was the music director at Station WOL in Washington, D. C.) has resigned from his position. The truth is! he is in need of a comparable position. The station has now embarked on the same format as that of WWRL in New York City. WOL, a station that has certainly been a dominant force in R & B for some 10 years, now is faced with, (it does appear, with the fact that it has been unable to find or develop, train a qualified black (in some ten years), or any man who really cares and understands what is cornin’ down, a man who is aware of the needs of the black audience. Bobby Bennett, Chuck Long and Carroll Hynson are other (back-to-work) on-the-air personalities who have been serving up the soul-power at the station for the Washington area residents. ... In the promotion areas of R & B music, black women are proving their mettle. Super gals, such as, Rowena Harris (national promo for All-Platinum Records) who has done her thing with the Moments release of “Sexy Mama”. Ellen Anderson (Polydor) who aids Joe Medlin, Nancy Pitts aiding Tom Draper at RCA are also exemplary of the new trend in promo. Gretta Hunter (promo with GRC) is a perfect ex- ample of what it’s all about. Many black women are doing super job on the radio front, such as, Wanda Ramos serving as Frankie Crocker’s assistant at WBLS-FM in NYC. One thing must be said about this new trend, and that is this—this is now the time for being—for real— the early BS era is over. It is an age of awareness and for-real individuality. The time is at hand! The unreal is being supplanted by the real, and this is especially true when it comes to black radio. Black radio for a black-white ratio (listening audience). If any- one does doubt this, sit down and spend a few moments with the truly for-real veterans in the record biz. Effie Smith (Stax); and Joe Evans (president of Carnival Records) can inform you. Joe is responsible for putting the Manhat- tans into the hit recording groove. Either one can enlighten the most unen- lightened. HOLLYWOOD — Cecil Holmes has joined Casablanca Records in Holly- wood as national vice president and general manager of R&B activities, according to Neil Bogart, president of the independent label. The Holmes—Bogart affiliation goes back nine (9) years to Cameo- Parkway when Bogart was national promotion representative, and Holmes national R&B director. The pair moved over to Buddah Records seven (7) years ago, and won numerous awards, earning thirty-six (36) gold records in that time. Bogart became co-ipresident of the label. Holmes, winner of the Bill Gavin award three years in a row as Record Executive of the Year, and the NA- TRA award, guided the careers of such artists as The Isley Brothers and numerous others. He was also instru- mental in signing Gladys Knight and the Pips. He supervised the recording careers of performers on the Buddah subsidiary labels, such as Sussex, Teaneck, Curtom and Hot Wax. His 1973 concept album, “Black Motion Picture Experience,” with the Cecil Holmes Soulful Sounds sold over 100,000 copies and Holmes him- self appeared on the TV commercial promoting the L.P. Holmes also did the “Music for Soulful Lovers” al- bum. In this re- snect, he will work closely with David Banks, national R&B director at War- ner Brothers, plus in artist relations. Al Green Strikes Fourth Gold Album NEW YORK — “Livin’ For You,” Al Green’s new Hi /London album, has been certified gold by the R.I.A.A. This is Green’s fourth gold album in less than two years. The others are “Let’s Stay Together,” “Pm Still In Love With You,” and “Call Me.” The now historic Al Green gold streak began in late ’71 with “Tired Of Being Alone.” Since then each suc- cessive single by Green has been cer- tified gold. A WORTHY CAUSE — Queen of The Most Holy Rosary, located in Roosevelt, LI., is operating an integrated school for youngsters through the 8th grade. The school is now forced to wage a fund raising campaign for the continuation of this school which has been serving the needs of the community. Donations, which are tax deductible, may be mailed to: QMHR, P.O. Box 344, Roosevelt, N.Y. 11595. A receipt will be returned. Anything you can do to help these children will be most appreciated. A concert is also being planned for March 2 and 3, to be held in the school auditorium which holds 700. Blinky To Reprise HOLLYWOOD — Soul artist Blinky Williams has signed an excusive re- cording contract with Reprise Rec- ords, it was announced today in Bur- bank by executive director—label management Don Schmitzerle and Mickey Stevenson, Ms. Williams’ manager. Blinky Williams was most recently heard in the film “Lady Sings the Blues” for which she recorded the song “Ain’t Nobody’s Business if I Do.” Prior to that she recorded for both Atlantic and Motown Records, the latter as a team with Edwin Starr, in addition to her own solo efforts. She has appeared with out- standing artists including the Temptations, Cannonball Adderly, The Four Tops, Flip Wilson, Quincy Jones and Sammy Davis Jr. Reprise plans to release Ms. Wil- liams most recent recording effort, with Stevenson producing, in the near future. NATRA AWARDS Dinner Mar. 9 NEW YORK—The Excellence Awards Dinner taking place March 9th, at the New York Hilton, is a combined ef- fort of the NATRA national, and Jack Walker Chapter. This important function is already receiving heavy response. The affair is to honor: Ben- jamin Hooks (FCC Commissioner); William ‘Boy’ Brown (who was pro- gram director in Houston) now para- lyzed. Joan Ganz Cooney (Sesame Street); Isaac Hayes; Michelle Clarke; Dick Gregory and the NY “Soul Show” (now off the air). Tickets for the function are as fol- lows; A table seating 10 is $750. In- dividual tickets are $75. The program is streamlined and it will be a highly entertaining event. Remember the price is tax deductible. It’s your din- ner so let’s have a big big turnout. CBS Records Sponsors Martin L. King, Jr., Benefit in Atlanta's ATLANTA — CBS Records recently sponsored a benefit concert in Atlanta on the occasion of Martin Luther King, Jr.’s 45th Birthday Anniver- sary. The concert, part of a two-day celebration hosted by Mrs. Coretta Scott King, the wife of the late Civil Rights leader, was held at Atlanta’s Omni Auditorium. Featured at the benefit, proceeds of which went to Martin Luther King, Jr. Center for Social Change, were: Epic Recording Group Sly and the Family Stone. Stax Recording Artist Omni Auditorium Albert King. Monument Recording Artist Maxine Weldon and Columbia Recording Artist Ramsey Lewis. Mrs. King presented each artist with a silver tray for their participation and gave an additional tray to Logan Westbrooks, director of special mar- kets for CBS Records, for his ef- forts in putting the entire show to- gether. Also cited by Mrs. King were Gloddard Lieberson, president, CBS/ Records Group, and Ii-win Segelstein, president of CBS Records, for their contribution to the affair. Participating Artists Get Awards ALL THAT’S JAZZ ‘Twofers’ Classics From Milestone BERKELEY — Milestone Records announces the release of six more re- issued “twofers,” jazz classics. In- cluded in the release are works by ’Thelonious Monk with John Coltrane, Wes Montgomery and friends. Mongo Santamaria, the Johnny Griffin Big Band, Coleman Hawkins, and a twofer featuring four drummers, Elvin Jones, Art Blakey, Philly Joe Jones, and Max Roach (M-47011 through M-47016). This release makes a total of 74 twofer releases on the Fantasy/ Prestige/ Milestone family of labels. The Fantasy twofer releases center around the blues, the Prestige twofers are jazz classics, primarily from the Prestige catalog; the Milestone two- fers, also jazz classics, are taken from the Riverside catalog. New Orleans Style Into Carnegie Hall NEW YORK — New Orleans jazz will be served at all temperatures, from the cool Ronnie Kole Trio, to the hot footstomping of Louis Cot- trell and the New Orleans Heritage Hall Jazz Band, featuring the Queen of the Blues, Blanche Thomas, the Onward Brass Band and the fifty- three voices of The Convent Gospel Singers, all for the benefit of the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center. The concert will take place Tuesday, Feb. 12 at Carnegie Hall at 8 p.m. The Heritage Hall Jazz Band, un- der the leadership of the great clari- netist Louis Cottrell is the finest that can be assembled. It is truly the last of the great, authentically honest New Orleans bands. The Onward Brass Band, also led by Cottrell, dates back to the 1890’s and was orig- inally led by King Oliver. 26 Cash Box — February 16, 1974

Ivory PLAYBOY CLUB L. A. — Ivory Pro- fessor Irwin Corey, renowned lecturer in thallophyte sciences and musicolo- gy was fortuitously on hand to deliv- er the opening remarks. His befud- dling introduction served as an ap- propriate prelude to Ivory’s generally good, but uneven set at the Playboy Club. A sextet, Ivory consists of two key- boardists, a pair of vocalists, a bas- sists and a drummer, all excellent mu- sicians whose performance seemed hampered only by the limiting nature of their material. From their opener, a boisterous tune, containing refer- ences to Hare Krishna etc. and through such songs as “Bringing Me Down,” the band appeared to be floundering in a structureless hodge- podge, mixing extended solos and en- ergetic vocals in a formula that never quite managed to coalesce. One bright spot throughout the evening was the drumming of Jim Divesek, whose precise and creative use of percussion remained crisp dur- ing even the most flacid portions of the set. In what amounted to an about face, Ivory presented their new Playboy Records single towards the end of the set. “Life Goes On,” penned by Paul Williams and Craig Doerge, 'was a perfect vehicle for their collective tal- ents, and the band’s sound became more disciplined, tighter and finally found the direction that had been lacking. Once having arrived at that plateau in their performance, the group remained there for the dura- tion of the set. A rendition of “Nature’s Way,” a slow, winding bal- lad, was again an effective showcase, especially for Lance and Grant Gul- lickson’s vocals. Ivory seems to be undergoing a very positive transition, one which should be watched closely in the com- ing months. e.s. = iX- r :SIC HALL, NYC I ; i.;:''' i.litedly was the finest ce a rock star (sorry there) in this giant i::, one of the great ladies i 'in (or perhaps Canadian/ o) music, delivered the mes- ; her many thousands of fans waiting for. The praised Philly quintet who are personable, polished, and precisioned sauntered thru their aggregate of Gamble and Huff hits like “If You Don’t Know Me By Now,” “I Miss You,” and “The Love I Lost.” Each member of the Blue Notes capably establish their o-vm distinctive personalities and voices. They also demonstrate some of the best harmony ever heard by this reviewer. Melvin himself is the suave, soigne sophisticate of the act responsible for several million selling records. Especially good was the song “I’m Weak For You,” off of their new Philadelphia International Album. On this particular number the group comically spoofed it up with a descant that invited audience participation. Opening The Harold Melvin and the Blue Notes Review was comedian Rodney Winfield who had some funny one liners. The one liner he seemed most impressed about was the one on the label in his jacket which said “Pierre Cardin.” Sandwiched between Rodney and Harold on the bill was songstress Sharon Page. At one point during her gospel sounding vocal workout someone spiritedly called from the audience “Let’s go to church,” however her “holey” seduc- tive sari probably wouldn’t allow her in a church gospel sounding or not. She was very good on “I Think I’ll Tell Him” but relied a bit heavily on hand gestures to both sell her song and her sari. r.b. piece of land, and settled in to give my spiritual side a chance to catch up with my sensual side. Anyway, I was sitting one night knitting myself a coat, when I thought I heard ap- plause outside. I walked out on the porch and looked around, but didn’t see anything, then I noticed that the sound was coming from an Arbutus tree, a very tough, independent tree with rubbery leaves and a will of its own. So I went back inside and thought about that for quite a while.” When Joni proceeded to sing the song about the Arbutus tree, her whole rap came into clear perspective as she retold the story in her unique poetic way. For too long Joni’s hesi- tance to tour has prevented her from receiving her just due. Lord STARWOOD, L.A. — Not since the early days of Gladys Knight and The Pips has a lady delivered r&b vocals with the impeccable precision and en- ergy of Catherine Mitchell. Together with fellow vocalist Richard Mosley, she led C. M. Lord’s performance at the Starwood through a vigorous set composed largely of fresh, original material. C. M. Lord, London Records’ newly signed sextet, also features organist Steven Hines, guitarist Victor Lewis, Jack White on drums and Mike Ziskin on bass and vocals. Their rhythm sec- tion is particularly strong, and Victor Lewis’ guitar work, as well as gener- ally excellent use of rhythms and har- monies on songs like “Hard Times Rocky Roads” should give their mate- rial, as well as their act, immediate cross-over potential. The group displayed great versatil- ity on a cover version of the O’Jays’ “Love Train” and with a number of medium-tempo songs that provided a perfect showcase for Catherine Mitchell’s rich, husky voice. Coming fresh on the heels of their rousing .success with Bloodstone, the signing of C. M. Lord should put Lon- don Records in an admirable r&b position. e.s. Charles Mingus And Old Friends With Rahsaan Roland Kirh CARNEGIE HALL, NYC — When Charles Mingus and Roland Kirk joined forces the jazz lovers came out in force. Such was the case at this Saturday night show. Before a sellout crowd the “New Audiences” presented the reunion of Charlie Mingus and Old Friends. And quite a reunion it was. Opening the show was the Charles Mingus Qunitet, consisting of Charles Mingus on bass, Don Pullen on piano, George Adams & Hamiet Bluitt on alto and tenor sax, and Danny Rich- mond, one of the best jazz drummers alive. The Quintet was joined by John Faddis, a truly surperb trumpet play- er and a friend of Charles Mingus. Because of the unusually responsive audience, the Quintet performed for two hours, spotlighting each musician several times. The knowledable audi- ence seemed to influence the Quintet, as they jammed on such numbers as “Peggy Blue Skylight,” “Celia” and “Big Alice.” After a brief intermission the audi- ence was anxiously awaiting the ar- rival of Roland Kirk, and his per- formance was no let-do-wn. The sec- ond set saw the Mingus Quintet, along with Roland Kirk, John Handy, Charles McPherson, and John Fad- dis work together. What resulted was an overwhelming jam session. Four saxophones simultaneously backed Roland Kirk with power. Roland played some leads with two saxes at once and jazz was played as it was meant to be played. In all, the show proved to be a quencher for a true jazz lovers’ thirst. s.o. Forrest Green BITTER END, NYC — An interest- ing assortment of roots, influences and techniques are incorporated into the fiery set of Forest Green. The opening night engagement of the Capitol recording artists proved to be an enchanting musical sojourn, taking us from rock to classical and im- provisational jazz. Forest Green has the ability to put these rather diver- gent elements together, and the result is a textural meld that proved itself to be both tight and musically satis- fying. The full instrumentation included a tenor and alto saxophone, flute, bass guitar, lead guitar, drums, bassoon and two electric pianos. At once the group began to cook coming up with intriguing rhythms, tight vocal har- mony, and instrumentation par excel- lence. A sophisticated rock ensemble, their choice of material was apt because it clearly reflected the polished musical diversity the group possesses both as a unit and as independent per- formers. “Movin’ To The Country”, a real rocking mover, began with a flash beginning that had the group imitat- ing a locomotive engine. And the cookin’ rhythms picked up speed and carried this superb rocker along. “Scream Fear,” an up-tempo tune with fine piano work is a song spiced with most provocative lyrics and fine horn accompaniment. “Mountain” had a serenely tranquil melody that floated forth from the group. A total mastery of form and instrumentation, carried this song very well. “Black Shepard” clearly incorporated classi- cal elements with an almost Baroque quality to the flute solos which left us all very mellow. “Beggar Man” and up-tempo tune employed moving rhythms with an excellent lyric and vibrant images. Closing their energet- ic set the group performed “Leave Your Love”. A complex series of mel- odies and great instrumental solo spots concluded the dynamic per- formance of this fine group. m.d. 32 Cash Box — February 16, 1974

The lovely and tender ballad “You and Me Against The World,’’ a beautifully orchestrated song, is placed for contrast after the short romantic spoof entitled “Nilsson Sings Newman" and gives an insight into Paul’s concept of the pacing and juxtaposition of his material. Paul uses no less than 50 musicians and singers to give this LP the richness which is its trade- mark. COME LIVE WITH ME—Ray Charles—Cross- 1 over CR9000 Every release of Ray’s is anxiously expected * and this unique collection is certainly not an exception. Highlighted by the hit title track, the LP is neatly divided into ballads and up- tempo tunes. “Somebody” looks like a great potential single, capturing the essence of the artist every bit as well as his classic “Hit The Road Jack’’ of 1961. For diversity, Ray has a wonderful version of the old Everly Brothers’ hit, “Problems, Problems” adorning side 2 of this LP, complimenting “Louise,” “Everybody Sing,” and “Where Was He” perfectly. His vocals are as spirited as ever, and the entire effort is one of his best. LOUD ’N’ PROUD—Nazareth—A&M SP 3609 In the great tradition of powerful British bands, Nazareth has come through in fine fashion on this rock ’n’ roll gem which will have knowledgeable fans everywhere up and boogie-ing around their record players before they know what hit them. “Go Down Fight- ing” is typical of the band’s straight forward approach, and we all know that the shortest distance between two minds is a thumping rock beat with solid vocals behind it. “Not Faking It,” “Child In The Sun,” and a great version of Joni Mitchell’s “This Flight Tonight” are further proof that this group is on its way to the very top. SKYLARK 2—Skylark—Capitol ST-11256 The quote from Kahlil Gibran on the back cover appropriately sums up the group’s philosophy when it says “. . . but who shall command the skylark not to sing?”, and this LP provides further emphasis that Skylark’s intention is to fill the air with beautiful music. “Love’s A River Flowing” is one of the pretti- est and most capably arranged ballads we’ve heard in quite a while and displays the excel- lent inner workings of the artists’ minds as they make difficult harmony parts sound ef- fortless. “If That’s The Way You Want It” and “It’s A Wonder” are our favorites from this worthwhile effort. SWEET FORTUNE’S DARLING—Hotspur—Col- umbia KC 32541 Exquisite harmonies and powerful, driving rhythms highlight this attractive debut LP for the talented quartet. “I Lost My Wings Ir Memphis” is a fabulous rocker with a steady, repeating chorus that gives it enough strength to be considered as a single. Throughout the collection, Hotspur effectively makes use of percussion, in much the same way as the Stones, using accents to bolster the feeling of the song. “I Wrote This Song,” “The Best I Can Do,” “Countryside Ride,” “You Can’t Lose (What You Never Had),” and “We Need A Captain” are all well worked pieces of music, showing promise for the band. StatusQua NEWCOMER PICKS JAZZ PICKS HELLO!—Status Quo—A&M SP3615 England’s number one boogie band has itself another stellar LP with this smokin’ collection highlighted by “Roll Over Lay Down,” “Claudie,” and the epic “Forty-Five Hundred Times.” Francis Rossi, Richard Parfitt, Alan Lancaster, and John Coghlan have gotten down to the essence of boogie and rock on this album and the effort may very well be re- warded by the group’s biggest sales to date. With tunes like “Caroline,” “And It’s Better Now,” and “A Reason For Living,” the band that has already established itself as a top box office draw in England, is surely headed for the top of the U.S. charts with this one. ETHNIC STEW—Tribe—ABC ABCX 807 One of the most versatile new groups to emerge this year does so with refreshing abandon on its ABC debut LP, a collection that starts out funky and just doesn’t let up. “The World Should Learn To Party Together,” “Think People,” and “Lovin’ On The Outside” are typical of the raw yet well paced fury the group puts together throughout the collection. Obviously well versed in the crucial arts of ar- rangement and dynamics, the band has that good time feeling in its songs that’s infec- tiously catchy. Listen to “Tribe,” “What Am I Gonna Tell My Wife,” and “Siggy Siggy” and you’ll fall for this band in a big way. VIRGO RED—Roy Ayers Ubiquity—Polydor PD 6016 Fascinating is the best word to describe Roy’s new Polydor LP, which combines jazz’s finest overtones and octaves with a steady, cookin’ feeling that’s altogether compelling. Featuring an interesting version of the Stories’ hit single, “Brother Louie,” as well as the memorable tracks "Love From The Sun,” “I Am Your Mind,’,’ “Des Nude Soul,” and the stunning title cut, the album is a rapturous sortie into the textures and modes of the present and future. The entire collection is permeated with constantly changing rhythmic patterns that are sure-fire dance numbers. Watch for the LP to take off very soon. '/J.ravj'isil CHILBREWS PICK SINGS FOR ALL THE BOYS AND GIRLS—Bob McGrath—Disneyland 1357 To all the kids who watch Sesame Street (and that includes a lot of older kids too) Bob is a household word, and his new Disneyland LP should provide one of the biggest treats of the year. Using the Jimmy Joyce Singers, as well as an excellent group of versatile studio musicians. Bob gets into “I’d Like To Teach The World To Sing,” "The Unbirthday Song,” “Black And White,” “It’s A Small World,” “Everything Is Beautiful,” and “Joy To The World,” rendering each in a classy, effective style, perfect for the young (and young at heart). Arrangements of the songs were done by the talented Lee Norris. SMNGEIZ BLLEl/lNS Pra/ious^ Unieteosed RcoDfdbgs ORIGIN .hviiieKcni in Lrnidon STAN GETZ & BILL EVANS—Stan Getz and Bill Evans—Verve V6-8833 This LP is something special, not just be- cause it highlights a whole series of previously unreleased recordings of great jazz artists op Verve (there are 6 such LP’s in all), but be- cause it brings two of jazz’s greatest masters together in a very impressive and distinctive collection along with Ron Carter, Richard Davis (who share bass duties), and the re- doubtable Elvin Jones on drums. Each of the six compositions on this album from “Night and Day” to “Melinda” is as well put to- gether as a fine Swiss watch. We particularly like Evans’ work on “But Beautiful,” a good description of the LP and the Verve series. AL CAST PICK JEROME KERN IN LONDON—Original Cast Re- cording—Monmouth—Evergreen MES/7064 The Monmouth-Evergreen label does musical theatre fans another big favor in bringing this import here from EMI. Featured performers in London productions of Kern shows sing such perennials as “I’ve Told Ev’ry Little Star,” “She Didn’t Say Yes,” “Look for the Silver Lining,” among others. “Among others” in- cludes a lovely neglected Kern-Hammerstein song, “Hand in Hand,” sung with surprising romantic flair by Stanley Holloway. To dis- cover this song alone is worth the price of the album. 38 Cash Box — February 16, 1974

BEST SELLING JAZZ ARTIST Donald Byrd-Blue Note (United Artists) Deodato-CTI Mahavishnu Orchestra-Columbia Herbie Mann-Atlantic ABKCO 1st Qtr Shows Declines NEW YORK - ABKCO Industries, Inc. has announced results of its op- erations, on an unaudited basis, for the first quarter ended Dec. 31, 1973 with revenues of $2,281,287 and a loss of $59,830 or 40 per share. This com- pares to revenues of $4,356,190 and earnings of $364,097 or 250 per share for the corresponding period in 1972. Wherehouse Earnings Up TORRENCE, CAL. - Integrity En- tertainment Corp., with headquarters in Torrance, Calif., has reported rec- ord sales and earnings for both the second quarter and the six months ended Dec. 31. Second quarter sales of $6,978,273 and profits of $178,676 compared to the year earlier sales of $3,480,244 and a profit of $134,428. For the six months sales were $10,- 995,466 (up 88%) and earnings were $266,501 (up 151%) compared to the same period for last year of sales and earnings of $5,838,490 and $106,144, respectively. Earnings per share for the six months rose 143% from $.07 to $.17 (fully diluted). Integrity Entertainment Corp. is the owner and operator of "The Wherehouse," a chain of 41 discount record and tape stores operating ex- clusively in California. The company announced the planned opening of five additional stores by June, 1974, bringing the total number of new stores opened in the 1974 fiscal year to 19. 13. Pointer Sisters-Blue Thumb (Famous) Steely Dan-ABC Art Wayne Dies HOLLYWOOD - Singer/composer Artie Wayne died in Nassau, The Bahamas on Thursday (14) at the age of 60. Death was attributed to a coronary. Wayne's most recent composition/ production effort of note was his `Moses and the Impossible Ten' re- leased by BASF Records. Wayne had performed as a singer with the Freddie Martin Orchestra, and later as a Mercury artist with such tunes as "Sleepy Baby," "Black Lace" and "Mahzel". He leaves his wife Vida Haliburton Wayne, one son and one daughter. RCA To Market London `Gypsy NEW YORK - RCA Records will release the British original cast album of the musical, "Gypsy," starring An- gela Lansbury coincidental to the be- ginning in March of an extended North American tour by the company. Miss Lansbury took the Jule Styne- Stephen Sondheim-Arthur Laurents musical to London last year in a pro- duction sponsored by Barry Brown and Fritz Holt, and it became a smash hit. RCA recorded the original cast album for its Red Seal label and the album became one of the hit imports of the year in the U.S. The tour goes from Toronto to Los Angeles to Denver, to Oklahoma City to Dallas, to Houston to Chicago to St. Louis to Detroit and finally ends with a limited New York engagement opening September 10 for nine weeks. Also starring with Miss Lansbury are Barrie Ingham and Zan Char- isse. CELEBRATING A THRILL-Following her only New York recital of the season, the celebrated soprano Leontyne Price was feted at a supper in her honor by Columbia Artists Management at the St. Regis Hotel. At the supper, she is shown here chatting with Kenneth Glancy, president of RCA Records. Miss Price is an exclusive RCA Red Seal artist, and her recording for the' label of Puccini's "Tosca" currently is one of the nation's best selling classical albums. Col Artist Strategy (Cont'd from p. 7) over success its specialized promo- tion department setup. This means that the label operates individual pro- mo departments in the Top 40, coun- try, R&B, MOR and FM areas. "Such concentration, where it can apply, en- ables us to lock -up airplay in differ- ent areas," Lundvall explains. These units are under the direction of Steve Popovich and Stan Monteiro (Top 40), Gene Ferguson and Bill Williams (country), Richard Mack (R&B), Chuck Taggard (MOR) and Mike Klenfner and Stu Slutzah (FM). Once the musical identity and "pic- ture" is established, the campaigns can be formulated on a specialized basis. Some examples follow: David Essex: his hit English single, "Rock On," aided by dealer invites to see act perform; makes three promo - only visits to U.S. for press, radio -TV interviews; massive English print publicity noted to U.S. press. TV cov- erage particularly noteworthy as breakthrough area. Billy Joel: "Piano Man" single from LP edited to make shorter; makes multiple visits to New York and Philadelphia and eastern areas; heavy Philly FM play on "Captain Jack" aids LP sales. Charlie Rich: country -wide tour in pop venues complements hit crossover single smash "The Most Beautiful Girl." Rick Derringer: heavy ad commit- ment ties -in with his role as a mem- ber of the Edgar Winter group. Aerosmith: heavy promo and ap- pearances in Northeast, where group has particularly large following; tours other areas with "compatible" artists. Herbie Hancock: close working relationship with Dave Rubinson, the artist's musical director, to incorpo- rate jazzist's progressive jazz ideas into larger musical framework; book- ings into larger, not generally jazz venues; press effort beyond jazz field; single edited for broader airtime cov- erage. MSFB: Philadelphia International act broke with their LP, "Love is the Message" last year and developed into a 250,000 seller, with a single, "TSOP," currently an R&B success. Press and ad coverage of black mar- ket plus spill -over into Top 40 area. Columbia, of course, is hopeful that it can "turn on" its entire organiza- tion to artists who are to be part of a strong merchandising effort. That is why the label at its various sales meetings, including its annual con- vention, makes a point to stress tal- ent performances featuring these acts. Such was the case at the label's recent sales meeting in Nashville. Even these internal artist showcas- ings, Lundvall points out, are subject to carefull screening so that top exec faith in an attraction is translated effectively to the entire label organi- zation. Ms Ivil Named Atlantic Pub Dir NEW YORK-Jerry Greenberg, Ate lantic Records senior vice president and general manager, has announced, that Ann Ivil has been named direc- tor of publicity for the firm. Ms. Ivil comes to Atlantic's New York head- quarters from London, where she has been head of creative services for Atlantic, as well as publicity director of WEA International. In her new post she will be in charge of Atlantic's publicity opera -4 tions throughout the country and will also liaison with the firm's interna- tional publicity activities. She will work closely with Bob Rolontz, vice president of public relations and ad- vertising. Ms. Ivil has been with Atlantic London office since it was started last fall. Before that she was in charge of publicity for the entire WEA In- ternational operation in London for, the previous two years. She had her own publicity firm in London for many years, which handled Dr. John, Frank Zappa, and others. Ann Ivil L.A. Indictment (Cont'd from p. 9) Records, 20th Century Records, United Artists Records and Warner Bros. Records. Twenty counts of the indictment, charging Taxe with mail fraud, said he advertised in national magazines that he was selling simulated stereo tape recordings when the tapes were actually duplicates of the original sound recordings. The indictment further charged that Taxe used the mails to transport the illegally duplicated sounds on the tapes to customers in Lakewood, Colo.; New Haven, Conn.; Houston, Tex.; St. Louis, Mo.; Freeport, Ill.; Colum- bia, S.C., and Spartansburg, Penna. The defendant was also charged with transporting stolen property in interstate commerce. The property al- leged to have been stolen are the sound recordings which were copy' righted by the recording companies. Maximum penalty for each of the copyright violations is one year in prison and a $1,000 fine. Maximum penalty for the mail fraud count is a $1,000 fine and five years in prison, and the maximum penalty for interstate transportation of stolen property is ten years in prison and a $10,000 fine on each count. The indictment is a result of an investigation by the U.S. Postal Service and the FBI. 24 Cash Box - March 2, 1974

Cash Box/RUB News Report Fifth Latin Fest. At Garden, Mar. 1st, Includes Rock & Soul NEW YORK - Richard Nader, pres- ident of the Richard Nader Organiza- tion, announced that on March 1st the -"5th New York Latin Music Festival of Jazz, Rock & Soul" will be presented in association with Madison Square Garden Productions in the main area. The production, which Nader origi- nated in November of 1972, features "Internationally famous Latin Music stars and top New York Latin attrac- tions. Celia Cruz (Tico Records), the fa - :nous Cuban songstress will headline the show which will feature Ray Bar - retto & His Orchestra (Fania), John- ny Pacheco & His Orchestra (Fania), Fausto Rey top vocalist from the Dominican Republic (Four Points), Machito & His Orchestra featuring his sister Graciela (Tico), and flying in from Puerto Rico especially for the Festival, Tipica '73 and special guest stars Apollo Sound (International). As a special added attraction Ro- berto Torres & Chocolate & his Or- chestra will make an appearance through the courtesy of Mericana Records. They currently enjoy the #1 position on the New York Latin charts with "El Caminante". The New York Spanish Music Radio stations will be represented by guest Master of Ceremonies Dick "Ricardo" Sugar (WHBI), Paquito Navarro (WHOM), Rubian De La Rosa (WADO), and Polita Vega (WBNX). Tickets are set at $7.50, $6.50 & $5.50. Nader said: "Two additional Fes- tivals are scheduled this year at the "Garden and plans are currently being completed to present similar Festivals in San Diego, Los Angeles, Puerto Rico and Washington, D.C. Peebles & Atlantic Come Together VAN PEEBLES AND ATLANTIC vOME TOGETHER - Ahmet Erte - gun, president of Atlantic Records, announced the firm had signed Melvin Van Peebles to a long term exclusive recording contract. Van Peebles' career already includes a long list of successful endeavors in virtually ev- ery phase of the creative arts. Van Peeples produced his first solo album for Atlantic, which features his own songs and his singing, and is entitled "What The *#%± You Mean I Can't Sing?" The album is sched- uled for release next week. Van Pee- bles continued his winning streak with his impressive accomplishments in Broadway musicals. Not only did he write the book music, and lyrics for "Ain't Supposed To Die A Natu- ral Death" and "Don't Play Us Cheap," but produced and directed one of them and saw both run simul- taneously. The two musicals garnered nine Tony Award nominations, and Van Peebles' six record albums in- clude the original cast recordings of these shows. Phonogram Names White To R&B Promo CHICAGO - Elzy White, formerly a business consultant for the Ohio Players, has been named to the post of National Promotion, R&B, for Phonogram, Inc. it has been an- nounced by Lou Simon, senior vice president/director of marketing. White comes to Phonoram after the business stint with the Ohio Play- ers. He is familiar with the music industry, having owned and operated his own publishing and artist man- agement in his home town of Louisville, Ky. In addition to White, Phonogram's national promotion staff includes Stan Bly, national promotion direc- tor, and Frank Mull, national promo- tion, country. Elzy will be working with the company's regional R&B staff, which includes: Ronald Patter- son, east coast, Robert "Flash" Gor- don, southeast, and Tommy Young, southwest. During the next two months, White will be visiting disc-jockeys and pro- gram directors throughout the coun- try as well as meeting all the R&B acts on the Mercury and Dial labels. Elzy White R&B Product From Mercury NEW YORK - Mercury Records has scheduled for immediate release three major R&B singles, all of which were recorded in New York by New York based artists. Charles Fach, Phono- gram/Mercury's vice president of a&r, sees this activity as a healthy sign for New York's R&B scene, which up until recently has taken a backseat to Detroit and Philadel- phia. Don Cavay, who recently has one of Mercury's largest -selling R&B hits with "I Was Checkin' Out She Was Checkin' In," has a new single, "It's Better to Have (And Don't Need)" scheduled for immediate release by the company. The single was pro- duced by Covay at CI studios. Covay is also at Mercury as a staff producer and is currently working on several other Mercury acts. He can be reached at the company's New York office. Roy C, whose own Mercury single, "She Kept on Walkin'," has currently broken out in the South East and surpassed the 100,000 mark, produced a record for the Mark IV. Disk is titled "I'm So Proud of You" and is also slated for immediate release. Just released by Mercury and re- ceiving airplay in Baltimore, Pitts- burgh, Buffalo and Richmond is the Joneses' latest single, "Hey Babe (Is the Gettin' Still Good?)." Jonses are managed by Glenn Dorsey, who also wrote the tune for the group. Dorsey is currently on a promotional trip throughout the East to promote the single. R 1.4 B INGREDIENTS-NATRA (National Association of Radio & TV Artists, a black organization) has been in existence approximately 18 years. Through the years, the organization has never had more than a handful of dedicated men (Jack Walker was one of them) believing in the aims and goals of NATRA, which should in every manner of speaking, be one of the most powerful groups on todays music scene. Now, renewed efforts and positive steps are in the works to strengthen and mold NATRA into a positive industry force. Altho, let's face it, it is not easy to restamp an image that has been implanted for 18 years. But, with proper and dedicated leadership it most assuredly can and should be done. Sheer force of numbers is not the answer. The answer is in the individual. Being able to put ego aside for the good of all, will, in the long run, put NATRA on the right track. (By the way, where is BAMA, PBA and FORE). Blacks, in every phase of the entertain- ment industry, have made valuable contributions. Taking black radio as an example, through the years, black d.j.'s have been responsible for selling records numbering in multi -multi -millions. And, at the same time their salaries have been low and they seldom are sitting in a secure position. But, a new awareness is at hand. Local NATRA chapters are now being restruc- tured and organized to give guidance and direction to blacks. Professional blacks realize that the time for the BS is over. The interest is there; and with forward -positive aims and goals, NATRA can, indeed, put it altogether. One of the best methods for keeping any organization from gaining stature and strength is to keep it in disarray. With Cecil Hale serving as national president, the indication is that this will no longer happen with NATRA. An eastern chapter, recently organized with Gerry Bledsoe as president, has an opportunity to show what NATRA is and will be, when the March 9th Excell- ence Awards Dinner takes place at the New York Hilton, NYC. It is up to you! ... Jimmy Brooks, who was dismissed from his R & B duties at Mercury, is now with Paramount Records. Jimmy will be handling midwest R & B promo for the label, as openers. Our congrats! . . . The Energy Crisis is a major topic with everyone these days. Has anyone stopped to think about the problems struggling young talented groups are going through in trying to get from one gig to the next. I'm referring to the problem of getting gaso- line. Acts working small to medium clubs usually cannot afford to fly from one place to another. They have to rely on their own transportation (for their equipment and luggage) to move about. Booking agents are going to have to concentrate more on booking their acts so that the acts are not leap -frogging half across the country to fulfil club dates, especially if gas is so difficult to get. . . .Attention Drummers-Bernard Purdie is holding a lecture and demonstration, showing the new Video Teaching method, 'Anato- my of a Drummer, Drumming & Drums', which will be used at the Pretty Purdie School of Music. LP Showcases `Jelly Roll' Morton NEW YORK - Columbia Records has released a special disk of com- positions by Ferdinand "Jelly Roll" Morton under its Masterworks logo. The album, produced for Columbia Masterworks by Leroy Parkins, show- cases works ranging from Morton's earliest compositions of the 1900's to his latest in the 1930's. Contained are some of Morton's jazz classics, in- cluding "King Porter Stomp," "The Pearls," "Grandpa's Spells," and "The Crave." Twelve compositions in all were transcribed for orchestra for the album with Dick Hyman arranging and performing all the tracks. "This release has put Jelly Roll Morton alongside other great Black composers of the past century. Until now, he has been relegated to a minor position as a mere songwriter and Audiofidelity Ent. Gato On The Go HOLLYWOOD - While most of the composers for the best original score written for a motion picture or a television special category in the Grammy Awards stem from the rock world (e.g. Bob Dylan, Neil Diamond, and Paul McCartney), Gato Barbieri is distinctly from the jazz scene. The 38 -year old composer for Bertolucci's "Last Tango in Paris" came into the spotlight last year when the film drew so much controversy and Barbieri's theme was covered by a multitude of artists ranging from Herb Alpert to Robin Kenyatta. Barbieri was in town recently to complete recording and mixing on his upcoming album on Impulse, "Latin America: Chapter Two." Working with producer Ed Michel at the Vil- lage Recorder, Barbieri played on the album's final track, "Gato, Gato," which features the tenor saxophonist in a musical dialogue with himself. The LP is scheduled for release this month. Cash Box - March 2, 1974 31
