cash box talent on stage Linda Ronstadt Jackson Browne CARNEGIE HALL, NYC-Although the billing was not nearly as "Super- star" oriented as the recent one that featured Bob Dylan and The Band, this show stood as one of the most eagerly anticipated ones in New York in some time. Before the evening was over, 5,000 completely satisfied pa- trons knew it would be some time be- fore another show as intensely enter- taining would come to pass. Linda Ronstadt opened the evening and her set was better than ever. Opening with her great "Colorado", the lady portrayed the ballad more stunningly than in any of her other previous performances and set the stage for an hour plus of mellow bal- lads and high spirited country rock- ers, each an absolute delight for the overflow crowd. During the course of her set, ma- terial such as "Love Has No Pride", "Silver Threads And Golden Needles", "Lovesick Blues", "Desperado", "The Fast One" and her still stunning "Long, Long Time" was portrayed perfectly as Linda again proved that she is by far the best female vocalist alive today. Her encore, a tune she claimed to have learned a few nights before, "Heart Like A Wheel", was a totally mesmerizing experience that generated a sincere, rousing standing ovation. Again, it's still a mystery as to why more folks have not yet picked up on her incredible talents. Her two current LP's on Asylum ("Don't Cry Now") and Capitol ("Different Drum") are excellent ways to begin a Linda Ronstadt love affair. Speak- ing for all of New York City, come back soon Linda. We adore you! Songwirter extraordinaire Jackson Browne continued the splendid eve- ning's entertainment with a perfectly paced set of his classic folk -country - rock material. While Jackson alter- nated between guitar and piano, his four man back up band perfectly complemented his material and great- ly helped in making the evening as magical as it was. Jackson's performances of "Rock Me On The Water", "Jamaica Say You Will", "Take It Easy", "For Everyman", "Doctor My Eyes" and his current single release, "Ready Or Not" were complete delights and had the crowd excited every step of the way. That's about when the frenzy set in. Jackson, with brilliant accom- paniment from David Lindley and Lowell George (from Little Feat) on guitars, as well as the rest of the band, started rocking and rolling. Carnegie was literally shaking. "Red- neck Friend", his recent single hit was the motivator and everything was letter perfect. With Jackson wailing away on vocals and Lowell on guitar (electric slide), the performance was as electric (if not more so) than any of the best of the best rock and roll shows to hit New York. Joel Grey FAIRMONT HOTEL, SAN FRAN- CISCO - There were two major mu- sic events being chronicled in all of the San Francisco papers while this reporter was there. One happened to be Bob Zimmerman (alias Dylan) and the other Joel Katz (alias Grey). Since Dylan tickets were being scalped for cents which made no sense, it was off to the Fairmont Ho- tel to catch Columbia Recording art- ist Joel Grey. This reporter advanced to the lengthy line and cooly waited for it to diminish so that he could go in. Lines? No one waits in lines any- more unless you're buying gas, going to see "The Exorcist," or happen to be seeing Dylan or Grey. When the turn to be admitted finally arose, the maitre d ushered this journalist to his charitable table, only a nose away from the entrance doors. However, as it turned out, the back seat at the cabaret was really the best, for one got a marvelous look at the audience, their faithful response to Joel, and of Joel's uncanny ability to transfix ev- ery corner of the showroom. Joel opened with "The More I See You," which was followed with his favorite country and western parody, "Romania," at which a table with a couple in their twenties and one with the teenagers roared with laughter. Next the energetic Grey did a George Cohan medley. Now it's time for Joel to saunter thru still another medley of another small giant in the music world, Billy Rose (Grey, statistically speaking would have towered him by three inches). Again the songs were performed with such verve and dedi- cation that anyone else doing them would only come off as a weak imita- tion. The grey Rose tribute included "Am I Blue," "Paper Moon," "Back in your Own Backyard" and a very effective, clever routine to "Me and My Shadow." For this number Joel danced and his shadow box, actually an old vaudeville trunk cavorted along with him. The trunk appeared floating as it synchronized itself to Joel's own fancy facile footwork. Next Joel segued into a very mov- ing interpretation of "Put a Little Love in Your Heart," done with a concerto sounding backgrouná. Dur- ing just a musical interlude of the song, Grey went around and tacitly touched members of the audience. Joel's silence and his careful pacing made it all profoundly moving. He saved his celebrated role of the mas- ter of ceremonies in "Cabaret," for last. Then utilizing a few props from that trunk he recreated the character he created on stage and also got to play in the movie. When Joel got the Cabaret song "Money," which was one of his last songs, it was most ironic to watch the waiters scurry once more to collect just that. Appar- ently this number was the signal amongst the waiters to tell them that the show had come to its end. There was a standing ovation from all gen- erations. His encore number was "Traveling Man." The house lights came on and the cabaret was over at least until his late show. r.b, Silverhead Fresh Start WHISKY L.A. - You can run through the whole gamut of cliche adjectives: gutsy, flashy, heavy and loud; all of them can be neatly and accurately applied to the performance of MCA's Silverhead. An England - based band, they've been through these parts several times before but have never sounded tighter, looked better or generally pulled their act off as well as they did recently at the Whisky. The group is fronted by singer Michael Des Barres, an emaciated shouter who comports himself with all the grace of a spastic Nureyev. Their compositions, almost all of which are collectively authored by the band, are of the hard-core rock vari- ety and range in lyrical content from the risque to the downright obscene. Such picaresque titles as "More Than Your Mouth Can Hold" and "Sixteen and Savaged" seem destined for a special place in the annals of rock 'n roll ethos. Although their act carries the re- quisite overtones of androgenous glitter, Silverhead relies more on a traditional stance of street -punk defiance. As vocalist Des Barres drooled, shouted and strangled his microphone, lead guitarist Robbie Blunt produced an endless series of provocative riffs and musical doodles, , providing a juxtaposition of remark- ably similar elements. And some cred it, please, for bassist Nigel Harrison,' whose competence was above and be-, yond the call of duty. As one might expect, the material Silverhead per- formed can be found, immortalized in vinyl, via an MCA LP titled "Sixteen and Savaged." Although they've been together for only eight months, for opening group, - Fresh Start its been time well spent. Their sound varies from funky r&b to,,, some simple and effective pop ar- rangements that are occasionally re- miniscent of the Doobie Brothers. The band consists of Milo Martin on bass, Fred Allen on drums, singer Bill Pratt and guitarist Paul Frank. Re- cently signed to ABC -Dunhill, Fresh... Start is presently in the studios and if their Whisky engagement is any indi- cation, they should have a good shot at both the r&b and pop markets. e.a. Cheech (i Chong Bachman Turner Overdrive ACADEMY OF MUSIC, N.Y.C. - In an exhilarating display of comic ver- satility, Ode recording artists Cheech & Chong, made an exciting return to the Big Apple, bringing with them several of their most memorable char- acters. The talented duo made a dozen costume changes and featured several selections from their current chart LP, "Los Cochinos," including Cheech's lip -sync version of the sin- gle, "Basketball Jones." Prior to the duo taking the stage, promoter Howard Stein's crew ran a five- minute animated cartoon based on the song, which is about a ghetto kid who grows up eating and sleeping basket- ball and winds up a star of the game. With professional rapidity, Cheech & Chong produced "Laid -Back Len- ny," everbody's favorite underground, west coast FM disk jockey, "Blind Lemon Chitlin," "Sister Mary Ele- phant," and "Sergeant Studenko," all of whom have become well known characters through the duo's satiric portrayal of .their roles in contem- porary society. Tommy Chong and Cheech Marin have enjoyed excep- tional popularity among a generation familiar with marijuana and other drugs, and while poking fun at the drug sub -culture, made some salient points about pushers, police, and drug users. One skit featured Cheech as a push- er and Chong as a supposedly hip undercover cop. In his role as the law, Tommy garbled such commonly used phrases as reefer and upper, substituting `roofer' and `speeder' in their places, much to the delight of the boisterous crowd, who yelled out their favorites to the stage as the pair went through the fast-moving stage act. In the skit, Chong is set to arrest Marin when the latter grabs his gun, and in a turn of events, brings the officer to his knees. It is obvious that Cheech & Chong rep- resent more than a recording or even concert act. Relentlessly poking fun at outdated morality and laws, the pair has become a symbol of freedom for the current generation, a fact made plain as day by the packed house's demand for a double encore, one the artists were happy to satisfy. The popular Mercury recording ar- tists, Bachman -Turner Overdrive opened the show with a raucous rock'n'roll set, which included high - r, lights from their two currently suc- cessful chart LP's, both named after - the group (numbered I and II). The quartet rocked through their previous hit, "Hold Back The Water" and treated everyone to a stunning ver- , sion of their current single, "Let It Ride," which is rapidly moving up the charts. Tight harmonies and well bal- anced (if slightly loud) instrumenta- tion keyed the set, which featured two' interesting change of pace jazz - flavored tunes that set up the group's', encore, "American Woman" (written by Randy Bachman) perfectly. d.b. Fairport Convention Eric Kaz TROUBADOR L.A. - Ominous En- glish ballads, frenetic Scots -Irish.' fiddling and a pop song or two made up their basic fare. Fairport Conven- tion, along with Pentangle and Steeleye Span, was among the pio- neers of the British electrified folkie movement and probably more than any other group in the genre, was+-' responsible for exporting the pheno- menon to this side of the Atlantic. The mainstay of the group in its present edition is Dave Swarbick, whose fiddling, mandolin playing and singing held the act together musical- ly and gave the audience a consider- able amount of highly watchable ani- mation. Swarbick moves about the', stage with the quickness of a le- prechaun, strutting impishly and grinning madly. His fiddle solos on songs like "Hexamshire Lass" (a cut from the group's latest A&M Records LP) were traditionally roguish at times, elsewhere employing an am- --, plified distortion to simulate the sound of a jaded slide guitar. á Sandy Denny, distinguished alumna of the band, took to the stage for a 4 guest appearance midway through theme set. Her voice, almost painfully ex- quisite and clear, lent itself well to.-.. the stark stuff in minor keys and to songs like Bob Dylan's legendary out -- take, "(Oh Mama) You're Gonna Miss Your Best Friend Now." " Eric Kaz, author of "Cry Like A Rainstorm" and "Love Has No Pride" has enjoyed great success as a -t-. songwriter. In performing the open- ing set at the Troubador, he was pushing his luck. e.a. 28 Cash Box - March 9, 1974

Rumors, of the ABC acquisition of the complex which includes 2 recording studios, 7 labels, 3 publishing co.'s and Ernies Record Mart, have been circulating throughout the industry for several weeks. However, R. E. Baulch, Jr. of the Crescent Co., the parent Company of Nashboro, said that all negotiations with ABC have been terminated and the complex will continue to operate as an independent enterprise. cash box/ (Awn :vedette LIVE RHYMIN'-Paul Simon In Concert with Urubamba and the Jessy Dixon Singers- Columbia PC 32855 An automatic number one album, Paul's latest is revolutionary because while recorded live at South Bend, Indiana and Carnegie Hall, it has an intimate "in -studio" quality that makes it as unique in its own way as "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band" was. Back- ing Paul on his great hits are South American expatriots, Urubamba and Chicago gospel group, the Jessy Dixon Singers, who augment "Loves Me Like a Rock," "Bridge Over Trou- bled Water," "The Sound of Silence," and "The Boxer" perfectly. We've never heard a live album done this well and our hats are off to Paul and chief engineer Phil Ramone for this excellent treat. OPEN YOUR EYES-Earth, Wind & Fire- Columbia KC 32712 The Earth, Wind & Fire machine keeps roll- ing along on this stunning LP that starts strong with a Sly-esque number called "Mighty Mighty" and never lets up in intensity. The eight -member group has built a prodigious streak of hit albums with solid music, carefully controlled dynamics and arrangements, and quality self -production, a facet they have con- tinued here. The LP is a product of the band's work at Jim Guercio's Caribou Ranch Studios outside of Boulder, and the result is spectacu- lar. We especially like "Drum Song" and "Tee Nine Chee Bit." HISTORY OF BRITISH ROCK-Various Artists- Sire sas 3702 It took nine months to put this package together, but the folks over at Sire are to be complimented for compiling the very best of British rock from Freddy and the Dreamers to Rod Stewart. This special two record set is amazing because it contains no clinkers, just 28 hits, and quality hits at that: The Kinks' "You Really Got Me," Dave Clark 5's "Glad All Over," "Mungo Jerry's "In The Summertime," Small Faces' "Itchycoo Park," Walker Bros.' "The Sun Ain't Gonna Shine," Donovan's "Catch The Wind," and, dig this one, the Trogg's immortal "Wild Thing." Only one way to sum this incredible package up-fantastic. ALIVE & KICKING-The Delphonics-Philly Groove PG 1501 Featuring the magic of "I Told You So," their recent single, the Delphonics new Philly Groove LP is a beautiful piece of work, exem- plary of the high quality craftsmanship that has been the group's trademark for years. "Ly- ing To Myself," "Pardon Me Girl," "Think It Over," "Seventeen," "Can't Go On Living," and "Start All Over Again" are top drawer tunes highlighting the group's impeccable har- monies and flair for soul that few can espouse. Throughout the package, careful arrangement and precision dynamics accent the multi- faceted talents that have made the act such a popular success. LONGHORNS & LONDONBRIDGES-B. J. Thomas-Paramount PAS 1020 Highlighted by B.J.'s version of Allen Tous - saint's "Play Something Sweet" and a slew of Randall Bramblett tunes (including "I'm Callin,' " "Too Many Irons," "Superman," and "40 Days and 40 Nights"), Mr. Thomas' latest Paramount LP is yet another excursion into the world of one of the music industry's most popular stylists. Steve Tyrell and Al Gorgoni produced the package and together with Paul Buckmaster's complimentary string arrange- ments, they have created a perfect musical vehicle to carry B.J.'s vocals. THOMAS THE ELEVENTH HOUSE-Eleventh House With Larry Coryell-Vanguard VSD 79342 11181 Larry Coryell, Randy Brecker, Alphonse Mouzon, Mike Mandel, and Danny Trifan, the Eleventh House's five parts, explode on the scene with a debut LP that's full of pleasant surprises and some interesting music that will have knowledgeable fans everywhere beaming smiles when they here it. Keyed by "Birdfingers," "Joy Ride," "Right On Y'AII," and "Theme For a Dream," the album is well paced and cleverly put together, with the dif- ferent themes and moods fitting together into an effortless unified whole. NEWCOMER PICKS ol WAR LIVE-War-United Artists-UA-LA193-J If you've ever caught War live, this album will mean a great deal to you, for the group not only presents its hits, such as "All Day Music," "Cisco Kid," "Lonely Feelin,' "' and "Slippin' Into Darkness," but an incredible amount of energy distributed over the entire two record set like thunderbolts from mighty Zeus. "Son Oh Son" is a ten and a half minute epic cut that reveals the tight, inner strength of the group and "Get Down," a twenty and a half minute cut taking up all of Side 4, is an exercise in unrestrained musical talent at its uninhibited best. This one can't miss. CLAUDINE-Original Motion Picture Sound- track-Sung By Gladys Knight & The Pips/ Written & Produced By Curtis Mayfield- Buddah BDS 5602 ST Whenever you're dealing with talents of the stature of Curtis Mayfield and Gladys Knight & The Pips, you know you have something great on your hands, and this stellar soundtrack LP from the film "Claudine" is a case in point. Packed with devastatingly powerful original tunes by Curtis Mayfield, the LP highlights the expansive genius of Gladys Knight & The Pips as they move briskly from "Mr. Welfare Man," "To Be Invisible," "The Makings of You," and "On and On," to "Claudine Theme" and "Hold On." Keep your eyes on this one, it will proba- bly rival "Superfly." SOMETHING'S HAPPENING-Peter Frampton A&M SP -3619 Peter has had a long and successful career, though he's only twenty-six, and his latest A&M LP gives every evidence that he's just now hitting stride. Featuring an interesting Doobie Bros.' interpolation appropriately enti- tled "Doobie Wah," the album is chock full of vivacious and bright material, all well executed with Pete's guitars, keyboards, percussion and vocals permeating each of the cuts. The over- all effect is that of a brightly lit stage with Frampton and co. doing what they do best- getting it on with heavy rock'n'roll and airy harmonies. A solid effort. DRAMATICALLY YOURS-Ron Banks and the Dramatics-Volt VOS -9501 Highlighted by their current single, "And I Panicked," the Dramatics latest LP is a self- made man's dream, a combination of opportu- nism and luck. The luck comes in when you realize how long it took to put this group together, the opportunism stems from the fact that the quintet has built its name from a smalltime club act, to one of the most presti- gious names in soul music. "I Dedicate My Life To You," "It's Hard Trying To Get Over You," "I Pray She'll Never Go Away," and "You Got Me Going Through a Thing" are exemplary of the group's masterful touch. PURE MUSIC-Chase-Epic KE 32572 Bill Chase has put a new band together and this new LP is a bright musical explosion, featuring six great tunes and some incredible dynamics that make it a pleasure to listen to from start to finish. "Weird Song #1" is a strange mixture of rhythms and textures, but the overall effect is a very convincing one. "Bochawa," "Love Is On The Way," "Close Up Tight," and "Twinkles" are exemplary of the band's tightness and discipline and each cut offers something different and exciting. The fusion of jazz and rock that Bill and Chase have put together here is well worth catching. "Run Back To Momma" is a great single. HIGHSTEPPIN' AND FANCY DANCIN'-Larry Raspberry and the Highsteppers-Enterprise ENS 7502 One of Memphis' and the South's greatest show bands has put it all together on its Enterprise debut LP, one that packs all the power of the group's live performances, and then adds some to that. Larry Raspberry is a stomper in the early Jerry Lee Lewis tradition and his energy mixed with that of the High - steppers is inescapably infectious. Listen to "Road Blues," "Rock'n'Roll Warning" (very Leon Russell-esque), "Baby Get Out of Bed (Once Is Enough For Me)," and "Jive Ass," and you'll get an idea where this band is coming from. With powerful harmonies and strong instrumentation, this LP is worth hear- ing. 40 Cash Box - March 16, 1974

KDAY R&B Scores HOLLYWOOD - On January 4, ra- dio station KDAY (1580 AM) changed from a Top 40 format to R&B. Early rating information indicates that KDAY has made the right move. The February Hooper shows that KDAY is in a strong position in all time periods, while leading the after- noon drive time (3 to 7 PM) slot. ARB figures released this week indi- cate further support for KDAY's de- cision to go with R&B programming. January -February ARB figures show KDAY leading its competition in the R&B ma ket in total cume figures (12+ Monday through Sunday 6AM to midnight). These strong numbers after only two months of R&B rmat demonstrate that KDAY is ell on the way to capturing major s ares of the Los Angeles market. Gary Price, general manager of DAY, stated that the station is con- e ntrating its energies on producing a s lid radio show for its market, and - developing a variety of community .- involvement projects. Jim Maddox, KDAY program director, is using the Top 40 c ncept for KDAY's R&B format, w ile concentrating the max- imum co mercial load of 8 minutes and 40 s conds an hour into four clustered ommercial spots. KDAY as put on a series of R&B concerts ith such top groups as Al - Greene, G adys Knight and the Pips, a d Barry White, and will continue to - d so in t e future. Mike Allen, news a d public affairs director, is using, f r the first time in Los Angeles, two b ack national news networks to sup - p rt and supplement KDAY's local n ws. He has also initiated a student o inion forum, "Youth Opinion," in hich Los Angeles youth are invited t express their views in 30 -second - i terviews on a subject of their own choosing. "All of these exciting, energetic programming approaches are helping KDAY to become one of the new 1 aders in this important market," Price declared. R f3 B INGREDIENTS-communicating, in the final analysis, is the name of the game. A record promotion man/woman is in truth applying communications expertise. When a product is properly promoted (to give it all possible exposure) the success of the product is still determined by the consumer. Of course, when the promo people are given a record that is right from the gitgo (This includes first the material (the song), an artist's honest interpretation and the production) then the promo job is somewhat easier. It should be increasingly clear to record companys as well as producer or artist/producer that it is almost impossible today to sell product that is not for real. The fault generally begins in the recording studio. An act may come into the studio feeling it can be another Stevie Wonder. When, in truth, the act should reveal what it is about. Then, if the talent is really there the stature of a Stevie Wonder may be achieved by doing 'your own thing.' Getting back to promotion. R & B (referring to it as root music) has grown by leaps and bounds in the past couple of years. And, it's only the beginning. Gus Redmond, na- tional promotion manager for the General Recording Corp., based in Atlanta, has been a standout in establishing the label (Aware) and artists (Ripple) as a solid R & B entity, He, along with his team such as Greta Hunter, understand- ing what it's all about, can stand proud. Bernie Block has a total understanding of his Baltimore/Washington markets. A veteran who stays with the trends and now happenings. Bernie is responsible for starting many records that have achieved national success. Bernie is now working the new single, "Come Down To Earth" by The New Censation on Pride (now distributed by United Art- ists). Those into the R & B field are well aware of what Jose Wilson has accom- plished at 20th Century Records ... Yours truly (Don Drossell), Curtis Jones in record retail (Bklyn) and Marty Mack (RCA) chaired a F.O.R.E. Seminar per- taining to the interrelationship between trade charts, radio stations, retailer, and, of course, record companies. The well attended session was highly re- sponsive and fired out the questions. This is the basic reason for seminars (to communicate and exchange views). The seminar was held March 13, and it was thoroughly enjoyed by me and I hope it was informative for those of you in attendance. Aki Aleong (involved with a pigeonnaper demanding ran- som) helped to chair the seminar. Aki has made front page in the New York Daily News two days running. Some culprits got 28 of Aki's prize pigeons the past weekend. The first pigeon returned had a note attached demanding $15. A second pigeon released demanded $50. 10 pigeons have been released but 19 are still missing. Good luck Aki! The record business can often be for the pigeons ... BOSTON - The sixth annual jazz ensemble festival for high school stage bands, hosted by Boston's Ber- klee College of Music and sponsored by the National Association of Jazz Educators, will be held at the College on Saturday, April 27th, it has been announced by Berklee Vice President Lee Eliot Berk. "Festival '74" will include individu- al band performances; improvisation and arranging clinics and demonstra- tions of the latest techniques, all con- ducted by Berklee's internationally - celebrated faculty such as Gary Bur- ton, Alan Dawson and John LaPorta. The day's program will culminate in an evening Concert/Competition, at which time awards consisting of Best Band Trophy, Citation for Excellence Plaques and Tuition Scholarships for study in music totaling $2500 will be presented. In its five-year history the Jazz En- semble Festival has attracted more than ten thousand student musicians from all over the United States and Canada. According to Young, the films are exhibited on a rental theater basis (four wall) as opposed to per- centage distribution, which he will do on a city by city basis, rather than a simultaneous national release. Dirt Band Helps Raise $35G For Prison Reform NEW YORK - The Nitty Gritty Dirt Band, a country -rock band, did pro- motion for special benefit concert in which they performed with John Den- ver, Steve Goodman and Oliver at Notre Dame University, South Bend, Indiana. Dirt Band members, John McEuen, Jeff Hanna, Jim Ibbotson and Jim Fadden, manned the phones to drum up press and radio support for and coverage of the story of the National Coordinating Committee for Justice Under Law, an organization formed several years ago to formulate new approaches to the rehabilitation of minor law breakers and offendors. Coordinating Committee chairman and founder, George Mische, took out more than $35,000 for the cause. The sellout house was just under 11,000 persons who paid in a total gross of $45,000. Mische, who was convicted in the Cantonsville draft records case, served 25 months in Federal prison. In an interview just after the concert, John McEuen, of the Dirt Band, ex- plaining that all members of the band endorse the program of the organiza- tion which seeks another answer than incarceration for all but the most serious crimes. The approach would be to achieve economic and social re- habilitation through actual job train- ing rather than imprisonment. N.Y. FOR THE RECORD PASSING REMARKS—First off, the answer to last week's “Rock And Roll: The Way We Were” quiz photo was that Philly early ’60’s group that coined, in song, that now classic line (and the one that named a generation), “Where do all the hippies meet?” Well, that song was "South Street,” and the group was the Orlons, They were the group in the photo. This week, the locale again changes, this time to Cleveland, where this group originated. Their hits were few, but they were big in the middle Sixties. Should you know the group, three hits should immediately come to mind. Let ya know next week . . . Steve Miller and his band have completed their follow up LP to the “Joker” for Capitol. As yet untitled, the disk is scheduled for May release and includes a new old member of the band’ Curley Cooke, rhythm guitarist, who was a member of the Steve Miller Band of 1966-67 . . . John Lennon has been in the news more of late, it seems, than most folks we know. If you remember his recent incident at the Troubader, in L.A., where he was bodily ejected for punching the Smothers Brothers manager following a heckling incident, and then doing the same to a lady photographer outside on the street in front of the club, well, here’s the latest. The lady photographer has dropped all charges against John, for one. Secondly, it is rumored that a major Las Vegas Hotel has offered John a few dates to perform. He hasn't yet refused the offer. Thirdly, a recent studio session found the newsworthy Mr. L at the Record Plant in L.A. recording some oldies with, believe it or not, Mick Jagger, Bill Wyman, Stevie Wonder, Jack Bruce, Harry Nilsson, Bobby Keys, Jesse Ed Davis, Billy Preston and “others.” One of the tunes said to have been recorded at this particular all night session was the Bobby Freeman (and Beach Boys) classic “Do You Wanna Dance.” Can’t say that John isn’t up and around, can you . . . Mott The Hoople, another group in the news of late, recently recorded a part of their Winterland concert (in San Francisco) as a part of a forthcoming live album . . . Mick jagger is thinking seriously of moving to Los Angeles, and is in the process of looking for that West Coast home. He, too, is contemplating an offer from Las Vegas . . . Steeleye Span, whose latest Chrysalis LP, “Now We Are Six” has just been released here, will tour the U.S. this Summer. They gave truly memorable performances here in New York last time around . . . Paul Horn recently recorded a new LP for Columbia. A few of his friends in on a few of the sessions were Joni Mitchell, the Section and the Crusaders . . . Guess it’s called being in the wrong place at the wrong time, but, Steve Hackett of Genesis was informed that his wife gave birth to a son, Oliver, in England only 12 hours after the group took off for their U.S. concert tour . . . The British will be invading Madison Square Garden in May when, for example, Alvin Lee and Ten Years After perform there on May 13, and Procol Harum steps in for two consecutive ROCK AND ROLL: THE WAY WE WERE #5 MID-SIXTIES CLEVELAND CHART BUSTERS 'A' evenings at the Felt Forum, the following two nights. May will also see such British pop luminaries as Graham Nash, Genesis, King Crimson and Robin Trower in the area . . . April 6 is the release date for Rick Wakeman’s “Journey To The Center Of The Earth” LP here in America. The disk, his second solo effort, will be on A&M . . . Speaking of Yes, the group returns to the States for their second concert tour of the year this Summer . . . Again, speaking of Yes, a streaker, a rather shapely, young, female streaker, did her act during the group’s encore in Long Beach, California. In front of 15,000 fans no less. No one knew how she was able to get backstage, disrobe and streak across the stage, but the fans loved it. When asked to comment on the incident, guitarist Steve Howe asked, "What’s a streaker?” Rick Wakeman stated “it’s a funny place to keep a hairbrush” and Jon Anderson, whose back was to the situation at the time, said simply, “I missed the whole thing. I wish I’d seen it. But it was really in bad taste” . . . Emerson, Lake & Palmer will hit the U.S. again this Summer to cover major market cities missed on their recently completed tour. The tour will include the mammoth "California Jam” on the Memorial Day weekend at the Ontario Motor Speedway . . . Telly Savalas the tube’s “Kojak,” will, believe it or not, sing the Academy Award nominated “Nice To Be Around” (from “Cinderella Liberty”) on the Gscarcast of April 2. Word has it he has also recorded an entire album of tunes. Who knew? . . . Gary Glitter and Suzi Quatro have been voted top male and female vocalists in the poll of BBC World Service Pop Club Members. Pop Club is a show broadcast three times a week in the World Service arid has more than 60,000 members in 100 countries in Europe . . . James Taylor (Carly’s husband, among other things) has finally recorded a new LP of new material. From what I’ve heard, the disk is his best since “Sweet Baby James.” Gotta say that it’s about time, too . . . Dan Fogelberg will be the opening act on the upcoming Eagles tour. Word has it he has also signed with Asylum and will have a new LP on the way shortly . . . Speaking of Eagles, their new LP, “On The Border,” is great, their best since that tremendous first outing. The group will be featured with Linda Ronstadt and Jackson Browne on the April 13 edition of Don Kirshner’s Rock Concert, the successful syndicated rock TVer. The show is simply incredible . . . Birthdays of those folks in the wonderful world of rock and roll that will be taking place this week include: Herb Alpert (Mar. 31), Ronnie Lane (of the Faces), (April 1), Leon Russell and Marvin Gaye (April 2), Richard Manuel (of the Band) and Jeff Barry (songwriter-producer) (April 3), Dave Hill, Hugh Masakela and Muddy Waters (April 4), and Ronald White (of the Miracles) (April 5) . . . Thursday, April 4, would have been the birthday of Berry Oakley, who met unfortunate death in a motorcycle accident. He was with the Allman Brothers . . . arty goodman ON THE ROAD AGAIN Pointer Sisters HOLLYWOOD — The Pointer Sis- ters, Blue Thumb recording artists have recently appeared at the Friends of Watts Benefit in Los Angeles and at the Narm Convention in Miami. Johnny Rivers NEW YORK — Johnny Rivers will debut the show he’ll take cross- country on a major concert tour be- ginning in April with a headline stand at the Troubadour, Los Ange- les, from April 2, through April 7. Backing Rivers will be the Nash- ville-based musicians used on his forthcoming Atlantic Records album, “Road.” It is Rivers’ first LP recorded in Nashville, includes the newly- released single, “Siftin' in Limbo,” which marks the performer’s debut with Atlantic. The Rivers band consists of Ron Oates, Piano; Jerry Carrigan, drums; Bobbe Seymour, steel guitar; Jack Williams, bass; Albert Lee,, guitar; Herb Pedersen, acoustic guitar and banjo. Musimart Sting Label Puts Spotlight On Canada Talent MONTREAL — George E. Erlick, president of Musimart Limited, a Montreal-based independent record importer and distributor since 1947, has announced establishment of a new label, Sting, to feature Canadian prod- uct. Initial release on the new label is three singles: “A Day Like Today” by Shonderiah; “Whispering Good- byes” by Brett McNaueal and “C’mon Mamma” by Stagg. National sales for the company is handled by Jack Inhaber, assisted by Jacqueline Lapointe. Michel Kordupel will handle national promotion. The Ontario market is under the supervi- sion of Ben Michaels, assisted by A1 Freedman. Musimart also employs resident sales personnel across the country. Production for the new label is under the direction of Ben Kaye, a Montreal producer. Founded by Erlick in 1947, Musi- mart has introduced many labels to the Canadian market including Angel, Polydor, Vanguard, Barclay, Blue Note, Elektra and Verve. In recent Epic Releases 1st Murphey LP NEW YORK — Epic recording artist Michael Murphey has had his latest album released this past week (26). The LP, Murphey’s first for Epic, is entitled “Michael Murphey.” Murphey has had two albums previously re- leased on the A&M records label. Murphey, who writes and sings a mixture of country, rock and gospel music, is currently on tour. The high- light of the tour will come in New York City during the IBS (Intercolle- giate Broadcasting System) Conven- tion, where Epic has arranged for Murphey to perform at the meeting of college radio programmers. His first Epic album was produced by Bob Johnston. years they have distributed the Prestige, Milestone, Savoy, Trip and Fantasy labels. The latter chalked up Canadian gold with Creedence Clear- water Revival. Musimart also released classical product through Vox, Turna- bout, Peter Pan and Ambassador. Im- portant to the Phonodisc structure has been the acquisition of ethnic product through Apon, Eurotone, Tifton and others. A national sales and promotion campaign is now being put together by Inhaber and Kordupel which will be launched for Sting within the next few weeks. CSP Re-Issue Of Monroe ‘Love’ LP NEW YORK — - Columbia Records Special Products has rereleased the soundtrack from the film Let’s Make Love as part of its Collector’s Series. The record, originally released in 1960, features singing performances by the movies’ three stars, Marilyn Monroe, Yves Montand and Frankie Vaughan. Included is Marilyn Mon- roe’s performance of Cole Porter’s “My Heart Belongs To Daddy.” The reissue has been spurred by rekindled interest in the late actress, a sex symbol from her teens until her suicide in the early 60’s. Among the nine tracks included in the album are “Incurably Romantic,” “Hey You With The Crazy Eyes” and “Let’s Make Love,” all of which were written by Sammy Kahn and Jimmy Van Heusen. Let’s Make Love is the latest in Columbia Records Special Products’ Collector’s Series, a catalog of special reissues. If you are reading someone copy of Why not mall this coupon TODAY! OTHER THE PLATINUM JOKER—Hollywood—Bhaskar Menon, president and chief executive officer of Capitol Industries-EMI, Inc. presents Steve Miller (1.) with a platinum album signifying the sale of one million units of his Capitol LP, “The Joker,” during local fete honoring the singer/ guitarist. Chicago VII Is Group’s 9th Gold NEW YORK —- Columbia Recording Group Chicago has struck gold for the ninth time with their latest al- bum, Chicago VII. The album had been released ten days prior to being certified Gold by the RIAA, signify- ing sales in excess of one million copies. The album was released on Mar. 8 and was certified on the 18th. Chicago has been awarded Gold disks for all six of their previous al- bums: Chicago Transit Authority, Chicago, Chicago III, Chicago At Carnegie Hall, Chicago V, and Chica- go VI. They have also achieved two gold, singles with “Saturday In The Park” and 1973’s “Just You ’N Me.” Chicago’s current single, “(I’ve Been) Searching So Long,” is riding high on the charts. The 7-man group has all of its material for Columbia Rec- ords produced by James William Guercio. ASCAP Names Rogers NEW YORK — - The appointment of Mel Rogers as district manager of the Cleveland office of the American So- ciety of Composers, Authors and Pub- lishers has been announced by James L. Cleary, national sales manager, general licensing. Rogers has served as an ASCAP field rep and assistant to the division manager in Cleveland for the past seven years. UA’s ELO Push HOLLYWOOD — United Artists Rec- ords has announced a major Ameri- can tour for UA rock group the Elec- tric Light Orchestra. In support of the tour the company is preparing an extensive advertising campaign and sending posters and promo materials to major stops on the tour. The group’s recently released single is “Ma-Ma-Ma Belle,” from their current album “On The Third Day.” The tour and promo campaign will be backed by a maior publicity campaign. Booked by CMA, major venues on ELO’s current tour include Detroit, Toronto, Philadelphia, New York, Camden, N.J., Pittsburgh, Baltimore, Columbus, Ohio, Louisville, Ky., Chi- cago, Minneapolis, Washington, D.C., Atlanta, Nashville, Kansas City, Los Angeles, Salt Lake City, and Seattle. Florida and Texas dates will soon be added. This is the group’s third American tour. King To Forest HOLLYWOOD — Charles “Casey” King becomes the production manag- er for Fun Productions, a division of The David Forest Company, Ltd. Also at Forest is Greg Mundy in charge of public relations for the management enterprise and Sue Finn, the compa- ny’s administrative coordinator. NO COLD FEET FOR HOT SOCKS—Sha Na Na held a first, as the first group to hold a party for their record company. Quoting from their invitation : “To commemorate the completion of our sixth album on the Kama Sutra label, “Hot Socks,” and to show our appreciation to the people at The Buddah Group, a party will be held.” The event took place at the Buddah home offices in New York on March 14. Seen here, just moments before the unveiling of the master tape of “Hot Socks” are: (1. to r.) Chico, Screamin’, Vinnie, Captain, Lenny, Johnny, Bowzer, Jocko, Donnie, Art Kass, president of The Buddah Group, Milt Sincoff, direc- tor of creative packaging, Denny, Bruce Bird, national director of pop promo- tion. Bill Able, director of FM promotion and Johnny Lloyd, national director of R&B promotion. Presiding (on the left) over all is the group’s manager, Ed Goodgold. “Hot Socks” is scheduled for release in the coming weeks. The album was produced by Bob Ezrin, the producer of four Alice Cooper LP’s and Lou Reed’s “Berlin.” Jack Douglas served as co-producer.

ABC Gets It Wright HOLLYWOOD — Due to a human error at ABC Records, Charles Wright’s latest single release was an- nounced as “That’s All That Matters, Baby—Part II.” The correct title for the single should have been “You Threw It All Away.” Both songs are from Charles Wright’s debut album on ABC Records, “Doin’ What Comes Naturally.” ‘Black American’ From Jewel Label SHREVEPORT — Stan Lewis, presi- dent of Jewel Record Corporation an- nounced the rush release of a record- ing by Don Evans entitled “The Black American”. Lewis stated “The record- ing is a masterpiece of black litera- ture telling the story of the black man as it has never been told before.” The story was written by a Ft. Worth, Texas lady, Adelle Jackson Martin. Her husband, Otis J. Martin, well known Ft. Worth business man auditioned several voices in reading “The Black American”. They both agreed that the voice of Don Evans was the one that did the work justice. Otis, who had never been inside a recording studio before, recorded the basic parts of the selection. The recording came to Jewel’s at- tention through a local gospel group in Dallas, Texas. A member of that group casually mentioned it to a vice- president of Jewel. Lewis immediately sent a representative to Ft. Worth, at which time the masterpiece was ac- quired. Lewis, who had been produc- ing many of the Jewel acts, went into the studio again to personally finish the product. Soul Surges At NEW YORK—Soul is surging at RCA: With singles and albums creating nationwide excitement, airplay and sales, RCA’s Rhythm and Blues sector is enjoying one of the best and most productive periods in its history. “We are hot,” states Tom Draper, Manager, Rhythm and Blues, “and we’re getting hotter.” Draper points to the heavy airplay Sammy Davis to MO Afro-American Gala At Spokane Expo 74 SPOKANE — Sammy Davis has ac- cepted the co-chairmanship of Expo ’74 World’s Fair Afro-American Heri- tage Day Festival, which will be launched via a special benefit gala on June 14 and 15. A “first” in the annals of World’s Fair history within the United States, the introduction of the Afro-American Pavilion marks the initial time an ex- hibition has been created to trace the history, culture and contributions to the environment by Afro-Americans from the year 1400 through 1974. En- dorsed by the Governor of Washing- ton and granted $200,000 for its de- velopment by the State Legislature, the Afro-American Pavilion will seek to raise another $100,000 as a result of the benefit gala which may itself result in still another “first” in terms of the largest assemblage of Afro- American entertainers to ever appear in concert. Michael Kobluk, Director of Visual and Performing Arts for Expo ’74, noted that the enthusiastic response by Sammy Davis to serve as co-chair- men for the Afro-American Heritage Day Festival has already been echoed by a host of top entertainers from throughout the nation, who have ex- pressed their desires to participate in the benefit gala. A roster of star names appearing on June 14 and 15 will be announced shortly, according to Kobluk. Blue Note, founded in 1939, and at 35 the oldest jazz-oriented label in existence, is currently represented by a new Donald Byrd album, “Street Lady,” and flautist Bobbi Humphrey’s “Blacks And Blues.” Plans call for the release of three albums from Blue Note during April, Alphonse Mouzon’s “Funky Snakefoot,” McCoy Tyner’s “Asante,” and an album by the late trumpeter Lee Morgan, the “Lee Morgan Memorial Album.” The Morgan album will include his jazz standard “Sidewinder,” and renditions of “You Go To My Head,” and “Just One Of Those Things.” The Blue Note Month campaign be- will also receive awards for the impe- tus she gave to jazz by her mag- nificent portrayal of Billie Holiday in the film ‘Lady Sings the Blues’ for which she received an Academy Award Nomination. Expands: More Courses NEW YORK — The Recording In- stitute of America’s (RIA) basic Modem Recording Techniques Course I, has been expanding in more cities throughout the country. The course is presently in Memphis at the Ardent Recording Studio. The instructor there is Jim Tarbutton. At Omega Studios in Chicago the RIA increased its course to six con- secutive classes with five different in- structors teaching the course. They are Ed Rehm, Murray Allan, Dave Purple, Richie Adler, and Bruce Swedeen. Harry Hetherington who is legal counsel for Peer Southern Publishing Co. in New York was sent to Pitts- burgh where he was guest speaker for the Recording Institute of Amer- ica at Audio Innovators Recording Studio. He discussed legal aspects of Recording. €^ashbox news CBS Posts Top First Quarter In Its History NEW YORK — CBS has reported the highest first quarter sales and operating earnings in the company's history, ac- cording to William S. Paley, chairman and Arthur R. Taylor, president. Income from continuing operations is estimated at $20.9 million, 22% ahead of the $1 7.1 million earned in the first quarter of 1973. Sales for the period increased to $414.5 million, a 14% rise over the $363.7 million in the comparable period last year. Estimated first quarter operating earn- ings per share were 734, 22% higher than the 604 operating earnings per share achieved in the first quarter of 1973. (First quarter 1973 earnings per share do not include a gain on discon- tinued operations of 184 resulting primarily from the sale of the New York Yankees.) Commenting on the first quarter results, Paley and Taylor said, “CBS has now enjoyed 12 consecutive quarters in which sales and operating earnings have improved over comparable year-earlier periods. " MCA Reports Record Income UNIVERSAL CITY — MCA Inc. has an- nounced a combined operating income figure of $18,234,000 in 1973 for its records and music publishing divisions. This represents an increase of 49% from the $12,246,000 figure reached in 1972. For MCA Records, under the ad- ministration of its president, J.K. Maitland, this figure represents an all time high, both in operating income and in gross revenues. Five singles and six LP albums achieved "gold " record status during 1973. The singles were "Half Breed " by Cher, “Drift Away " by Dobie Gray, “Gar- den Party" by Rick Nelson, “Crocodile Rock " and “Goodbye Yellow Brick Road " by Elton John. The LP records were “Hot August Night " by Neil Diamond, “Quadrophenia" by The Who, “Don't Shoot Me, I'm Only The Piano Player" and "Goodbye Yellow Brick Road " by Elton John, and the movie soundtracks from “Jesus Christ Super- star” and “American Graffiti, " RCA Promo Man Back On Disks NEW YORK — RCA Records' Cincinnati based promo man Rob Hegel has traded his promo bag for the studio. Hegel has just cut his first single for RCA, “New York City Girl.” In addition to singing, Hegel also wrote, produced, and played piano on the session. Hegel went from music director at WFIB at the University of Cin- cinnati, to doing independent promo in that city. C. S. N. & Y. Reunion NEW YORK Crosby, Stills, Nash and Young will reunite this summer, their manager confirmed last week. They got together two months ago in Hawaii and discussed getting back together. Prior commitments had Neil Young the last to confirm. The first date will be June 29 at Fort Collins, near Denver on the Colorado State University Campus, according to Bill Graham, the San Francisco promoter who will produce some of the concerts. The official opening will be in Southern California on July 6th at either the Los Angeles Coliseum or the Ontario Motor Speedway near Los Angeles. Phil Jones Joins Polydor, Inc. As Assistant to Pres. Beltran NY Times Co-Pub, Admn Ties With Jackie DeShannon NEW YORK — Murray Deutch, president of the New York Times Music Publishing Corp. has announced a long-term co- publishing and administration agreement with Plain & Simple Music, which includes a writing and in-house production agreement with singer/- writer/producer Jackie De Shannon. Plain & Simple has a staff of five writers in addition to Ms De Shannon and a catalog of over 250 copyrights including “Vanilla Olay." Ms De Shannon, who currently records for Atlantic Records, won five Grammy nominations for “What The World Needs Now” and "Put A Little Love In Your Heart. " Her writing reflects her background in pop, blues, folk and country music. She has starred in vir- tually every major TV variety show and has presented an Oscar-nominated song on the Academy Awards telecast. A highly prolific writer, her hits include "Put A Little Love In Your Heart,” "Dum Dum,” "Heart In Hand," “So Deep, " “When You Walk In The Room, " "The Great Imposter " and "Come Stay With Me. " The current agreement adds to the New York Times Music Corp.'s recent acquisitions of Metromedia Music, the Clyde Otis pop-soul catalog and the score to the smash hit Broadway musical “Over Here.” Clapton ToU.S. To Cut New Set NEW YORK — Eric Clapton arrived in the United States last Sat. (13) to start work on a new album. The album, to be produced by Tom Dowd, has been ten- tatively set for a late summer release by RSO Records. Musicians working with Clapton on the album will include bass player Carl Radle, formerly with Derek and the Dominos. Robert Stigwood ad- ded that no tour plans for Clapton have yet been finalized. Bill Oakes, president of RSO Records, noted that it will be Clapton's first new studio recording since "Layla,” the multi-million selling double album re- corded nearly three years ago. His two most recent albums for RSO, both cer- tified gold, were live recordings — "Derek and the Dominos in Concert " and “Eric Clapton's Rainbow Concert. " Clapton hosted a celebration party in London at the China Garden Restaurant in Soho for more than 300 guests, in- cluding his friends George Harrison, Ringo Starr, Elton John, Jimmy Page, Ronnie Wood, Steve Winwood, Pete Townsend, Rod Stewart, Alvin Lee, among others. Good News Ends U.A. Ties Acquires “Love Song” LP HOLLYWOOD — Freddie Piro, Good News Records president, has an- nounced that the label had recently con- cluded negotiations with United Artists Records to acquire all the distribution rights for the Good News label, thus en- ding a two year association. Included in the agreement were the entire distribution rights to the first album by Love Song, titled "Love Song”. Since its initial release in 1972, the album, a mixture of rock, folk and western, has received widespread ac- ceptance in all areas of the gospel market. It became the top selling gospel album in the nation for 1973 as well as receiving various awards. HOLLYWOOD — Phil Jones has been named assistant to the president at Polydor, Inc., the new organization which includes the Polydor and MGM labels. Beltran, head of the operation, stated that the vet music man’s "unique marketing and promotion expertise will assure all Polydor labels greater success in the future. ’ Jones comes to Polydor Inc. after 12 years in the Motown Records organization, where he was instrumental in establishing the marketing and promo activities for the label. Jones has also served on the NARM Manufacturers Ad- visory Board. Jones' career in the music business began in the early 50 "s with one-stop and rack jobbing situations in Detroit. Al Riley Dies NEW YORK — Al Riley, national promo director of Chess/Janus Records, died here last week of cancer at the age of 36. Riley started as R&B promo director of Janus in 1970, and when Janus merged into Chess in Dec., 1971, he was named national promo director of the combined labels. Riley spent six years with Liberty Records and its affiliate labels, leaving as national promo director of Minit/Blue Note/Solid State Records. He started as a clerk at Liberty and subsequently rose to salesman in the greater New York area, branch promo man, east coast regional promo man, east regional promo director for Blue Note/Solid State Records and national sales and promo director for Minit before joining Chess. Riley is survived by two daughters. CBS records has released the first album under its new distribution agreement with Kirshner Records. The releases will feature three album releases on the Columbia label; Earth, Youth Movement Institutes ‘Black Record’ (James Brown First Recip NEW YORK — The National Youth Movement (NYM), the black self help youth organization has instituted a series of awards to be presented to black re- cording artists. The award will be called. The Black Record’ which will cite those songs considered relevant to Black young people by NYM. "Traditionally, gold records have been given to recor- ding artists for a record that sells a mil- lion copies or more, the NYM Black Record will be the black communities’ answer to this ritual, ” said Rev. Sharp- ton. The Rev. Alfred Sharpton, NYM’s 19 year old Chairman stated, "Our Black Record will salute those artists that record a song that has particular relevance to Black America in its present condition. White people give gold records to those recording, stars that make large sums of money for white companies, it is now time for black people to salute those who have stayed black both musically and in other areas. Black people must at this time demand the proper music and proper lyrics that relate to our plight as a people. This award will be given to tunes that are at- tuned with the community." Rev. Sharpton presented the first Black Record to the Godfather of Soul, James Brown at his Manhattan Center concert Friday, April 6, 1974. The award was designed and made by a young Harlemnite named Samuel Spencer. Rev. Sharpton, during the presentation said, “Everyone knows that James Brown has been a brother on many levels for many years. His new release, the "Payback, " expresses the sentiments of many young blacks. We cite him because many white and Uncle Toms refused to give him what he is due. We, the young people both love and respect him, and in the final analysis, it is we, the young consumer that really counts.” NEW YORK — Black Ivory signed an ex- clusive recording contract with Kwanza Records, distributed by Warner Bros. The Jazz Zone’ New Nile Show CHICAGO — "The Jazz Zone," a new radio show featuring the jazz sounds of the "50s and "60s, premiered Wed- nesday, March 27, at 5:30 p.m. on WB- MX-FM, stereo 1 03 on the dial. Illinois Bell is the sponsor of The Jazz Zone, which will be hosted by black jazz musician Morris Ellis. The show, nostalgic in mood, is aired from 5:30 to 6:30 p.m. Wednesdays through Fridays, and from 1 1 p.m. to midnight Saturdays. Ellis, who is an orchestra leader and owner of a commercial production firm in Chicago, will play and analyze records from the past by jazz artists such as John Coltrane, Billie Holiday and Wes Mon- tgomery. He will display his jazz exper- tise through comment on the musical style and personality of famous jazz musicians. He will also interview jazz performers and develop insights into their works. Ellis is a graduate of Howard Univer- sity, where he majored in psychology and political science. He is 44 years old and lives on Chicago's South Side with his wife, Barbara, and their two children. Mrs. Ellis is a schoolteacher. "We think The Jazz Zone will fill an im- portant niche in Chicago radio, " said Robert Campbell, Illinois Bell's adver- tising manager. “It offers listeners an ap- pealing alternative to the traditional soul-rock and pop format. Illinois Bell also sponsors "Lu's Notebook," a five-minute news commen- tary by black journalist Lu Palmer heard twice a dqy, Monday through Saturday, over four black-oriented radio stations in the Chicago area. 28 Cash Box — April 20. 1 974

Chet Atkins, guitarist and RCA executive, and Cecil Null, songwriter and president of Old Masters Records, donated the instrument on T ravis' behalf. Atkins noted that "the guitar includes many features which later became stan- dard on electric guitars. The strings are attached through the body from the guitar's back and the turning gears are all on one side of the peghead. It is obvious from a glance at the guitar that it inspired the Fender line. " The guitar — the first solid-body in- strument actually used in professional performance — was designed by Merle Travis in the late 1940's, and was hand built by Paul Bigsby in 1948. Atkins add- ed that "the guitar still sounds good. It has a pickup designed and hand-wired by Bigsby, and it has a particularly full and rounded tone even in the highest register of the instrument. " Diane Johnson — curator of the Hall of Fame and Museum — accepted the donation of the rare instrument. Cash Box — April 20, 1 974

U.S. A. Runstein Book NEW YORK — Robert E. Runstein, for- mer chief engineer and technical direc- tor of Intermedia Sound of Boston, and currently a&r director of North Country Productions, Ltd. announced publication of his book "Modern Recording Techniques" by Howard W. Sams and Co.. Inc. He has focused on equipment, con- trols, and techniques used in the modern multitrack studio with descriptions and explanations designed for producers and artists as well as engineers. The text is intended for individual study as well as tor use in classrooms and engineer training programs. Among the topics in- cluded are the recording chain, sound and hearing, microphones, and magnetic tape recording. The book is available tor $9.95 at elec- tronic parts distributors and bookstores that stock Sams publications, or directly from the publisher in Indianapolis. ‘Men Upstairs’ Aid Famous In All Music Areas Contribute Varied Music Success Pattern To CBS/Records Top 1 st Qtr NEW YORK — Famous Music Publishing Companies’ turnaround from a traditional film company subsidiary, leaning heavily on its film catalog, to one of the more competitive operations around (Lobo, Jim Stafford, The Hollies), could well become a “classic case of how conglomerate acquisitions in our business can pay off," according to Mar- vin Cane, chief operating officer for Famous Music Publishing Companies. Cane continued, “immediately following the Paramount Pictures acquisition, Gulf & Western board chairman Charles Bluh- dorn and David N. Judelson, president of G&W, breathed life into the film com- pany, and, at the same time, made the commitment to revitalize the music divisions.” FRONT COVER: Aretha Franklin is indeed the heir to the legacy of Billie Holiday, and as the reigning 'Queen of Soul' it is only ap- propriate that she is currently repre- sented on the Cash Box singles chart with “I'm in Love,” pulled from her char- ted Atlantic album, "Let Me In Your Life. ” She has meant a great deal to music fans since her first hit, “I Never Loved a Man,” hit big in 1967. Aretha’s string of successes, which have led her to a dozen gold records, are mirrored by the constant demand for her to appear in concert, something which she does lovingly, if all too sparingly. With each step in her career a triumph, Aretha Franklin has earned the deserved respect of fans and peers alike. INDEX Album Review 18 Coin Machine News 35-39 Country Music Section 19-25 For the Record 15 Insights 32 Looking Ahead 28 New Additions to Playlist 31 On the Road 15 Past Hits 28 Radio Active Chart 28 R&B News Report 27 Radio News Report 29 R&B Top 70 42 Single Reviews 16 Talent On Stage 30 Top 170 Albums 41 Vital Statistics 28 "What’s so great about these men up- stairs Js that they made themselves available,’’ Cane states. "We com- municated with them, bounced ideas around. We’ve all heard stories about what happens when big companies acquire smaller operations. Our set-up is different. This ’open-door' attitude and the accessibility of Top Brass makes the adrenalin flow and has boosted morale in the publishing division. The best part is that word got around the industry that the G&W management supported with action the professional commitment made by the music publishing divisions." This resulted in our first big year under Gulf and Western with ‘Love Story,' Make It Easy On Yourself,’ Me And You And A Dog Named Boo,' and Come Saturday Morning. ' You can see from the results that our strategy to balance the pop and film music worked great.” Yablans Role Cane said the division "got another break when Frank Yablans was named president of Paramount Pictures. Hall NEW YORK — Irving Berlin and George Gershwin are the two musical creators among the 10 major talents selected as the first inductees into the Entertain- ment Hall of Fame. The 10 were select- ed in a nation-wide poll of entertainment editors, and will be honored at the first annual awards ceremony scheduled for the MGM Grand Hotel in Las Vegas this week (23). The other inductees include Charles Chaplin, Judy Garland, D. W. Griffith, Katharine Hepburn, Lord Laurence Olivier, Eugene O'Neill, George Bernard Shaw and Tennessee Williams. The awards presentation will be televised on May 23rd over ABC-TV's "Wide World of Entertainment." Host of the show will be Gene Kelly, and John Green will produce the special. NEW YORK — The CBS/Records Group’s first quarter of 1974 was the most successful in the group's history. Goddard Lieberson, president, said that the achievement was a tribute to the ef- forts of Irwin Segelstein, president of CBS Records, and Walter Yetnikoff, president of CBS International, and their division associates both in A&R and in marketing. All areas of recorded music contributed to the company's sales growth, Lieberson stated. Columbia For the Columbia label, the first quar- ter brought six gold records, including Chicago’s single, "Just You ’N Me" and album Chicago VII; David Essex’ "Rock On"; Barbra Streisand's "The Way We Were"; Johnny Winter’s “Johnny Winter Live" and Jim Nabors' “The Lord's Prayer ”, In addition to the records which reached gold, there were many other major releases which boosted overall sales for the first quarter. On Columbia, such artists as Paul Simon, Herbie Han- also gives us an opportunity to present technical descriptions — for the first time publicly — of some of Disco-Vision’s in- novative techniques which have heretofore been kept confidential, pend- ing filing or granting of necessary patent applications." The high-density 12-inch Disco-Vision disc is the audio-visual equivalent of an LP record. It revolves at 30 revolutions per second and its microgrooves are scanned by a low-power laser beam — rather than a needle — to relay sound and pictures from the disc to the screen of any standard TV set. Disco-Vision will enable viewers to see the subjects of their choice on home TV screens when the system's relatively inexpensive player or player/changer unit is attached to the VHF input terminals of any stan- dard television receiver, tuned to a chan- nel not used for regular programming. Rodgers, Harnick To Team On New Broadway Musical NEW YORK — Composer Richard Rodgers and lyricist Sheldon Harnick will collaborate for the first time on a new musical, “Rex," to be produced next season. The storyline centers around Henry VIII, according to producer Richard Adler, and will have a book by Jerome Lawrence and Robert E. Lee. In more than 50 years of composing for the professional theatre, Rodgers, who will be 72 this June, has had only four collaborators. They are Larry Hart, Oscar Hammerstein, Stephen Sondheim and Martin Charnin. Harnick's chief col- laborator in recent years has been Jerry Bock ("Fiorello!” and "Fiddler on the Roof,” among others). After the death of Oscar Hammerstein in 1960, Rodgers began to write his own lyrics, supplying additional songs for the film re-make of “State Fair" and a totally new score for "No Strings." He teamed with Sondheim and Charnin for one musical each, "Do I Hear a Waltz?” and “Two By Two," respectively. cock, Billy Joel, Earth, Wind & Fire, Tanya Tucker, Johnny Winter and Mac Davis have all had new product, either during or just prior to the first three months of 1974. Also, the continuing sales strength of previously released albums by Columbia artists such as Neil Diamond, Loggins & Messina, Lynn An- derson, Garfunkel, Santana, Sonny James, The Mahavishnu Orchestra, Johnny Mathis, Ray Price and Barbara Fairchild helped to bolster the high sales volume. Epic/Col Custom Epic and Columbia Custom Labels have been a major factor in the success- ful sales performance in this quarter, with releases by such artists as Rick Der- ringer (Blue Sky), Redbone, The Staple Singers (Stax), George Jones, David Houston & Barbara Mandrell, Albert Hammond (Mums) and Charlie McCoy (Monument). Steady sales on previously released albums by Epic/Custom artists such as Edgar Winter, Sly & The Family Stone, Tammy Wynette, Isaac Hayes (Stax) and Poco also contributed to the company’s enormous first-quarter results. The Philadelphia International Custom Label earned two gold records with The O’Jays’ "Ship A hoy" and MF- SB's "TSOP" as well as steady sales with other artists on their roster including Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes and Billy Paul. Rich Success Of all the Epic artists, the greatest suc- cess was achieved by Charlie Rich who won the following awards during recent months; NARM’s Award for Best Selling (continued on P. 12) Taylor: CBS/Records Sales Up 22% In 1 st Qtr ATLANTA — In achieving it’s best first quarter in history the CBS Records Group increased sales 22% over last year, according to CBS president Arthur Taylor. Taylor, addressing a stockholders meeting here last week, said that "Measures taken to halt the deterioration of profit margin have started to show positive results." The recording division, he said, faces “severe cost pressures, particularly in the area of recording talent, and (vinyl) is still in short supply (but) long-term contracts are helping to assure the vinyl supplies we require, and careful planning has helped to control cost increases ..." CBS Records International, Taylor said, continues to be "One of our fastest-growing divisions. Though it ex- perienced first quarter softness in France and Germany, sales were strong in Latin America, Canada, Australia and, surprisingly, Great Britain. We cannot be certain what impact current fluctuations, inflation and political instability around the world will have on the rest of the year, but the indication is that the great popular acceptance of our roster of American and foreign artists should enable us to perform well in almost any climate.” Taylor also said that the Retail Stores division, with Pacific Stereo and Discount Records operating under a common management, saw '"im- provement" from Discount, while Pacific Stereo "has rebounded from slower sales growth in Feb., and in Mar. ran well ahead of last year's record pace." New Acts Break During the past months, Columbia Records has paid special attention to breaking new artists and expanding the sales levels of established performers. Herbie Hancock's “Headhunters" album opened up a new audience for him as well as other jazz/ rock artists on the CBS Records roster. David Essex and Billy Joel have also broken into top chart position with their singles, David Essex' “Rock On" reaching No. 1. Barbra Streisand scored with “The Way We Were," and the soundtrack and studio albums of the same name. (Both the single and the studio album reached No. 1 on the charts). Also, through a carefully planned effort, Columbia has begun to expose Tanya Tucker to the contem- porary music audience thus adding to her already vast country following. Epic and Columbia Custom Labels cites several break-throughs with new ar- tists. Epic recording group Redbone rose high on the charts with their single "Come And Get Your Love." Philadelphia International recording group MFSB has topped the charts with their single "TSOP," which the Epic/Custom staff helped to cross over from the soul market into all other musical formats, making it the #1 single and the #1 album. Blue Sky recording ar- tist Rick Derringer was brought out from the shadow of superstars Edgar and Johnny Winter and hit big with his own album, “All American Boy” and his single, “Rock N Roll Hoochie Koo." Classic Success Responsible for six of the total of 11 Grammy Awards won by CBS Records artists was the Columbia Classical Division. Among these six was another Grammy for Vladimir Horowitz, the 12th of his illustrious career (the largest num- ber by any classical performer). CBS Int’l CBS Records International, a division which has grown 400% in the past four years, enjoyed its most successful quar- ter in the initial months of 1974. High sales volumes in England, Holland, Brazil, Mexico, Australia, Canada and Japan spearheaded this success. Charlie Rich, Robert Knight, the Three Degrees and Harold Melvin & The Blue Notes were among the U.S. acts which CBS U.K. broke in this first quarter period. England reconfirmed the star status of Andy Williams, whose "Solitaire" single and album remain best sellers there. English television and recording act the Wombles achieved constant success. Tiara, a newly formed music company based in Chicago, is owned and operated by Jerry Aaron, president and Carter Russell, Jr., vice president. The company will be formally introduced to press and public at the Continental Plaza’s Cotillion Room. Kelly Mann will do the honor of presenting Tiara the three-point crown company to the media. Tiara's first release "Come And Ask Me" will be performed by The 5 Wagers. Yvonne Daniels of WLS is to be mistress of ceremonies. Joe Cobb (WVON) and Richard Steel (WJPC) will anchor the entire show. It shapes up to be a big night in Chicago ... Mayfield Sets 6th Solo LP NEW YORK — "Sweet Exorcist," Curtis Mayfield's sixth solo album on the Cur- tom lable, is being released by The Bud- dah Group this month. Mayfield who has three gold albums, “Curtis,” "Super Fly” and "Back To The World," denied the LP title is connected with the film. In talking about the tone of his album, as well as this song, Curtis added, "There is also a timely element in it, of people generally feeling depressed, going through hard changes and down feelings.” Among the songs on the album is "To Be Invisible," from Curtis, "Claudine" soundtrack which deals with the crushing weight of the world for many people. “But instead of giving up to these bad feelings, what I am speaking of is can- celling them out, getting beyond them, through a ‘sweet exorcism’,” said Mayfield. SESSION TIME - Buddy Killen, executive vice president of Dial Records, Annette Snell, popular Dial Recording artist, and Paul Kelly, Dial producer, are shown during Annette's recent recording session at Soundshop Studios in Nashville. Kelly and Killen co-produced the session. Award To Charles NEW YORK — “Ray Charles,” children's biography penned by Sharon Bell Mathis and illustrated by George Ford, has been selected to receive the 1974 Coretta Scott King Award at the American Library Association's annual convention, meeting in New York in early July. The award is presented yearly to honor authors and publishers who produce books that inspire young people to use their talents to make Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.’s “Dream ” their own. Ray Charles will be honored with a plaque commending him for “his own courage and determination to hold fast to "his Dream' and become one of America's outstanding performers.” Ray Charles' current album on Cross- over Records is “Come Live With Me." Jazz Interactions Honors Ellington April 28th In NYC NEW YORK — More than one hundred performers will help celebrate Jazz In- teractions' ninth anniversary in a marathon fund raising affair in honor of Duke Ellington on his 75th birthday. This event will take place at Pub Theatrical on Broadway at 51st Street in New York City, starting at 5 p.m. Sunday April 28th, 1974, and continuing into the morning of the 29th. Benny Goodman will be among the many outstanding musicians to pay tribute. Jazz Interactions will present a special award to WRVR’s Max Cole for his dedication to Jazz. cashbox/news Instrumentals Take The Spotlight Adams’ New Term As Musical 1974 Marks A New Trend As ASCAP Prexy NEW YORK — A phenomenon currently in existence in the music industry is the success of the instrumental of late, suc- cess that seems, for the most part, to have been all too rare over the past few years. The fact that three instrumentals are currently listed in the Cash Box Top 10 Singles chart bears that fact dramatically. Of these three, "TSOP" by MFSB has already topped the charts (currently listed at #7), “The Entertainer" by Marvin Hamlisch (currently charted at #4 with a bullet) seems headed in that same direction, and “Tubular Bells (Theme From The Exorcist)" by Mike Oldfield (this week #6) has also that same chart topping potential in the coming weeks. Other Media Tie-In An interesting aspect of all three disks is that each is not only a music industry success but is part of other media suc- cess stories. "TSOP" is the main title song from the soul-oriented television series, “Soul Train". "The Entertainer” was culled from the academy award win- ning soundtrack of “The Sting”, and “Tubular Bells" appears as part of the soundtrack of “The Exorcist" (although only half of the song actually appears in the film). The marriage of the media seems to be working well both sides (film & music, television & music) and a definite trend seems to have been established, at least on the instrumental level. Of those other instrumental successes of the year thus far, another obvious disk to note is "Love's Theme" by Barry White's Love Unlimited Orchestra, a for- mer #1 charted disk that may have been the one to have opened the flood gates for the instrumental. Other successes thus far, as we stand in only the fifth month of 1974, have been "Jungle Boogie" by Kool and The Gang (there were not nearly enough lyrics to qualify as anything but an instrumental success), BURKE’S DREAM - Solomon Burke, veteran performer, has recently signed with ABC Records, who will be releasing his debut LP titled "I Have a Dream” this week. The album draws its inspiration from many of the speeches of Dr. Martin Luther King. Pictured are, from left to right: Herman Rush, Solomon's manager; Otis Smith, vice president; Howard Start, vice president; Solomon Burke (seated); and Jay Lasker, president of ABC Records. Jerry Tiefer, vice president and general manager of ABC/Dunhill Music, Inc. (BMI) and American Broadcasting Music, Inc. (ASCAP), has announced the appointment of James Krondes as east coast professional manager of the ABC Music Publishing companies. Krondes has a vast background in music publishing and in the production and promotion of records. His most recent assignment was as east coast professional manager of Metromedia. Music. Prior to that he was east coast professional manager of Sunbury/Dun- bar, Inc. "Jessica" by the Allman Brothers Band, “Pepper Box" by the Peppers (also a smash European hit), "Chameleon" by Herbie Hancock (currently on the rise on the single chart) and Cozy Powell's "Danc£ With The Devil" (also currently in The Cash Box singles chart). The reasons for the successes of these disks not associated with other media are varied. The return of the discoteque, at least on the east coast, and the dance, may have something to do with it. People may be dancing a bit more now than they were five years ago, maybe to take their minds off of their problems. Some say that the generation that brought rock to the prominence it reached in the mid & late sixties has now grown up and can more greatly appreciate music for music's sake. If so, that maturity definitely shows in current sales figures. Still another reason, an offshoot of the maturity belief, is that instrumentals are not longer considered "musak” and studio musicians along with their producers, engineers, etc. are finally realizing that instrumentals can be suc- cessful when taken from the background and brought into the foreground. Hence, the better quality of the instrumental and better quality always generates greater sales, in any market selling any product. How will the trend affect the remain- der of the year? Only time will tell, ob- viously. But people are beginning to sit up & take notice. Both music folk and the consumer are fully aware of the times and the importance of entertainment. The return of Herb Alpert and his Tijuana Brass is an important step in that future. From the current vantage point, things look very positive. There’s an ex- cellent chance that we ll all have lots more "good" music to listen to in the future. Weiser Named To Board At ASCAP NEW YORK — Norm Weiser, president of Chappell Music Co., has been ap- pointed to the board of directors of ASCAP, president Stanley Adams has announced. Weiser will complete the unexpired term of Jacques Chabrier, who has resigned after six years of ser- vice on the board of the performing rights society. Weiser started his career as a reporter for "Radio Daily" and "Film Daily," moved to "Billboard" as music editor and later became publisher of “Down Beat" and 14 other magazines. He also wrote a music column syndicated to 200 newspapers. In 1960, he was named vice president of records and publishing at United Ar- tists. In 1962, he went to 20th Century Fox as vice president of music activities, later rejoining UA as vice president and director, west coast music division. After representing Paramount in London as director of European operations, he joined Chappell in Aug. 1969 as vice president and general manager. Commented Adams, "Norman Weiser brings a breadth and variety of solid ex- perience to the ASCAP Board, and his practical knowledge of the music world promises a substantial contribution to the 16,000 writers and 6,000 publishers who comprise our membership. His ability, his knowledge and his energy have made him a dynamic figure in the music community, and we are confident that he will be a most valued addition to our Board."
