RCA Adds It All Up: Denver Sales Bonanza NEW YORK — Just before the end of April, RCA Records made a tally, the results of which show that John Denver's album, "John Denver's Greatest Hits,” had sold more than one and one half mil- lion copies since Jan. 1. Added to the sales it had garnered in the late months of 1973, the album pushed ahead of the 2-million sales mark. Ken Glancy, president of RCA Records, noted: "And this is domestic commercial sales only ... it does not in- clude RCA Record and Tape Club sales, nor any sales in any other country of the world. Glancy had company researchers dig farther, and described the results as "ab- solutely phenomenal!" In the first four months of the year, Denver's entire album catalog has sold more than 2V2 million units. Another album, “Poems, Prayers and Promises," has added another half a million units and its total sale is approaching 2 million. Another big seller is “Rocky Mountain High," also pushing toward the 2- million-unit plateau. All those figures are on the domestic commercial sales basis alone. Also in the first four months of this year, the single, "Sunshine on My Shoulders," which went gold soon after its release, has sold more than a million and a half copies. "There is no doubt," said Glancy, "that John Denver, in the first third of 1974, has been the hottest selling artist in the entire recording industry in America. This has been a marvelous campaign in ! which we have worked closely with Jerry Weintraub and have had the fullest cooperation. MCA, Inc. McCartney Sees No Reunion Of The Beatles NEW YORK — Paul McCartney's rep has "categorically denied and refuted” rumors and reports of a reunion for in- person appearances of The Beatles. As far as McCartney is concerned, the Beatles will not be performing together at any time, nor have any offers by promoters for any type of performance been discussed. McCartney points out that being seen with other Beatles is merely social since they are still friendly and any professional collaboration might be assisting each other on recording tracks. McCartney further states that he is devoting all his talents and attention to the reforming of his 'Wings Band for recording and other projects to take place later this year or early 1974 Sung Suh to UA LOS ANGELES— George Boyle, vice president and controller of United Artists Records, has announced the appoint- ment of Sung Hee Suh to the post of director of accounting for United Artists Records. Suh will also assume respon- sibility for UA s royalty department. A native of Korea, Suh was most recently with the accounting firm of Peat, Marwick, Mitchell and Co. where he was heavily involved in the entertainment in- dustry. It is McCartney’s contention that the proliferation of rumors and stories in the print and electronic media that the Beatles will reunite are "a flagrant misrepresentation and a great disservice to the public.” McCartney feels that he, as well as the other former members of the group, are involved in their own projects which are ultimately accepted or rejected by the public. To lead this same public into believing a reunion is imminent, says McCartney, is damaging to all of the Beatles as individual artists. Womack Injured LOS ANGELES — United Artists Records artist Bobby’ Womack has can- celled some of the dates on his current concert tour because of illness.’ Womack sustained a slight concussion when he tripped over an amplifier while recording in the studio the week before last, and thereafter he complained of dizziness and impaired vision. Upon advice of his doctor,' Womack en- tered Hollywood Community Hospital that Friday for neurological tests which proved negative. After being released from the hospital on Sunday,’ Womack's doctor ordered a complete rest for him. OS ANGELES — ATV Music Group has made its first major publishing j acquisition through the purchase of the i entire catalog of Attache Music, formerly \ owned by Lee Hazlewood and Joe Nixon. Chapin Is Keynote Speaker At AGAC NEW YORK — The bi-monthly meeting of the American Guild of Authors and Composers took place April 24th at Kings Court, located in the Barbazon Plaza. Ervin Drake, president of AGAC, summarized the basic tenets of AGAC and how the organization works to protect the writer. He then introduced the guest speaker of the evening, who was Elektra recording artist Barry Chapin. Also, WHEW DJ Alison Steele acted in the capacity of moderator, inter- jecting and expanding on audience questions. Chapin, who was at one time a film maker between 1965-1971, has always had an interest in the music industry. He then wrote his #1 "Taxi" and from there got it all together. As he said, "The key is will and determination. Desire is the most important thing an artist must have. I've maybe met one out of any 10 tal- ented artists who had the desire to follow it through ” Chapin feels that managers are merely frustrated performers who never made it. Also, commenting on the writer who wishes to play place his material with an artist, Chapin said it was very difficult and that he at one time had the same idea but ended up singing himself because he couldn't find anyone to perform his material. Chapin proved to be an in- teresting spokesman for a variety of topic . concerning the industry. Blue Note “Cooking” LOS ANGELES — Blue Note Records, under the direction of George Butler, is, in the parlance of the trade, "cooking." The United Artists-distributed label, the oldest jazz-oriented label in existence (founded in 1939), is currently strong on the pop charts with Donald Byrd’s "Street Lady” and Bobbi Humphrey's “Blacks and Blues;'' the recent release of Alphonze Mouzon's “Funky Snakefoot insures more soulful sounds from the label that likes to call its music "the sound of the street,” music which incor- porates jazz, soul, and rock into a sound that crosses over in many different direc- tions. Butler said that “we are trying to incor- porate a musical universality in which the music expressed by various artists on the label can reach a wide spectrum of musical tastes. " Bobbi Humphrey's “Blacks and Blues" broke in Baltimore/Washington, Seattle, New York, Detroit and Chicago, and, with the release of her "Chicago, Damn” single off the album, her career is in high gear. Blue Note's breakthrough began some 14 months ago, when Ed Levine, then director of promotion and sales for the label, and his assistant, Jere Hausfater, began a campaign to convince people that the artists and music on the label could become general market records. Says Levine: "Donald Byrd's "Black Byrd” began with jazz play and crossed over to R & B and pop. We even had some MOR’son the album. If the music is in the grooves, then it doesn’t matter what the label copy says. April was Blue Note Month at United Artists, with the entire organization get- ting behind a massive Blue Note sales program. Merchandising aids included a much-in-demand poster made from a painting by artist Francisco Toledo. Stut- ters for retail stores with minis of the top sellers on Blue Note were also used. Butler, who acts in creative and ad- ministrative capacity, works closely with Ed Levine, who was upped at the begin- ning of the year to the post of national director of promotion for United Artists and with Hausfater, once Levine's as- sistant, who is now in charge of Blue Note promotion. cash box talent on stage Fanny Chris Rush TOWN HALL, NYC - In a rare but delightful appearance, Casablanca recording artists Fanny played a memorable set before a small, but ap- preciative audience of enthusiastic fans. The all -female quartet whose live perfor- mances have become known for their lack of inhibition took the stage dressed in long flowing robes and masks. The group's music centered on feminist themes, but had the substantial rocking quality to maintain audience in- terest. The girls themselves, particularly new addition Patti Quatro (sister of British rock star Suzi) deported them- selves with poise and professionalism throughout and drew an enthusiastic response from their following. Hope to have them back again soon. Opening for Fanny was super comedian Chris Rush who, in typical fashion, brought the house down with his unique brand of 'humoristic realism' in which he draws from true -life experien- ces to make his routines effective. Rush's approach seemed to have everyone in the house identifying with him at one time or another and his presentation of early childhood ex- periences caused one youthful observer to literally fall in the aisle. Chris is curren- tly considering several major record company offers and will announce his new affiliation shortly. JUST A FACE IN THE CROWD B/W THIS COULD ONLY HAPPEN TO ME BY kittie dowsell H2468 r; Where The Musk and Entertainment People Meet To See and Be Seen it's IDEAL FACILITIES FOR ARTIST'S PROMOTION PARTIES CALL YOUR HOST TONY RICCIO 1523 CAHUENGA 466-3441 Todd Rundgren's Utopia CARNEGIE HALL - NYC - Whenever Carnegie Hall is invaded by rock perfor- mers, a carnival atmosphere prevails that seems to remove, or at least part asunder the clouds of Victorian dignity that have so long stood as cornerstones of the establishment. Such was the case when the futuristic Todd Rundgren and his band Utopia took over the building on W. 57th St. for three hours of madness and rockin' mayhem. Make no mistake, there is a legion of die'hard Rundgren fans who make all his shows (though his last one in New York was over two years ago), but the singularly striking impression Todd gave his audiences was that he was there to perform regardless of the number of people in the house. The fact that the show was a sellout obviously stimulated the performer and his six piece back-up band, and he encouraged the audience to participate in the show, handing out orchids and generally serving as master of ceremonies at a musical party whose backdrop ws replete with trees, festoons, and baubles of all kinds. Todd started the show solo, leaping on stage and, with the aid of programmed tapes sand "International Fee/Never Never Land," "It Wouldn't Have Made Any Difference," "I Saw The Light," and "Hello It's Me." He then introduced Utopia consisting of Ralph Schuckett and Mark Klingman on keyboards, John Siegler on bass, Kevin Ellman on drums, and M. Frog on synthesizer. Rundgren played guitar. They played the "Utopia Theme," "Black Maria," "Everybody's Going To Heaven," "Kiríg Kong Reg- gae," and an oldie, "Open My Eyes." The fact that there was an intermission bet- ween the segments featuring Todd and Utopia added to the Rundgren hysteria that had obviously swept even the post - pubescents off their feet so that when the entire ensemble closed with a 90 minute jam and then three encores (finishing with "Just One Victory," the audience applauded as if there were no tomorrow. Of course with Todd, there's always a tomorrow. d.b. Electric Light Orchestra Elvin Bishop SANTA MONICA CIVIC, L.A. - The Electric Light Orchestra has by now carved out its own peculiar niche in rock music, a place inhabited by smirking caricatures of teutonic masters, the logo of a corporate giant and the ghosts of an- cient rock 'n' rollers who haven't even died yet. Their enormous popularity rests upon admirable, often dazzling musicianship and the downright chut- zpah of their musical collage. In performance, surprisingly little in- tricacy within their extremely studied sound was lost. Instead, the band managed to demonstrate startling musical effects while simultaneously exhibiting the flash and polish associated with the best English rock bands, a sort of minimalist choreography that remains exhilarating even as it treads on predic- table ground. Cellist Mike Edwards bore his cumbersome instrument with capricious ease, and the remainder of the band was likewise animated. There were seven members on the stage led by guitarist, lead vocalist and composer Jeff Lynne, all combining to produce a sound that was deceptively full and varied in texture. Hitmongers among the audience were titillated by such songs as "Showdown"; they boogied to "Ma Ma Belle" and waited patiently for "Roll Over Beethoven," whose familiar strains were left for a rousing encore. Also featured in the finish was a neon incarnation of E.L.O.'s smartly designed logo and an early song of theirs, the "10583 Overture." Satisfied but not quite satiated, the audience clapped, cheered and went home. Opening act was Elvin Bishop's new group. Elvin, who became near to legen- dary for his early work with Paul Butter - field's band, can still be considered among the foremost guitarists in rock. Recently signed to Capricorn Records, he previewed some material from a forth- coming LP. e.s. Richard Pryor Main Ingredient Billy Paul APOLLO THEATRE, NYC - Richard Pryor, headlining a top-notch show, was a box office smash for this week long gig. On closing night, it was still standing room only business. Richard, is probably one of the hottest names on the comic scene. His newly released LP, "That Nig- ger's Crazy" on the Partee label, is one of the hottest and fastest moving items in several areas. Pryor accurately reflects the feelings and mood of the street. He knows what it is all about. His cutting wit and humor can strike a heckler dead in a second. His routines are classic and highly descriptive. Those who have seen him live are familiar with his 'Wino & Junkie' routine and "Have your ass home by 11 o'clock". They come across with uproarious response. He is earthy and dirty, but acceptable in all degrees. A natural genuine talent, he tells it like it is. Check him out. The Main Ingredient, with a release called, "Just Don't Want To Be Lonely" which seems to be headed for gold, also holds the audience spellbound, with past and current hits to its credit. The group performs with ease and perfection. Cuba Gooding, carrying the bulk of the lead chores, is now a solid get down deliverer. "Girl Blue," a Stevie Wonder gem, is matchless with the Cuba Gooding rendition. These three gen- tlemen are backed by a solid group, cal- led "The Human Revolution." The group's latest RCA recording, "California My Way" is in a solid swing groove. The Main Ingredient does turn an audience on. All three can make a woman swoon. Cuba, also in a mellow mood, turned it on with "Summer Breeze". Aside from the fact that their portion ran somewhat long, they were as usual impressive. But, it's Cuba Gooding that stands tall. Billy Paul, in the estimation of this reviewer, turned in one of the finest per- formances of his career. He has got his thing together. Billy, is backed by three soulful California chicks who also know what going down. Billy Paul turned it on and completely captivated all. His turn about from previous was shockingly great. "Me & Mrs. Jones", came off as fresh as today. "Thanks For Saving My Life", set everyone standing. The audience knew and felt where he was coming from. He was home. d.d. Leo Sayer TROUBADOUR, L.A. - Well, Jolson wore white face and we've all seen Mar- cel Marceau before; there were people wondering what the point of the whole thing was. It's been, after all, a long and gimmicky season in the world of rock 'n' roll. But Sayer, Leo the songwriter, artist and latent class clown, makes good use of his harlequin get-up. Its detachment, a wall of make-up that reveals nothing and keeps eveyone guessing what he's going to come up with. He comes up with songs. Cleverly, the set gets going with familiar stuff, a pair of songs that Leo co-authored for the "Daltrey" LP - "One Man Band" and "Giving It All Away" - and the audience identified immediately. Leo was an in- stant cultural hero within fifteen minutes of his set. ("Funny, he doesn't look Whoish," someone said.) His attack varied between the aggres- sive and the wispish; delicate little tunes had a habit of turning on the audience with mock fury. There was more than a little bit of showmanship - pure theater - but it was the music that really grab- bed the crowd, the pretty neatness of his compositions. Like a southpaw boxer, Leo had the right hook every time. Backed by an impressively competent group of musicians, Leo performed the majority of his "Silverbird" LP (Warner Bros.) and for a brief interlude combined his singing with only a piano and cello for a rendition of "The Dancer." Capping the set was the well-known song, "The Show Must Go On," and there was no disputing that the song belongs to Leo Sayer. e.s. The Eleventh House Larry Coryell and TROUBADOUR, L.A. - There have been vague murmurings, reports from obscure sources and a lot of cultish an- ticipation preceding the appearance of Larry Coryell and the Eleventh House. Something about how he used to jam with Hendrix and Winter in the days when Steve Paul's Scene was flourishing, and how he'd put together this great band with the drummer from the Weather Report. And then, when he opened, it was on the bottom of the bill with Leo Sayer, a really tough act to precede. Openers at the Troubadour usually get subjected to a rumble of chairs, a buzz of conver- sation and a generally uninterested crowd. But not so Larry Coryell. Within minutes after his opening piece, the club kept its collective mouth shut and listened. They were rewarded with some of the most cohesive and inventive progressive jazz-rock that this reviewer has ever heard. With Alphonse Mouzon simulating a loosely mechanized marionette hovering over his drum set, the other 4 members of the band created a maze of melody and rhythmic pattern. Unlike many of the "progressive" groups, the Eleventh House avoided the temptation to lapse into a mere display of acrobatics, and compositions like "Joy Ride," "The Funky Waltz" and "Yin" remained acces- sible in their intricacy. "Joy Ride," in par- ticular, with its theme and variations on a simple, pretty melody was an excellent vehicle for the group's considerable talents. Larry Coryell and the Eleventh House record on the Vanguard label and the bulk of their material was drawn from their recent LP. e.s. 32 May 18, 1974 www.americanradiohistory.com

cash box; 'news Ember To Glow in U.S. HOLLYWOOD - "I'm determined to establish artists for longevity," averred Jeffrey Kruger, president of Ember Records, after a luncheon launching his new artist Denny Doherty's initial Em- ber/Paramount single "You'll Never Know," held here last week. Kruger's aim for "longevity," is a bit of a double enten- dre since the tune itself which Doherty has recorded was written in 1943. This Bregman/Voceo. & Conn (20th Century Music) published song won the Oscar that year for the film "Hello, Frisco, Hello." In a way Kruger's own Ember label is saying "Hello, U.S., Hello," via his new distribution deal with Famous Music and by establishing west coast of- fices headed by John Madara, who was just appointed Ember vp in charge of creative development. Madara produced the new Doherty single and will be producing several of the new artists sig- ned to Ember/Paramount, among whom include Mother Trucker (an all girl's group from England), Susan Maughn (a Melody Maker poll winner set to open the Persian Room next month), and Rick Sandler (a songwriter/composer who Krueger likened to Elton John). Kruger and Tony Martell, president of Famous Music are also very excited about the forthcoming LP release of Desmond Dekker's "Greatest Hits," (which in- cludes his "Israelites," hit). Krueger also disclosed that Dekker is currently in England recording some new material for Ember/Paramount. Also operating out of Ember's Los Angeles office is Rick Palladino, the label's new director of national promotion. Governors To NARAS Named LOS ANGELES - The Los Angeles Chapter of the Record Academy (NARAS) reports that voting members have elected 21 new governors to serve 2 year terms on the chapter's Board Of Governors. Those elected and the mem- bership categories they represent are: Vocalists/singers: Ray Charles, Sally Stevens; leaders/conductors: Don Ellis, Peter Matz; producers: Kelly Gordon, Bones Howe; songwriters/composers: Mel Larson, Jerry Marcellino; engineers: Bruce Botnick, Ben Jordan; instrumen- talists: Jay Cooper, Vince DeRosa; ar- rangers: Dave Dexter; spoken word: Milt Larsen, Ruth White; and classical: Peter Christ, Don Christleib, and Mario Guar- neri. The governors -elect will attend their first Board meeting Tues., June 4, when they will join incumbent governors who have another year in office. At that time, new chapter officers for the coming year will be elected. Blaskey To Haven HOLLYWOOD - Lindy Blaskey has joined Lambert and Potter's Haven Records as general professional manager of the company's publishing divisions, announced Eddie Lambert, Haven's general manager. "We feel that acquisition of Lindy Blaskey," com- mented Brian Potter, "marks a step for- ward for our company, in becoming a viable and competitive publisher." Blaskey's responsibilities, according to Lambert, will encompass ad- ministration of Haven's two publishing divisions, Touch of Gold Music Inc. (BMI) and Natural Songs Inc. (ASCAP), as well as One Of A Kind Music, affiliated with ABC Dunhill Music. Prior to joining Haven, Blaskey was professional manager of the Music Publishing Division of ABC. Takoma, Briar Distrib Pact SANTA MONICA, Calif. - Takoma Records president Charles Mitchell has announced the signing of Briar Records to a five year distribution agreement. Briar prexy John Delgatto plans the immediate delivery of 3 finished LPs; "The Doc Watson Family Album," The Kentucky Colonels" with Clarence and Roland White, and Byron Burline's "Stone Mountain Boys." Avco Rushes Hit Via Eng. NEW YORK - Hugo & Luigi have an- nounced that Avco Records is rushing out the release of the Limmie & Family Cookin' current British hit, "A Walking Miracle." Originally from Cleveland, Ohio, Lim - mie & Family Cookin' spends a great deal of their time in England, where they've had three consecutive chart hits. The new record was produced by Steve Metz and Alar Klein and arranged by Van Mc- Coy. "A Walking Miracle" was a hit in the 60's by The Essex on Roulette Records. Joseph Forms Jasmine Music HOLLYWOOD - Rick Joseph, executive head of Dawnbreaker Music (BMI) an- nounced formation of Jasmine Music (ACAP) to meet expanding needs of the publishing company. The first two writers Jasmine has signed are Kay Dunham and Walter Heath. Dunham has placed songs with such artists as Eddie Kendricks, Three Dog Night, Harry Belafonte, Thelma Houston and Hoyt Axton. His latest material can be heard in the movie, "The Last Detail," which used two of his songs. Walter Heath has recor- ded for A&M records under the name Lawrence Heath, and is currently opening the show for Seals & Crofts on their national tour. Also signed with the newly formed Jasmine is Jack Goga, former staff writer for Jobete Music and producer at Motown Records. He was co-author of the Temptations gold record, "You", as well as having penned songs for Martha and the Vandellas. Pictured here (I. to r.) are Rick Joseph, head of Dawnbreaker; Walter Heath (seated) and Kay Dunham. Acording to an estimate recently released by the U.S. Census Bureau, the population growth of blacks in the U.S. over the past three years is more than double that of whites. The figures show an approximate five percent increase in black population between 1970 and 1973, totalling 23,900,000. The white increase was two per cent, to 183,500,000. These figures continued in a trend. Between 1960 and 1970, the black population increased by nearly 20 percent; whites by about 1 per cent. Today, with these pertinent statistics at hand, it would seem as a reasonable estimate that at least 5 per cent of the black population would have to be considered having purchasing power (referring to leisure -time action, such as records and equip- ment). Taking this 5 per cent figure of some 24 million, the total shows up as having plenty of clout (purchasing power that is . .. HOLLYWOOD - United Artists Records, a subsidiary of Trans America Cor- poration (NYSE), has announced un- precedented sales of $33,640,000 since 1971 of records featuring the seven member rock group, War. According to Michael Stewart, United Artists Records president, no large progressive Black ensemble in history has ever achieved sales of a similar nature. "The total has been attained with five albums and five single records," Stewart said. "Three of the albums have ex- ceeded platinum status (more than $2 million in sales) and a fourth, the current "War Live," is approaching the coveted horizon," he added. War is composed of Charles Miller, saxophone; Howard Scott, guitar; Lonnie Jordan, organ; B. B. Dickerson, bass; Harold Brown, drums; Dee Allen, conga drums; and Lee Oskar, harmonica. The group is managed by Steve Gold of Far Out Management and produced by Jerry Goldstein of Far Out Produc- tions. RCA Appoints Harris NEW YORK - Ray Harris has been ap- pointed manager, merchandising rhythm and blues, RCA Records. The announ- cement was made by Jack Maher, direc- tor, product merchandising, to whom Harris will report. Harris joins RCA Records from adver- tising Contractors, Inc., where he was an account executive servicing such organizations as Carson Chemical Co., Monarch Wine Co. and the Wella Corp. primarily in the radio and TV areas. His specific account responsibilities in- cluded the coordination of media plans and subsequent radio and/or TV buys. A native New Yorker, Ray Harris is cur- rently attending Bernard Baruch Evening College, where he is majoring in advertising. Platters Set For MGM Grand NEW YORK - Las Vegas fans of The Platters will be pleased to learn that MGM Grand Hotel buyer Bernie Rothkopf has just signed The Platters for three forthcoming appearances in the Lion's Den - the first four weeks to begin July 10, 1974. Buck Ram, musical director and foun- der of The Platters, has just signed con- tracts with Phonogram International of Holland to produce three LP's and several singles, which will be released as quickly as possible once he delivers them to Phonogram. Ben Bunders, Inter- national A&R Manager of Phonogram, is planning on being here from Holland for The Platters' opening and bringing representatives from their United States staff. Since The Platters have been breaking attendance records at all their appearan- ces, Jean Bennett, manager of the group, who resides in Las Vegas, stated, "You haven't seen anything yet! The Platters' act today is so polished and professional, and they complement each other so completely now, that it's really a refreshing act. They delight every audience with the many reminiscent sounds of their golden hits and at the same time add their own contemporary youthful presentations of today. The Brown Brandy combo that accompanies The Platters is composed of such dedicated musicians, under the direction of Henry Lee, that they've also become a valuable and integral part of the act as a whole. We'll have no qualms about our opening night, even at the impressive and beautiful MGM Grand Hotel." "In an era of instant trends and over- worked nostalgia, there are certain musical "institutions" that appreciative audiences can look to for longevity, professionalism, and, simply, classic in- terpretations of great songs," said Buck Ram. Despite stars who flash on the horizon never to be heard from again, The Plat- ters - founded by Buck Ram in 1954 - will celebrate their twentieth year in the music business with their July 10 -August 6 engagement in the Lion's Den in the lavish new MGM Grand Hotel in Las Vegas, to be followed by a posh date in New York in the early fall. The Platters have proved that there has always been and continues to be an audience for their classic interpretations of the Buck Ram -written hits "Twilight Time," "The Great Pretender," "Only You," or the Buck Ram -arranged "My Prayer" and "Smoke Gets In Your Eyes." Over the last 20 years, Buck Ram has been responsible for 16 gold records for CASH BOX WELCOMES BUNNY SIGLER. Earth, Wind & Fire Hit Gold Status NEW YORK - Columbia Recording group Earth, Wind & Fire has garnered its second gold record with their latest album, "Open Our Eyes." The disc was certified Gold by the RIAA, signifying sales in excess of one million dollars. For Earth, Wind & Fire, an eight -man group from Chicago, this is their second gold album. Their second Columbia album, "Head To The Sky," went gold last year. The two previous Earth, Wind & Fire LP's were produced for Columbia by Joe Wissert and "Open Our Eyes" was produced by Wissert and group leader Maurice White. "Open Our Eyes" reached gold status less than three mon- ths after its release in February, 1974. McCann Store Promo PHILA. - Les McCann, Atlantic Records recording artist and one of the top names in jazz, made a highly successful per- sonal appearance recently at Franklin Music's center -city Philadelphia store. McCann, who was appearing at one of the city's clubs at the time, spent two hours meeting the public and signing autographs at Franklin's newest store of the five -store Delaware Valley rec- ord/audio chian. The appearance was the most recent in a series of in-store promotions and visits by famous recording personalities that has helped lend support to Franklin's major"Music Man" advertising effort, a campaign which has sought to establish Franklin's personnel as people who "know something about the music they sell." McCann's appearance was supported by newspaper ads and in-store signing. Commenting on the purpose and suc- cess of the appearance, Edward H. Rosen, president of Franklin's parent company, Raymond Rosen and Com- pany, said, "Philadelphia is really becoming the music capital of the coun- try. And we felt we should help add to the aesthetic momentum, rather than just capitalizing on the retail benefits. By doing more and more of this type of thing, we're giving the people a chance to meet, in person, the kind of major talent our city's attracting." The Platters alone. cash box,- news CBS Publishes Book On Progress Against Pirates NEW YORK - CBS Records has written and published a booklet, Progress Against Piracy, which has been distributed throughout the music in- dustry. It is estimated that there are over 4,000 copies of the booklet currently in circulation. The booklet, which was compiled through the efforts of the CBS law de- partment, describes the progress that has been made in legislation, civil litigation and criminal litigation to protect recording artists and record companies against record and tape piracy. The booklet cites the steady progress that has been made in the courts against unauthorized duplication of sound re- cordings. It has been estimated that tape pirates alone have been selling more than $200 million of pirated tapes each year. CBS Records has distributed the booklet not only to its own employees, but to customers, state legislators and retailers as well. Copies were given out at the NARM convention and at a recent Eastern Regional Conference of Attor- neys General in Newport, R. I. By making people more knowledgeable on the subject of record and tape piracy, CBS Records feels it's making another important contribution towards gaining more effective anti -piracy legislation, both on the state and federal levels. Set LMI Series HOLLYWOOD - Lee Magid, president of LMI Records, has announced that the label is starting a blues -jazz series featuring a cross section of artists. Set for release this month are two Ip's, "Boss Man Of The Blues" featuring Big Joe Turner and backed by The Dirty Blues Band and "Blues Man," premiering Rod Piazza as a featured performer on har- monica. Dept NEW YORK - Bob Altshuler, vice president information services, CBS Records Group, has announced two shifts in the CBS Records west coast publicity office: Pat Siciliano has been promoted to the newly created position of west coast manager press and infor- mation, Epic and Columbia Custom Labels and Charley Copien has been ap- pointed to Siciliano's former position as general publicist Columbia Records, west coast. Both appointments were made by Judy Paynter, assistant director press & information, west coast. These two appointments come as an expansion of the responsibilities of the west coast publicity office. In his new capacity, Pat Siciliano will be responsible for maintaining press relations on behalf of Epic and Columbia Custom labels with various publications, both consumer and trade, throughout the western region. He will also perform other publicity functions, including in- volvement with the Epic and Columbia Custom artists based on the west coast. Siciliano joined CBS Records in 1972 as general publicist in CBS Records' west coast office, a position he has held until his new promotion. Prior to joining CBS Records, he worked for A&M Records in their publicity department. Charley Copien joins CBS Records af- ter having worked at ABC/Dunhill Records as a publicist. Before that, he was a writer for Cash Box in Los Angeles. In his new capacity at CBS Records, Copien will assist Judy Paynter in the direction of all press and information ser- vices for the west coast area. Siciliano, Copien Wartoke Makes 2 WC Appointments LOS ANGELES - The Wartoke Concern has announced the opening of a West Coast office here staffed by Barbara DeWitt and Mary Greifinger, who join Pat Costello, Jane Friedman and Rod Jacobson as full partners in the publicity and public relations company. Assisting DeWitt and Greifinger in the Los Angeles office will be Janet Ferguson. Ms. DeWitt, whose career in the music business spans 10 years, began doing publicity for New York's Bitter End, before joining United Artists in promotion in New York. She later headed up UA publicity in London for three years before opening her own publicity company there, Three's Com- pany, which specialized in arrranging tours and tour publicity for American acts touring Europe. She then returned to the U.S. to do worldwide publicity for Frank Zappa's film "200 Motels", and later rejoined UA publicity where she remained in various capacities until joining Wartoke. Greifinger, a veteran of eight years in the music business, also comes from United Artists, where he was in UA's publicity department. Before moving to the West Coast, he spent four years as director of publicity and artist relations in UA's East Coast office. Greifinger began his career as a freelance writer and published his own magazine, Teen's Top Ten before joining United Artists five years ago. The Wartoke Concern is cur- rently celebrating it's fifth anniversary. 12 June 8. 1974 www.americanradiohistory.com

cash box/album reviews SAVE THE LAST DANCE FOR ME - The DeFranco Family featuring Tony DeFranco - 20th Century T-441 It's really a pleasure to watch hitmakers emerge especially when they're as talented as the DeFranco Family. Keyed by the runaway hit title track, this new LP sparkles with all the verve and gusto of their last effort, but looks to have even more sales potential judging by the in- credible response to the group's live dates. Naturally, Tony's vocals out front are a key to the DeFranco sound, but don't overlook the fine har- monies the rest of the group provide. We like "Poor Boy." "Baby Blue," "Write Me a Letter," and the title track. IN MY LITTLE CORNER OF THE WORLD - Marie Osmond - Kolob/MGM M3G 4944 Marie Osmond has come a long way in a relatively short space of time and with her suc- cess in the country market already well documented, she now ventures forth with a highly commercial new LP that is certain to gar- ner for her an equally impressive number of pop fans. The album, produced by Sonny James in conjunction with Mike Curb, spotlights the artist singing a variety of tunes from "True Love's a Blessing" and "Invisible Tears" to "Singing The Blues" and the great title track. This should be quite a coup for Marie. BINGO - The Whispers - Janus JXS-7006 Featuring the group's r&b hit single, "A Mother For My Children," the Whispers new Janus LP is just what the doctor ordered for a case of the blues. Distinguished by impeccable harmonies and a strong feel for arrangement and dynamics, this LP stands out for a number of reasons, not least of which is the excellent material found in the grooves. Bunny Sigler is featured on piano and leads an all star cast of musicians backing the Whispers who are incredible from start to finish. We look for this LP to be a big plus for a big group. MYSTERIOUS TRAVELLER - Weather Report - Columbia KC 32494 Josef Zawinul, Wayne Shorter, Alphonso Johnson, Dom Um Romao, Ishmael Wilburn, and Miroslav Vitous have every reason to take great pride in their new LP, one that combines the strengths the group has come to stand for, and some bold and innovative musical steps forward into the future of progressive music. Particularly effective are "Nubian Sundance," "Scarlet Woman," "Jungle Book," and the title track. Throughout the entire package, the group's pride and unity shine through. A big step for Weather Report. COME A LITTLE CLOSER - Etta James - Chess CH 60029 Etta has long been regarded as one of the finest pure vocalists on the scene and here she further distinguishes herself, adding to that reputation with a fine selection of material writ- ten for the most part by the likes of Gabriel Mekler, T. Lawrence, Randy Newman, and peerless Don Covay. Her treatment of "Sooki Sooki" is fantastic and she shines on "Out On the Street, Again," "Mama Told Me," "St. Louis Blues," "Gonna Have Some Fun Tonight," and "Let's Burn Down The Cornfield." We really go for this package. DIFFERENTLY - Ralph Graham - Sussex SRA 8033 Ralph Graham's album like its title, is not something that comes along everyday. As both singer and writer, Ralph explores a variety of directions, but all with one goal in mind - com- munication. It is this singular ability that makes his LP such a treat to get into. From "I Don't Want To Play This Game" and "Stay On The Good Side" to the title cut and "My Love Goes With You," the LP moves in strange and fascinating directions. In terms of arrangement and dynamics, the LP is flawless and the overall creative effort is well worth catching. pop picks SAVE iNE +' CE FOR ME '- 0 s i : ANDREWS SISTERS OVER HERE! iW1N71'S(''s1 1'Flit (FNTI iF %i111111 1114 \.1 newcomer picks RALPH GRAHAM MY LOVE - Engelbert Humperdinck - Parrot APAS 71065 Engelbert's track record alone would make this LP a big seller, but for the uninitiated, suffice it to say that his new LP is probably his best ever. PROMISED HEIGHTS - Cymande - Janus JXS 7004 From the moment we heard Cymande's great single, "Together," we've expected big things from the powerhouse group and all indications point to this album as the wedge that will break them big across the board. TWENTY SONGS OF THE CENTURY - Arranged, Conducted & Musically Designed by Michel Legrand Bell 4200 Picking a personal Top 20 melodies of this century - modestly excluding his own fine works - the ever -inventive. Michel Legrand brings highly listenable, melodically sensitive colorations to songs spanning from 1914 ("St. Louis Blues") to 1969 ("Bridge Over Troubled Water"). In between, of course, there's plenty to go after, including "My Funny Valentine," "Autumn Leaves," "One Note Samba" and the Beatles' "Yesterday." This is 2 -LP's worth of pop orchestral beauty that revives a lost disk art. LAND'S END - Jimmy Webb - Asylum SD 5070 Featuring Jimmy's great single "Crying In My Sleep," the artists brand new Asylum LP is one of the most interesting he's ever done. The master songwriter has distinguished himself over the past few years with dozens of top hits and on this album he shows the potential to put together another impressive string of chart -busters. Alter- nately contemplative and outspoken, Jim has meshed a number of textures and moods together beautifully. We particularly dig "Ocean In His Eyes," "Lady Fits Her Blue Jeans," and the title track. KING BISCUIT BOY - King Biscuit Boy - Epic KE 32891 King Biscuit Boy (or Richard Newell as his mother knows him) has every reason to be proud of his brand new Epic LP, his first in this country. Already a legend in Canada as a harp player, songwriter, and singer, KBB is likely to take off very rapidly as a top selling artist once this LP starts receiving some much deserved airplay. Particularly enjoyable in this package are "River Boat," "Mind Over Matter," "Mean Old Lady," and "The Greatest Love." Distinguished throughout by sensitivity and strength, we look for this LP to do well. 16 June 8, 1974 www.americanradiohistory.com

for the record EAST COASTINGS - Off and running, the answer to last week's "Rock and Roll: The Way We Were" photoquiz #12, was The Serendipity Singers, whose name was almost enough to make p.d.'s from coast to coast sit up and take notice whenever the folk ar- tists released a new disk. They were giants in that early and mid -Sixties folk revolution. This week's mystery artists, #13 in this series, were super British hit - makers during that British Invasion period, but had little success here in America. This five -man band's hits in Great Britain were many and their name should be familiar to any British rock fan of the period. Answer here next week. Talk about rock and roll getting tougher, Yes had an experience recently they may care to forget. The concert was held at the Palais des Sports in Paris, but was held up because the group's equipment arrived late from America. When said equipment did arrive, it was immediately noticed that two of Rick Wakeman's Moog synthesizers were smashed by the airline, unintentionally, of course. Then, 700 ticket forgeries were discovered at the door. The unruly mob waiting outside was repelled by firemen sporting hoses ... The annual Schaeffer Music Festival begins in New York City's Central Park (Wollman Memorial Ice Skating Rink) on June 12. All tickets, priced at $2.50 and $1.50, still remain as the best pop music bargain in the world. Some of the acts to be appearing this Summer in the Big Apple include; the original Righteous Brothers (billed with the original Sam and Dave); Melanie; the James Gang (with Maggie Bell and Steeleye Span also on the bill); John Sebastian; Todd Rundgren's Utopia; John McLaughlin's Mahavishnu Orchestra; King Crimson (billed with Golden Earring); ZZ Top with Brownsville Station; Robert Klein (with Melissa Manchester and Jim Dawson; the anxiously awaited new trio of Richie Furay, John David Söuther and Chris Hillman (billed with the incredible Leo Kottke); America; Jesse Colin Young, Linda Ronstadt, Martin Mull (all on the same bill); Harry Chapin; Poco; Dave Mason; Boz Scaggs, Anne Murray & Brewer and Shipley (on the same bill); Uriah Heep and Manfred Mann together; the Earl Scruggs Revue (billed with the Charlie Daniels Band and David Bromberg); the Marshall Tucker Band; Don McLean; Billy Cobham, billed with Deodato; Peter Frampton and Montrose; the Pointer Sisters; Foghat; Lynyrd Skynyrd; and Savoy Brown. An excellent line-up of talent. It all promises to be a super -Summer in New York (that is, of course, if the weather ever gets itself together). COMMENT ... With Summer just about here, it's time I mentioned the aspect of rock and roll and it's almost medicinal value on the big city populous. Here in New York, Summer has always meant an amazing number of pop concerts, therefore a place for the young to congregate when the streets (and tempers sometimes) get hot. The Schaeffer Festival is probably the best case in point, due, not only to the low price, and pleasant concert (outdoor) atmosphere, but to the low price that has the young wallet in mind. The out -of -school youngster not only gets the best possible entertain- ment, but can afford it and has a good time in the process. Summer in the city is tough, but it's getting easier thanks to promoters with the consumer in mind. arty good man POINTS WEST - Early summer activity is gurgling all around us these days with a flurry of movement stepped up in local recording studios, concert promotion offices et al. Regarding the news story about The Platters, which ran in the May 25 issue of CB R&B News Report, picking up some history of the Buck Ram Associated Platters from 1954, Ralph Bass informed this office that the story begins in 1953. Ralph says that he founded The Platters in 1953 by placing Toni Williams with a local Los Angeles group called The Platters. Ralph also says that he cut several sessions with them before Buck Ram came into the picture. "I recorded them for a label called Federal a subsidiary of King Records. In fact, "Only You their first hit was recorded for me as their producer before they re-recorded it for Mercury," said Ralph. Sorry for the goof. Just trying to set some platters ... Top jazz names will continue to appear at these noon time sets. don drossell Soulvation Records From Pittsburgh PITTSBURGH - A new soul label known as SOULVATION ARMY RECORDS has been formed in Pitt- sburgh as a division of Western World Music, located in suburban Carnegie, Pennsylvania. Bill Lawrence who also owns and operates Pittsburgh's largest one -stop heads the Western World complex which houses a complete sixteen track studio, custom pressing plant and the label's of- fices in a brand new luxury building. Reporting directly to Lawrence will be director of Sales and Promotion, Alan Leeds. Leeds is best known for his leng- thy relationship with James Brown Productions where he served as publicity director and later as booking manager for the James Brown roadshow. Leeds' experience also includes stints with Kool and the Gang, Starday-King Records, Gene Redd Productions and as a deejay for WANT Radio in Richmond, Virginia. Leeds is quick to admit that a strange story surrounds the debut release on SOULVATION ARMY, "Yesterday Stan- ding By" by These Gents. "Initially the record came to us as an outside master and we released it on the parent label, Western World. Response in many key markets was strong but we felt the production quality could be im- proved. We decided to re -cut it in our own studios. We have no reservations anymore and indications are already that we have a hit!" Leeds has set out on a lengthy promotional tour which will include the Carolinas, New York, Philadelphia, Boston & the Midwest. Playboy Signs Willie Henderson `Dance Master' Hot LOS ANGELES - Hillery Johnson, director of R&B Products for Playboy Records has announced the signing of Willie Henderson to the label, as well as the purchase of his single "Dance Master" for the U.S. "Dance Master," which is on the Decca label in the U.K., has been getting exten- sive discotheque play in New York, where copies of the import were being sold for as high as five dollars a copy. The single was brought to the attention of Hillery Johnson, who immediately recognized the potential of the single as well as the artist. Willie Henderson's career has span- ned almost every aspect of the music business. He was musical director for five years at Brunswick Records and helped establish name acts such as the Chi -Lites, Barbara Acklin, Lost Generation, Jackie Wilson, and Tyrone Davis. As a producer, his credits include several national chart hits, and he has produced such acts as Tyrone Davis, Lit- tle Richard, Laine Kazan, King Curtis, and the Beautiful Zion Choir. Tyree Glenn Is Dead At Sixty -One NEW YORK - Tyree Glenn, who played the trombone and vibraphone during the big band era died Saturday (18) in Englewood (N.J.) Hospital. He was 61 years of age and lived at 308 West Englewood Avenue in Englewood. Glenn joined Louis Armstrong's All - Stars in 1964 and stayed until Arm- strong's death in 1971. Armstrong and Glenn would switch parts when Arm- strong was not capable of hitting the high register. Glenn organized á sextet which played at the Royal Box in the Americana Hotel. He picked up the vibraphone while with Lionel Hampton, and played five years with the Ethel Waters group. In 1949 he was asked to join the Duke El- lington group. He also was a member of a quintet that was part of Jack Sterling's early morning WCBS program. Survivors include his widow, Gloria, and two sons, Tyree Jr. and Roger. The funeral was on Thursday (23) in the Cen- tral Presbyterian Church, 593 Park Avenue. cash box," news Emmy Sparks Sales Marlo Thomas LP NEW YORK An Emmy Award to "Marto Thomas and Friends In Free To Be ... You And Me," produced by Carole Hart, as "Outstanding Children's Special of the Year" has sparked sales spurts for the Bell Records album from which the ABC-TV special was adapted. "Free To Be ... You And Me" has been on the trade charts three separate times since the album's release in November of 1972. The album, which has now sold 250,000 units, appeared on the national best selling album charts after its initial release. A year rater Christmas sales and a Grammy as Best Children's Album of the Year again put the LP in the winner's circle and now tv has provided a whole new surge to the album's saleability. The March 11 airing of the special of "Marto Thomas and Friends In Free To Be .. . You And Me" had the impact of a brand new release. "In addition to mentions of the album in all of the advertising for the TV show, we geared for the television exposure," commented Bell marketing vice president Gordon Bossin. "Bell Records put its own promotional and sales depart- ments behind the TV special and was fully prepared to take advantage of the sales opportunity it provided. 'Marto Thomas and Friends In Free To Be .. . You And Me' had impact both in the television ratings and for album sales. The LP was back on the charts almost im- mediately. The subsequent Emmy nomination and now, the Emmy Award, added to 'Free To Be ... You And Me' album content, have turned this LP into a catalog album from which we can expect sales with annual spurts at Christmas. In all, 'Free To Be ... You And Me' has been on the charts for 39 weeks, with more undoubtedly to come." Kress To RCA Legal Dept. NEW YORK - The appointment of Alan H. Kress as a counsel in the law depart- ment of RCA Records has been an- nounced by Myron Roth, Senior Coun- sel. Kress joins RCA Records after having been associated with the law firm of Schumann, Bession, Kennelly and Dor- ment in Jersey City for the past 21 months. A graduate of New York University with a Bachelor of Arts degree, Kress was given his JD degree with honors in 1971 from the George Washington School of Law. For a year following his degree and before joining the Jersey City firm, Kress was Law Secretary to the Hon. Donald G. Its publishing arms include Sorayda Music (BMI) and LP Music (ASCAP). 3 Campus Honors For Eubie Blake NEW YORK - Eubie Blake, apparently recovered from his recent medical problems, has been honored by three Eastern universities for his contributions to American music. On May 30th, the 92 -year -old writer -performer received a Doctorate of Fine Arts from Rutgers University, New Brunswick, New Jersey. The New England Conservatory of Music in Boston honored him with a Doctor of Music Science on June 2nd, and a week later Blake and his wife journeyed up to Hanover on June 9th for the presen- tation of his Doctor of Humane Letters at Dartmouth. PER HOUR OFF -TIME SPECIAL 8 TRACK RECORDING PHONE: 212-765-8499 Screen Gems/Col Pub. Rush Release BTO Book NEW YORK - Screen -Gems -Columbia Publications. a division of Columbia Pic- tures Industries. Inc., have announced that they are rush -releasing a Bachman - Turner Overdrive songfolio according to the company's vice-president, Frank J. Hackinson. The songbook will contain all of the material found on their Mercury albums. including their singles, "Blue Collar," "Let It Ride, and "Taking Care of Business, which is currently riding the nation's pop charts. In addition, the book, arranged for piano/vocal and guitar, will contain stories and biographies on the group, as well as action photographs of their television and personal appearan- ces. The songbook follows the recent sign- ing of the group's leader and founder, Randy Bachman, to Screen Gems - Columbia Music for copyright ad- ministration of his publishing companies, Ranbach and Top Soil Music. Unart Gains WFL Theme HOLLYWOOD - Wally Schuster, vice- president of the United Artists Music Group announced that Unart Music has acquired the rights to the "World Foot- ball League Theme" by Dominic Fron- tiere. The WLF theme will be heard over both the animated opening credits and closing titles of all televised WFL games throughout the continental U.S. and Hawaii. Marketing plans for this latest theme by composer/artist Frontiere, who also wrote the Academy Award nominated song from "Hang 'em High" and the "Theme from the F.B.I.," include march- ing band arrangements to be sent to all high schools and colleges and a com- mercial record release deal to be an- nounced shortly. 'Red Back Book' Angel's Best Seller HOLLYWOOD - Guther Schuller's album "The Red Back Book", a recor- ding of authentic orchestral ar- rangements of Scott Joplin's classic rags, has become the all-time best- selling Angel Records album, announ- ced Brown Meggs, vice-president and chief operating officer of Capitol Records. "Palm Leaf Rag," the companion Joplin album, released in March, is already Angel's ninth best-seller. New arrangements of Joplin standards, in- cluding many featured in the Academy Award winning film, "The Sting,' "Palm Leaf Rag" is played by the Southland Stingers, conducted by George Sponhaltz. 30 June 22, 1974 www.americanradiohistory.com

cash box; ' album reviews LET IT FLOW - Elvin Bishop - Capricorn CP 0134 Its been a long time for the one time rhythm guitarist of Paul Butterfield's Band. but now it looks like he's ready to explode with the stored up vitality of a decade of hard work. Capricorn has become a home for many artists and it's evident that Elvin is happy with this new record- ing environment. Listen to "Watermelons." "Can't Hold Myself In Line." "Bourbon Street," "Honey Babe," and "Ground Hog" and you'll get an insight into the essential Elvin Bishop. We certainly hope that PD's and one stops are hip enough to get into this LP quickly. PARADISE AND LUNCH - Ry Cooder - Warner Bros. MS 2179 The man responsible for a good deal of the "Performance" soundtrack LP and a moving solo on the Stones' -Sister Morphine," not to mention some brilliant solo LP work of his own, is back again with a blistering Warners album that con- solidates all of his strengths as a guitarist/singer into one package. We admire the way Cooder has stayed with his sound. resisting the "Easy" commercial lure in hopes of producing an aesthetically pleasing piece of work. We enjoy "Tamp 'Em Up Solid,- "Ditty Wa Ditty." "If Walls Could Talk." and"Its All Over Now." GYPSY SYMPHONY - Wendy Waldman - War- ner Bros. BS 2792 Wendy's debut album was quite impressive. but as is the case with dynamic talents. her second offering is even better. Her enchanting vocals are the soul and substance of this package, but no one should overlook her in- credible writing talents (Maria Muldaur recorded one of her songs on the RIAA certified gold "Maria Muldaur" LP). Wendy is indeed a self con- tained expressionist and her strengths are abun- dant throughout this collection. We lean in the direction of such gems as "My Love Is All I Know." "Baby Don't You Go," and of course, "Mad Mad Me." STEPSON - Stepson - ABC ABCX-826 Homegrown in Los Angeles. Stepson is one of the most promising new groups to hit the scene in quite some time. Capable of provoking ex- treme reaction when engaged in live perform- ance, Stepson comes across on record equally powerfully with a triumphant collection of brash and brazen rock 'n' roll numbers including "Rule In The Book." "Lil" Bit," -Suffer." "Burnin' Hurt," and"Back To Bama." The group's selective ar- rangements and dynamic flair keys this product which ought to have heavy appeal to teen and college audiences. WHERE OR WHEN - Norman Feels - Just Sun- shine JSS-3502 It's always pleasing to hear a sensitive artist caught in the right mood at the right moment. Certainly Norman's new album is a collection of "right" moments for each cut comes back time and again to haunt the senses with a provocative flair seldom found in today's records. An excel- lent vocalist, Feels does outstanding work on "Shame," -Movie." "Mr. Wanna Be,""You Can't Stop My Love" and"I'll Always Love Just You," but his talents are in no way confined merely to those cuts. His flair for lyric interpretation is un- deniably distinctive and augers well for him. THE DRUMS - Various Artists - ABC/Impulse ASH -9272-3 The liner note on the front cover appropriately states that this tremendous three record set is. "A critical analytical guide to the major trends in the development of the tradition of the principal percussive and rhythmic force in jazz." But beyond that the LP is a sensuous delight featuring some of the greatest drummers in the world. Featured are the likes of Art Blakey, Max Roach, Kenny Clarke, Philly Joe Jones, Sid Catlett, Joe Jones. Connie Kay. Roy Haynes. Buddy Rich. Louis Belson. Elvin Jones. and Shelly Manne to name a few. Super LP get it. pop picks 4i111111-1111171» LET rTFLOW U1Cocd¢n e`nc- JOHNNY 1NATHIS da newcomer picks stepson jazz picks WHAT'LL I DO - Johnny Mathis - Columbia C 32963 Featuring Johnny's single title track, this LP is a demand item. Though Johnny has been pur- suing an impressive contemporary musical direc- tion (a la his Thom Bell produced LP), he decided that he would do this album based on the heavy demand for him to record the stan- dards that appear here. Featured on this disk are -More." "Put On A Happy Face." "Under A Blanket Of Blue." and "The Touch Of Your Lips." and naturally each is engraved with the match- less Mathis grace that has caused so many hearts to dream in the past. An easy listening treat, this LP is pure Mathis. I, IN THE MEMBERSHIP OF MY DAYS - Richard Harris - ABC/Dunhill DSD-50159 In one of the most intriguing and moving albums of the year, Richard Harris and family have come up with a stirring piece of work based on the renowned actor/singer's own poems and songs. Each cut on the album defines a different aspect of the artist's introspection and obser- vations and each speaks lovingly of the col- laboration with his children who are pictured on the back cover of this package. Harris' dramatic voice alone could sustain any such concept, but t s interesting that he has chosen to make it a family affair. FERDINAND "JELLY ROLL" MORTON - Tran- scriptions By Dick Hyman - Columbia M 32587 The entire title calls this album a collection of rags and stomps and a little blues, but that's put- ting it mildly. The masterful transcriptions for or- chestra that Dick Hyman has arranged and per- formed (on piano) suggest the greatness of the original genre and provide a picturesque insight into what we now lovingly call "the good old days." Featured in this package are "King Porter Stomp," "The Pearls," "Fickle Fay Creep." "The Finger Breaker." and "The Crave" each of which sparkles with individual brilliance. CROSS ROADS - Jae Mason - Buddah BDS 5604 The interpretive genius of Jae Mason is the first thing that jumps out of the tracks of his new Buddah LP. one in which the artist gives full rein to his creative flow. "Cross Roads" is for Jae more than a debut album, it is an emotive piece of the man's life and one that speaks highly of his relationships with man and nature. Particularly effective on this LP are the songs, "Poor Folks." "Please The Crowd." "Little Girl." "Lady Pearl." and "Monday Morning Blues." If this record proves anything it's that Jae has his finger on the pulse of what's happening - and that's not bad for openers. DARRYL WAY'S WOLF - Wolf - London XPS644 As exciting as its cover the new Wolf LP is as powerful as the forest animal represented on the cover and as "foxy" as the music inside the package. The group has all the essential rock 'n' roll ingredients down pat and a little exposure on the tour circuit ought to earn them the prestige of the likes of ZZ Top and Orphan. Particularly strong cuts on this album include "The Ache." "Two Sisters." "Go Down." "McDonald's Lament," and "Toy Symphony." Enjoyable on a number of levels, we look for this LP to do well for the Wolf. SOLO CONCERTS - Keith Jarrett - ECM ECM3-1035/37 ST In a stunning tour de force recorded last year in Bremen and Lausanne, Keith Jarrett takes off in a million different directions at once. The result is this beautifully packaged three record set which features Keith playing his heart and soul like no other musician. Refraining from con- trived titles, Jarrett has simply called his com- positions ""Bremen. July 12. 1973 Part 1," "Lausanne. March 20, 1973, Part IIB," etc. In reducing the titles to basic elements. the artist has reflected the content of his music. It's elemental and cosmic alternately and points to the tremendous amount of creative energy that Keith Jarrett stands for. 22 June 29, 1974 www.americanradiohistory.com

NEW YORK - Pictured at a recent press conference at Madison Square Garden held in anticipation of his upcoming con- cert at the Garden on the fourth of July is Godfather of Soul James Brown and National Youth Movement spokesman, Reverend Sharpton. Said Kass, "This cer- tification represents the fifth con- secutive gold record by Gladys Knight & The Pips for The Buddah Group." "Claudine" joins the group's initial Buddah LP, "Imagination," as well as the singles "I've Got To Use My Imagination," "Midnight Train To Georgia," and "Best Thing That Ever Happened To Me" in the certified gold status. In addition, their most recent single, "On And On" (the first from the "Claudine" album) is moving up the charts and has crossed the three-quarter mark on its way to gold certification. Kass further noted that the album "Imagination" which has been on the charts for almost 40 weeks, has now sold in excess of a million units. According to record industry custom, "Imagination" has therefore reached the status of a platinum album. In addition to the mil- lion -sellers "Midnight Train To Georgia," "Imagination," and "Best Thing That Ever Happened To Me," the album con- tains the group's first Buddah hit, "Where Peaceful Waters Flow." JAZZMOBILE ROLLS OUT 10th SEASON OF FREE OUTDOOR CONCERTS - The first of 81 concerts got a royal send off, July 1 on the steps of City Hall, hosted by Of- fice of Manhattan's Borough President, Percy Sutton. Billy Taylor, founder and president of Jazzmobile, Inc., and the Jazzmobile All Stars performed at the opening concert. Among the highlights of this season's program will be concerts at the New Harlem State Office Building on July 10 at 7 p.m. at which Horace Silver will appear, and the Willowbrook State School for the Mentally Retarded in Staten Island on Aug. 16 at 7 p.m. Some of the artists slated to perform in subsequent weeks include: Dizzy Gillespie, Charles Mingus, Sonny Fortune, Louis Hayes, Charles Sullivan, Junior Mance, Andy Harlow, Ray Bryant and Robin Kenyatta. The cities of Buffalo, Rochester, Albany, Syracuse, Schenectady, and Westchester County areas, plus New Jersey, Washington, D.C. and Baltimore. A major part of the over-all Jazzmobile, Inc. picture is the Jazzmobile Workshop, an ongoing, energetic program which has, since 1969, successfully provided hundreds of talented young, aspiring musicians with the opportunity to study free of charge with professional jazz artists on a weekly, year-round basis in order to improve and expand their musical skills. A not incon- sequential part of this phase of Jazzmobile is the more than two hundred jazz lecture concerts that have been presented in public schools throughout the Metropolitan area since 1968. "My Ebony Princess" on Pi Kappa. don drossell GRC Names Anderson To Midwest R&B Post ATLANTA - General Recording Cor- poration (GRC) president Michael Thevis, has announced a major cor- porate expansion within the firm's r&b division with the appointment of Les An- derson to the position of midwest r&b marketing manager. Anderson will be responsible for the Midwest region including promotion, sales and merchandising of GRC, Aware and Hotlanta label product in Chicago, Cleveland. Columbus, Detroit, Milwaukee, St. Louis, Buffalo and Toledo. GRC's releases which Anderson will be marketing feature singles and albums by artists Ripple, John Edwards, Jimmy Lewis, Dorothy Norwood, The Counts and Deep Velvet. Prior to joining the GRC record com- plex, Anderson was an independent promoter for several major record labels. Preceeding this affiliation he worked with Warner Brothers in Hollywood as director of special projects, handling national r&b promotion for the label. His background experience in the record industry also includes the post of operation manager of WDIA in Memphis and program director of WHAT in Philadelphia. He was co -manager for the O'Jays and Valentino's and handled "promotions for several radio stations in Houston, Baltimore and Cleveland. Lou Munson CTI/KUDU VP Of Sales NEW YORK - CTI/KUDU Records has announced the appointment of Lou Mun- son to the position of vice president in charge of sales and marketing. In making the announcement, Creed Taylor, president of the company, com- mented on Munson's unique ability due to his strong and varied background as an executive in the entertainment field. Prior to breaking into the recording in- dustry, Munson, a native of Pittsburgh, spent a number of years in radio. He also was heavily involved in the artist management and booking agency business. Munson was previously associated with Liberty/United Artists Records. He joined CTI Records in 1971, shortly after the company was formed. Gus Redmond VP Nat'l Promo For Innovation CHICAGO - George Williams, vp marketing and sales for Innovation Records (distributed by Warner Bros.), has announced the appointment of Gus Redmond as vp in charge of national promotion for the label. Redmond re- cently was with GRC Records where he handled R&B promotion. Redmond was also responsible for helping to establish Ripple (GRC) as a major R&B act. Redmond will be based in Chicago. His first project will be a Quadraphonics release, "Bet You If You Check It Out." Also, a Lost Generation release, "If You Decide (Your Mission)." Lowrell Simon, who is a co -writer and co -producer of the movie score, "Three The Hard Way" is a lead singer with the Lost Generation. The Innovation label is headquartered in Chicago. Motown To Dist. CTI/KUDU NEW YORK - Motown Records and CTI/KUDU Records formally announced a trend -setting arrangement in which Motown will distribute CTI product nationally, according to a joint statement by Ewart Alner, president of Motown Record Corp., and Creed Taylor, president of CTI Records. The move marks Motown's entry into the jazz market, and the first affiliation CTI has made with another label in its four years of operation. Under the terms of the agreement, CTI will retain its corporate and artistic iden- tity, and will have autonomous control over its product. CTI will also retain its key distributors in addition to the Motown distributors, giving it greater national coverage. Coor- dination of all marketing for CTI product will remain the same, and CTI does not anticipate any changes in its field per- sonnel as a result of the new agreement. On the CTI talent roster are such ar- tists as Esther Phillips, Bob James, Airto, Grover Washington, Jr., Milt Jackson, Hubert Laws, George Benson, Paul Desmond, and Joe Farrell. Also, Jackie Cain and Roy Kral, Ron Carter, Don Sebesky, Garbor Szabo, Eric Gale, Johnny Hammond, Hank Crawford, Jim Hall, Joe Beck, Chet Baker, the Phil Up- church and Tennyson Stephens band, and Idris Mohammed; further, there is Lou Christie, on CTI's Three Brothers label, and Jayson Linin on the Metronome label, distributed by CTI. Commenting on the new venture, Ewart Alner said: "We are enormously pleased with our new relationship with CTI Records, and I look forward to working with Creed Taylor. "This new venture brings Motown Records into the jazz field, a very impor- tant and growing area of the recording industry. CTI has established a track record for excellence in that field, and sales of its records have reflected the quality of the CTI product." In discussing the agreement, Taylor stressed that "the precedent -setting as- sociation between our two companies is based on mutual respect and under- standing. It also brings CTI/KUDU into the realm of mass marketing." The distribution agreement with Motown covers only the United States and will not affect the CTI network of in- ternational licensees. `v/iiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiii/N{.viiiiiiiii iiiiiiiiiii« a , , iixA, iiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiriiiiiiiiiíJi qe,' ' I,I_--- 1.: . the hats On! Robert Thompson, executive director, SESAC Nashville, has been named to head the Anti -Piracy Committee of the Nashville Chapter of the National Academy of Recording Arts & Sciences (NARAS). In a meeting held this week Thompson announced that the committee was formed and would con- sist of six members and the chairman. Other committee members include Mary Reeves Davis, president of Jim See Energy Crisis As Aid To Pianos NEW YORK - Are America's pianos bet- ter off because of the energy crisis? Well, they are, according to the Piano Technicians Guild Convention now taking place at the Statler-Hilton in New York. F. M. Ward, president of the Guild, ex plained it this way: Pianos usually go out of tune due to changes in temperature and humidity; the more drastic the change, the worse the piano ends up sounding. With homes not being heated or cooled to the extremes they used to be, the temperature and humidity are more constant year-round, and thus help pianos hold their tone better and longer. While there is no substitute for regular piano service, Ward says circumstances like this make the job much easier. Producers, Stars Get Mike At KMET HOLLYWOOD - Mikel Hunter, program director, at KMET FM Metromedia in Los Angeles announced that August 3 will be "Producer's Day." Some of rock's best known producers will have at least an hour to play the music that they consider made contributions to the rock idiom, im- portant milestones in music. Among producers contributing are: Jerry Wexler, Thom Bell, Kenny Gamble, Lamont Dozier, Todd Rundgren, David Rubinson, Joe Wissert, Jeff Barry and Russ Titleman. Hunter said that "listeners are interested in what influ- enced the people who influence the people who make the music." The same program with the point of view of the recording artist will be aired on July 27th. KMET will exercise no control over the music that is chosen by their guest d.j.'s. Programming consultant Sandy Gib- son, will coordinate all arrangements for producers and recording artists to do their shows at KMET as well as KMET sister stations in N.Y. (WNEW FM), San Francisco (KSAN FM), Philadelphia (WMMR FM), Chicago (WDHF) and Detroit (WOMC FM). Book Review: Vet music exec C. A. Schicke's "Revolution in Sound" (Little, Brown & Co., $6.95) is exactly the kind of book tradesters - or the general public - can use to get a highly readable historical perspective of the music industry, from the very point of its birth almost 100 years ago. Subtitled a "biography of the recording industry," it covers, often engrossingly, the growth and develop- ment of the industry, including the many colorful and exciting men who either in- sisted that a commercial recording in- dustry was a viable one or who pushed ahead in scientific, business and creative segments of the business. Some years ago, a book called "From Tin Foil to Stereo," told the music industry story in greater detail, but Schicke provides more passion in addition to being inform- ative, yet concise. There is some faltering in the spelling of current -day names of executives and companies, but the overall impression is one source that answers a recent Cash Box editorial that called for greater knowledge of the in- dustry's history by its very members. i.l. 18 July 27, 1974 www.americanradiohistory.com
