cash box/news Soul Train's 4th Season HOLLYWOOD - Producer Don Cor- nelius will launch the fourth television season for the all black variety show "Soul Train" August 5 at KTTV with the syndicated show scheduled for airing in 95 markets. Cornelius will continue to host the show that is directed by B. J. Jackson. Cornelius stated, "that while the format of the highly successful show will remain essentially the same, the show will be in- corporating certain changes throughout the season to utilize the special guests to the best advantage." Some of the guests scheduled for the new season include James Brown, The Temptations, Billy Preston and The Miracles. `Night Train' To Feature `Bloodstone' HOLLYWOOD - Bloodstone will score and star in the muscial-comedy, "Night Train," written by Dan Gordon, for The Crystal Jukebox Film Corporation, scheduled to go into production in mid - October. Harry Williams, Charles McCormick, Willis Draffen Jr., and Charles Love, known collectively as Bloodstone, will play dual roles in this film written specially for them, plus doing the music and lyrics. The original soundtrack album will be available on London Records. The London Records artists' were voted the #1 new vocal group in 1973, Cash Box polls, when they went gold with "Natural High" and have been top- ping the charts ever since. The Crystal Jukebox Film Corporation has signed D. Scott Easton as producer. Bloodstone's record producer, Mike Ver- non has been set as musical director with Pip Williams doing the arrangements. GOLDEN LADIES - The Pointer Sisters gather with members of Blue Thumb Records' staff back -stage at the Univer- sal Amphitheater as news arrived that their second Blue Thumb LP, "That's A Plenty" had received R.I.A.A. gold cer- tificiation. Their latest album, "The Poin- ter Sisters Live At The Opera House" is being shipped this week. Pictured in the photo (back row, from left) are Ruth, Anita, Bonnie and June Pointer. Sur- rounding them, in "opera house" tee- shirts, are Blue Thumb staff members. Stax Releases 4 Singles, 1 LP HOLLYWOOD - The Stax Organization will release four singles and one album, it was announced today. Singles on Stax Records include, "Get It While It's Hot," by William Bell; "Run Around Sue," by the Second Society; "That's The Way I Want To Live My Life," by Mel and Tim; and "Little Gold Band" by The Gentrys. The new album release, by The Staple Singers, is called "City In The Sky." Al Bell Wins Youth Award HOLLYWOOD - Al Bell, chairman of the board of Stax Records of Memphis, was one of five award winners at Reve, Gip - son's Fourteenth Annual "Youth on Parade." He was presented with the first Grant Harris Award, named for the founder of the Good Shepherd Baptist Church in Los Angeles, where the event took place on Sunday, July 28. In all there were five award winners, chosen by poll of the black youth of Los Angeles as public figures they best believe personify those who have over- come racial problems, poverty and economic barriers to become nationally recognized leaders in their field. The four other winners were: Anthony and the Imperials, Johnny Mathis, Bobby Womack and Billy Paul, making Mr. Bell the only non -performer so designated in the popularity poll. Mr. Bell was also presented with a citation by Mayor Tom Bradley, proclaiming his good works for the people of Los Angeles. HOLLYWOOD - Al Bell, chairman of the board of Stax Records of Memphis, receives the first Grant Harris Award from Reve' Gipson and is presented with a color portrait of himself prepared by ar- tist Allen Harper, drawn from a black and white photo of Bell "Hollywood Swinging" Goes Gold New Kool Disc Has 400,000 Advance NEW YORK - Kool & The Gang, cur- rently one of the hottest groups on records and in -person, have received a third gold record in less than six months for their current million -selling hit, "Hol- lywood Swinging." Fred Fioto, president of De -Lite Records revealed that ad- vance orders for the group's next release "Higher Plane," have already topped 400,000 copies. The Kool & The Gang gold rush started with their smash #1 single, "Jungle Boogie," earlier this year. Their "Wild And Peaceful" album, which includes both "Jungle Boogie" and "Hollywood Swinging," gave the group their first gold LP. A new Kool & The Gang album, "Light Of The Worlds," will be released in August. Highlights of the busy group's per- sonal appearance schedule include the Braves Stadium in Atlanta, Ga. with Mar- vin Gaye on August 5 and the Apollo Theatre in New York with Nancy Wilson and Dick Gregory from August 9 to 15. Kool & The Gang will headline a major concert tour in the fall, with dates to be announced shortly. De -Lite Records is distributed by P.I.P Records, a division of Pickwick International. Candi Staton To WB Records HOLLYWOOD - In conjunction with this week's NATRA convention, Warner Bros. Records has announced the signing of Ms. Candi Staton to a long- term exclusive recording contract. Present for the signing formalities in Muscle Shoals were (left to right) producer Rick Hall, Candi and John Salstone, representing Warner Bros. The deal which brings Candi to Warners includes the continued production ser- vices of Hall, who produced all of the successful soul stylist's past hits on his own Fame label, including "Stand By Your Man," "Sweet Feeling," "He Called Me Baby," "I'm Just A Prisoner," "In The Ghetto" and many others. Photo was shot during a break in current recording sessions at Muscle Shoals Sound for Candi's first Warner Bros. album to be released this fall. A single from the ses- sions will be released by the end of the summer. Rocky G. Promotions Expands NEW YORK - The independent black promotion company, Rocky G. Pro- motions, now in its second year serving the Boston to Washington market, an- nounced that it will expand its operations from black AM and FM stations, to in- clude "all mainstream FM stations." Stated Rocky G., "There are a number of reasons for this move, but first among them is the quality and number of black LPs. Black music is at the beginning of a tremendous new growth cycle, and it is clear that the entire FM spectrum is where these new albums belong and where they are going." Rocky G. also noted the recent emergence of black FM stations as a major force in each market, citing, for example, WBLS in New York City, WDAS in Philadelphia and WHUR in Washing- ton, D.C. "In this boom situation," he said, "one must not overlook the power- ful influence of jazz albums and jazz stations. While jazz is being heard with increasing frequency on the major pop and rock FM stations, FM jazz stations have broadened their format to include music from the fine new black pop albums." In this latter situation, Rocky G. mentioned WRVR in New York and WWDB in Philadelphia. Joining Rocky G. in his expanded operations are his two daughters, Maria and Michelle, both college students, who have worked informally with their father for the last several years. The young women will be responsible for store and discotheque contacts and reports. Along with the excellence of the new product, Rocky G. stated that the expan- sion of his operations was the fruit of his strong relationships with "the wonderful program and music directors at the major Northeast stations. Everywhere, there is a new awareness of the importance and appeal of black album product. I have found radio personnel receptive and en- thusiastic throughout the area." Concluded Rocky G., "With so many brilliant young producers currently at work, I am looking forward to a very ex- citing year. The amount of genuine creativity to be found in black music is it- self a very positive indication of the future success of these expanded operations." Rocky G. Promotions is located at 1247 Hastings Street, Teneach, N.J., (201) 836-0395, and in midtown Manhat- tan at 810 Seventh Avenue, 21st floor, New York, N.Y. 10019, (212) 582-6900. cashbox, -news r - Industry Stresses Search For Ways To Reach Consumers NEW YORK - The record industry's big- gest problem today is to find methods of reaching the consumer with important new product without depending as heavily as it does on radio. Although this hurdle has confronted the industry for years, it was brought home again, more vividly in the addresses of execs at the Columbia Convention as well as in the many seminars held during the conven- tion week in Los Angeles. Many people have addressed this problem at various industry forums through the years but in the most recent discusssions in this area there seems to be greater acceptance of three basic axioms: 1) radio's interests are not the same as the record industry's even though it appears on the surface that they are the same. 2) Continuous com- plaining about tight programming for- mats will not change things appreciable, since formats seem to be getting tighter each year. 3) The record industry will just have to apply its innovative minds to finding new avenues to expose new product if it hopes to make strides in the coming decade similar to the tremen- dous growth the industry enjoyed from the beginning of the Beatles era to the present. In the past decade. FM radio's coming on the scene as an important new vehicle for exposure of artists normally not programmed by AM radio, played a major role in the growth the industry en- joyed. But in recent years, FM radio's sound, seeking to enlarge its audience, has begun to sound more like AM radio, cutting -off, to a large extent, this produc- tive avenue. Grateful Dead Settles Pirate Suit Out Of Court HOLLYWOOD - The lawsuit filed by Grateful Dead Records and Ice Nine Publishing Company against Ramont Company, dba Kester Marketing, Charles Schlang, and Edward Barsky has been settled by all the parties to the suit. The suit, which involved the purchase and sale of infringing pirated records of the album "The Wake of the Flood," has been dismissed. The defendants, who obtained copies of the album without knowledge of the album's illegal source, are cooperating with the plaintiffs in an attempt to determine the source of manufacture of the pirated albums and to aid federal authorities in commencing appropriate prosecution under the Copyright Act. I FRONT COVER The Righteous Brothers, the singing duo that prompted the term blue-eyed soul into existence, have travelled a long way since their first smash single, "You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling" in 9164, but Bill Medley and Bobby Hatfield have a whole new bright future ahead of them thanks to their bottomless reservoire of talent and their association with Haven Records (distributed by Capitol). The Righteous Bros.' impact was felt strongly when they debuted in the sixties as their two gold LP's and gold single bear witness to, but they may well have their biggest success ahead of them. Their new Haven LP, "Give It To The People," highlighted by the smash single, "Rock 'n' Roll Heaven," is already starting to make a lot of folks happy and prompting heavy demands for them to go on the road. It's great to see skill and enthusiasm rewarded by a knowledgeable public and industry. UA Re -Organizes Operation: Stewart To Chair 5 Divisions HOLLYWOOD - Eric Pleskow, president and chief executive officer of United Artists, announced the formation of United Artists Music and Records Group, to be headed by Michael Stewart, who has been named chairman of the board of the group. Within the newly formed group there will be five divisions: United Artists Records of America, which will act as the domestic record company and be responsible in the United States for the acquisition and development of talent and the production, marketing and ex- ploitation of recordings issued under the United Artists and Blue Note labels; the music publishing division, consisting of Robbins Music, Big Three Music and United Artists Music, all of which rank among the largest music publishers in the world; the mass merchandising division, which includes Musical Isle of America, one of the nation's leading rack jobbing operations; the manufacturing division, consisting of All Disc, located in New Jersey, Research Craft, located in Los Angeles, and LTD., the tape duplicating operation, located in Omaha, Nebraska; and the international division, which includes the wholly owned and operated subsidiary companies in England, Canada, France and Germany. Pleskow stated that as a result of this reorganization Stewart will be better able to concentrate on the overall policy and planning of the entire group, which is necessary for the continued growth and expansion of United Artists' ac- tivities in the record and music publishing fields. cash box,- news Polydisc Convention Report (cont'd) Beltran Cites MGM/Polydor Goals In Address To Phonodisc Distribs ago," he declared. "Today, it is one of the leading companies in the world with established international ties in 35 coun- tries." He bolstered his remarks with a slide presentation showing regional and inter- national growth breakdowns. He closed his remarks mentioning that the music publishing, audio-visual products and marketing services which are the cornerstones of the corporation are continuing to show growth on all levels, with the upshot again falling on the key word of the entire morning's ac- tivities - optimism. The final speaker on the opening day's agenda was Phonodisc vice president Don England, who made a spirited sales presentation, commencing With a group of Phonodisc personnel pictured on slides backed with the music from the song "People" which was to be his key theme. In fact, the final slide stated bluntly, "Phonodisc Is People." After a brief personal introduction, he turned quickly to the subject of record industry growth in the last quarter cen- tury and of the incredible tasks and great challenges that have arisen as a result of this growth. "We have grown into a giant," he declared. "Many changes have nurtured our forward motion but the in- dividual, or the little guy, is still the heart- beat." England then outlined his raw of compatibility. He said, "The success of any organization depends on the ability of people to function cooperatively with mutual respect, toward a common goal." He stressed that a common goal was es- sential and observed that he saw the fall of many a record company due to divisive, rather than unified, policy. He stressed that bridges should be built not islands created. To do this, Phonodisc must create hit product through mer- chandising, sales promotion and distribution. "I think it's about time we eliminated the time -worn tag of 'promo man' or 'sales rep'," he said. "I think we ought to refer to ourselves as 'record marketing specialists'." He said he was more impressed with collective individuals rather than team, the word team implying a rather "happy- go-lucky, mindless conglomeration." It is his point, from a sales perspective, to gather from individuals their strengths and energies and to motivate them to work together as a team without sacrificing their own individuality. He stated that in all facets of the business, today's music men, particularly salesmen, promotion men, merchan- disers and distributors must be "multi- talented." "A renewing cycle of this talent is necessary to establish new ar- tists, to maintain the stature of hit acts and to keep catalogs active," he declared. England mentioned areas that he wanted Phonodisc personnel to be acutely aware of: account coverage, product line selling (including all ac- counts no matter how small), overall catalog sales and support of artist tours. As an incentive, England said the com- pany's policy was to upgrade and promote personnel from within the cor- poration rather than to go looking out- side. He stated that the company's recent policy proves this with the last slate of promotions coming at a 90% rate from within the company, and he promises this ratio will continue. Beltran's address was as follows: "We are a record company - a creative, highly explosive, very special kind of company. Hits is the name of the game' - new releases, airplay, chart - action, product in the market, sell through, etc. are everyday occurrences. "But a record company is a company like any other company and therefore, we must be concerned with the overall objective of achieving economic results, very often referred to as profits. For this to happen, the whole must be greater than the sum of its parts, our returns on investments must be larger than our initial outlay. The secret of success is to allocate resources to 'potential hits,' before we know in actuality that they are, and that's why the most crucial decisions in a record company are very subjective decisions. "Total awareness of today's music is a must - alertness to changes of attitudes by the ultimate judge, that is the con- sumer, is a requirement for success. "There are no real rules or standards by which to predict what is going to hap- pen next. Likewise, there is no such thing as a "sure hit." By and large, we're dealing with intangibles, gambling and taking calculated risks every time a decision is made. The only certainty is the faith the people that make up the company have in the product. Being able to properly expose new talent to the con- sumer requires ingenuity, tenacity, en- thusiasm, careful planning, hard work and lots of luck. One of the keys in the music business today is the ability to look and plan ahead, to constantly seek out new talent and to remain completely open. "Let's evaluate our opportunities by the feelings, the emotions, and the sen- timents that our product can potentially arouse in the consumer. Let's not forget that there is a very wide market out there that could and will react to a very large variety of product. "I said earlier that the whole must be greater than the sum of its parts. And I say now that the whole cannot exist without all of its parts. "You, as our distributors, are an in- tegral part of the system. You are our arms and as such you must take our product to the consumer, and return to us with the facts and figures that represent the reaction of that complex demographic, the positives and negatives, so that we can make a timely shift in our efforts if necessary. "Everyone on the Polydor Incor- porated team, that is MGM and Polydor, is aware of their involvement in the never ending search, and thoroughly ab- sorbed in every phase of new product from conception to release. Our belief in the product includes belief in the final consumer as well. There's no denying it. God knows we've got a tremendous task before us ... but it's countered by an overwhelming desire on the part of each and every one of us to make MGM and Polydor the hottest labels in the country. I have yet to meet a man who is in this business who isn't completely captivated by the challenge. "And so, in closing, we're going to present to you our product. We're going to tell it like it is - how we see it, what it means, where it should be taken.... "A famous poet once said 'Our reach must extend our grasp, or what's a heaven for?' He must have been talking about the record business. We may not be able to win 'em all and all that glitters is not gold, but you can bet WE'RE GONNA TURN UP EVERY NUGGET TILL WE FIND IT!! cash box R&B news Bar -Kays Set College Dates MEMPHIS - Stax artists The Bar -Kays begin a series of concerts at 45 mid - western and eastern college campuses September 16. winding up two months later at the end of their most heavily con- centrated tour to date. Coming off smash appearances at Pall's Mall in Boston, Richard's in Atlanta, The Bottom Line in New York, and a homecoming at the Club Paradise in Memphis, The Bar -Kays are em- barking on the tour in conjunction with the release of their new album, "Cold Blooded" on Volt, a division of the Stax Organization. The Bar -Kays were chosen by the National Entertainment Conference as the showcase act for the meetings last February in Houston. The block bookings for 45 colleges came as result of the NEC showcase performance. The seven members of The Bar -Kays, the Stax house band for years, have backed such gold -record artists as Isaac Hayes, The Staple Singers, Albert King, Carla Thomas and Otis Redding. The group is listed in the credits of about 50 million dollars worth of records. For live dates The Bar -Kays are joined on stage by one or more of lead singer Larry Dodson's pet boa constrictors - Cecil, Clarence and Clyde. Their ap- pearance usually gives the Bar -Kays a lit- tle more room around the stage to work. The college tour runs September 16 through November 15 and includes the following campus dates: In Michigan: Sept. 16, Alpena Com- munity College, Alpena; Sept. 17, Aquinas College, Grand Rapids; 19th, C.S. Fantasy Declares CBS Launches Tyner `Month' Jazz Program BERKELEY - Milestone Records has declared McCoy Tyner Month, from Sept. 15 to Oct. 15, with an all-out promotional campaign to be spearheaded by the simultaneous release of two new McCoy Tyner albums. One new LP is "Echoes of a Friend", a solo piano album dedicated to John Coltrane, with whom Tyner played for many years. The second album is "Sama Layuca", which further explores the genius of this remarkable pianist/ - composer, and features an all-star group including Bobby Hutcherson, Gary Bartz, and Azar Lawrence. During McCoy Tyner Month, the entire Tyner catalog of albums and tapes, in- cluding the new releases, will be available to distributors on a "buy ten, get one free" basis. Milestone is particularly proud of its continuing relationship with Tyner, and of the rapidly expanding audience for his recent recordings. The list of honors bestowed on Tyner this year is indeed impressive: in the 1974 Down Beat Inter- national Critics' Poll, he won first place as combo leader of the year, tied with Keith Jarrett as top pianist, and was voted tops for deserving wider recognition as a composer. His Milestone album, "Enlightenment", tied for first place in the same poll for Record of the Year, and was awarded the "Diamond Prize" by the Montreux jazz jury for the year's best recording. McCoy Tyner Month will be backed by heavy consumer advertising, radio spots, special radio programs of Tyner's music throughout the country, posters, and special slick book covers. cash box,- news GRC Sets 12 Anka Orig. Hits Singles, 5 LP's Via Sire In Oct. ATLANTA - In response to increased airplay and sales reaction of current product releases, GRC Records has an- nounced the mid -fall premiere of 12 new singles and 5 albums from the firm's label. GRC President, Michael Thevis, said product releases will begin Sept. 24 and feature the country singing duo Lonzo & Oscar with "He Came Back" followed Oct. 1 with GRC's country/pop band Heartwood. Heartwood will release "Guaranteed To Win" produced by Paul Hornsby. Additional product slated for October release includes R&B vocalist Dee Ervin "I Love What You're Doin' To Me"; pop vocalist Eddie Reeves "What Are We Doin' "; pop singer/guitarist Jim Turner and Houston singer/performer Bill Nash. Releases on the label, the r&b sub- sidiary of GRC, feature return singles by R&B songstress Loleatta Holloway and soul singer John Edwards. Edwards is currently enjoying top 30 R&B position on the charts with his single "Careful Man." From the success of "There's Got To Be Rain" released early this year by Dorothy Norwood, GRC returns with a new single and album from the former gospel-turned-R&B artist. Also marked for release is the vocal/instrumental funk -sounding septet, Ripple. This band brought in the first breakthrough for GRC in an R&B/pop crossover during the label's first six months of operation. Ripple's current single is "You Were Right On Time." Joe Hinton, songwriter for many Motown artists will release a single on GRC's Hotlanta Label. Heading the list of November single releases are the Rhodes Kids. This seven -member youthful set, making their debut with "Voo-Doo Magic," plan to follow with "I Like You," backed by an extensive multimedia promotional cam- paign. New albums slated for Oc- tober/November include The Counts, Eddie Reeves, Dorothy Norwood and the Rhodes Kids. According to Buz Wilburn, president of GRDC, "We have produced a diversified selection of product releases including the areas of pop, R&B, country and MOR. Our overall sales have increased within the past three months and we have expanded our artist roster heavily in country and pop music. Combining this with our marketing staff, field promotion force and A&R push, we feel the successes of GRC will continue developing." Wilburn also commented that GRC will be releasing a complete new line of jazz product in mid -November by Ebony Godfather, thus initiating the world-wide label into yet another phase of the music industry. NEW YORK - The original recordings of Paul Anka's greatest hits, which have not been available since 1962, will soon be released in a specially packaged and priced two -record set by Sire Records following an agreement reached be- tween Bill Buster of American Record Sales, who holds the exclusive license to this product and Sire's managing direc- tor Seymour Stein. These recordings cover the period from 1957-1962 when he was under con- tract to ABC -Paramount. Titles include "Diana," "Lonely Boy," "Put Your Head On My Shoulder," "Puppy Love," "You Are My Destiny," "It's Time To Cry," "My Home Town," "Dance On Little Girl," all of which were top 10 hits for Anka and all of which will be contained in this package. Sire plans to release the double album in October as part of their first release since signing their new ABC distribution pact, as an historic package filled with photos and memorabilia with special liner notes by Greg Shaw, editor of Phonograph Record Magazine. Plans for future releases from the Anka catalog of over 100 masters have not yet been set. Sire's rights cover the United States only, but include tape rights, through their licensee GRT. Buster has done separate deals for Canada and the rest of the world with Pòlydor of Canada and CBS International respectively. In commenting on the deal Stein stressed, "We are indeed pleased that Sire has been entrusted with the task of bringing back on the market these great Paul Anka recordings. Our timing is ex- cellent! With Paul back on the top of the charts, this album will appeal not only to collectors who have been waiting years for this material to be re -issued, but to all markets as well." Pryor's 'X' Rated Hits Gold Status MEMPHIS - Comic Richard Pryor's cur- rent album, "That Nigger's Crazy," has been certified gold with over a million dollars in sales, combining the figures for both records and tapes. The LP on the Partee label (a division of The Stax Organization) is distinctive in that it reached its status virtually without the benefit of radio airplay, because of the nature of Pryor's material. Clearly "Rated X" on the cover, the Pryor album is done with scenes and language straight off the ghetto streets which in- spired most of Pryor's routines and characterizations. Lead guitarist Adrian Fisher has left the band, meanwhile, and there pres- ently are no plans to replace him. Scoring strongly in America, mean- while, is the debut Sparks album, "Kimono My House," and the single, "This Town Ain't Big Enough for Both of Us." "This Town" and "Amateur Hour" were major chart entries for the group upon release overseas, the former establishing Sparks' reputation as pos- sibly the best new band of 1974. cash box/ album reviews pop picks LOOK AT THE FOOL - Tim Buckley - Producer: Joe Falsia - DiscReet DS 2201 Tim's last effort, "Saffronia," was a remarkable LP, but all Buckley fans will be delighted to learn that his current effort is at least as good and in many respects an improvement over his last record. Tim's vocals continue to have a haunting quality to them even when he reaches back and lets it rip, but the overall strength of the record is in its sense of unity. Wé think that "Bring It Up," "Tijuana Moon," "Down In The Street" and the title track are particularly strong and give the LP a good foundation. ASTRALSIGNAL - Gene Harris - Producers: Keg Johnson, Jerry Peters, Jim Shifflett - Blue Note BN-LA313-G Watch for Gene Harris! Not only is this Blue Note LP an exercise in brilliance, but his live stage act is incomparable. This record explodes with such tracks as "Rebato Summer," "Don't Call Me Nigger, Whitey," "My Roots." "Love Talkin," "Green River" and Gene's great new single "Higga-Boom" and Harris' piano playing throughout is incredible. If people start hearing this album, they're not going to rest till it's a part of their collection. It's that good and so is Gene Harris. URUBAMBA - Urubamba - Producer: Paul Simon - Columbia KC 32896 If you were impressed by Paul Simon's "Live Rhymin" LP, then you were at least subcon- sciously influenced by Urubamba, the South American quartet Paul met in Paris in 1965 and whom he used to back him on one side of the aforementioned Gold album. This collection puts into focus the collective as well as the individual brilliance and sensitivity of the members of Urubamba and gives them a very strong debut product in which they can all take pride. We like the cuts "Heart Of The Inca King" and "Kachar- pari." HOME AT LAST - Wayne Berry - Producer: Norbert Putnam - RCA CPL1-0603 One of the most pronounced talents to emerge this year, Wayne Berry can be very proud of his new RCA LP, one that reflects the sincerity and depth of emotion he's capable of reaching, seemingly at will. Recorded in Muscle Shoals (with the appropriate heavies) and Hollywood (where most of the remaining heavies now reside) the LP has a flair to it that ranges from the fine song selection to Norbert Putnam's skillful production job. Rustic Wayne's at his best on "Dixie's Pride" and "All I Needed." UNICORN - Unicorn - Producer: David Gilmour - Capitol ST -11334 As enigmatic and mysterious as the group's LP cover, Unicorn is a different kind of band, one whose spirit is tied to its flesh in a remarkable pattern of interweaving harmonies and melodies. The group's new Capitol LP is a strong one, a mixture of derivative and original styles that come together neatly. The production is clear and the arrangements clever, resulting in some rather pleasing sounds. Particularly good tracks include "Holland," "Electric Night" and "Just Wanna Hold You." DON'T FIGHT THE FEELING - Sound Experience - Producer: Stan Watson - Soulville PS 1650 The name of the group added to the famous Flip Wilson expression that serves as the LP title just about sums up the message of this fine new Soulville package. As adept at pretty ballads as they are at rendering super -funky material, the Sound Experience is a group of skillful, polished professionals who know what they're about - good music. Our faves off this new disk include "You Don't Know What You're Doing," "Devil With The Bust," "Your Love Belongs To Me" and the great title track. ft). jazz picks best bets 3O1ND 3/C,EFIENiCE )H'T FIGHT HE FEELING i321LY..D JILL). D!' 41) 'elf! Billy ThuncierKloud and the Chiffons DORY PREVIN - Dory Previn - Producer: Nikolas Venet - Warner Bros. BS 2811 Dory Previn has always been one of the most enigmatic and uniquely gifted singer/song- writers to perform in the pop genre and her cur- rent LP is an expansion of the talents she has am- ply displayed in the past. The LP cover is sym- bolic, for Ms. Previn has always placed a high priority on lyrics and this collection is one of the most intriguing we've seen this year. VIVA EMILIANO ZAPATA - Gato Barbieri - Producer: Ed Michel - ABC/Impulse ASD-9279 The obvious saxophone genius of Gato Bar- bieri pours forth on this LP as well as his marked proclivity towards 6/8 time and the resultant product is one of wonder and magic. GINO CUNICO - Glno Cunico a- Producers: Ar- tie Ripp, Gino Cunico, Toxie French - Kama Sutra KSBS 2601 A dynamic talent capable of sounding like Billy Joel or Maurice Gibb (of the Bee Gees), Gino Cunico has a very bright future ahead of him in- deed. From the moody quintessence of "Faith" to the more emphatic "Hold On To Your Lady" and "Free Love" the album has a vivacious quality about it that is challenging and compelling simultaneously. Look closely both to the heavens and to your local one stop for this one. OFF THE RESERVATION - Billy ThunderKloud and the Chieftones - Producers: Farah Produc- tions, Jim Vienneau - 20th Century T-452 An interesting LP to say the least, this new 20th Century package features Billy Thun- derKloud and his group stylizing such tunes as "Sunny," "Kick The Can," "Endless Sleep," "You Touched My Life" and "Come To Me." The har- monies are good and tight, the production com- plimentary, the arrangements succinct and the dynamics well thought out. It's hard to pick a favorite off the LP because the group doesn't fit into any established "bag." So listen and decide for yourself. 28 September 28, 1974

cash box R&B news Chris Jonz To Taurus Production HOLLYWOOD - Motown Records superstar Stevie Wonder has appointed Chris Jonz as manager and business ad- ministrator for his independent com- pany, Taurus Productions, effective im- mediately. Jonz's duties will include overall su- pervision of all of Wonder's activities as well as personal direction to coordinate all promo ttional activities between Won- der's New York and Los Angeles offices. Jonz, formerly with Motown Records, had functioned as national promotion director and manager of artist relations. Prior to his tenure at Motown, Jonz held the position of national promotion direc- tor of the New York based Scepter Records. In another move, Wonder has ap- pointed Reggie Wiggins road manager for Wonderlove, Stevie's musical and vocal backup ensemble. Additionally, Wiggins, drawing from his vast entertain- ment background, will function in related business affairs. Prior to joining Taurus Productions, Wiggins served with the Jackson Five for 21/2 years, and before that, a 4 year stint with Diana Ross and the Supremes. DeJohnette Signs Exclusive Contract With Prestige BERKELEY - Jack DeJohnette has signed an exclusive recording contract with Prestige Records. His first album for the label, "Socery" (P-10081), will be released this month. DeJohnette produced the album, and wrote all of the music. Although he is best-known as a drummer, the album also features his keyboard work. (DeJohnette actually began his musical career as a pianist, and only later gravitated to the drums.) DeJohnette is a highly innovative and original musician. He has, until now, spent most of his career as an accom- plished sideman, playing on four Gram- my -winning albums by Bill Evans, Miles Davis, Freddie Hubbard, and Hubert Laws. He has also worked with John Coltrane, Sonny Rollins, Stan Getz, and Charles Lloyd. While not on the road, DeJohnette teaches improvisation to private students at his home in upstate New York. He is presently scheduling an ex- tensive college tour of the east coast. Others on the new album, "Sorcery," are Bennie Maupin on bass clarinet; John Abercrombie and Mick Goodrick on guitars; David Holland on bass; and Michael Fellerman on metaphone. Notable Music Obtains Song Fest R&B Winner NEW YORK - Cy Coleman's Notable Music (ASCAP) has obtained the publishing rights to the American Song Festival's R&B winner, "And A Little Child Will Lead You" by Gloria Nissen - son and Marcia Defren. The song was performed at the fest by Al Wilson. In other activity at Notable, the one- time Jackson Five hit, "Never Say Good- bye," has been released as a single by Gloria Gaynor on MGM. Also, composer Coleman has written instrumental music for the American version of the hit English play, "Equus," which Kermit Bloomgarden will bring to Broadway next month. Vinnie Bell, who had suc- cess with the "Airport" theme, has re- corded the piece, with a label deal in the works. cash box R&B news report r&b ingredients KINSHASA, ZAIRE - The ambitious dream of bringing together the top black musical artists of Africa and America became a reality here with the presentation of the first of three Zaire '74 stadium concerts in this Central African capital city. James Brown was the opening night headliner, and despite the handicap of going on at 3:30 a.m., he brought the audience to life and dazzled them with his pyrotechnics. Brown, sticking with his roadshow format, didn't make his appearance until the second half of his show, but his faithful fans waited him out and cheered him. The concert was held in the newly refurbished 60,000 -seat soccer stadium where Muhammed Ali and George Foreman were scheduled to fight until Foreman's eye cut resulted in the post- ponement. Ali was among the spectators at the opening night concert and received a roaring salute from the crowd. Preceding Brown on the opening night show were several African acts and American entertainers. The Fania Allstars with Pacheko in command ignited the audience first with a rousing set of Afro -Latin rhythms that brought calls for an encore. The Pointer Sisters were less successful in clearing the language barrier with their slick and imaginative act. Better suited for Las Vegas than Central Africa, their show is largely a sendup of the American music of 30 years ago. Promoters Don King and Lloyd Price expressed the feeling that the concerts represent a tremendous cultural achievement in bringing the two continents together with music. Certainly the technical achievement was remarkable, and the concert stage assem- bled by Bill McManus and Chip Monck was second to none with the most professional equipment. Twenty-five American technicians installed the massive amount of equip- ment and excellent sound system. The opening night concert pulled an estimated 25,000 persons, the ticket sales being handicapped because of an advance sale and the high range ($2 to $3) of the prices in this country where many people work a day for less than the minimum ticket. King said plans were being made to lower the ticket price to $1 for all seats for the final concert to give everyone an opportunity to see at least one of the history -making concerts. Price said, "The primary thing is the film for the world to see rather than just filling up the stadium, but we want as many people as possible to enjoy the concert in per- son. The fact that we spanned 9,000 miles and put more than $2 million into this project makes it unlike anything ever attempted before." King added, "We promised that we would deliver the artists and the equipment, and we did. We are all very proud that we got to take part in this remarkable cultural event.- . The Supremes, Mary Wilson, Cindy Birdsong and Scherrie Payne have been set for a one week tour of Brazil starting on October 14, which will see them performing at the Teatro Tuca Theatre in Sao Paulo, The Brune Theatre in Rio de Janeiro, the Circle de Las Artists in Rio, the Blue Cassara and the Circulo de Militar in Sao Paulo. ... The group is comprised of Damita Jo Freeman, Perry Brown, Pat Davis, Eddie Champion, Jimmy Foster, Wanda Fuller and Burt Woods and has just signed with Daniel Ben Av Productions for personal management. ... On A Wonderful Day Stevie Gets Keys; Gives Charity Concert DETROIT - Accepting an acknowledgement of his talent, Motown Records' superstar, Stevie Wonder, was presented with a city proclamation and the key to the city of Detroit by Mayor Coleman A. Young to welcome him to the city. The mayor also declared Sep- tember 27 to be Stevie Wonder Day. Getting his start in Motown as a young boy as "Little Stevie Wonder," he per- formed and lived for many years in Detroit. On his "Day" he performed to a sold - out concert at Olympia Stadium. Proceeds from the show were donated by Wonder to be used in summer bus- sing programs to transport culturally disadvantaged children from the ghetto to the country. The singer -composer vowed that this "was the beginning of the beginning" and that he would be re- turning to Detroit for more charity con- certs. Tying in the promotion with radio, Stan Fantich, Motown's national field promotion manager, successfully ar- ranged for the following stations to hold Stevie Wonder Days: CKLW, WJLB, WGPR and WERZ. Free albums and tickets to the concert were given to listeners. Additionally, all retail stores in the area featured Stevie Wonder albums and displays. Two parties were held to celebrate Stevie Wonder Day. Before the concert, Ewart Abner, president of Motown Records, hosted a reception for Stevie at the Grand Ballroom of the St. Regis Hotel, and after the concert Stevie hosted another party for 300 guests and friends at the hotel. Coliseum HOLLYWOOD - Philadelphia Inter- national recording artists the O'Jays, at a recent performance at the Greensboro Coliseum in Greensboro, North Carolina, instantly became the fourth largest grossing attraction in the Coliseum history with a total gross of $84,437. This put the group in line with such artists as Elvis Presley and the Osmond Brothers, who have successfully sold out the Coliseum. According to H.E. Wheeler, the Coliseum owner, the group had the largest walk up ticket buys in the Coliseum's history. "The group did a larger walk up gross than they did in ad- vance sales," Wheeler stated. Also performing that evening as special guest attractions were Rufus and the Ohio Players. Promoter for the date was Quinton Perry for Taurus Produc- tions. cash box,- news CBS 3rd Qtr, Nine Months Set New Highs NEW YORK - CBS 1974 third quarter and first nine months sales and earnings have set company records for those periods, according to William S. Paley, chairman, and Arthur R. Taylor, president. The execs noted that sales im- provement by the CBS/Records Group came "primarily from the international unit." Estimated 1974 third quarter income from continuing operations is $25.8 mil- lion, compared with $23.4 million earned in the third quarter of 1973, a 10% in- crease. This is equivalent to 90e per share for the third quarter of 1974, com- pared with 82e for the third quarter of 1973, the company's previous record high for that period. Estimated 1974 third quarter net sales are $415.2 million, compared with $370.7 million achieved in the same period in 1973, a 12% im- provement. Paley and Taylor observed that, "The third quarter was the 14th consecutive quarter in which CBS earnings from con- tinuing operations have improved over comparable year-earlier periods." For the first nine months of 1974, estimated income from continuing operations is $76.1 million, compared with $64.1 million earned in the first nine months of 1973, a 19% increase. Estimated nine months per share income from continuing operations is $2.66, compared with $2.25 earned in the first nine months of 1973. (The first nine months 1973 earnings per share do not include a gain on discontinued operations of 17e resulting primarily from the sale of the New York Yankees.) Estimated net sales for the first nine months are $1,249.8 million, compared with $1,088.6 million for the first nine months of 1973, an increase of 15%. RCA Sales Over Nine Months Set New Label High NEW YORK - RCA Records sales for the first nine months of 1974 were the highest in its history, according to Jack Kiernan, vp of marketing. "Our fine roster of artists," Kiernan said, "has given us product of consistent high quality which has created a very high demand throughout the year. Heavy sales, based on this, have given us the record nine months as well as a larger share of the total record market. We have great strength and with a con- tinuing flow of the kind of product that should give us a banner sales year." Ending Mar. 31 NEW YORK - Decca Limited of London, England, the parent company of London Records, showed gains in sales and profits for the year ending Mar. 31. The group turnover, converted to dol- lars at the exchange rate of $2.394 on Mar. 31, 1974, increased by $48,358,800 and profits before taxation rose $1, 967,868 to $38,074,176. Decca's turn- over on consumer goods, which includes records, tapes, TV and audio, was up from $165,186,000 in 1973 to $192,717,000, and pre-tax division of profits on consumer goods shows a total of $23,844,240 against last year's figure of $23,590,476. The capital goods aspect of the com- pany's trading, which includes elec- tronics, navigation and radar, grossed $134,303,400 in the trading year against $113,475,600 in 1973. Directors recom- mended a final dividend of 14.42487 cents per share (last year 14.32809 cents per share) making 19.45227 cents for the year (last year 19.35549 cents). CBS Gets Temp. Court Order In Suit Vs Stax MEMPHIS - CBS Records was granted in U.S. Federal District Court in Memphis last Thursday (10) a temporary restraining order against Stax Records as a result of a suit filed by CBS to prevent what it terms a "violation' of its distribution agreement with the label. The Court, with the consent of Stax, is- sued the temporary restraining order fol- lowing CBS' contention that Stax had repudiated its agreement with CBS "without justification or cause." That agreement was made two years ago this month. CBS said its action against Stax sought to enjoin the label, reported to be in financial difficulty, from "distributing through other distribution outlets and reducing the label's artist roster." Anderson To UA VP Promo Post LOS ANGELES - President of United Artists Records of America, Al Teller, has announced the appointment of Ray Anderson to the post of vice president, promotion. In his new position, Anderson will be responsible for all radio promotion ac- tivities for both the United Artists and Blue Note labels and will supervise the day to day activities of United Artists' national promotional staff. In announcing the appointment, Teller stated that "Ray Anderson is one of the most respected and effective promotion executives in the recording industry. I am confident that his contribution to the future success of United Artists Records of America will be a most significant one." Anderson, a veteran of ten years in the promotion field, was most recently manager, national singles promotion, for RCA Records and, prior to assuming that position, was RCA's Los Angeles field promotion representative. Anderson will be headquartered in United Artists' Los Angeles offices. Anderson `Labels' Act Barrage Lifts Sales Sight For 4th Qtr NEW YORK - Recording companies are fueling what is traditionally the industry's best quarter of the year - the period of Oct. thru Dec. - with some of their strongest product lineups ever. The heavy barrage of strong talent being made available in the year's final surge of sales activity comes, in- terestingly enough, in an era when LP scheduling of key acts in a single burst of product announcements is difficult in view of greater artist control in the creation and marketing of album mer- chandise. The boost psychologically at this time is important, too. This is due to the anxiety over the economy and its pos- sible impact on the industry. Whatever the future holds, the business realizes that strong sales contenders find it in- creasingly less formidable to reach the 1 million unit sales milestone, with many albums going far beyond that point. The availability of new albums by key performers is, of course, a big traffic draw, and the fact that so much in the way of star acts are comirrg at a single period - happily the industry's best - is also seen as a big boost to general catalog sales. House Agrees to Anti -Pirate Bill; Penalties Increased WASHINGTON - The House approved by a voice vote last week a bill increasing penalties against tape and disc pirates. The measure, recently passed out of a House committee, subjects violators to a maximum fine for a first offense of $25,000 and a maximum jail term for a subsequent offense to two years. The Senate recently agreed to stiffer penalties, making the manufacture and sale of bogus recordings a felony, with possible jail terms of three years for a first offense and seven years for a second violation of the law. A com- promise measure now has to be worked out by the House and Senate. See Special Country Section In This Issue October 19, 1974 7

for the record POINTS WEST - It can safely be reported that all rumors of Dr. John's leaving Atlantic Records are totally false. The good Doc (Mac Rebbennack to his family) is cur- rently in the studio recording the followup LP to his "Desitively Bonaroo" album and it's for Atlantic.... Dec. 15 is the tentative release date for Alice Cooper's new flick according to Bob Brown who, along with Shep Gordon, ably pilots Alive Enterprises, handling the likes of Alice and Anne Murray. Title is yet to be decided upon.... His Master's Wheels, the fine recording studio that scored heavily with their recent work on the Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young tour (they did the recording for the quartet's up- coming live LP) will be busy recording the Grateful Dead's last live concert for at least a year at San Francisco's Winterland Ballroom (16-20). Looks like Eliot Mazer and Gary Haber won't be getting much rest during that hectic four day stint.... Lenny Wil- liams, lead singer of Tower of Power, was so impressed with His Master's facilities he laid down some basic tracks and will return to cut his first solo LP for Warners shortly. ... Tubes, another hot Bay Area band just signed to A&M, is also working on their debut LP at the studio - keep on truckin', fellas. The Village Recorder studios here in West L.A. is also the scene of a lot of activity. Producer/arranger Jim Price is well into the completion of the followup LP by Joe Cocker whose current A&M release "I Can Stand A Little Rain" is a chart success (2 on the Cash Box LP chart this week). They're into overdubs and mixing, and Price, who did Cocker's last, is very pleased with how this one's turning out. Price is also producing Wayne Shorter's solo LP for Columbia at the studio with guest artist Brazilian singer/songwriter Milton Nacimento sitting in. And Cocker's former business manager, Mark Aglietti, has joined Village Recorders as director of operations. Price's projects at the studio find him working with the best, the studio's chief engineer, Rob Fraboni.... Also at the facility Bloodstone finishing their new London LP and the soundtrack for their upcoming film "Night Train." Mike Vernon producing with engineer Rich Heenan at the console. Finally, Kiss has just finished its new Kerner & Wise produced LP at the studio. At Elton John's Hollywood opening which was attended by a number of celebrities including Elizabeth Taylor, Harry Nilsson, Ringo Starr and Henry Mancini, among others, RCA regional promotion man Don Whittemore had a practical joke played on him by parties unknown. The loudspeaker announced about five minutes before the lights dimmed, "Would Mr. and Mrs. Whittemore please call your home immediately, your baby sitter called and said she can't find the fire extinguisher." This might sound like black humor on the surface, but insiders such as Nilsson and Mancini (who record for RCA) laughed because they know Whittemore is unmarried -or do they? cash box/news cash box" album reviews New Guess Who GRT Sets To Be Held Up Oct. Release HOLLYWOOD - Burton Cummings, lead singer of The Guess Who, and new guitarist Dom Troiano, have co -written the next album for the RCA group, called "Flavors." A release date has been set for early January, according to manager Don Hunter. There is a good chance the label will not distribute the record for some time, since The Guess Who's "Road Food" LP is doing well in sales and on the charts, while their single "Clap For The Wolf - man" is currently a hit. Speaking about his newest writing partner, Cummings said: "Things are a lot better than they've been for years." As for "Flavors," Cummings thought there might even be a country hit off the album. "I used to know what hit singles were, and I don't really any more," the lead singer admitted. "I never expected 'Star Baby' or 'Wolfman' to be hits. They were flukes. But we've got pretty good com- mercial roots - I grew up on AM radio, and it comes round to that again, sooner or later. So here we go again." NARAS Readies Lecture Bureau NEW YORK - A new Recording Academy Lecture Bureau has been for- med by NARAS. It will be administered by the American Program Bureau of Boston. Bob Walker, president of the American Program Bureau, is presently coor- dinating plans for a series of seminars and lectures at colleges and universities across the country. Recording Academy members from all sectors of the industry will be invited to participate in either one- or two-day group seminars or in- dividual lecture appearances before campus audiences. Emphasis in both lectures and seminars will be placed on educational information, with special attention given to the professional opportunities open to college students who wish to pursue a career in the music industry. Edvard Moritz Dies NEW YORK - Edvard Moritz, composer and symphonic conductor in both the United States and Europe, died in New York City on Sept. 30. Mr. Moritz, who was born in Hamburg, Germany on June 23, 1891 was 83. A member of the American Society of Composers, Authors and Publishers since 1939, he wrote many orchestral works. His compositions included four symphonies, two piano concertos, and many works for chamber groups. He is survived by his widow, Johanna. Darius Brubeck and his ensem- ble as well as Chris and Dan Brubeck join their talented father in a tour de force that reinforces the concept that the family that plays together stays together. Particularly enjoyable cuts here include "Mr. Broadway," "The Duke," "Temp- tation Boogie," "Christopher Columbus," "It's A Raggy Waltz" and "Sky Scape." A fun and ex- citing LP. FIRST LIGHT - The Family of Mann - Atlantic SD 1658 Herbie Mann's impeccable musical reputation is further enhanced on this new Atlantic LP which features super 'family' members Pat Rebil- lot, David Newman, Tony Levin, Armen Halburian, Steve Gadd and Sam Brown. The relationship that develops musically between Herbie and these talented journeymen comes across strongly in bold, powerful strokes, especially on cuts such as "Toot Stick," "Sunrise Highs," "Lullaby For Mary Elizabeth," "Music Is A Game We Play" and "Thank You Mr. Rushing." A thoroughly enjoyable LP. UPON THIS ROCK - Joe Farrell - Producer: Creed Taylor - CTI 6042 S1 Joe Farrell's mastery of tenor and soprano sax as well as flute has never been more evident than on his new CTI LP, one that features the talented jazz artist accompanied by Joe Beck on guitar, Steve Gadd ("I Won't Be Back") and Jim Madison on drums, Herb Bushier on bass, Her- bie Hancock (piano on "I Won't Be Back") and Don Alias (also on "I Won't Be Back"). "I Won't Be Back," an epic piece of some ten minutes, is one of the most compelling pieces of music we've ever heard -and the interplay between Far- rell and Hancock is breathtaking. THE FINAL SWING - Trapeze featuring Glenn Hughes - Producer: John Lodge - Threshold THS 11 Glenn Hughes may have broken the group up with his decision in 1973 to join Deep Purple as its bassist, but the memories of Trapeze in some of its finer moments are captured here in a powerful retrospective set that features the band in those moments of blazing fury when they were masters of all they surveyed. Dave Holland on drums and Mel Galley on lead guitar com- plement Hughes' work on these tunes, notably "Send Me No More Letters," "Medusa," "Coast To Coast" and "Dats It." October 19. 1974 25

cash box talent on stage Steppenwolf Dalton and Dubarri UFO HOLLYWOOD - As soon as the band stepped out on stage and the swirling, pounding sound of "Born To Be Wild" poured through the enthusiastic audience at UCLA's Pauley Pavilion, everyone knew that Steppenwolf was back. After an incredible career, in- cluding numerous gold records and world wide concert success, the band had broken up and 'gone their separate ways. But with a new album release, en- titled "Slow Flux" on Mums Records, John Kay and company were acting like they had never left. Their set included generous doses of the past hits - "The Monster," "Magic Carpet Ride," "The Pusher" and "Hey Lawdy Mama" - and equally generous portions from the new album. Much of their political material, as Kay was quick to point out, has stayed remarkably topical in the intervening years because of Watergate. But topical or not, the nearly patented Steppenwolf sound was much in evidence. High points of the set included "I'm Moving On" which Kay had recorded on one of his solo outings and which was particularly powerful in its Steppenwolf arrangement, and "Straight Shootin' Woman," the band's single from "Slow Flux." Present day Steppenwolf includes originals Kay, Goldy McJohn and Jerry Edmonton, and newcomers George Biondo and Bobby Cochran. Their stage act is particularly enhanced by the unique amplification system they employ which keeps all unsightly amps and wires out of the spotlight and allows Kay to prance about undistracted. Dalton & Dubarri played the set im- mediately before Steppenwolf and warmed up the audience with a series of tunes from their new Columbia album called "Good Head." Good harmonies and an ability to get an audience up on their feet helped the duo keep the vibrations high and handsome. They had most success on their opening number, called "Got To Have My Rock 'N' Roll," which was the crowd's favorite and which allows for plenty of audience response. UFO opened the show with a hard rock, shiny metal set which included "Rock Bottom" and other tunes that called to mind Led Zeppelin and other power units. Cleo Laine John Dankworth CARNEGIE HALL, NYC - The somewhat excited Carnegie Hall audience sat in eager anticipation for the first lady of song to appear. Her ap- pearance brought resounding applause as the "Empress Of Song" graced the Carnegie Hall stage. Her husband, John Dankworth, who functions as conductor of the tight backing ensemble as well as woodwind player par excellence, is Cleo's perfect complement. He an- ticipates her every mood and his well poised professionalism carries a charac- teristic dignity with it. Cleo was exuberant and full of the kind of song that has increased her popularity greatly from her Carnegie Hall concert last year to this present concert. Her material is well thought out, contains bril- liant arrangements (by Dankworth) and spotlights the unique throated sophisticated songstress. Her repertoire spans Gershwin (That Certain Feeling), Legrand (The Summer Knows), Gilbert and Sullivan (The Sun The Moon And I), to the works of such poets as e. e. Cum- mings, Sir John Betjeman, and Shakespeare. The poetry is set to music and Cleo's dramatic sense augments the Lou Reed Hall & Oates FELT FORUM, NYC - Daryl Hall and John Oates have changed a great deal since their "Abandoned Luncheonette" LP was done for Atlantic. The LP produced by Arif Mardin marked the group as a soulful duo who gave their special taste of funk an electronic flavoring. This LP, and "She's Gone" in particular, was a unique outing for the talented duo who mix sharp and tren- chant lyrics with superb blending har- monies cushioned by mellow syn- thesizers. Since the "Abandoned Luncheonette" excursion the group has gone through an acute musical metamorphosis. They are now produced by Todd Rundgren and "War Babies" is the title of their new Atlantic LP. The transformation has en- tirely altered their sound and style and now these angry young men have come across with a strong attack on the society of which we are all a part and taken elec- tric music with a pulsating beat to depict the horrors and atrocities of war and the nightmare of the atomic age. Included in their new repertoire is an electrified ver- sion of "She's Gone," which has inciden- tally been covered by two r&b acts. All the rest of the material was taken from the "War Babies" LP and included "Is It A Star," "War Baby Son Of Zorro," " '70s Scenario," and "Better Watch Your Back." The eager anticipation of the crowd reached its zenith as the divine Mr. Reed was led on to the stage by his group of at- tending valets. Clad like a 3 -dimensional cutout of the picture of him on his latest RCA LP entitled "Sally Can't Dance" the bizarre Lou has dyed his hair a very light blonde and has donned large sunglasses which obfuscate part of his face. Wearing tight fitting jeans and sleeveless midriff the maniacally decadent Lou went through the famous stylized talk nar- rative with musical accompaniment that he has become so very famous for. Numbers included "Sally Can't Dance," the title track from his new LP, "Vicious" and "Walk On The Wild Side." Older material was taken from his "Tran- sformer" LP and the audience was very receptive to Lou's bizarre shenanigans. From Velvet Underground days Lou per- formed "Heroin" with a really macabre sequence of getting off which was initiated by a graphic tying -off segment. Yes, Lou Reed positively epitomizes the decadent rock and roll we have all dug at one time or another. He is one of the precursors of this rock movement and if he did not have an audience that was into his act then he would not have sold out the Felt Forum. m.d. wonderfully poignant presentation. The strongest part of her performance was her older material. Billed as a request medley, the songs included "Day By Day," "On A Clear Day," "I'm Going To Sit Right Down And Write Myself A Letter," and a magnificent ren- dition of Carole King's "Music." She seemed most natural and aesthetically spontaneous on these selections, and her exceptional vocal flexibility was best exercised. And using the audience as an index of response, the crowd clamored for more when she hit her superlative notes within the medley. Ms. Laine certainly has a unique tim- bre to her voice. At times sounding a bit rough, she slid into her casual scat singing or remarkably soothing pitch. "Birdsong," written by Dankworth was a particularly moving number. "All In Love Is Fair," which has been covered by the likes of Barbra Streisand, is a Stevie Wonder penned tune that was given a polished interpretation. m.d Santana Tower Of Power ACADEMY OF MUSIC, N.Y. - It never fails. Just ask a New York audience for a minute of silence and you'll end up with the most boisterous response of the evening. Such was the greeting bestowed upon Carlos Santana when he requested a minute of silent meditation preceding the group's appearance on Oct. 12. Being generally regarded as the pur- veyor of Latin -rock in the '60s, the music of Santana was a wholly influential source of inspiration to the music scene at the time. An unfortunate series of in- cidents a couple of years ago including drug and managerial problems zapped the group of their creative juices, but a spiritual awakening on the part of Carlos Santana has resulted in a recent flurry of recording activity and a reformation of a touring group which includes three original members. The new 8 -man lineup parallels the earlier group in that much of their material has been culled from the first three albums ("Soul Sacrifice," "Oye Como Va," and "Black Magic Woman"), but the arrangements have been spiced up to include synthesizer, and the flute and saxophone of Jules Broussard, while the role of the guitar has in turn been de-emphasized. The newer material presented by the Columbia group re- flected Carlos Santana's inclinations toward a jazzier sound with results which were most encouraging. The im- provisations, thrust by a trio of percus- sionists, explored dissonant themes and provided ample opportunity for solos, yet an overriding sense of control per- meated the music not heard since the very early days of the group. Opening the show was Tower Of Power, whose five -man horn section colors and bolsters the driving sound behind buttery voiced lead singer Lenny Williams. They played a short but precise set highlighted by their latest Warner's single, "Don't Change Horses," but ap- peared inhibited by the concert hall am- bience of the Academy. b.t. Weather Report AVERY FISHER HALL, N.Y. - Weather Report's music is a cosmic theatre of the mind. The notes, like actors in a drama, contest and confirm each other. In isolation, each note, each measure, and each composition, in fact, appears remotely detached, as if suspended in mid-air. Yet, the sensitive organization of the musicians, based as it is upon an un- canny understanding of each player's ability and emotional affectability, ener- gizes the music and anchors the pieces to a supportative stage of signification. Each note, each composition, however, like the many acts of a play, can only be understood after the curtain has dropped and the end has been revealed. The Columbia group's music was based upon a strong and vibrant wall of rhythm. Al Johnson on bass, Dom Um Romao on percussion instruments and Darryl Brown on drums raised the pulse of the sound. Weather Report's opening numbers, "Nubean Sundance," and "Milky Way," were bursts of power, ac- cented on the first by Wayne Shorter's flowing musical tempest on soprano sax, and on the second by Joe Zawinul's haunting bell -like symphony of sound on electric piano. Zawinul sees the sen- suous backing as the link connecting the audience and the group. The listeners' impassioned response to those com- positions and the funkier "125th St. Congress" and "Boogie Woogie Waltz" was proof that the jazz-rock fusion is cor- rectly structured upon a recognition of percussion and rhythm as the foundation of music. s.m. Temptations Staple Singers URIS THEATRE, N.Y. - Rock and roll and the Broadway stage sounded like an interesting combination when the idea was formulated about two years ago. The Temptations and the Staple Singers, who opened a six -day stand here on Oct. 8, raised some questions as to the feasibility of such a combination and the results were dubious at best. For starters, the Uris sound system proved incapable of handling the or- chestrated sound of the groups, and at times distorted the sound so badly that the lyrics could have been sung in Esperanto for all the clarity that was af- forded them. Furthermore, at $12.50 a ticket, a group is limiting its audience and when they respond with a meager 50 minute set, they are beginning to stretch their credibility. Needless to say, the 50 minutes saw the group work out a smooth, well-oiled set which included over twenty numbers - most of them culled from their reser- voir of great hits including "My Girl," "Cloud Nine," "Get Ready," and "Papa Was A Rolling Stone." Witty dialogue, split second timing, and razor sharp choreography from the Motown group provides an appealing visual aspect while the traditional Temptation vocal harmonies are ever present even if only two original members remain. Still, an air of predictability prevailed while the group gave the audience everything they could have asked for while offering nothing more. The Staple Singers, who opened the show, served up a compelling blend of songs which ranged from their own Stax hit singles ("Come Go With Me," "Respect Yourself") to adaptations of songs like "Feel Like Making Love," and "I Honestly Love You." Mavis Staples has emerged as a major talent over the last couple of years and would have probably turned in a superior per- formance if the group was not pitted against a faulty amplification system. b.t. Mountain RADIO CITY MUSIC HALL, N.Y. - The arrival of Mountain on the rock scene in 1969 came about at a particularly oppor- tune time for the group. With memories of Cream still vivid in the minds of many, the group was considered the brightest hope to fill the void created by the demise of the trio. Though Mountain has never lived up to the expectations of many due to a somewhat erratic string of recordings (seven live sides on three consecutive albums not including the live West, Bruce, and Laing LP) and several personnel changes, Corky Laing, Felix Pappalardi, and Leslie West ap- peared confident at Radio City on Oct. 3 and seem poised to make up for lost time. With a filmed backdrop of an active volcano and a curtain of dry ice smoke, the group rose from the depths of the or- chestra pit and erupted with a frenzied version of "Whole Lotta Shakin' Going On" from their recent "Avalanche" album. Other numbers from the album included "Thumbsucker," "Back Where I Belong," and "Satisfaction" but it was the older material which managed to detonate the audience into a state of near hysteria as the windfall group ram- paged their way through "Mississippi Queen," "Theme From An Imaginary Western," and "Nantucket Sleighride." The latter, a twenty minute showcase for Leslie West, wore a bit thin, but he left no doubt as to his expertise which grows sharper with each successive visit to the city. b.t. 26 October 26, 1974

cash box,' news Capitol Makes Shifts In PR Dept. HOLLYWOOD - Dan Davis, director, creative service and press, Capitol Records has announced a realignment of the Capitol Records' press depart- ment. Remaining in her post as national publicity manager is Patti Wright whose duties include the coordination of national press activities in relation to Capitol artists. Ms. Wright will provide national tour support for the company's major acts. in addition to providing publicity material for national trade and consumer publications. She will report directly to Davis. Effective immediately, Michael Leh- man has been named western publicity manager. Lehman was formerly an as- sistant to the vice president of the enter- tainment division of Rogers & Cowan, in addition to his freelance work for periodicals. His duties include working closely with Capitol sales and promotion in order to coordinate all efforts on behalf of Capitol artists appearing in the western half of the United States. He will also be responsible for generating album and concert reviews, and maintaining liaisons with the trade magazines and west coast consumer publications. Leh- man replaces J.R. Young who has been appointed manager, press and editorial services. Both will report directly to Ms. Wright, and all will work out of the Capitol Tower in Hollywood. Lehman's counterpart in the New York offices of Capitol is Soozin Kazick, eastern publicity manager. She has been with Capitol Records two years after ser- ving as the director of publicity for Bud- dah Records and then as the director of publicity and promotion for Grossman/ - Glotzer, a managerial firm based in New York. Kazick's duties will be the same as Lehman's except her operations will be east coast oriented. Kathy Wagner, national publicity coor- dinator, remains at her post in the Hol- lywood offices, and her duties include the production of publicity material, in- cluding bios, photos, and clippings of Capitol artists. She also maintains Capitol's mailing list to the press throughout the entire country. She has been with Capitol Records for five years. Says Davis: "We are delighted with the latest changes within the department, and we feel that this new fully experi- enced staff will be able to coordinate not only with the trade and consumer press, but also with the various related depart- ments within the Capitol Tower itself. No longer will the press department be separate from the other departments, but will integrate its activities closely with sales, merchandising, promotion, and the art departments. Private Stock, GRT Tape Ties NEW YORK - Larry Uttal, president of Private Stock Records and Tom Bonetti, president of GRT Music Tapes, have an- nounced a long-term agreement covering the manufacture and distribution of all Private Stock tapes in the United States. Uttal called the arrangement, "a positive step forward in building the kind of solid marketing base from which Private Stock Records can grow. The merchandising of pre-recorded tape is a specialized area and one in which GRT excels. They are experts." "Larry Uttal has a proven affinity for product that sells," Bonetti commented. "We are proud to be associated with him and his exciting new label, Private Stock." Bill Levy To Polydor; Tops Creative Svcs NEW YORK - Bill Farr, president of Polydor, Inc., has announced the ap- pointment of Bill Levy to the newly created position of director of creative services. Levy, who held similar positions at MCA and Columbia - as well as most recently for Famous Music, will be responsible for all packaging, graphics and advertising for Polydor, MGM and their related labels, and will report directly to Farr. "It's rare," said Farr, "that you find a person with such a varied creative background, that also has a sense of merchandising and marketing. With an organization growing like ours, I feel most fortunate in acquiring the talents of Bill Levy." Jay Warner Joins Wes Farrell Org. NEW YORK - Jay Warner. a multi- faceted music industry figure who has been involved in composing, production and management, has been promoted to the position of East Coast Director of Professional Activities for the Wes Far- rell Organization's publishing com- panies. Since his arrival at the company, War- ner's accomplishments have included originating and compiling the publishing industry's first musical quiz promotion, "Musi -Quiz", placement of songs with a number of acts, including Dawn, Johnny Winter, The Shirelles, and the First Class. Prior to joining the Farrell Organization in 1973, Warner served as assistant to the president of S.A.S., Inc., management company for B.B. King and Gladys Knight and the Pips. From 1970-72 he served as General Manager of Record on Film Inc. and its affiliates, Exhibit Records and Hello Music Publishing. A record producer and song- writer, he has also written commercial and motion picture theme music. Feigen Resigns Columbia A&R HOLLYWOOD - Ted Feigen has an- nounced his resignation from Columbia Records as vice president A&R, West Coast, for the past 15 months. "I feel that my tenure at Columbia was an invaluable learning experience, and I have nothing but admiration for all of the people I was associated with there. My reasons for leaving were based only on significant policy differences." Feigen joined Columbia in April 1973 as assistant to the president, and moved to the West Coast in July to assume head of the A&R department. Sparago Named LP Sales Mgr. At Buddah Label NEW YORK - Lewis Merenstein, vice president and general manager of The Buddah Group, has announced that Ber- nie Sparago has been named national album sales manager. He will report directly to Merenstein. Initially, Sparago will be based out of Buddah's offices in Los Angeles. "Sparago has had enormous ex- perience in this area of the industry," commented Merenstein, "and has worked closely with distributors, one - stops, rack jobbers as well as national chains. He will be involved with the marketing of all Buddah product, and his entrance into the company signals a sig- nificant reorganization of our marketing procedures. Working closely with the promotion staff, Bernie's efforts will be a part of the company's commitment to highly energize our operations." Prior to his appointment at Buddah, Sparago was vice president and sales manager with Nehi Records in Califor- nia. Before joining Nehi, Sparago had worked for five years with United Artists Records as general manager for Sunset Records, then as sales manager of the Blue Note label, and finally as sales manager for all of UA's labels. Ms. Ylvisaker GRC Appoints Mazur Director Creative Services HOLLYWOOD - General Recording Corporation announced the appointment of Ruby Mazur to the position of director of creative services for GRC, Aware and Hotlanta labels. Mazur was named to the creative post by GRC president Michael Thevis and GRDC president Buz Wilburn. In joining the GRC record complex headquartered in Atlanta, Mazur brings an experienced background in both executive and creative capacities, en- compassing over eight years in the music industry. His previous affiliations include positions with ABC/Dunhill as executive art director; Paramount Records as art director, and, most re- cently, creative director of Ivy Hill Packaging. During his tenure in the industry, he has designed and overseen the com- pletion of many national campaigns in- cluding such top selling artists as the Rolling Stones, Jim Croce, Rufus, Dusty Springfield. the James Gang, B. B. King, Dave Mason, Billy Joel, Elton John, James Brown, the Four Tops, etc. Mazur is credited with designing the Rolling Stones (single sleeve) "mouth and tongue" logo, recognized worldwide as the rock group's trademark. His background also includes a year's work in England where he designed album covers, posters and media adver- tising campaigns for various labels in- cluding Columbia, Warner Brothers, Polydor and M.C.A. In 1971 his album cover concept for the group, Crowfoot, brought a nomination for the Grammy Award com- petition. Two years later he received the Society of Illustrators Award for his Cur- tis Mayfield cover design. In his new post as creative services director for GRC Records, Mazur will be completely responsible for all album cover designs, marketing aids, adver- tising, press and photographic services.
