Al Peckover Dies At 48 NEW YORK - Albert Peckover, vice president of Midland International Records, died suddenly of a heart attack Fri., Oct. 18 at thé age of 48. A veteran music man with a background in finance, administration and dealing with foreign based music publishing firms, Peckover had been af- filiated with Big 7 Music and was general manager of M.R.C. Music prior to joining Bob Reno, president of Midland, at the label's inception He leaves his wife Dorothy and two daughters Celia and Karen. The family is receiving people at 574 Winchester Avenue, Union, New Jersey. Lanzetta continued from 10 "Full utilization" is the catch phrase for Lipman's approach. In a recent television spot campaign for Jim Stafford's album, Lipman and Lanzetta personally con- tacted each participating store prior to airing the spots. "Dealer awareness is always crucial to the success of any cam- paign," says Lipman. "I wanted to make inventory checks with each store in each chain before we ran the spots. While I was at it I made sure in-store display material was up and that individual store management knew exactly where, when and how often Stafford spots would run in their market." After the campaign Lip- man and Lanzetta called back each store for a first-hand response. In Stafford's case the response was very favorable. Lipman is also finding ways to make "full utilization" work in radio and print campaigns. "There is an album on Bang Records by Paul Davis, called "Ride 'Em Cowboy." We decided to start with a full page ad in National Lampoon. To get the most out of this ad we dealer -tagged it region by region and worked out a program of in-store play and point of pur- chase material with each store when we placed the ad. When the ad ran, we called back each store to coordinate the program and then called back once more for store reports." For a Mac Davis campaign, Lipman decided that the best way to capitalize on Davis' summer television exposure was to feature the new album, but to include catalog wherever possible. The results brought Mac's current album to gold status and caused a tremendous surge in his catalog at the same time. A particularly gratifying experience for Macey Lipman Marketing is the Randy Edelman "Prime Cuts" album on 20th Century Records. "So far, we have been very successful and we've only done a small amount of trade magazine adver- tising to call this album to people's atten- tion." The bulk of the campaign has been direct contact on the dealer and radio levels. Posters designed like those seen in butcher shops were sent out as teasers by Lipman to 500 key dealers across the country. A few days later, this mailing was followed -up by the album and a few days after that 500 prime cut steaks were packed and shipped directly from Chicago. Winners of the market by market Randy Edelman "best window" contests were treated to steak dinners for two. Lipman believes that unusual promotions like this one can be effective in calling dealer attention to a particular project. "They're not right for everyone, but when they are right they can be very useful." The appointment of Tony Lanzetta will give Macey Lipman, "more time to deal directly and on a creative level with large accounts and racks ... to set up chain - wide promotions." for therecord POINTS WEST — Well, we saw Elvis emerge in the fabulous 50s, watched with dismay and then awe as the Beatles led the vanguard of the new rock of the 60s, and now, as 1974 draws to to close we will all soon be witness to the latest dance craze to sweep America and perhaps herald the arrival of the next BIG star, Tom Seufert. Who? Seufert is not to be trifled with my friend, nor his new Epic single “Casablanca Belly Roll." Complete with a snake charmer, shiek and belly dancer (who unfortunately wasn't either Little Egypt or Fatima), Tommy and producer Dave Kirshenbaum displayed the new product at our popular Sunset Blvd. offices before an astounded staff. What shook everybody up so much was the impact the disk had — I mean, Manu Dibango, look out! We've got a record here. It’s got Hollywood in a frenzy and when that happens, can Ames, Iowa be far behind. “The Phantom of the Paradise,” after a long series of legal delays, finally debuted in Hollywood (Oct. 31). With music by the film’s star, Paul Williams, the comedic horror flick runs the gamut of tongue in cheek industry one liners while providing an up- tempo story line of music and mayhem. Jeffrey Commanor and Keith Allison play cameo roles, while William Finley plays the elusive Phantom . . . Lee Radziwill was spotted at the Marvin Gaye concert at Radio City Music Hall in the Big Apple (NY) boogieing like mad with Robert Stigwood and Andy Warhol — soul is where you find it . . . Andy Kim is in L.A. working on the follow up single to his recent #1 smash, “Rock Me Gently.” Iron Butterfly will soar into Paramount studios to cut their first LP with MCA starting this week with all new material. The eyes and ears of the world will be tuned in for the results of those sessions to see if the magic of “Inna Gadda Da Vida” is still there. Check us in January for the results . . . David Gates, former lead singer of Bread will be Al Schlessinger’s special guest Nov. 3 at the Sherwood Oaks Experimental Col- lege. Apparently the series of lectures is going quite well and generating con- siderable interest. Where was it when I was slaving away in History 235 at Syracuse? Enjoyed a fascinating talk with veteran studio engineer Lee Kiefer, particularly his anecdotes about the various hits he’s tracked. Recently, while taking a break around 5:00 o’clock in the a.m. at a record plant session, Lee and the “artist" shared a couple of drinks to relax, then said artist solo'd into the studio, sat behind the keyboards and in one take knocked out a thing called “Nothing From Nothing Leaves Nothing.” Billy Preston, natch, and Lee says it was a bit of magic. “We never intended really doing anything, just kind of filling up time when Billy did his thing. First take, too, and his foot tappin’ against the piano gave us the guide for the background laid down later on. Tom Seufert (behind Fatima) Bellies Up You can hearthat foot tapping on the record,” Lee says, “if you listen closely.” Of the more than 1000 LPs I've reviewed this year (so far) for Cash Box, perhaps the most exciting and rewarding one has been “The Gregg Allman Tour” featuring Boyer & Talton along with a 24 piece orchestra backing Gregg. I’ve mentioned the cuts I dig in the album review section, but I feel compelled to praise Gregg for going out on his own not only to tour, but to make (with the invaluable assistance of Johnny Sandlin) such a fine record. In my estimation it rivals “Live Rhymin' ” for “in studio" quality which is remarkable considering the much funkier music that’s dealt with on this two record set. Most bands and probably individuals would have folded up after sustaining losses like Gregg did with the death of his brother Duane and bassist Berry Oakley, but Gregg Allman’s a proud man and should be singled out for extraordinary merit and praise for carrying a tremendous load on his shoulders and doing it with such soul and dignity. Sure, the Stones are greatest, but Gregg, my hat’s off to you and I’m sure all the folks at Capricorn and in Macon are every bit as proud as I am of this superb new LP. Dave Loggins, while doing a series of college dates with Jim Stafford became friendly with the "Spiders and Snakes” man and the two have decided to collaborate on a number of tunes and hopefully an LP. Which label, Epic or MGM, will get it is still up in the air, but it sounds like a great team . . . Booker T. Jones has his new band ready and will be out on the road in November playing some oldies like “Green Onions” and some of his great new material culled from his “Evergreen” LP released two weeks ago. Booker’s fantastic and his professionalism never gets in the way of his idealism though the two do go nicely together . . . One of Epic’s hot new acts, Honk, as a part of its upcoming tour, will open for Poco and Loggins & Messina, Dec. 14 in L.A. I always did believe in the sink or swim principal myself. The late Wes Montgomery’s brother, Monk, who is currently touring Africa, intends to start a “bring jazz to Las Vegas” campaign when he gets back. Hope it works . . . Donovan’s first west coast dates in over two years will take place in Berkeley Dec. 8, Santa Monica Civic (11) and San Diego (12) . . . Dan Fogelberg recently sold out six consecutive dates at Denver’s Ebbets Field . . . all that’sjazz Clear Skies Ahead For Weather Report picksoftheweek The music of Weather Report, like its meteorological namesake, is a uniquely sub-, tie combination of different sounds, moods, and emotional attitudes. The com- positions utilize elements from different musical mediums. The notes, like clouds in a storm, contest and confirm each other. In isolation, each note, each measure, and each composition, in fact, appears remotely detached as if suspended in mid-air. Yet, the sensitive organization of the musicians, based as it is upon an uncanny under- standing of each player's proficiency and emotional affectibility, energizes the music and gives the pieces their meaning. Each note, each composition, however, like the daily passage of climatic elements, can only be understood after the sun has set and the end has been revealed. Joe Zawinul is one of the energetic leaders of the group. Yet, as Zawinul said, the title of “leader” is a misnomer. “The total sound is the product of five unique musicians. Each of us is very sensitive to the other's feelings. We all take a humble at- titude towards the other musicians. Our creative philosophies fit together very well. All the musicians are great improvisors and a creator is always looking for fellow creators, rather than followers. Everyone has an equal voice and the same impor- tance." The present members of the group — Zawinul, Wayne Shorter, Dorn Urn Romao, Darryl Brown and Alphonso Johnson — put together three improvisational lines to produce the total sound. Supporting the melodic excursions is a strong and vibrant wall of rhythm. Zawinul said that “rhythm is life, there’s nothing without rhythm. Only through it can you communicate life. Dorn on percussion and Darryl on drums bring the music closest to the people. Their backing exudes warmth and yields a strong rap- port with the audience.” Zawinul on keyboards and Shorter on tenor and soprano sax are the primary soloists. Yet Al Johnson on bass provides a smooth harmonic undercurrent that ac- cents the lead lines and that can also articulate the difficult melodies without a hitch. The total sound is electic, borrowing elements from rock, “cool” jazz, and the genius that is Ornette Coleman. Each musician is recognized as a distinct musical individual, who may take the music in the direction he feels it is best defined. "We always solo, but we never solo,” Zawinul said. “Whatever you play, even if it is accompanied, is JAZZ: IT’S THE ESSENCE THAT COUNTS always a solo. Though everyone is playing away from each other and everything is ap- proached soloistically, it is never completely individualistic, because the solos fit together. One could play background, but it isn’t really just background, dig?” The band was formed in the late ’60’s. Zawinul and Shorter were both in Washing- ton during the early part of the decade, Zawinul playing with Cannonball Adderly and Shorter with Art Blakey. Zawinul related that “Wayne is such a great writer and musician. We used to play and talk music all night long.” When Shorter joined Miles Davis' band, the two separated. However, their musical ideas were developing in similar directions: a relaxed, free-form style of improvisation based upon strong melodies. They both played with Miles on “In A Silent Way,” “Bitches Brew,” and “Nefertiti." Zawinul, in fact, wrote many of the key pieces for the group, including “In A Silent Way,” which was, in many ways, the precursor of the present jazz-rock fusion. "After Wayne left Miles and I went back to Cannonball, it was kind of natural that we’d eventually get together. We hooked up with Miroslav Vitous, who had similar ideas. He, too, is a great improvisor. We added Airto on percussion and Alphonso Mouzon on drums. No one dominated the other, we just had a good deal of reciprocity. " In 1971, the first album, “Weather Report,” was released to unanimous critical ac- claim. Since that time, the group has released three additional albums on Columbia (they are presently in the studio cutting their fifth album). Except for Darryl Brown, the present personnel is featured on the latest record, “Mysterious Traveller.” It may seem ironic that the early albums have begun to sell only as a result of “Traveller’s” commercial success. However, Zawinul reflected, “It takes time, because our music can only be understood retrospectively, like history. Even when we compose, there is a lapse of time between the actual writing and the time you can understand it. Each part only makes sense in light of the whole. The albums will do better as the people begin to appreciate them. The last album has the most strength, bottom, and, I think, the most emotional sensitivity. The music is more secure and less fragile. People can really get off on it.” A band as philosophically and musically unified as Weather Report can remain coherent even as the relaxed, free-form improvisation suggests an absence of musical structure. The emotional respect each musician has for the others sensitizes the music and gives Weather Report its unique power. Zawinul smiled and said, “Our music is always fresh, we feel like we haven’t even started. When we get started on the material we now have, when we can really get it down, it’s going to be some trip!” Steven marks THE BADDEST HUBBARD - Freddie Hubbard - CTI 6047 S An anthology of Hubbard’s work at CTI. The first chorus in "First Lights" shows Hubbard at his best as his melodic variation on the theme creates a suggestive textual blend with Ron Car- ter's bass. Echoes of Miles dance on the album's most interesting piece, “Red Clay,” as Hubbard plays notes devoid of ornamentation in a relaxed style that still manages a few rhythmic surprises. The accents in it are often shifted to the even beats. Of interest, also, is his dialogue with Her- bie Hancock on piano. The all-star personnel in- cludes Keith Jarrett (piano), Billy Cobham (drums), and George Benson (guitar). IN MEMORIAM - The Modern Jazz Quartet - Lit- tle David 0698 The final album by the “third stream” in- novators who have been together for 23 years. "In Memoriam’s Second Movement,” is a tribute to some of the world's greatest musicians, in- cluding Schoenberg, Dolphy, Parker and Lester Young. The MJQ explores the motif announced by the orchestra in the third chorus. The perfor- mance is based on Parker’s innovative use of ac- cents and unstated notes that the listener yearns to fill in. The third riff of “Jazz Ostinado” is an in- teresting rewrite of a piece originally penned for Eric Dolphy. Milt Jackson on vibraphone sug- gests here the melodic textures of Ornette Coleman. NO ANSWER — Michael Mantler — Watt/2 Michael Mantler has set Samuel Beckett’s “How It Is” to music. The album captures the confusion that is the meaning through repetitive piano phrases accented by discordant blasts that signify Beckett’s two voices. The trumpet on Side A, "Part 3," is a brilliant example of the voice that speaks yet receives no answer. The two sides are variations on a similar theme. The second is somewhat more lyrical than the first. Carla Bley is on piano, clavinet, and organs. Don Cherry plays trumpet and Jack Bruce voices the Beckett narration and plays the bass. FEEL - George Duke - BASF M C 25355 George Duke’s second solo album for BASF. A member of the Mother’s of Invention, Duke’s music reflects many of the group’s charac- teristics: short phrases of percussion-like notes and simultaneous voicings of the melody line by differently pitched instruments. Duke most ef- fectively utilizes the latter technique in “Funny Funk" by overlapping statements by his piano and synthesizer. "The Once Over” is an in- teresting implementation of electronics. The percussion instruments take the lead and are backed by Duke's electric piano. Ndugu and Airto are on percussion, an unnamed Mother Ob- dewl’X on guitar, John Heard on bass and Flora Pu rim vocals. JUST ONE OF THOSE THINGS - Stephane Grap- pelli — Black Lion 211 Grappelli, here heard live at the Montreux Jazz Festival of 1973, re-interprets many old up- tempo standards and ballads. He adds certain lit- tle twists which keep them interesting. The in- troduction and the first chorus on "More” are subtle shifts in harmony and rhythm. On Cole Porter’s “Just One of Those Things," the unex- pected is struck as the piano chorus jumps out of the medium fast tempo into a more ballad-like 4. “Honeysuckle Rose's" combines stop-chords with Grappelli’s linesflying over the accom- paniment. Grappelli is on violin, Marc Hemmler piano. Jack Sewing bass, and Daniel Humair drums. for the record POINTS WEST - Well, we saw Elvis emerge in the fabulous 50s, watched with dismay and then awe as the Beatles led the vanguard of the new rock of the 60s, and now, as 1974 draws to to close we will all soon be witness to the latest dance craze to sweep America and perhaps herald the arrival of the next BIG star, Tom Seufert. Who? Seufert is not to be trifled with my friend, nor his new Epic single "Casablanca Belly Roll." Complete with a snake charmer, shiek and belly dancer (who unfortunately wasn't either Little Egypt or Fatima), Tommy and producer Dave Kirshenbaum displayed the new product at our popular Sunset Blvd. offices before an astounded staff. What shook everybody up so much was the impact the disk had - I mean, Manu Dibango, look out! We've got a record here. It's got Hollywood in a frenzy and when that happens, can Ames, Iowa be far behind. "The Phantom of the Paradise," after a long series of legal delays, finally debuted in Hollywood (Oct. 31). With music by the film's star, Paul Williams, the comedic horror flick runs the gamut of tongue in cheek industry one liners while providing an up - tempo story line of music and mayhem. Jeffrey Commanor and Keith Allison play cameo roles, while William Finley plays the elusive Phantom ... Lee Radziwill was spotted at the Marvin Gaye concert at Radio City Music Hall in the Big Apple (NY) boogieing like mad with Robert Stigwood and Andy Warhol - soul is where you find it ... Andy Kim is in L.A. working on the follow up single to his recent #1 smash, "Rock Me Gently." Iron Butterfly will soar into Paramount studios to cut their first LP with MCA starting this week with all new material. The eyes and ears of the world will be tuned in for the results of those sessions to see if the magic of "Inna Gadda Da Vida" is still there. Check us in January for the results ... David Gates, former lead singer of Bread will be Al Schlessinger's special guest Nov. 3 at the Sherwood Oaks Experimental Col- lege. Apparently the series of lectures is going quite well and generating con- siderable interest. Where was it when I was slaving away in History 235 at Syracuse? Enjoyed a fascinating talk with veteran studio engineer Lee Kiefer, particularly his anecdotes about the various hits he's tracked. Recently, while taking a break around 5:00 o'clock in the a.m. at a record plant session, Lee and the "artist" shared a couple of drinks to relax, then said artist solo'd into the studio, sat behind the keyboards and in one take knocked out a thing called "Nothing From Nothing Leaves Nothing." Billy Preston, natch, and Lee says it was a bit of magic. "We never intended really doing anything, just kind of filling up time when Billy did his thing. First take, too, and his foot tappin' against the piano gave us the guide for the background laid down later on. Tom Seutert (behind Fatima) Bellies Up You can hear that foot tapping on the record," Lee says, "if you listen closely." Of the more than 1000 LPs I've reviewed this year (so far) for Cash Box, perhaps the most exciting and rewarding one has been "The Gregg Allman Tour" featuring Boyer & Talton along with a 24 piece orchestra backing Gregg. I've mentioned the cuts I dig in the album review section, but I feel compelled to praise Gregg for going out on his own not only to tour, but to make (with the invaluable assistance of Johnny Sandlin) such a fine record. In my estimation it rivals "Live Rhymin' " for "in studio" quality which is remarkable considering the much funkier music that's dealt with on this two record set. Most bands and probably individuals would have folded up after sustaining losses like Gregg did with the death of his brother Duane and bassist Berry Oakley, but Gregg Allman's a proud man and should be singled out for extraordinary merit and praise for carrying a tremendous load on his shoulders and doing it with such soul and dignity. Sure, the Stones are greatest, but Gregg, my hat's off to you and I'm sure all the folks at Capricorn and in Macon are every bit as proud as I am of this superb new LP. Dave Loggins, while doing a series of college dates with Jim Stafford became friendly with the "Spiders and Snakes" man and the two have decided to collaborate on a number of tunes and hopefully an LP. Which label, Epic or MGM, will get it is still up in the air, but it sounds like a great team ... Booker T. Jones has his new band ready and will be out on the road in November playing some oldies like "Green Onions" and some of his great new material culled from his "Evergreen" LP released two weeks ago. Booker's fantastic and his professionalism never gets in the way of his idealism though the two do go nicely together ... One of Epic's hot new acts, Honk, as a part of its upcoming tour, will open for Poco and Loggins & Messina, Dec. 14 in L.A. I always did believe in the sink or swim principal myself. The late Wes Montgomery's brother, Monk, who is currently touring Africa, intends to start a "bring jazz to Las Vegas" campaign when he gets back. Hope it works ... Donovan's first west coast dates in over two years will take place in Berkeley Dec. 8, Santa Monica Civic (11) and San Diego (12) ... all that's jazz Clear Skies Ahead For Weather Report The music of Weather Report, like its meteorological namesake, is a uniquely sub tle combination of different sounds, moods, and emotional attitudes. The com- positions utilize elements from different musical mediums. The notes, like clouds in a storm, contest and confirm each other. In isolation, each note, each measure, and each composition, in fact, appears remotely detached as if suspended in mid-air. Yet, the sensitive organization of the musicians, based as it is upon an uncanny under- standing of each player's proficiency and emotional affectibility, energizes the music and gives the pieces their meaning. Each note, each composition, however, like the daily passage of climatic elements, can only be understood after the sun has set and the end has been revealed. Joe Zawinul is one of the energetic leaders of the group. Yet, as Zawinul said, the title of "leader" is a misnomer. "The total sound is the product of five unique musicians. Each of us is very sensitive to the other's feelings. We all take a humble at- titude towards the other musicians. Our creative philosophies fit together very well. All the musicians are great improvisors and a creator is always looking for fellow creators, rather than followers. Everyone has an equal voice and the same impor- tance." The present members of the group - Zawinul, Wayne Shorter, Dom Um Romao, Darryl Brown and Alphonso Johnson - put together three improvisational lines to produce the total sound. Supporting the melodic excursions is a strong and vibrant wall of rhythm. Zawinul said that "rhythm is life, there's nothing without rhythm. Only through it can you communicate life. Dom on percussion and Darryl on drums bring the music closest to the people. Their backing exudes warmth and yields a strong rap- port with the audience." Zawinul on keyboards and Shorter on tenor and soprano sax are the primary soloists. Yet Al Johnson on bass provides a smooth harmonic undercurrent that ac- cents the lead lines and that can also articulate the difficult melodies without a hitch. The total sound is electic, borrowing elements from rock, "cool" jazz, and the genius that is Omette Coleman. Each musician is recognized as a distinct musical individual, who may take the music in the direction he feels it is best defined. "We always solo, but we never solo," Zawinul said. "Whatever you play, even if it is accompanied, is JAZZ: IT'S THE ESSENCE THAT COUNTS always a solo. Though everyone is playing away from each other and everything is ap- proached soloistically, it is never completely individualistic, because the solos fit together. One could play background, but it isn't really jusfbackground, dig?" The band was formed in the late '60's. Zawinul and Shorter were both in Washing- ton during the early part of the decade, Zawinul playing with Cannonball Adderly and Shorter with Art Blakey. Zawinul related that "Wayne is such a great writer and musician. We used to play and talk music all night long." When Shorter joined Miles Davis' band, the two separated. However, their musical ideas were developing in similar directions: a relaxed, free -form style of improvisation based upon strong melodies. They both played with Miles on "In A Silent Way," "Bitches Brew," and "Nefertiti." Zawinul, in fact, wrote many of the key pieces for the group, including "In A Silent Way," which was, in many ways, the precursor of the present jazz-rock fusion. "After Wayne left Miles and I went back to Cannonball, it was kind of natural that we'd eventually get together. We hooked up with Miroslav Vitous, who had similar ideas. He, too, is a great improvisor. We added Airto on percussion and Alphonso Mouzon on drums. No one dominated the other, we just had a good deal of reciprocity." In 1971, the first album, "Weather Report," was released to unanimous critical ac- claim. Since that time, the group has released three additional albums on Columbia (they are presently in the studio cutting their fifth album). Except for Darryl Brown, the present personnel is featured on the latest record, "Mysterious Traveller." It may seem ironic that the early albums have begun to sell only as a result of "Traveller's" commercial success. However, Zawinul reflected, "It takes time, because our music can only be understood retrospectively, like history. Even when we compose, there is a lapse of time between the actual writing and the time you can understand it. Each part only makes sense in light of the whole. The albums will do better as the people begin to appreciate them. The last album has the most strength, bottom, and, I think, the most emotional sensitivity. The music is more secure and less fragile. People can really get off on it." A band as philosophically and musically unified as Weather Report can remain coherent even as the relaxed, free -form improvisation suggests an absence of musical structure. The emotional respect each musician has for the others sensitizes the music and gives Weather Report its unique power. Zawinul smiled and said, "Our music is always fresh, we feel like we haven't even started. When we get started on the material we now have, when we can really get it down, it's going to be some trip!" The first chorus in "First Lights" shows Hubbard at his best as his melodic variation on the theme creates a suggestive textual blend with Ron Gar- t'er's bass. Echoes of Miles dance on the album's most interesting piece, "Red Clay," as Hubbard plays notes devoid of ornamentation in a relaxed style that still manages a few rhythmic surprises. The accents in it are often shifted to the even beats. Of interest, also, is his dialogue with Her- bie Hancock on piano. The all-star personnel in- cludes Keith Jarrett (piano), Billy Cobham (drums), and George Benson (guitar). IN MEMORIAM - The Modern Jazz Quartet - Lit- tle David 0698 The final album by the "third stream" in- novators who have been together for 23 years. "In Memoriam's Second Movement," is a tribute to some of the world's greatest musicians, in- cluding Schoenberg, Dolphy, Parker and Lester Young. The MJQ explores the motif announced by the orchestra in the third chorus. The perfor- mance is based on Parker's innovative use of ac- cents and unstated notes that the listener yearns to fill in. The third riff of "Jazz Ostinado" is an in- teresting rewrite of a piece originally penned for Eric Dolphy. Milt Jackson on vibraphone sug- gests here the melodic textures of Omette Coleman. NO ANSWER - Michael Mantler - Watt/2 Michael Mantler has set Samuel Beckett's "How It Is" to music. The album captures the confusion that is the meaning through repetitive piano phrases accented by discordant blasts that signify Beckett's two voices. The trumpet on Side A, "Part 3," is a brilliant example of the voice that speaks yet receives no answer. The two sides are variations on a similar theme. The second is somewhat more lyrical than the first. Carla Bley is on piano, clavinet, and organs. Don Cherry plays trumpet and Jack Bruce voices the Beckett narration and plays the bass. FEEL - George Duke - BASF M C 25355 George Duke's second solo album for BASF. A member of the Mother's of Invention, Duke's music reflects many of the group's charac- teristics: short phrases of percussion -like notes and simultaneous voicings of the melody line by differently pitched instruments. Duke most ef- fectively utilizes the latter technique in "Funny Funk" by overlapping statements by his piano and synthesizer. "The Once Over" is an in- teresting implementation of electronics. The percussion instruments take the lead and are backed by Duke's electric piano. Ndugu and Airto are on percussion, an unnamed Mother Ob- dewl'X on guitar, John Heard on bass and Flora Purim vocals. JUST ONE OF THOSE THINGS - Stephan Grap- pelli - Black Lion 211 Grappelli, here heard live at the Montreux Jazz Festival of 1973, re -interprets many old up - tempo standards and ballads. He adds certain lit- tle twists which keep them interesting. The in- troduction and the first chorus on "More" are subtle shifts in harmony and rhythm. On Cole Porter's "Just One of Those Things," the unex- pected is struck as the piano chorus jumps out of the medium fast tempo into a more ballad -like 4. "Honeysuckle Rose's" combines stop -chords with Grappelli's linesflying over the accom- paniment. Grappelli is on violin, Marc Hemmler piano, Jack Sewing bass, and Daniel Humair drums. The Jazz Composers Orchestra Association The problems of creating a small in- dependent record label devoted to quality music are well-known. Limited by moderate audience interest and insuf- ficient funds for promotion, the indies are often overpowered by the facilities of the large conglomerates. One indepen- dent organization that has managed to succeed in spite of generally hard economic times and the pressures from more secure firms is the Jazz Composers Orchestra Association. Originally devoted to giving free public concerts and workshops for com- posers interested in writing extended works for large jazz orchestra, the non- profit JCOA has formed a record label which has released three major pieces stemming from those workshops: Michael Mantler's "The Jazz Composer's Orchestra," Carla Bley's "Escalator Over The Hill," and Don Cherry's "Relativity Suite." From the onset, JCOA sought to distribute their own records. The music is one of the primary examples of jazz' avant-garde and its creative cutting - edge. Though the initial number of buyers was small, the listening population grew at a rapid rate. As a result, the New Music Distribution Ser- vice was created and within two years, the service has taken on consignment and resold some 80,000 LP's of imported and domestic jazz work. NMDS has recently added 40 albums on 23 labels to the catalogue, bringing the total listings to 275 albums on 67 musician operated companies. The music handled by the Association. now extends beyond the jazz field. Ethnic music and modern "classics" are among the varied mediums distributed. The only qualification the JCOA makes in accepting new records is that the recordings be examples of "the new music." Pop and folk are not handled because the organization believes that mass -market music is better handled by commercial distributors. Even though the NMDS has suc- ceeded in the past, the service is finding it difficult to continue its progress within the tighter economic structure. The profits from JCOA Records, in fact, are turned into the main source of expen- ditures for the distribution service. JCOA is trying to advertise NMDS' records through an internal promotion campaign. The second edition of "Corrective News Distribution," a service newsletter, is being prepared by Carla Bley. Ad- ditionally, a press release on the 40 new albums acquired for distribution is being sent to all the standard sales outlets. Bill Ewell of JCOA explained the sim- ple economics of the Association. Both the JCOA and NMDS are non-profit organizations, he said, and added that the former receives money from the New York State Council of the Arts for their workshops. All other activities, such as distribution and pressing of the records, are funded through private grants and profits from the first three JCOA albums, he remarked. Actively engaged in the difficult process of raising money in a depressed market, the JCOA has recently received a grant from "The Martha Baird Rockefeller Fund for Music." The money has been allocated for the expansion and development of the distribution service, Ewell explained. He said that a person was added to the staff to boost new ac- counts and, hopefully, increase the fundings. If, he emphasized, the JCOA had a person to handle the business af- fairs, then they could release another in- dividual for distribution. The cash flow from NMDS' more established com- panies - JCOA, Watt, Strata -East, CRI and PM Records - is a solid source of in- come for day to day activities, Ewell said. The problem for all independent com- panies, Ewell concluded, is that more time is needed for expansion. However, tight money limits the personnel who can be released for the most important ac- tivity: distribution, he said. steven marks STANLEY'S THE MAN - Stanley Turren - tine is shown surrounded by fans and autographing copies of his first Fantasy album, "Pieces Of Dreams," during an engagement at Chicago's Jazz Showcase. BELL INKS GIL SCOTT -HERON - Gil Scott -Heron has been signea to the Bell group this week, announced Clive Davis, the label's president. Gil Scott -Heron, only 25, is an accomplished poet and songwriter. His first two albums, on Flying Dutchman, included "Home Is Where The Hatred Is," "Lady Day And John Coltrane," and "The Revolution Will Not Be Televised," which has become a black rallying cry. More recently, Scott -Heron's album "Winter In America," was propelled by the single, "The Bottle." all that's jazz picks of the week CIRCLE/PARIS - CONCERT - Anthony Brax- ton, Chick Corea, David Holland, and Barry Alt- schul - ECM 1018/19 ST One of the best performed ad most cohesive jazz albums recently released. Though a com- bination of solos and duets for the most part, the album somehow remains extremely unified. It demands serious listening, but the enjoyment is well worth the effort. On Wayne Shorter's "Nefertiti," Corea opens the piece with a har- monic introduction. Then both he and Braxton develope changes to the popular melody, enough snatches of which are present to keep the listener oriented. Dave Holland's bass solo is a rhythmic tour de force, consisting of multi - octave leaps and changes of rhythm. SORCERY - Jack DeJonette - Prestige P10081 Jack DeJonette's third album as a leader. "Sor- cery" is a combination of solos based upon a highly rhythmic theme first announced by Dave Holland's bass and then repeated at various in- tervals throughout the piece. John Abercrom- bie's guitar chorus reminds one of the guitar work done in the late '60's by the Jazz Com- posers Orchestra. Of interest, too, is Bennie Maupin's bass clarinet solo, which seems to tran- scend the limits of the instrument's range. "Reverend King Suite" is an interesting com- bination of sounds and textures reminiscent of Carla Bley's "Tong Funeral." BLACK BEINGS - Frank Lowe - ESP 3013 A devotional album, in John Coltrane's sense of the word, dedicated to the "musicians who gave their all." Side A consists of Lowe's exten- sive "In Trane's Name." The piece is an emotional powerhouse. The free -blowing music typical of Coltrane's middle -to -later works (see "Ascension") is based upon a combination of solos and dialogues by Lowe on tenor sax and Joseph Jarman of the Art Ensemble of Chicago on sop and alto sax. The sax dialogues utilize the two instruments Coltrane made his own, yet ex- tend the bounds of his performances. The piece does not exist in time, but explodes as a spatial wonder. THE PHIL WOODS QUARTET - Phil Woods - Testament T-4402 Phil Woods' sound is an interesting synsthesis of music's development from the late '40's to the present. At times, it is a tightly structured com- bination of two melody lines emphasizing rhyth- mic and harmonic variation (on "Yesterdays," for instance, though Woods occasionally lapses into some perfunctory arpeggio scales). At other times, the music works a freer form. Time sig- natures are varied, electronics are utilized, and choruses only appear connected to the melody by the requirements of intervallic logic (see "Nefertiti" and "Riot"). IT COULD ONLY HAPPEN WITH YOU - Duke Pearson - Blue Note - LA 3176 A combination of Latin rhythms and sensuous bossa nova jazz. Flora Purim's vocals, especially on "It Could Only Happen," and "Stormy," are husky and earthy, and possess a remarkable range and timbre. Note the interaction of her voice and the tenor sax on "Round and Round." Pearson's piano solo during the first paraphrase of "Emily" is a controlled manipulation of the main theme which explores some interesting rhythmic changes before depositing the listener back in the lap of the melody. LEONARD FEATHER PRESENTS THE EN- CYCLOPEDIA OF JAZZ, VOL. 5 - MCA 2-4063 A musical counterpart of "The Encyclopedia of Jazz" covering the period of the '50's. The various sounds and textures include post -bop developments, the big band (Doc Severinson is heard on a cut with Sal Salvador's band) and "cool" jazz. The avant-garde is noticeable by their absence. Tony Scott and The All -Stars "Lester Leaps On" revolves around the bass work of Oscar Pettiford. George Wallington's guitar solo suggests the direction later guitarists will take. Coleman Hawkins' variation of "Body and Soul" originally recorded in 1939 is a rhap- sodic joy to behold. 28 November 16, 1974

cash box R&D news report r&b ingredients Barry White announced the addition of a creative department to his music produc- tion companies, and the appointment of Bernie Butler to head up the newly formed operation. Operating under the umbrella of Barr-Larr Inc., the primary purpose of the creative department under the direction of Mr. Butler, will be to handle the operations and merchandise of the newly formed "Maestro Barry White Fan Club," that launches its initial membership drive and kick-off campaign during the month of November. Barry White has also contracted the services of Warren Lanier Enterprises Public Relations Agency, to work hand in hand with Bernie Butler, to publicize and promote the special projects associated with Barry Whites production companies and the creative department. Barry, Love Unlimited, and the Love Unlimited Orchestra left Los Angeles Nov. 4 for a month long concert tour that will cover the East Coast in- cluding dates at New York's Felt Forum, the New Haven Coliseum and the Toledo Sports Arena. Barry White, Love Unlimited and the Love Unlimited Orchestra will also be making a guest appearance on "The Midnight Special" on Friday, Nov. 15. Mayfield Starts New LP While `Mimi' Waits HOLLYWOOD - Curtis Mayfield, his starring role in the motion picture "Mimi" pushed back until next spring, is now writing material for his next album, a fol- low-up to "Sweet Exorcist." The Curtom Records star was to have also written the score for "Mimi," but Columbia Pictures pushed back the star- ting date until early 1975. Film will be shot in New Orleans, as an updated remake of the opera "La Boheme." Mayfield is working out of the Curtom studios in Chicago, according to executive Mary Stuart. °'Jays In Studio Completing Album HOLLYWOOD - Philadelphia Inter- national recording stars the O'Jays, com- posed of Eddie Levert, Walter Williams, and William Powell, are in the process of completing their newest LP tentatively titled "The Law." The album, which is scheduled for release at the beginning of the year, is produced by Gamble and Huff and ar- ranged by Bobby Martin. The LP is being recorded at the Sigma Sound Studios in Philadelphia, with the MFSB Orchestra accompanying the O'Jays. Tunes featured on the album include "Just Don't Seem To Be My Day," "Just Let Me Love You," and "What Am I Waiting For" by Bunny Sigler, who penned such O'Jay songs as "Sunshine" and "When The World's At Peace." Pro- ducers Gamble and Huff wrote "Can't Nobody Break Us Up," "The Rich Get Richer and The Poor Get Poorer," "How Time Flies," and "Living In The Boun- daries Of The Law" (the title tune) for the album. The new LP release will mark the fifth collaboration of the O'Jays with the Gam- ble and Huff producing team. "Live In London," the O'Jays' current album release, has just been certified gold, signifying album sales have reached the one million dollar mark. The trio is currently rehearsing for their headline appearance at the famed Waldorf-Astoria Hotel's Empire Room in New York City. "Zaire '74" Crew Finishes Filming HOLLYWOOD - Eight camera crews have concluded filming for "Zaire '74," which includes a music festival that features such performers as the Pointer Sisters, the Crusaders, Hugh Masekela, James Brown, B. B. King and many others. In addition to the music festival, the camera crews also shot 19 hours of film on the country of Zaire, and the events leading to the championship fight be- tween Muhammad Ali and George Fore- man. Leon Gast is in charge of editing for the film, which will be released early in 1975. Crusaders & Pointers Set For Japan Tour HOLLYWOOD - Two top American acts, The Crusaders and the Pointer Sisters, have been signed to perform in Japan for the first time. They will tour that country briefly as of mid -November. The instrumental group and the vocal group will give a joint recital on Nov. 15 at Nakano Sun Plaza Hall, according to UOP, which is promoting the show. The Crusaders last concert was at the Zaire Festival, while the Pointers headlined a recent European concert tour, then performed at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville. Latest album for The Crusaders is "Southern Comfort," distributed by ABC Records. Sister Sledge Signs HHV HOLLYWOOD - Sister Sledge has signed for exclusive worldwide publicity and public relations with Hecht Harman Vukas Creative Communications, Inc. Consisting of four young girls, Sister Sledge is the only girl group currently signed with Atlantic Records. Their first single, "Love Don't You Go Through No Changes," set for a Nov. 1 release, was arranged by Bert Decoteaux and produced by Tony Sylvester. HOT SOUL EXPLOSION - A pre- planning meeting for the Atlantic/ATCO "soul explosion" campaign involving 10 of Atlantic's artists, and also a pre - strategy meeting on Gene Page's new LP "Hot City" were held in New York recently. Attending the meeting were, from left to right: Bill Staton (east coast special projects,) Sonny Woods (regional mgr. -south), Clarence Bullard (local NY promotion), Gary Johnson (regional mgr. -east coast), Henry Allen (vice- president for R&B product), Paul John- son (national promotion director for R&B), Tommy Phillips (west coast manager-R&B), Eddie Holland (regional mgr. -mid -west), and Alan Lott (director of album product.) FOR ART'S SAKE - Shown at the very first Blue Note Records "Jazz for Art's Sake" mini -concert held at Alan McKen- zie-Watson's photo studio in Los Angeles are (from left) Eddie Levine, head of promotion for Blue Note; Bobby Hut- cherson, who appeared at the Art's Sake concert; George Butler, general manager for the UA -distributed jazz label; famed jazz journalist Leonard Feather, who led a discussion of the music and jazz in general after the con- cert; and producer Keg Johnson, co- producer of Gene Harris' recent Blue Note album "Astralsignal." COOL WATERS - Everybody's all smiles as Waters signs with Blue Note Records, the first vocal group ever signed to the prestigious 35 -year -old jazz label. Hancock's "Death Wish" Released HOLLYWOOD - Herbie Hancock's soundtrack album for the film "Death Wish" has been released by Columbia Records, though the picture has been out for some time. David Rubinson produced the record. Hancock's latest album on Columbia is his "Thrust" LP, a follow-up to his big - selling "Headhunters" record. 32 November 16, 1974

POSTMASTER -Send form 3579 to CASH BOX, 119 West 5710 cr uew v,,.I, u v 101110 cash h box editorial `Greatest Hits' As Great Sellers In these days of spiralling costs, stagnation, and recession, records remain one of the cheapest and most accessible forms of entertainment, making them the perfect gifts for the holiday buying season. The "Greatest Hits" album, traditionally a popular gift giving item, once again looks to be one of the approaches labels will be keying on for strong sales. These albums, which are usually in the form of studio or "live" versions of previously released material, have also proven helpful in stimulating the sales of artists' catalogs. Released in just the last two weeks have been live recordings by Gregg Allman, David Bowie, the Four Tops, Fairport Convention, the Marshall Tucker Band, Mott the Hoople, and Frank Sinatra - all containing previously released material. "Greatest Hits" albums of studio material have been marketed by groups and artists like Elton John, the Moody Blues, the Partridge Family, Jan and Dean, Bobby Womack, B.J. Thomas, Dionne Warwick, Bobby Goldsboro and Billy "Crash" Craddock. This is in addition to studio or live "Greatest Hits" albums which are already charted by the Beach Boys ("Endless Summer") and Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young (both former #1 LPs on the Cash Box charts), Jim Croce, the Pointer Sisters, Emerson, Lake and Palmer, the O'Jays, Santana, Bread, Marvin Gaye, Rory Gallagher, John Denver, Nitty Gritty Dirt Band, Duane Allman, and Alice Cooper. The trend has apparently also carried over to the jazz field as evidenced by CTI Records' "Baddest" series which comprises previously released material culled from albums by Stanley Turrentine and Freddie Hubbard. ABC has released "John Coltrane - The Greatest Years Vol. III" and has added to the "Impulse Years" series, two record sets featuring material by Elvin Jones, Milt Jackson, and Duke Ellington. With "live" albums promised by artists like Joni Mitchell, Cat Stevens, Argent, and Brian Auger, and "Greatest Hits" collections by Andy Kim, the Turtles, Rick Nelson, the Ventures, Paul Anka, the Hollies, and Jay and the Americans due for release imminently, all indications point to another holiday season of good sales catalyzed by the strength of the "Greatest Hits" LP. THE TURTLES' GREATEST HITS - The Turtles - Sire SASH - 3703-2 Subtitled "Hoppy Together Again," this fabulous Turtles' two record deluxe set is a refreshing blast from our romantic past and features one of the sixties' most popular groups doing a number of chart hits they offered con- secutively over the span of several years. The Flo & Eddie duo, so popular today, emanated from the Turtles and their influence is laced heavily throughout the hits "It Ain't Me Babe," "Elenore," "Happy Together" and "Can I Get To Know You Better." "You Are The Sunshine Of My Life," "My Little Girl" and "San Francisco Lights." On each cut the lady proves that she's a genuine genius. THE BEST OF TYMES - The Tymes - Abcko AA4228 The Tymes, currently on the charts with "You Little Trustmaker" now find themselves the sub- ject of a 'tyme'-ly LP featuring some of their finest hits of the sixties. St. Louis Mayor Declared Nov. 3 O'Neal Twins Day HOLLYWOOD - The O'Neal Twins. Shelter Records premier Gospel artists celebrated their twenty-fifth anniversary of performing together with a concert at the Kiel Auditorium (St. Louis) Sunday Nov. 3. Headlining the show along with the O'Neal Twins were The Staple Singers and Reverend James Cleveland. Other notable gospel groups were the Brooklyn All Stars, Reverend Maceo Woods and the Interfaith Choir. In addition to the concert, Mayor John Poelker honored the Twins for their many years of faithful service to the St. Louis community by proclaiming Sunday O'Neal Twins Day. Shelter Records under the direction of Leon Russell and Patrick Henderson taped the concert with the assistance of Fedco (well known for its fine job on the "Mad Dogs and Englishmen" LP). The Twins first Shelter album just re- cently released was produced by Leon Russell and Patrick Henderson and de- buted on the Gospel charts at number thirty-one. Jazz Presented On Cable TV NEW YORK - An advanced concept in musical entertainment has started on Sterling Manhattan cable television. Every Monday night at 11:30, on public access channel D, the Experimental Television Coop is presenting "live" jazz and contemporary musicans, performing in a relaxed, intimate format that stimulates creativity on a level not pos- sible on commercial television. The name of the show is "Jamming." Frank Watkins is the producer/director of the show and Mike Garr acts as asst. producer. Motown Marketing And Creative Services PowWow Held In LA HOLLYWOOD - Motown Records held a marketing and creative services meet- ing for all Motown regional promotion and regional sales managers last week at the Holiday Inn in Westwood. The pro- motion and sales managers were brought to town for the two day session to discuss the November release. The first day of the meetings, directed by Tom Noonan, acting director of marketing, was devoted to promotion, sales, distribution and the formation of the plans, contests and assignments to work this product. The regional managers were told how all were to coordinate their efforts with Motown's distributors, the tours of the artists, and with radio stations. Ewart Abner, president of Motown Records, made a special presentation dealing with each person's responsibilities and discussing Motown's future and their part in that future. Herb Belkin, vice president of creative operations, presided over the second day's meetings. These meetings outlined support plans of the new product dealing with advertising, merchandising, publici- ty, graphics, artists relations and the in- troduction of the new releases. Belkin presented a new image in an- nouncing the recent acquisition of dis- tribution rights for Manticore Records and introducing the new Melodyland label, Motown's C&W wing, thereby broadening the base and giving the corn- pany greater diversification in terms of artists, product and potential. Drum, picksof the week YESTERDAYS - Gato Barbieri - Flying Dutch- man - 0698 The first side is an interesting combination of Kern and Harbach's standard, "Yesterdays," and the Trane's "A John Coltrane Blues." On the former, the first few bars of the intro remind one of Pharoah, yet, the Latin rhythms are clearly Barbieri's. Gato always rhythmically enlivens the somewhat sterile bossa nova percussion line. See the first chorus here. 8 -bars of congas open "The Blues." The instruments are introduced in- dividually (note Paul Metzke's guitar work). After Gato announces the head, his choruses blend the Trane's mysticism with his own musical anarchism (see the twisted notes, weak -beat syn- copations, and multi -octave excursions). SINGERELLA - Gary Bartz - Prestige - P-10083 The fairy tale is one of "rats, roaches, and melon coaches." "St. Felix St." epitomizes the album's mood. At times, the music, like ghetto life, labors under the logic of a dominant force. Yet the human, and the humor involved in the in- visible world is also present. Bartz' sop sax chorus portrays all the tension lurking below the apathy of the depraved existence. The vocals are matter-of-fact statements, or better, exhorta- tions, that can lay bare frustration and ac- complishment in a single phrase (see "Singerella" and "Nation Time"). FRESH FEATHERS - John Klemmer - Impulse ABCD-836 John Klemmer's 9th album. The record blends a rock beat with jazz improvisations. The first side, however, seems to revolve around Klem- mer's changes of the melody lines within a tightened 4/4 structure. He adds certain little rhythmic twists to keep the tracks interesting. On "Fresh Feather's" second chorus, Klemmer ac- cents the weak beat and ties notes across measures, breaking the restrictions of the bar line. The second side is more loosely structured and open-ended. Note "Stinger," with a modal intro which nicely blends into the scalar theme. JOE & ZOOT - Joe Venuti and Zoot Sims - Chiaroscuro CR 128 A meeting of two masters. The album's in- teresting sound arises from the empathetic com- bination of two radically different instruments. Because the two musicians are sensitive to the different qualities of the sax and the violin, the music works and assumes an airy quality. "Some- day, Sweetheart," has counterpointed duets which are devoid of excess ornamentation -a common fault of swing - and which still manages a few rhythmic surprises. On "C Jam Blues," note the woven melody lines which create a spatial wonder reminiscent of the Duke himself. POUM - Fischer, Robinson, Whitecage, Cook, Pavonex - Composers Collective 721 The Composers Collective was formed in 1972 in order to produce music that is not commercial- ly available. The music demands that the listener put aside all notions regarding normal musical structure, that he try to listen to the music from a perspective similar to that of the musicians who composed the pieces. That perspective is enlightened, indeed. "Sinfonia" is quite abstract and proceeds over spatial planes as well as over time. Yet it also, interestingly, seems to double back upon itself. The "Apollo" series is thematically structured around the first moon landing. THE JAZZ PIANO OF JOHN COATES, JR. - John Coates, Jr. - Omnisound N 1004 The second production of Omnisound, Inc. and the first album for Coates. Note the two resolutions in "Love Is Enough." After the first, Kay on bass and Davis on drums join in accom- paniment. The piece is sharpened by interesting dischords, and arpeggio runs which confront the piece's time signature. Immediately preceeding the coda is a fine example of Coates contrapuntal harmonic technique. After a modal opening on "Yesterday," Coates creatively explodes the tunes harmonic and rhythmic structure. 36 November 30, 1974

cash box,- album reviews ALL THE GIRLS IN THE WORLD BEWARE!!! - Grand Funk - Capitol So -11356 - Jimmy lenner The title indicates that the Grand Funk machine is out to capture the hearts of women everywhere with super developed masculinity, but the capturing is done in the grooves even more than on the hilarious cover artwork. Featur- ing their latest single "Some Kind Of Wonderful," the disk is an exercise in power, rock power at its commercial best. Particularly effective tracks in- clude "Life," "Wild," "Look At Granny Run Run" and the great title track. You've got to pick this LP up. THE MAGIC OF THE BLUE - Blue Magic - Atco SD 36-103 - Norman Harris Another soulful adventure from the fabulous "Stop To Start" quintet that has shaken the world of soul from top to bottom. On this LP, the group plays off a more classic entertainment theme, even working circus noises into the LP's opening cut. Vernon Sawyer, Richard Pratt, Keith Beaton, Wendell Sawyer and Ted Mills, the members of the group, work their harmonic magic to a tee on every number. We especially like "Three Ring Circus" and "Let Me Be The One." SPECIAL EDITION - Paul Horn - Mushroom MRS 5502 The title of Paul's new LP is very apt because it reflects the special nature of this brilliant two re- cord set that captures some of the flautist's finest performances ever. Side three, for instance, is entirely devoted to the incredible epic piece, "Dusk," which is a brilliantly painted musical tableau filled with provocative musical images. If ever there were a time for Paul to become re- cognized as the super performer he is, it's now. Listen to "Freedom Jazz Dance," all 3 parts of "Tribute To Jobim" and "Willow Weep For Me" and you'll agree. THE HOBBIT BY J. R. R. Tolkien - Narrator: Nicol Willaimson - Argon APL 1196/9 - Harley Usill A monumental and eloquently packaged four record set featuring Nicol Willaimson's readings from the famous Tolkien best seller, this effort is certainly right on the money for any undecided Christmas shoppers - especially those with a bent for "The Hobbit." Nicol Williamson's read- ings are extremely communicative and the adap- tation into recorded form by Harley Usill bespeaks an insight and professionalism we ad- mire. Each track draws you deeper into the mystery and fantasy of the great tale. You'll love it. JELLY ROLL MORTON 1923/24 - Jelly Roll Morton - Milestone M-47018 One of six spectacular anthology LP's includ- ing sets by Louis Armstrong & King Oliver, Blind Lemon Jefferson, The New Orleans Rhythm Kings and Ma Rainey, this classic Jelly Roll Morton set is an indication of the way things used to be and a clear look at some of the primary roots of today's popular music. A de- finitive and authoritative original collection, this LP offers such tracks as "Wolverine Blues," "My Gal," "Tiger Rag," "Steady Roll" and "High Society." MY EBONY PRINCESS - Jimmy Briscoe & The Little Beavers - Pi Kappa PK 6000 - Paul Kyser The dynamic stage act that has delighted audi- ences across the country also proves again that it has all the ingredients to communicate a soulful message via records too. The quintet, dis- tinguished time and again in the r&b field, once again returns to its strength, but also offers strong possibilities for pop crossovers on this disk. Especially fine selections include "Forever," "Marching ToHigher Ground," "Pack Up" and the fantastic title track. pop picks lIE ML.GICGE THE BLUE PAUL HORN IP:CJ!Y B'fMCilE 6 !Tg LITTLE 1E Lo ooW t; 4 T lot AS I SEE IT NOW - Melanie - Neighborhood NB 3000 - Peter Schekeryk "Madrugada," Melanie's last LP, was an in- teresting and exciting departure from her unique style and her latest goes even further in delineat- ing the growing maturity, both musically and spiritually, that mark this fine performer. Of special interest is the song "Autumn Lady," a beautiful tune which was to be the title track of her last LP until she and husband/producer Peter Schekeryk came upon "Madrugada." We dig "Yankee Man," "Chart Song" and "Stars Up There." KUNG FU FIGHTING AND OTHER GREAT LOVE SONGS - Carl Douglas - 20th Century T-464 - Biddu Highlighted by Carl's current number one hit single, "Kung Fu Fighting," the artist's new 20th Century LP is a complete package of musical dynamite with Douglas at its center, generating enough heat to drive a train. Using the Kung Fu theme intermittently throughout the disk, Douglas establishes an interesting presence here, on that will obviously carry him past the novelty stage and into other musical dimensions. There are some other fine cuts on this LP and we dig "Witchfinder General" and "Never Had This Dream Before." SHE'S GONE - Lou Rawls - Bell 1318 - Norman Ratner The fabulous Lou Rawls has taken one of the finest songs ever written (the title track) and given it a whole new dimension on his latest LP, a masterful combination of song selection and powerful vocal delivery. Lou is excellent render- ing such classics as "You Don't Miss Your Water" and Roberta Flack's "Feel Like Makin' Love," but is equally fine on other selections such as "Keep The Faith," "You're A Lady" and "Baby You Don't Know How Good You Are." HOT WIRE - Trapeze - Warner Bros. BS 2828 - Neil Slaven, Trapeze Not to be cute, but Tapeze is one of the most acrobatic music acts recording in rock today. Originally a trio, the group now boasts four mem- bers; Dave Holland, drums; Pete Wright, bass and vocals; Bob Kendrick. guitar and vocals and Mel Galley, guitar and lead vocals. A high energy group that is capable of turning the juice on at any time, Trapeze is featured best on cuts such as "Back Street Love," "Goin' Home," "Wake Up, Shake Up" and "Turn It On." Precision dynamics and tight arrangements augment the fine material, all original. KINKY FRIEDMAN - Kinky Friedman - ABC ABCD-829 - Producer: Steve Barri, Willie Nelson When Kinky Friedman first emerged with his band, the Texas Jewboys, the reaction was WHAT? But Kinky has gone to great lengths to establish himself not just as a satirist, but also as one of the most talented country rockers on the scene today. The humor doesn't hurt, of course. as you'll discover when you listen to "They Ain't Makin' Jews Like Jesus Anymore" and "Wild Man From Borneo." Kinky's style is unique and carries the unmistakable charm and talent of a star who's going to be around for a long time. THE ROTO ROOTER GOOD TIME CHRISTMAS BAND - Roto Rooter Good Time Christmas Band - Vanguard-VSD 79347 - Tom Hensley One of the most provocative LPs of the year. this package is slightly deceptive because of the name of the group, but so thoroughly enjoyable that you'll have difficulty determining exactly what holiday spell you're under the influence of. This is a super party record and the band deports itself with poise and confidence throughout the effort. If you've got a sense of humor you'll dig this one for sure. We like "Martian March.' "Swamp Lake" and "Pico and Sepulveda" (a natural). 20 December 14. 1974

For LA LP Sessions LOS ANGELES - The Jackson Five, Motown recording artists who recently closed a headline engagement at the MGM Grand Hotel in Las Vegas, have cancelled all personal appearances for the month of Jan. and will spend the time recording at MoWest studios. According to a group spokesman, "the group will not only be recording a new group album, but will concentrate on new individual albums for members of the group. "Since they are already contractually committed for appearances in Las Vegas, Lake Tahoe, three foreign tours, aside from their regular theatre -in -the -round appearances and concerts, we decided to block out some time for recording prior to hitting the road again." The innovative musician, long known as the father of the "soul school" of jazz, is scheduled to release a new Blue Note album early next year. Just Released "Bus Stop" Abet LP #406 8 track tape #80406 MY"' #1 Disco in England Oliver Sain 'NUS STOP' Abet x$9457 Most requested disco in New York City Excellorec Music 1011 WOODLAND STREET NASHVILLE, TENN. 37206 (615) 227-5081 picks of the week MOVIN' DAY - Grady Tate - Janus JXS 7010 Grady Tate's first album as a lead vocalist. Tate has a mellow timbre and an extremely attractive tone. He can handle a soulful ballad as well as an uptempo pop tune. The selection of material ex- ploits his enormous musical knowledge. The in- strumental backing swings within the tight vocal structure. Check Ron Carter's bass on Van Mor- rison's "Moondance." On the second verse, his triplet and dotted 16th groups energize the vocals. "Sitting in Limbo" is a blues number, highlighted by Elliot Randall's guitar work. Also appearing on the album are Joe Farrell, Joe Newman, and Jimmy Johnson. THE WORLD OF SWING - Various Artists - Col X698 This double LP fills in many gaps in previously released swing collections. Many of the cuts are obscure; some, in fact, have never been issued before. The tracks are arranged chronologically and show the developments in the band struc- ture. Stanley Dance, the author of "The Worlds of Swing," provides excellent liner notes. Chick Webb's "Stompin' At The Savoy," highlights the drummer and Sandy Williams on trombone. Ell- ington and Basie's Orchestras are heard together on "One More Once." The cut features the two band's sax sections. Checkout Paul Gonzalves' coda. LOVE IS IN US ALL - Pharoah Sanders - Im- pulse - ASD 9200 The album has two extended cuts. The first is entitled "Love is in Us All," while the second side is an ode "To John." The title track is very rhythmic and, as expected, is replete with percussion instruments. The two -bar ostinado is developed in two sections. In the first, the melody is sung, while the polyrhythms are woven about the lyrics. There is an interesting chordal break by the piano before the first sec- tion closes. The tempo is slowed down in the second section, which consists of Sander's alto work counterpointed with the piano. STORIES TO TELL - Flora Purim - Milestone - M-9058 Flora Purim, "downbeat's" top female vocalist of 1974, has released her second album. The ti- tle track, composed by Miroslav Vitous and Purim, includes titles and phrases from Neville Potter's pieces for the first Return to Forever. Check out Vitous' Moog work here. Purim has composed lyrics for McCoy Tyner's "Search for Piece." Her voice on the piece is sensuous and haunting; it readily evokes the sentiments of the song. George Duke's superb accompaniment on acoustic piano creatively utilizes Tyner's pen- tatonic chord structure. FACING YOU - Keith Jarrett - ECM 1017 ST Keith Jarrett again performs solo piano. Though the LP was released in Europe in 1972, it is now readily available through Polydor in the States. The record is more consistent than the "Solo Concerts" triple LP, and has none of the "Concert" LPs' sterile, "technique -for -technique - sake" lapses. Jarrett's work includes both strong chordal rhythms and light legato arpeggios. "In Front" steps right out and brightly dances over the heavy bass part. "My Lady; My Child" is a soft and striking ode. The chord progression here is quite interesting. ALONE TOGETHER - Joseph Jarman and An- thony Braxton - Delmark DS -428 The record features Joseph Jarman of the Art Ensemble of Chicago and Anthony Braxton, a one-time member of Circle and an outstanding composer. Both are extremely talented reedists. The compositions on side 1 are Braxton's, while the second side is devoted to Jarman's work. The title track begins with the two saxes in un- ison. Though they play together, the single voice sounds isolated and alone. Yet, the voice divides and Jarman and Braxton creatively play against each other. "CK7 (GN)" is non -structured, polyrhythmic, and extremely abstract. The piece tries to clarify the relationship between pure sound and music. 24 December 14, 1974

cash box,- international news GRC, Nippon Columbia Sign Distribution Pact ATLANTA - Continuing their interna- tional expansion, GRC finalized a licens- ing agreement for the distribution of their GRC, Hotlanta and Aware catalogues (all to be issued on the GRC label) in Japan with one of the leading record and tape manufacturing com- panies in that country, Nippon Columbia Co., Ltd., it was jointly announced this week by GRC president Michael Thevis and T. Hanzawa, general manager of the International Repertoire Department of Nippon Columbia. Nippon Columbia will officially launch the GRC releases the end of Dec., con- centrating initially on Sammy Johns and Ripple, to be followed by other products of the GRC catalogues. Nippon Colum- bia is preparing an extensive campaign aimed at the record dealers, radio, TV, press outlets plus the public with unique merchandising aids, point -of -purchase promotions, extended publicity cov- erage, etc. "Recognizing that Japan is one of the key record and tape markets worldwide and realizing the stature of Nippon Columbia in the Japanese marketplace, I am extremely pleased and proud to be associated with Mr. T. Hanzawa and his energetic and most enthusiastic staff," stated GRC's Thevis. Sought by many record companies in Japan, GRC sent their international licensing consultant Bobby Weiss of One World of Music, to Tokyo to personally survey the complete music business scene and it was a result of his extensive research and talks with more than 35 record companies (and music publishers) that the record licensing plans were finalized with Nippon Colum- bia. "It was their keen desire to represent GRC supported by their impressive marketing plans that really convinced me," said Weiss, "plus checking Nippon Columbia's stature with the dealers, pre- ss, radio and TV, which confirmed my opinion that GRC's best interests would be served via Nippon Columbia's representation." Discussions have been underway for some weeks about GRC artists Sammy Johns and Ripple making a promotional tour of Tokyo, Osaka, etc., to appear before the dealers, press, the public, plus appearing on selected and impor- tant radio and TV programs, it was con- firmed GRDC President Buz Wilburn. "I am hopeful that booking time can be cleared for both of these artists to work into Nippon Columbia's plans for ap- pearances in Japan sometime early in 1975, as if so, I would like to extend their appearances to other areas of the Far East." Said T. Hanzawa of Nippon Columbia, "For many months, we have recognized the growing importance of the GRC artists and it was our desire to acquire their record and tape rights because Nip- pon Columbia's staff has such tremen- dous enthusiasm and belief in their artists for our expanding market. GRC will not only bring their outstanding 'Atlanta-Hotlanta sound,' but because of their involvement internationally with numerous important record sources, other leaders and future stars of the record business to Japan." Plans are already underway for GRC and Nippon Columbia executives to visit each other in their respective home of- fices during the coming months to map plans for 100% cooperation between the two firms and to set day -and -date release of key product so that Japan may share in the USA impact of the GRC best- sellers. The first GRC label releases will be is- sued by Nippon Columbia in time for the last week of December business. Discussions are still being held with various music publishers in Japan con- cerning sub -publishing rights to the Thevis Music Group of catalogues con- sisting of six companies and Bobby Weiss expects to finalize an agreement shortly via his One World of Music negotiations. Thus, Nippon Columbia joins EMI Capitol of Canada as an international licensee with contracts now in the finalization stage for other territories to be confirmed shortly for both records and music publishing representation. London: Pye Changes, Island USA Debut LONDON - Following last week's an- nouncement of John Fruin's resignation from Polydor London comes news of the resignation of Ronnie Beck of Feldman (part of EMI Publishing Ltd). Beck is to join Fruin in a new record label venture to be known as State Records. Also in- volved will be Wayne Bickerton and Tommy Waddington. Because of Beck's departure, EMI Publishing have an- nounced that as from Jan. 1, 1975 Feldman and Robbins Music Corpora- tion will be under the direction and general management of Terry Slater who was previously general manager of Robbins Music Corporation. The identity of these two publishing companies will be maintained and some further staff ap- pointments are in the pipeline. Island Records has inaugurated a new r&b/soul label to be known as Island USA with which the company makes a re-entry into the British soul market. Em- phasis will be on singles market and material will come primarily through the purchase of masters from small indepen- dent record labels and production com- panies in the United States. Island did much to introduce r&b into Britain in 1963 when it licensed the catalogues of the American based Sue label. Much the same pattern of promotion will be de- veloped for the new Island USA label; i.e. initial exposure through clubs and discotheques. However, where specific records are considered to have max- imum commercial potential they will be promoted through all conventional chan- nels. In addition to soul and r&b masters material will also come from the New York based Latin American label Fania with which Island has just signed a licensing agreement. Deal was con- cluded between Island's Chris Blackwell and Fania president Jerry Masucci and marks the introduction of Fania's catalogue in the U.K. Label manager for Island USA is Danny Holloway. Sparks Deny Permanent U.K. Departure HOLLYWOOD - Sparks is expected to move operations to the United States following a final Christmas concert in England on Dec. 20. While the move is described as tem- porary and motivated by expanding com- mitments in the U.S., speculation is growing in the U.K. that Sparks is plan- ning a permanent departure because of the country's severe tax system. This is denied by Sparks' nucleus, Ron and Russell Mael, and their manager, John Hewlett, who've indicated winter '75 concert dates in Britain already are on the itinerary. First up, however, is a February tour of the U.S. Additional dates are con- templated for the fall and, in between, Sparks hopes to record its third album somewhere in the States. "It's just a case of staying there for some time once we get there," Ron Mael explained from London. "Let's just say that Sparks will now be based wherever we happen to be at any one time." While Island Records continues to pro- mote Sparks' heralded debut album, "Kimono My House," as well as a single newly -released from the LP, "Talent Is An Asset," the follow-up album was re- leased in Britain simultaneous with a tour there that concluded Nov. 28. A final holiday concert is set for Leeds on Fri., Dec. 20. Called "Propaganda," the second album is targeted for American release in tandem with the Feb. U.S. tour. Temps Storm Japan HOLLYWOOD - The Temptations, Motown recording artists, have em- barked on a concert tour of Japan, it has been announced by Don Foster, the group's manager. The 6 -city, 14 -engagement tour follows their previous highly successful tour of Japan, earlier this year. The dates are scheduled to coincide with the re- lease of their present Motown single, "Happy People." The Temptations schedule is as follows: Dec. 5, Shibuya Kokai-Do, Tokyo; Dec. 5, Club El Morocco, Tokyo; Dec. 6, Osaka Kosei Nenkin Hall, Osaka; Dec. 7, Nagoya Shi Kokai-Do, Nagoya; Dec. 9, Fukuoka Shimin Kaikan, Fukuoka; Dec. 10, Hiroshima Uybin Chokin Hall, Hiroshima; Dec. 11, Shibuya Kokai-Do, Tokyo; Dec. 11, Club New Latin Quarter, Tokyo; Dec. 12, Shibuya Kokai-Do. Tokyo; Dec. 12, Club Canterbury House #3, Tokyo; Dec. 13, Shizuoka Sumpu Kaikan, Shizuoka; Dec. 14, Sun Plaza Hall (2 shows) Tokyo.
