cash box, talent on stage Guess Who BOTTOM LINE, NYC - In one of their rare club appearances, the Guess Who captivated standing room audiences with a homogenous presentation which suc- cessfully combined elements of nostalgia with selections from their new Flavours" LP, released concurrently with this three day engagement. The group's new members, Dominic Troiano and Bill Wallace join stalwarts Burton Cummings and Garry Peterson to comprise a sleek. well-oiled unit whose express confidence carried through both past hit singles and new album material. Cummings, with one of rock's most dis- tinctive vocal styles remains the focal point of the group while Troiano, a veteran of the Canadian music scene. in- jects the flash that has been traditionally lacking through over a decade of shifting line-ups. Troiano is the consummate rock and roll guitarist. with an arsenal of elec- tronic devices that either modify or in- tensify the sound with a flick of the switch. Through numbers like "Star Baby." "No Time." and "Dancin' Fool." his sense of timing was deadly; un- leashing avalanches of notes and en- compassing gusts of chords. With this obviously intuitive sense of rock's energy and motion. it is unfortunate that Troiano felt it necessary to resort to grandstand ploys like his unaccom- panied solo during "Show Biz Shoes," which was both overlong and uninspired. From there, the group fought an uphill battle to regain their stride, but through songs like "Long Gone." "Hoe Down Time," and their recent "Dancin' Fool- single. the obvious strengths of the veteran RCA group cemented before the evening was capped off with a pair of well earned encores. b.t. Miles Davis THE TROUBADOUR. L.A. There can be no denying the immense influence Miles Davis has had on the American jazz scene in the past decade and a half. The list of musicians, for instance, who have graduated from his groups to form bands of their own is a staggering testa- ment to his talents and it includes luminaries like John McLaughlin. Tony Williams, Chick Corea, Herbie Hancock, Billy Cobham and dozens of others. Therefore when Davis isn't in top form it is a real disappointment and when he can barely play at all it is a tragedy. For the Troubadour set Miles brought along some sensitive sidemen including Sonny Fortune on sax and flute, Mike Henderson on bass and percussionist Mtume. but at no time in the one hour set did Davis show that spark of genius which is uniquely his. Often he could barely stand and supported himself by leaning drunkenly on an electric organ and playing long, droning chords while the six man band tried to shape a sound around the dissonance. Rarely bothering to play trumpet at all. Miles was more concerned in staring his sideman down and ordering his roadie to fetch him cigarettes. When he did take the horn to his lips the solos were short, grunting bursts that failed to excite the audience. Playing half the time on his knees. curled into a small. white -clad ball, he appeared totally disconnected from what was going on with the rest of the musicians. But even in a set as bleak as this one the music contained fleeting moments of brilliance. When the band wasn't ex- cruciatingly loud they managed to create some sexy. sensual sounds and towards the closing moments they played some variations off the standard twelve bar blues that were truly mind boggling. j. b. Neil Sedaka Ed Begley, Jr. HOLLYWOOD - Looking much like a Beverly Hills attorney, Neil Sedaka climbed onto the Troubadour stage, amidst rounds of hearty welcome, im- mediately capturing the room with his astonishingly beautiful voice on "The Other Side Of Me." Past references to Sedaka's history as an all-time, all-star music maker were ignited and verified, as he whipped through a set that could only delight the conscious and bring the passed -out to a sitting -up position. This man Sedaka is a master, both at songwriting and performance. Comedian Ed Begley Jr. had brought the Troub audience to the verge of hilarious tears with his fast -paced monologue, interspersing take -offs on product advertisements for Skippy Soylent Butter and Pop and Gobble breakfast cereal. His twisted version of Nun's Story was especially humorous as was his Alistair Cooke at DisneyWorld routine. Begley gets nothing but better on each outing and he's a man to look for when hard up for a smile. Also provided was Begley's one big non -hit, "Does The Name Pavlov Ring A Bell." But Begley was merely a warm-up for the sensation that Sedaka was. Most of the audience was old enough to have grown up on Sedaka items, such as "Calendar Girl," "Hey Little Devil," and "Happy Birthday, Sweet 16" and Neil de- livered those and other familiar tunes with a gusto that moved the unmovable. Backed by a top-notch band, com- prised of Lee Sklar (bass), Jeff Baccaro (drums). Richie Zito (guitar). Danny Kootch (guitar), David Foster (keyboards) and Brenda and Brian Russell and Abigail Hanness on vocals, Sedaka captured the evening's mood when he sang the lines "Tonight's The Night." Indeed it was a night worth wait- ing for. Moving at a fast clip through his huge catalog of tunes. Sedaka and this crispest of bands delivered everything that one familiar with his history could desire, from the earliest to the most re- cent material from "Sedaka's Back" in- cluding his recent smash success "Laughter In The Rain," which brought the house down with it's timely quality. Sedaka at the piano, often paid short -riff tributes to his mentor. Elton John, bring- ing additional smiles to those in atten- dance. His voice is in as fine a shape as ever and his God-given talent for com- posing heart-warming tunes is an asset worthy of envy. Sedaka is definitely back and this reviewer is proud. t.h. Gil Scott -Heron Gene Harris THE BOTTOM LINE, NYC - The poetry of the black man is the song of the street. It describes anguish and frustration, con- tentment and accomplishment. In many ways, the finest young black poet is Gil Scott -Heron. The Bottom Line performance was his first since joining Arista Records and it coincided with the release of his "The First Minute Of A Brand New Day" LP. The lyrics, most of which were com- posed by Scott -Heron and Brian Jackson, are intense evocations of the black world and its people's conscious- ness. On "Winter Sunrise," Victor Brown and Scott -Heron's rough, provocative voices called to mind the splendor of re- birth from the ashes of decay. So. too, "The Liberatión Song" echoed the spirit and unity of a struggle for social and political independence. Scott -Heron's Midnight Band is com- posed of ten musicians, many of whom concentrate on percussion instruments. Though, at times, the band does not seem to be as technically proficient as it might be. the performers have a unique feel for the music and for Scott -Heron's personal conception of his art. Like him, the band members are musicians of the street. In this case, the music tightly fuses with the lyrics and sensitively evokes the moods and ideas behind the words. It would be an understatement to say that Gene Harris has changed his act. The old Three Sounds keyboardman was best known for his uncluttered, blues - directed performances. However, the Blue Note artist has recently formed a seven -piece band whose sound might best be described as "soul -jazz." Harris worked primarily on electric piano and synthesizer while accompanying his two female singers. Kitty Doswell and Ersel Magitt. The two women have different, yet complementary vocal styles. Ms. Doswell demonstrated her husky, sensuous singing on "Dr. Feel -good." Her stop -time coda, though a bit too long, was exhilarating. She was followed by Ms. Magitt's crystal, almost clear fragile rendition of "Last Day Of Sum- mer." Harris did keep his older listeners oriented by performing a nice 24 -bar blues chorus on "Summer." s.m. Etta James & Surprise Guest THE TROUBADOUR, L.A. - Any time you get a chance to see Etta James perform, take it. You'll never know what magic and excitement she can generate till you catch her shaking, shouting and pouting the blues in her own inimitable style. Her stint at the Troubadour was doubly exciting because Gregg Allman, a man known for his jamming penchant, sat in with Etta's band for one of the most memorable experiences of its kind in re- cent history. Etta was magnificent calling out the name of 'Mr. Blue' as only she can and her band cooked with the fervor of wild nights on 115th and 7th Avenue. When Allman joined the band (a totally unex- pected turn of events) there was an im- mediate gasp of recognition from the blues thristy audience and Allman filled it with numbers like "Stormy Monday Blues," "Queen Of Hearts" and Sweet Little Angel." The combination of explosive, powerhouse riffs complimented by the most soulful vocals anywhere (on both Etta and Gregg's parts) was overwhelm- ing and it's easy to see why Allman takes such delight in showing up unexpectedly to perform with blues musicians whom he respects. d.b. Z. Z. Top Kiss SWING AUDITORIUM, SAN BERNARDINO - Z. Z. Top is a magnifi- cent boogie band and an overflow crowd of 7900 jammed the Swing to be blasted by the Texas trio and Casablanca record- ing artists, Kiss. Z. Z. Top didn't miss a trick in performing a variety of selections from their current hit LP, "Tres Hom- bres" (on London) as well as several songs from their previous LP's. The crowd pressed close to the stage. strug- gling to touch the colorful cowboy outfits the boys sported and several had to be carried away when they succeeded in climbing on stage. However when the band returned for the first of four en- cores and launched into a spirited version of their hit single "La Grange," the audience nearly overpowered the security force in their sensuous ecstasy. Throughout the concert, Z. Z. Top main- tained total control of their dynamics, though at times they strained to get down low enough to hear the monitors. Make no mistake though, Z. Z. Top got down. Kiss, who opened to a very en- thusiastic crowd themselves. let their brand of heavy metal hard rock and uni- que makeup and clothes speak for them, though three times they exhorted the au- dience to "Get it on!" Their theatrics and loudness worked to their advantage and they paced themselves well enough to earn two encores for themselves. Make no mistake, the crowd had already gotten down before reaching the Swing in good ole San Berdoo. d.b. Ray Manzarek Camel HOLLYWOOD - The Whisky is packed to the rafters, the excitement level hard- ly contained within it's rock -soaked walls. The stars are huddling with the press in the infamous booths and then ... the white suited Ray Manzarek hits the stage and all hell breaks loose. It seems that Mazarek had_ well established the fact that when he plays, there's a fun time to be had by all and indeed, again, Ray de- livered. Backed by an all-star review of talent as band -members, the joint was rocking and rolling like it was the last chance. Snuffy Walden, former mainstay of Stray Dog, on sizzling guitar, Nigel Harrison, formerly of Silverhead, provid- ing the bass line and Hunt Sales (yes, Soupy's son) on drums and sexual moans. Manzarek has left behind his in- tellectual -musical bastardization and gotten down to the roots of rock reality, singing of love on the run and the high times in-between. His soaring keyboard work qualifies memories of Doors -days, yet he's move from the Doorish mold into something more of his own and believe us when we say Manzarek has a hot thing going. Featuring the entirety of his second solo LP, "The Whole Thing Start- ed With Rock and Roll - And Now It's Out Of Control," Ray scorched those in attendance with his heated moments, in- termittenly cooled by gushers of dry ice shooting from specially -rigged boxes towards the ceiling. If what we saw is any indication of what Manzarek's pending tour will be like, let's just say, there'll be some hot nights in towns all across the country. Camel opened the set, attracting a healthy percentage of those who saw them at Long Beach the previous week- end, proving that they are indeed a good club band. Despite initial sound system problems (the expected at the Whisky, rather than the unusual), keyboardist Peter Bardens led the quartet through an interesting array of material from their un -released first album and their recent Janus release, "Mirage." t.h. 28 February 1, 1975 www.americanradiohistory.com

cash box/album reviews pop picks RIDDLE OF THE SPHINX - Bloodstone - Lon- don PS 654 - Producer: Mike Vernon The LP title may deal in riddles, but Bloodstone's latest LP is a clear picture of a super group doing its thing - playing music like few groups in the world can. Whether crooning softly or whipping into a soulful uptempo number, the band displays an excellence that sets them apart from most competitors. We especially like "For The First Time," "The World Is Funky," "Young Times, Old Times." "Nobody But You" and "Just Learned To Walk." Maturity and depth mark this LP. THE BEST OF THE STYLISTICS - Stylistics - Avco AV -69005 - Producers: Thom Bell, M. Bryant, B. Perry, Hugo & Luigi, V. McCoy Truly a "Greatest Hits" of the highest caliber, the Stylistics' new package is loaded with nothing but the finest - chart hits including "You Make Me Feel Brand New." "Betcha By Golly, Wow," "Rockin' Roll Baby," "Break Up To Make Up,"I'm Stone In Love With You," "Heavy Fallin' Out" and "Let's Put It All Together." The quin- tet's popularity keeps growing geometrically and a single listen to this collection will convince you that the Stylistics have style. GOT MY HEAD ON STRAIGHT - Billy Paul - Phila Int'l KZ 33157 - Producers: Gamble, Huff Mr. Soul, Billy Paul, has come a long way in a relatively short space of time and with each new LP, he improves. His latest, a stunning collection of catchy tunes, typifies the stylized brilliance that has become synonomous with his name. His vocals are rich and powerful and his presence is commanding on such cuts as "Black Wonders of the World," "When It's Your Time To Go." "Billy's Back Home" and the impressive title track. An exciting LP. SO MUCH LOVE - The Three Degrees - Roulette SR -3015 - Producer: R. Barrett The Three Degrees have come up a long way from that first radio spot for Coca Cola and this Roulette collection of some of their earliest material provides an interesting insight into the dynamism that has turned the three lovely singers into one of the most sought after acts in the record business. The special quality the gals possess is found on such tracks as "Magic Mir- ror," "Love The One You're With," "Who Is She (And What Is She To You)" and "Maybe." SILK TORPEDO - Pretty Things - Swan Song SS 8411 - Producer: Norman Smith Led by the venerable Phil May, the Pretty Things return via this Swan Song debut LP that's different from the original group's sound, but much more refined and with far greater com- mercial potential. The group now has six mem- bers and the result is a skillfully blended com- bination of textures and moods that lend itself to any discriminating ear. Particularly good cuts on this record include "Dream (Povey)," "Singapore Silk Torpedo." "Bruise In The Sky" and "Joey." THE VERY BEST OF JAY & THE AMERCIANS - Jay & The Amercians - United Artists UA -LA 357-E Another of the great United Artist retrospec- tive albums. this set by Jay & The Americans is a memorable slice of sixties' nostalgia. The package includes such classics as "Cara Mia." "Gypsy Woman," "Let's Lock The Door (And Throw Away The Key)," "When You Dance." "This Magic Moment," "She Cried." "Stand By Me." "Save The Last Dance For Me." "Only In America" and "Come A Little Bit Closer." If you're into the sixties. this set is an absolute must. OHIO PLAYERS GREATEST HITS - Ohio Players - Westbound WB 1005 The Players have got it made in the shade and it's fitting that we should be treated to a selection of some of their finest material. This record is a case in point, displaying the consummate ability of one of the finest and most well prepared vocal quintets working today. NEVER CAN SAY GOODBYE - Gloria Gaynor - MGM M3G 4982 - Producers: T. Bongiovi, M. Monardo, J. Jimmy Castor and his Bunch certainly have their act together here and it's reflected throughout on such tracks as "E -Man Boogie," "You Make Me Feel Brand New," "Hallucinations," "Bertha Butt Boogie" and "Potential." Make no mistake. Jimmy, Bertha and the Bunch are here to stay and their horizons are limitless. THE VERY BEST OF LITTLE ANTHONY AND THE IMPERIALS - Little Anthony & The Imperials - United Artists UA -LA 382-E Part of an impressive set of 21 releases of vin- tage material by the biggest stars in the history of pop music, this package featuring Little Anthony & The Imperials is a classic for sure. The best is here, including the greats: "Tears On My Pillow." "Shimmy Shimmy Ko Ko Bop," "Two People In The World" and the memorable "Goin' Out Of My Head." One of the greatest groups of all time gets its just due on this set that also features "Hurt So Bad." Other LP's in the release feature Cher. cash box,- news RCA Plans Major Denver Promo For LP, TV Appearance NEW YORK - RCA recording artist John Denver will have his new album, "An Evening With John Denver" re- leased on Feb. 18. The album will also be available on stereo 8 and cassette. "An Evening With John Denver" is a live two album package recorded during Denver's appearance at the Universal Amphitheater in Los Angeles last Aug. In addition to being Denver's first live album, and first two record set, the LP contains five songs never recorded before by him. In support of Denver's new album, and in conjunction with his Mar. 10 ABC-TV special, RCA Records has proclaimed the period from Feb. 18 through Mar. 31 as"Denver Spring" and the week of Mar. 3 as "Denver Spring Week," leading into ,telecast of the Denver TV Special. Traffic Platinum HOLLYWOOD - Traffic's "Low Spark Of High Heeled Boys" album, on the Island label (distributed by Capitol), has at- tained "platinum" status this week for sales in excess of 1,000,000 units, it was announced by Don Zimmermann, senior vice president, marketing, Capitol Rec- ords, Inc. The LP is one of 50 Capitol albums to qualify for the platinum award. Two other fast -selling Traffic LPs in the Capitol catalog are "Shoot Out At The Fantasy Factory" (R.I.A.A. certified gold record) and "On The Road." "Denver Spring Week" will be heralded by a saturation major market TV buy from Feb. 28 through Mar. 10. Two different thirty second television spots have been prepared for it. One of the spots will key on "An Evening With John Denver" and his catalog, the other will again key to the new album and to the television special. A large part of the "Denver Spring" campaign will be devoted to RCA's local offices which will design plans around their local markets needs. Plans call for individual radio and in-store contests all designed to give "An Evening With John Denver" the widest possible market penetration. Heavy London Push On Bloodstone LP NEW YORK - Bloodstone's fourth LP for the London label is entitled, "Riddle Of The Sphinx." The LP will be receiving a massive promotional push, reports Herb Goldfarb, vice president in charge of sales and marketing. The album, re- leased this month, will receive heavy radio saturation in key major markets in the U.S.A. The LP has already received full page trade ads and is also scheduled for heavy consumer advertising within sixty to ninety days. Special in-store promotional material is being supplied with a cut-out easel, empty jackets for window display, and a two-color salesmen's discography with tape configuration. NEW YORK - Atlantic/ATCO Records has announced the release of 18 albums for Jan. and Feb., comprising its entire post -Christmas release. Spearheaded by the sixth album by Led Zeppelin, a two - record set entitled "Physical Graffiti" on Swan Song Records, as well as Roxy Music's fourth album, "Country Life." Pretty Things' debut on Swan Song Records is called "Silk Torpedo," pro- duced by ex -Beatles arranger Norman 'Hurricane' Smith. Other key albums in the pop release include the debut of Donnie Fritts, whose album, "Prone To Lean" was co -produced by Kris Kristof- ferson and Jerry Wexler in Muscle Shoals, the solo debut of Joe Vitale, formerly with Joe Walsh & Barnstorm, whose "Roller Coaster Weekend" was produced at Criteria Recording Studios in Miami; the second ATCO release from Germany's Passport, featuring Klaus Doldinger, called "Cross -Collateral"; the debut on Big Tree Records of Greek singer/composer Demis Roussos, with a program sung entirely in English for the first time; and the re -issue (after years). of Margouleff and Cecil's Moog syn- thesizer project, known as "Tonto's Ex- panding Head Band." Atlantic's soul album release is highlighted by a second album for the label from The Jimmy Castor Bunch, titled "Butt Of Course." From ATCO comes the debut of Sister Sledge with "Circle Of Love," produced by Tony Silvester and Bert De Coteaux, and, the debut from Major Harris, formerly of The Delfonics with "My Way." Atlantic's jazz album release consists of "Mingus At Carnegie Hall," produced by Joel Dorn and Ilhan Mimaroglu, and John Coltrane's "Alternate Takes" featuring selection of tracks from entire- ly unreleased sessions of 1959-60, as well as alternate takes, also unreleased. of familiar Coltrane standards. Rounding out the release is the debut from Karen Phillips on Ilhan Mimaroglu's Finnadar Records, titled "Viola Today." Also, three albums from Virgin Records have been released - Robert Wyatt's "Rock Bottom," David Bedford's "Star's End" and Gong's "You." Ohio Players `Fire' Goes Gold CHICAGO - The Ohio Players have had their second consecutive Mercury single certified gold by the RIAA for sales in ex- cess of one million units for their current top 10 record "Fire." This brings a total of four gold awards the Ohio Players have received since joining Phonogram, Inc. less than one year ago. Previous gold was for the "Skin Tight" single, the "Skin Tight" album, and the "Fire' LP. The "Skin Tight" album was also awarded a platinum LP by Phono- gram late last year for sales in excess of one million units. The "Fire" LP is also approaching platinum status. Blue Note will be releasing the following albums this month: In new releases, Blue Note will be out with Donald Byrd's "Stepping Into Tomorrow," Bobby Hutcherson's "Linger,- Lane," Marlena Shaw's "Who Is This Bitch Anyway?" Blue Note also reports strong pop and r&b action on Gene Harris' new single "Losalamitos-,r latinfunklovesong" culled from the jazz - blues pianists' latest Blue Note album "Astralsignal." Newbury, Orleans Highlight E/A's Feb. Release HOLLYWOOD - Elektra/Asylum/None- such Records' second album release for 1975 will comprise two new albums set for national release Feb. 24. The albums are Mickey Newbury's "Lovers," his fifth album for the Elektra label, and the Asylum debut for Orleans, titled "Let There Be Music." "Lovers" was produced by Chip Young at Youngun Recorders and is being re- leased in conjunction with a series of public and TV appearances by Newbury. The title track is also being released as a single, with marketing and promotion to focus on both the single and, at the re- gional level, on Newbury's club and con- cert appearances. The first Asylum album from Orleans, a Woodstock -based quartet, was produced by Charles Plotkin, Elektra/Asylum director, a&r. "Let There Be Music" is be- ing released amid touring by the band, and the title song is set for release as a single. Promotional support will focus on the group's live act, while marketing sup- port will include instore display items, notably a special full -color "dangler" dis- play utilizing reproductions of the album art. for the record EAST COASTINGS - If Led Zeppelin's first of three concerts at Madison Square Garden last week was any indication, the group's cross-country tour of Americana's massive areas will be remembered as an unqualified artistic success. The visuals alone, from dry ice smoke to laser beams to one of the most elaborate uses of lighting in rock and roll are all impeccably executed, yet the magic radiated by Mssrs. Page, Bonham, Plant, and Jones managed to transcend all their accounterments. As one of the few remaining purveyors of flash rock and roll, Led Zep reaffirmed their place in rock's upper echelon. Jimmy Page's attack was uncompromising and razor sharp, especially in "Dazed and Confused" which hadn't been performed until opening night at MSG in over a year. A couple of the brightest moments of the eve- ning were the swashbuckling version of "Kashmir" from the forthcoming "Physical Graffiti" album and a final onslaught which included "Stairway To Heaven," "Whole Lotta Love," and "Communication Breakdown." It's refreshing to see that a major group like Led Zeppelin can return to the stage after nearly two years and still rock with the best of 'em. BITS & PIECES: Atco Records is planning to repackage Roxy Music's "Country Life" album; something about the cover offending people. The new cover, without the green cellophane, will have "lush green foliage" instead of the girls. The original looks like it will become a collector's item ... Martin Mull is planning to collaborate with former National Lampoon editor Michael O'Donoghue on a play to be titled "Lin- coln: The Man, The Car, The Tunnel" ... Muddy Waters is in Woodstock recording his next album for Chess with members of the Band ... Humble Pie's upcoming concert at the Academy of Music later this month is being billed as their "Farewell Performance" ... Japanese rock act, the Sadistic Mika Band make their U.S. label de- but next week on Harvest Records. There's nothing very sadistic about them as far as we can gather (lyrics are in Japanese), except that lead singer Mika reportedly walks on stage swinging a samurai sword. It seems that Mika was making her husband, Kazu Kato, who is also in the group, do all the housework one day. Kazu called her "sadistic" and the name stuck. Hence, the Sadistic Mika Band. You may remember Jonathan King as the guy who sang "Wooly Bully" with Leslie Gore and Ramsey Lewis on the Hullaballoo show in 1965. You may remember him as the balladeer who crooned through five million copies of "Everyone's Gone To The Moon," or even as the tycoon of tacky tunes by fictitious groups like the Weatherman, the Piglets, and Shag. Chances are that by next month, with the release of his new album, "A Rose In A Fisted Glove," whatever preconceived notion you may have had about Jonathan King will have to be revised. "When people start buying my records and think they've got me figured out, it's time to change my style," King told Cash Box last week. The album, which should be more accessible than his bastardizations of pop classics on the "Bubblerock Is Here To Stay" LP and the wry humor of "Pandora's Box," his last solo effort, continues to brim with eccentricity, After all, the combina- tion record executive (he founded U.K. Records in 1972) - recording artist - pro- ducer - founder of the Kim Novak fan club openly admits that humor is an asset. "A Rose In A Fisted Glove" (the title is taken from a line in Stephen Stills"Love The One You're With') is partly comprised of songs that King has admired while the other half are original. Of the former, King has chosen to lead off with Joni Mitchell's "Free Hand In Paris." "It's a song that should always have been sung by a record executive," he says. Also in that category is a solid c&w interpretation of Ann Peebles' r&b hit, "I Can't Stand The Rain," and a very palatable version of Jerome Kern's "The Way You Look Tonight." Of King's originals are the weird but brilliant "Let's Not Get Dirty," the bizarre"Mental Diseases," and a sultry"A Very, Very Melancholy Me." Another project King has recently involved himself in is the importation of 10,000 copies of the London cast recording of "The Rocky Horror Show" in time for the Broadway opening next month. "We recorded the soundtrack two weeks after it opened on Kings Road and we managed to capture it while it still sparkled with the in- itial feeling of excitement HOT FLASHES: Return To Forever, who are currently on an extensive European tour will embark on an American jaunt next month which will coincide with the re- lease of their next album, "No Mystery" and new single, "Jungle Waterfall ... "The Myths And Legends Of King Arthur And The Knights Of The Round Table" is the official title of Rick Wakeman's next album. Heard with Rick are the regular rhythm group, a 45 -piece session orchestra, the 48 -piece English Chamber Choir, and an eight -piece male voice choir. Wakeman was recording "Arthur" right up to his departure for tours of Japan and Australia. It is based on the life of King Arthur, his knights, and the magician Merlin. Rick plans to stage a "King Arthur Day" at Tintagel Castle in Cornwall in spring this year. "I would like it to be more of a pageant than a rock show - with jousting, medieval bands and knights in armor," he says. Roy Rogers has been set guest on ABC -TV's "Tonight Show" Tues. cash box R&B news report Kendricks To Headline Benefit HOLLYWOOD - Eddie Kendricks, Tamla recording artist, has been set to headline a benefit show for The Edwin Gould Services For Children. The benefit show will be held at New York City's Felt Forum, located at Madison Square Garden, on Feb. 8, with two performances scheduled at 7 and 11 pm. The Edwin Gould Services is a volun- tary non-profit child welfare agency that has programs aimed at adoption, foster care, residential treatment facilities and their own group home for children. Appearing on the bill with Kendricks are Harold Melvin and The Bluenotes, Carl Douglas, and Disco Tex and The Sex -0- Lettes. Bell Honored At Image Awards HOLLYWOOD - Al Bell (right), board chairman of The Stax Organization, was honored by the Hollywood Beverly Hills Chapter of the NAACP at the 8th Annual Image Awards Banquet. Bell was pre- sented the coveted Founder's Award by branch founder Maggie Hathaway (center) in recognition of his outstanding contribution to the national business community. Bell accepted the award before a star- studded audience of over 1,000 at the famous Hollywood Palladium and in response he shared philosophically, "I am proud to say that I serve a master who can calm troubled waters. I can no longer just say I believe, for those who merely believe are manipulated by those who know. I can no longer just sing 'We Shall Overcome' because I know it's time now to 'Come On Over'." Also widely honored by several awards was producer -writer -performer Barry White, who swept the music categories with his multiple talents. Stax artist Billy Eckstine emceed the event along with actress Denise Nicholas. Shirley Brown (Truth label, a division of the Stax Organization) performed her gold record, "Woman To Woman," at the event. Gladys Knight Honored On Far East Tour TOKYO - Gladys Knight and the Pips, currently on tour in the Far East, were guests of honor at a reception hosted by the dept. of U.S. information services in Tokyo, Japan last week. The guest list of about 100 names in- cluded members of the Japanese press, performing artists, critics of the arts, and members of the diplomatic corps from all over the world. Also invited to meet Gladys Knight & the Pips at this recep- tion was a small contingent of orphans from local institutions. Tokyo was the first stop on a three- week concert and promotional tour which will also take the Buddah record- ing artists to Hong Kong, Australia, New Zealand and then back to the U.S. via Hawaii. Wonder Sweeps Ebony '75 Poll HOLLYWOOD - Stevie Wonder, Tamla recording artist, the winner of five covet- ed Grammys in last years awards com- petition and a multiple contender in this years grammy awards with seven nominations covering the field of singer, songwriter, album of the year ("Fulfilling- ness' First Finale"), and the newly creat- ed producer of the year category, has swept the 2nd annual Ebony Magazine Black Music Polls. In making the announcement, Ebony Magazine stated, "In the area of rhythm and blues or whatever one might wish to call the popular soul music of today, one man reigns supreme. Stevie Wonder is the unquestionable ruler of the roost and his highly publicized excursions into electronic music have served to bolster his appeal. Stevie, 24, now a giant in his own right and one who was inducted into the Hall of Fame the first time around, placed first as Innovative Artist, Instrumentalist, Composer, Male Singer and led with his album, "Innervisions." The winners of the second annual poll were announced in the Feb. issue of Ebony. The final winners were selected after the votes polled from the over 12 million subscriber readership of Ebony magazine were tabulated. Ventures Into Jazz Field ATLANTA - Mike Thevis, president of GRC, has announced that the General Recording Corporation of Atlanta, Georgia has begun an intense undertak- ing into the jazz genre of music. The new jazz venture has been stimulated by the GRC album success of the Ebony God- father. Oscar Fields, vice-president of sales. stated that "This jazz era we've evolved into is not totally different from the post- war period of music after World War II. At that time jazz and big bands were a major trend in the American music force. I can see a smiliar post-war jazz evolution." Bob Harrington, GRC vice-president, marketing, believes that "The jazz record buyer is unusually well-educated musically. He is a very tasteful individual. Because of these characteristics, marketing concepts will be uniquely dif- ferent, tasteful and current with the musical trends of the period. We are gearing our marketing towards the more sophisticated audience." cash box; 'news NARM Lists'74 NEW YORK - The National Association of Recording Merchandisers, Inc. has named the nominees for the 1974 NARM Awards, which are given annually for the best selling recorded product in the United States. The annual NARM Awards are based on actual sales of re- cords and tapes to consumers, and therefore based solely on dollar volume. The annual awards will be presented at the NARM Awards Banquet, which climaxes the annual convention. This year's NARM Awards Banquet will be held on Thurs. evening, Mar. 6, in the Los Angeles Ballroom of the Century Plaza Hotel. It will be the final event of the Seventeenth Annual Convention which convenes there on Mar. 2. All NARM regular members, the merchandisers of recorded product, vote for the award winners. Their votes are based on actual sales in their retail out- lets, leased departments, and in the de- partments serviced by rack jobbers. The categories for this year's awards FRONT COVER RCA recording star John Denver aside from having a perfect score (seven gold LP's in seven trys), he nas also had five platinum LP's and 4 gold singles. Clearly, Denver has emerged as one of the major music forces in America in the '70's. His personal appearances couples with TV specials and guest spots on major shows has made him into a cultural folk hero across the land and his influence has ob- viously been felt by thousands who now emulate his outdoors, clean living style. "An Evening With John Denver," his just released 2 record live set, is a sure bet to shoot up the CB charts and once again prompt his personal manager Jerry Weintraub (chairman of Management Ill) to handle the flood of offers that con- tinually pour in for his presence in con- cert. The other thir- teen categories and their nominees are as follows: continued on pg 27 Jazz Disks Spur Pop Activity In Crossover Trend NEW YORK - The number of jazz artists charted on the pop listings has con- tinued to expand in recent weeks. Ac- cording to this week's Cash Box LP charts, over 10% of the albums fall into the category of either jazz or jazz - oriented music. This development reflects the tendency of jazz musicians to borrow elements of rock and r&b while more commercial soul and pop acts have begun to utilize jazz structures. The goal for most has been to fuse the various sounds and, thus, make jazz a more com- merially viable product. Among the jazz artists who have chart records with a pop/r&b flavor are Billy Cobham, StanleyClarke, the Crusaders, Jerry Goodman & Jan Hammer, George Duke, Gil Scott -Heron, Miles Davis, George Benson, Stanley Turrentine, Flora Purim, Chick Corea, and Bobbi Humphrey. The highest charted record as of this week is Gil Scott -Heron's debut LP for Arista, "The First Minute Of A New Day," which is bulleted at 59. Stanley Clarke's first solo LP for Nem- peror Records, "Stanley Clarke," is bulleted at 68, and George Benson's "Bad Benson" on CTI is positioned at 75 with a bullet. Several soul/rock artists who are charted with albums having distinct jazz influences are Chicago; Ramsey Lewis and Earth, Wind, and Fire; Santana; the Blackbyrds; Gene Page; and Tower Of Power, Sergio Mendes and Jade Warrior are among this week's new additions. Ramsey Lewis' "Sun Goddess" on Columbia is the highest charted record in this category at 39 with a bullet. Tower Of Power's "Urban Renewal" on Warners is positioned at 41 with a bullet, while the Blackbyrds' "Flying Start" on Fantasy follows at 53 with a bullet. Further proof of the crossover poten- tial of jazz records is evidenced by the continued on pg 29 Analitto Loses Piracy Decision BOSTON -A four -day jury trial in Mid dlesex County Court here ended in the conviction of Walter Paul Analitto, doing business as Poor Paul's, on three counts of wholesaling pirated tapes. It was the first conviction under the Massachusetts Anti -Piracy law which became effective on Oct. 31, 1973. Analitto received a suspended one- year sentence on each count but was placed on probation for two years. Among some 18,000 suspected pirat- ed tapes that were seized from Analitto's warehouse were recordings by Lynn An- derson, Blood, Sweat & Tears, Johnny Cash, John Denver, Glen Cambell and Van Cliburn Assistant District Attorney Bonnie McLeod -Griffin prosecuted the case. HOLLYWOOD - Motown Records has entered into a distribution pact with Gull Records, a London based record label. Gull will be distributed in the United States and Canada. Motown also has the right to acquire all future Gull artists for distribution. Announcement was made jointly by Herb Belkin, Motown's vice-president of creative operations and Derek Everett and David Howells, founders and co - directors of Gull Records. Belkin stated: "Gull represents, to us, the highest professional experience and taste to have surfaced from the U.K. re- cently. The principals have a tremen- dous history of record success. The pro- duct, thus far, promises that their suc- cesses will not only continue but prosper." Derek Everett and David Howells, the two men responsible for the formation of Gull in 1974, played a large part in bring- ing the talents of The Zombies, Argent, The Average White Band, Soft Machine, Wishbone Ash, Osibisa (among others) to the attention of the American public. cash box,' insight&sound , Ike & Tina Turner -Its Worked Out Fine Billy Taylor - The Subject Is Jazz One of the nicest and most deserved success stories in music belongs to Ike & Tina Turner. Tina, sartorially elegant in her office at Bolic Productions in Hollywood, reflected back on the first gig she and Ike ever did together: "We were travelling in a station wagon to do a gig in Cincinnatti with Dee Clarke and the car was overflowing with instruments and amplifiers and musicians. I was thinking about what the show would be like when all of a sudden the station wagon flipped over on the road and rolled to a stop. Everyone was shaken up. but fortunately there were no serious in- juries, not even a broken bone. When we finally got to the date, we saw that it was a funky old ballroom with no dressing rooms, but we got ourselves together and went on ahead and did our show. The audience really loved us and from then till now I've never been sorry." Now Bolic Productions alone employs six people (when recording is going on the number triples) and the Ike & Tina Turner show travels with seventeen people, 14 of whom perform on stage. In between the funky Cincinnatti ballroom and a position of eminence in rock music, Tina remembers the dues paying days, the ultimate recogni- tion of their show as top drawer and her own growth as an individual. Tina Turner is possessed of the unique ability to transform from high voltage sexy entertainer to mother of four teenage boys without any trouble. "My home life." said Tina, "means more to me than my career. I don't have to be a star when I'm home with Ike and the kids because I can adapt to any situation I'm in." It is this singular ability to become a part of any given enviornment that sets Tina apart from so many performers who can't (or don't know how) to separate their private and professional lives. For in- stance, her role as the acid queen in the Robert Stigwood-Ken Russell film production of "Tommy" gave her the opportunity to fulfill a life long dream to act. Though she has no speaking parts (the story is conveyed through the songs in the rock opera), Tina was excited about getting to express herself dramatically for the first time. "When I was a little girl in Tennessee, said Tina, "I'd come home from a movie and act out parts that I liked for my mother. When Ken Russell told me that the scene in "Tommy" was a physical one, it opened up a new perspective for me and gave me a chance to use my hands and facial expressions along with the song lyrics. When I saw a playback, I was surprised at how much I was able to convey." Though Tina looks forward very much to the New York premiere of "Tommy" Mar. 18 and subsequent premieres in Philadelphia and Hollywood, you can bet that as soon as she gets home, she'll devote as much time as she can to her family. "Craig is into sports and hasn't really expressed a desire for a musical career, but Ike Jr. plays the drums and has even done some backing vocals for us. Ronnie has his own group and they work around schools and Mike plays guitar and piano. I try to re- late to them as their mother not as a star and I think they respect me for it." As much as she's into helping her kids through their teenage years, she's con- sumed with a passion for self-improvement and reads voraciously every chance she gets. "I'm particularly interested in re -incarnation," she said, her eyes dancing, "and though I've only read four or five books on the subject, I'm really into it." Tina is JUST RELEASED GARY U.S. BONDS NEW SINGLE "GRANDMA'S WASHBOARD BAND" r egAis, PRODIGAL RECORDS Management/Direction toll Ente>pprrIlneez Ltd. 315 West 57 St New York, N Y 10019 Suete 200 212 248.7134 "Education is so important," Dr. William Taylor reflected. "In fact, it's the most im- portant thing I'm doing now. Our cultural institutions are in danger. Many people are trying to save the so-called European art forms. To my mind, however, there are no organized groups working for jazz or other non -establishment cultural expressions. I'm very concerned about this and I've found out that the best way to keep these structures from disappearing is education." As a member of the National Council on the Arts, and as a consultant and an advisor for The International Art of Jazz, Jazz In- teractions, and the Newport Jazz Festival, Taylor has tried to publicize the historical significance of this musical genre. So, too, in his educational seminars and in his "artist -in -residence" programs at various schools and colleges, he has tried to insure that the traditions, musical styles, and esthetic philosophies of jazz are transmitted to the young. The aim of Taylor's instruction is to cultivate the creative potential of young musi- cians and to prepare the local teachers for their daily lessons. Taylor said, "It's impor- tant to get the talented kids into performing and it's equally important to get the non - players involved in areas they can relate to. People can love music so much more if they know where it's coming from or what improvisation is, for instance. And, you know, these things are really not as technical as they are made out to be." "However, the most important thing is to get the teachers involved so that they can really carry the ball," Taylor added. "In our D.C. program, we're trying to show them how to teach this music. What we do is to give them a bibliography and a discography and tell them that this is one form of music which has been documented from its earliest days. Jazz has a fantastic reservoir of material. In Washington, we have pre- pared field trips and other activities. We have structured a fine program for the D.C. schools. Perhaps the most interesting of Taylor's projects is the Jazzmobile. Organized in 1974 as the first major initiative of the Harlem Cultural Council, the Jazzmobile is a non-profit organization which shares the creative contributions of jazz greats with communities which might not otherwise he able to hear these musicians in person. Among the artists who have appeared with the Jazzmobile are Duke Ellington, Dizzy Gillespie, Lee Morgan and Charlie Mingus. Taylor, the organization's fund-raising, talent -coordinating president, explained "The Jazzmobile is unique. I felt that there were too many writers and critics between the musicians and the audience explaining the music. So, we tried to instill a direct, one-to-one relationship. In this case, either the music gets to you or it doesn't. If not, that's our problem. On the street, if one starts playing and somebody doesn't like it, then he turns on his heels and you have no audience. It's as basic as that." Taylor laughed and added. "So far, we've had some success. Only a few people have run out on us." "The kids really keep you on your toes," Taylor smiled and said. "They have an ear for this music and it's not really difficult to get people involved in music that is part of their heritage." That jazz heritage, in fact, is the legacy of America's classical music art form. Taylor explained, "Jazz has all the elements which make up a classical music. This can he seen from various structural or temporal perspectives and one can trace the development of these elements from the earliest forms to the present." Taylor is extremely qualified to discuss the historical development of jazz. He has taught the history of jazz at the Manhattan School of Music and is currently working towards a Ph. D. in musicology at the University of Massachusetts. Taylor has also re- ceived an honorary doctorate from Yale University. Most importantly, Taylor has played with the giants. Upon his arrival to New York in the late '40's, he began playing with the Ben Webster Quartet on 52nd St. Before being ostracized by the hop musi- cians for refusing to use heroin, Taylor gigged with Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Art Tatum and Lester Young. The pianist has been the guiding force behind many big band acts and has performed around the world with his Trio. One of his compositions, "I Wish I Knew How It Would Feel To Be Free." is performed at many civil rights gatherings and black school commencements. It has also been published in many church hymnals. Taylor stated, "Jazz started as an expression of the black conscious- ness. The spirituals and the blues are the bedrock of jazz and they stem from different forms of black thought. But jazz has now gone beyond them. Even though black thought is the core, the many layers are not black. What we're now talking about is American music. Stan Getz is as authentic a jazz artist as John Coltrane. Milt Jackson is an original as is Gary Burton. Many musical statements made by blacks have become a part of the general jazz frame of reference." All of Dr. Taylor's efforts have served to clarify the purposes of music education. "As Americans, we have a serious problem." Taylor exclaimed. "We look at education in the wrong way. We look at it as a tool. We say, 'Get a high school education and get a job.' Baloney! Learn something and get a job. I hope that in terms of music, I have counteracted some of our problems. Every chance I get, I try to set the record straight. Hopefully, it's working." steven marks familar with Dr. Maxwell Maltz's theories on biorhythms and is constantly reaching our for more and more knowledge. "I believe in a life circle," she said. "and I feel that each time we're here we should seek to learn as much as we can." Her belief is rein- forced by the fact that she would like to be a teacher someday and perhaps even study and perform in opera. Meanwhile, Tina Turner cooks on stage like no one else and when she speaks of Ike, love and respect are in her voice. "Ike's a very special person." she said softly, moving slightly in her large chair. He's got a great quality about him that's hard to define. Sure, he's got his moods, but then again we all do, and when he's working he's got more concentration than anyone I've ever seen." Working used to mean 11 months a year on the road for Ike & Tina, but now they only do special tours (like with the Stones) and weekend dates. They're a huge success in Europe and even recorded a tune live in Germany ("Baby. Baby. Baby, Get It On"). Their new single on United Artists. "Come Back and Finish What You Started" is great and is another example of the dynamic sound they've created together. The duo has seen six complete sets of Ikettes come and go and some have done well. but Tina prefers to think about what will be happening in her future. "I know there are lots of things in this world that I can do well and I intend to try to do as much as I possibly can." For many, this would be just another pipe dream. but for Tina, who with Ike is a vibrant life force, the statement harkens back the title of one of their first big hit singles - "I Think It's Gonna Work Out Fine." david budge 26 February 22, 1975 www.americanradiohistory.com

Hal Davis: Versatility Is Production Key HOLLYWOOD - "When you are produc- ing for Motown you really have to know what you're doing," says Hal Davis, a pro- ducer who has helped shape some of the most successful music in the past several years. "Motown is a great school for pro- ducers and if a producer leaves them he can work easily for other people because his background makes him a solid pro." Davis has been responsble for records by such artists as the Supremes, Stevie Wonder, the Temptations and many others irticuidng the Jackson Five. Hav- ing produced the recently released solo Michael Jackson album and the soon to be released Jackson Five product he knows of what he speaks. He worked last year with the group on their successful "Dancing Machine" besides directing other projects like the Marvin Gaye/ - Diana Ross duet LP. But some of his best shots are still coming in 1975. "I look forward to doing some more outside work during the year like the new Bette Midler LP which I produced half of." Having started out as a performer himself he shares a rapport with artists and can communicate with them easily. "The main thing I want is a challenge` I like to accomplish what other people say is impossible. But I'm not consistent when I produce, I have no "system." You can't let the people in the business know where you are coming from because then you'll find your style stolen." "A producer has to be versatile," Hal adds with a smile. "he has to be able to change with the times. That's why I'm still around today." Assemblyman Attacks Pirates LOS ANGELES - Tougher penalties will be imposed on those who illegally copy or pirate recordings or tapes upon passage of legislation introduced last week by Assemblyman Mike D. An- tonovich (R-Glendale/Burbank). "The bill, AB 684, is directed at curtail- ing the multi -million dollar industry in pirated recordings, which has skyrocket- ed in the past few years," said An- tonovich. "Under my legislation," he con- tinued. "it will be unlawful for any person to knowingly manufacture, distribute, or wholesale any recording without the consent of the owner. "Such violations will be punishable by both imprisonment for not less than one year, and a fine not exceeding $25,000. A second conviction will result in a prison sentence for not less than three years and not to exceed ten years, and a fine not exceeding $100,000. This legislation also makes it a misdemeanor for any person to knowingly retail any re- cording which has been pirated." NARM FINALISTS coni fr pg 7 1. cash box/country news CMA/Opry Fan Fair Set For June 11-15 NASHVILLE - Advance registrations are running far ahead of last year and at- tendance at 1975's Country Music Fan Fair could easily exceed all previous records, according to Country Music As- sociation spokesman Ray Pradines. Scheduled for June 11-15 at Nashville's Municipal Auditorium, the event will include more than 25 hours of live entertainment featuring top Country Music artists, a Bluegrass Concert, an Ole Time Fiddling Contest, picture tak- ing and autograph sessions with the stars, a large fan club and record label exhibition, tickets to Opryland USA and the Country Music Hall of Fame, and three lunches. A free -to -the -public Fan Fair slow pitch softball tournament will be held on June 9 and 10. This year's tourney will be held at Nashville's Two Rivers Park, located near Opryland. Last year's win- ning team, the ABC -Dot Record's "Coun- try Shindiggers," will be facing de- termined competition for possession of the Fart Fair softball trophy from the likes of Bill Anderson's "Po' Boys," Conway Twitty's "Twitty Birds," WKDA's "High Hurlers," Loretta Lynn's "Coal Miners," Billboard's "Music Row Rebels," RCA's "Country Cookers," and WSM's "Big Country Machine." Several all Country - Girl teams are expected to participate. Teams are made up of Country Music performers, radio and television personalities and recording industry personnel. Any organization wishing to enter a team in the competition should contact Ray Pradines at the Country Music Association, 1511 Sigler, Nashville, Tennessee. The phone number is (615) 244-2840. A teams' meeting will be held later on this month. Free transportation from Municipal Auditorium, Opryland and various hotels to the Two Rivers Park will again he available. Pre -game entertainment is slated for both days; during the games, record albums and autographed softballs will he given away to fans in attendance. The Fan Fair registration fee is $25.00. Checks should he made out to Fan Fair and mailed to P.O. Box 100, Nashville. Tennessee 37202. Fan Fair is co- sponsored by the Country Music As- sociation, Inc. and the Grand Ole Opry. UA Music Taps Two NASHVILLE - Jimmy Gilmer, pro- fessional manager of United Artists Music here. has announced the signing of two Nashville music business veterans. Richard Mainegra and Milton Blackford, to exclusive songwriting con- tracts. Words & Music - Mickey Newbury The song is the most important thing' "You can't teach someone to write. You can help, but every mind is different so every writer and his approach is cifferent," said veteran songwriter Mickey Newbury in a recent visit to the Cash Box Hollywood office. Whether or not one has heard of Mickey Newbury, everyone is familiar with at least one of his songs. In fact, there was a time when he was, as he says, "hotter than a firecracker" with a hit on every chart. "I Just Dropped In (To See What Condition My Condition Was In)" was a top 10 hit on the Top 40 charts for the First Edition; Andy Williams represented him on the MOR charts with "Sweet Memories;" Solomon Burke rode the R&B list with "Time Is A Thief," while "She Even Woke Me Up To Say Good- bye" was a top country record. Newbury, who is in his twelfth year as a staff writer for Acuff -Rose, his first publisher, says "when you find a good one, stay with them," and good they have been for Newbury as he's had songs recorded by almost everybody. Noting his success as a writer, it is difficult to understand why Newbury has yet to hit big as an artist (although "An American Trilogy" was a recent regional hit mainly in the East and South). He has, in the past, recorded for Mercury, RCA and is presently on Elektra. Perhaps it is because he's hard to categorize. "I'm not considered pop by the pop people; I'm not considered country by the country people; and I'm the wrong color for R&B. The only outlet I really had for my own records were the FM 'underground' sta- tions but there aren't many of them left anymore." Mickey does sing well, in a clear yet at times gravely tenor, and his records have been simply produced. "The song is the most important thing," he said. "Singers are a dime a dozen," he continued, "I'm into somebody moving me and making me believe what he's saying and reach me. That's my approach to recording." "Naturally, I want to reach the people - if you don't want to communicate, you may as well lock yourself up in a closet - but on the same hand, I have to like it myself. When I get a letter from someone saying that they got one of my albums seven years ago and still play it, that's more important to me than having a million seller and not being heard from again." In many ways, Newbury's attitudes on his recordings parallel what he attempts to achieve from his writing. "It's not so much what you play, but what comes out of your head and onto your fingers and whether the listener's then able to hear what the artist is hearing. That's why I try to write on a simple level yet communicate on other levels at the same time. The listener participates through his personal interpretation. Some of my songs will mean one thing when you hear them and something different when you read the lyrics. I write about my environment to reach the people around me." Newbury's catalogue contains some 500 songs, many of them recorded. What does he want to reach for next? "I'm not concerned anymore on what my acceptance is today as much as I am about thirty or a hundred years down the line. I want to write that one song that will last and last. bed bogash COUNTRY ARTIST OF THE WEEK Lois Johnson "20th Century Lois" - Lois Johnson comes from Maynardville in Union Coun- ty, Tennessee and is the only child of school teacher parents. Her first performances were on school programs and she could sing and keep perfect time before she could walk. Winning a talent contest when she was eleven years old gave Lois her chance to appear on Knoxville radio and television and really started her professional career as a singer, first as a member of the "Cas Walker" shows and later the "Midday Merry Go Round," and CBS "Tennessee Barn Dance." After graduation from high school she moved to the "World's Original Jam- boree" in Wheeling, West Virginia and toured the northeastern United States and Canada. She later joined the Abbie Neal Show in Las Vegas and with this group toured the Far East, including Hong Kong, Japan, Korea, The Philip- pines and Hawaii. With this experience behind her, Lois came to Nashville and was a featured artist on the Ernest Tubb syndicated TV show. She recorded on the Columbia label where her best known records were "To Chicago With Love" and "Dad- dy, Don't Hang Up The Phone." She has also had parts in two feature movies. Leaving Columbia for MGM, Lois had "When He Touches Me," "Good Morning Dear," and "Love Will Stand." She also had two very successful albums with Hank Williams, Jr.. "Removing The Shadows" and "Whole Lotta Lovin'." She is presently under contract to 20th Cen- tury Records and her first release is "Come On In And Let Me Love You,' which was written by Don Silvers the other half of the very popular Lois John- son/Don Silvers road show. Lois has an unusual voice range and control, and plays guitar, bass, piano and accordian. Buddy Lee handles exclusive management and booking and Jim Vien- neau, head of 20th Century Records in Nashville is her producer. Her latest chart climbing single on 20th Century is "Loving You Will Never Grow Old." ARISTA PROUDLY PRESENTS ORNETTE COLEMAN, CECIL TAYLOR, RANDY WEBTON, ROSWELL RUDD, GATO BARBIERI 8( DOLLAR BRAN ALBERT AYLER, CHARLES TOLLIVER, AND MARION B'.WN THE GREAT LONDON CONCERT by ORNETTE COLEMAN This two record set is the complete first concert of Coleman outside of the United States and one of his most stunning and creative perforºnances. With the trio of bassist David Izenzon and drum- mer Charles Moffett, Coleman makes an aesthetic statement underlining the elements of beauty, swing and funk that are within the language of the new music. CATO RAF BIERI DOLLAR BRAND A. / CONFLUENCE CONFLUENCE by GATO BARBIERI & DOLLAR BRAND This intimate duet comes from two major jazz fig- ures whose origins lie in South Amer- ica and Africa respectively. Well known as leaders in their own right, Barbieri and Brand interact to create a beauti- ful music of the Third World. CECIL TAYLOR w p SILENT TOBICUES SILENT TONGUES by CECIL TAY- LOR This solo piano tour de force, recorded live at Montreux 1974, con- sists of a five movement suite and two encores, demanded by an astounded and enthusiastic crowd. Taylor's stat- ure as a major musical innovator are clearly set out in this exciting and mov- ing piece. ALBERT AYLER VIBRATIONS VIBRATIONS by ALBERT AYLER This album captured the music of a great jazz innovator at the peak of his creativity. With his working trio of bassist Gary Peacock and drummer Sonny Murray and guest artist trum- peter Don Cherry, the unique tenor saxophonist laid down a wholly new music that was simultaneously very appealing and very powerful. Included is his anthem of the new music "Ghosts". RANDY WESTON p CARIIILVAL CARNIVAL by RANDY WESTON Recorded live at Montreux 1974, Wes- ton and his quintet set down a driving set of rhythmic jazz of West Indian and African influence with some im- pressive soloing from Billy Harper. Randy's solo piano tribute to Duke Ellington was a highlight of the fes- tival. CHARLES T O E l I V E R M f PAPER RAN PAPER MAN by CHARLES TOLLI- VER Tolliver is a leading trumpeter and composer in contemporary jazz circles. His bristling, fluid style is com- plemented on this special album by Herbie Hancock, Gary Bartz, Ron Car- ter and Joe Chambers, a spectacular cast to say the least. i O S W E L L RUDD Alk R FLEXIBLE FLYER FLEXIBLE FLYER by ROSWELL RUDD With his working quintet that includes the unusual talents of singer Sheila Jordon, this trombonist com- bines his interests in the new music, bop and older jazz traditions for an album that will satisfy his fans and will him a new following. This is Rudd's first album in six years. MARION BROWN A a 66666 NOVO PORTO NOVO by MARION BROWN One of the best known of the sixties new music circles, Brown explores his alto saxophone to the fullest with the sympathetic and spirited support of just bass and drums. The store's spacious eighth floor auditorium will be utilized for the sale and Lieberman will provide $150,000.00 glue Jays 11," CARNEGIE HALL MARCH 10,1975 worth of soul -oriented merchandise to back the effort. Firm hosted a similar"ex- plosion" last year which resulted in sub- stantial sales of soul product and re- ceived extensive media coverage in the Chicago area. POWERFUL PEOPLE GOTTA MOVE - A&M Records' Gino Vannelli chats with "Soul Train's" Don Cornelius during the taping of Gino's performance on the na- tionally syndicated television program. Vannelli sang his current hit single "Peo- ple Gotta Move and previewed his newest single release "Powerful Peo- ple," from the album of the same name. Motown Donates LP's To E. Mich. U. Archives HOLLYWOOD -A complete selection of Motown albums and tapes has been donated to The Eastern Michigan University's sound archives in Ypsilanti, Mich. The donation was made possible through the efforts of Mrs. Esther Gordy Edwards, senior vice-president of the Motown Record Corporation. Patricia Freedman, curator of the archives, stated: "We are quite pleased and thankful to have been given this memorable collection. It is very definite learning material for persons who want to do constructive musical research." The sound archives, which is a division of the university's library system, now houses over 10,000 albums and tapes. In addition, the musical artifacts include over 3,000 cylinder disks, reconditioned cylinder and record players, press clip- pings on musical history, sheet music, and back issues of the three national music trade magazines, Cash Box, Billboard and Record World. The archives are primarily used by the faculty and students of the university but are also available for use by qualified outside organizations and individuals. "We are constantly looking for material to further build up our archives catalog, Freedman stated, and we welcome any contributions that can be made." Withers `Greatest' Due From Sussex HOLLYWOOD - Sussex Records, Inc.. has announced the forthcoming release of "The Best of Bill Withers" due to ship the first week of March. A marketing campaign is being planned which will utilize in-store merchandising aids, radio advertising for key markets, a sales in- centive program, and radio station give- aways. Concurrent with the release of the LP will be a single containing two cuts from the album which were among Bill's big- gest hits, but were never released as singles, "Harlem" and "Who Is He (And What Is He To You)." According to Bob Davidson, senior vice president of Sussex Records. "The tunes for this LP have been very careful- ly selected and sequenced to give the listener the broadest possible taste of Withers' enormous talent and range. The cover concept is in keeping with our at- tempt to capture the total mood created by Withers." for the record EAST COASTINGS - In the wake of New Orleans' Mardi Gras celebrations, Paul McCartney and Wings held an informal press conference aboard a riverboat to dis- cuss future plans. Along with Linda, Denny Laine, Jimmy McCulloch, and session drummer Joe English, McCartney fielded questions about the next album currently being recorded with Allen Touissant at Marshall Seahorn's Sea -Saint Studios. Release date for the LP is scheduled for sometime in April. McCartney claimed that New Orleans was a good site to record because "it's warm and it's a musical city." He also mentioned that a Wings tour of the U.S. could materialize sometime in the not too distant future. After the press disembarked, the boat was taken over by celebrities from N.O., musicians, and friends from the studio. A five hour party/boatride ensued with music provided by the Meters and Chocolate Milk, with all of the partygoers including McCartney, Touissaint, Lee Dorsey, and Ernie K -Doe joining in for a rollicking jam session BITS & PIECES: Ron and Russell Mael of Sparks have been asked by French film- maker Jacques Tati to star in a motion picture to be shot in France later this year .. . Foghat bassist Tony Stevens has left the group. His replacement, Nick Jameson, an American, has already taken up the vacant spot and will appear with the group during their upcoming tour with the Faces ... The new Alexis Korner LP, "I'm Tired Of Being In Everyone Else's Reviews" will feature guest appearances by Keith Moon and Mick Jagger. Speaking of Jagger, he and the Mrs. were at Madison Square Garden with David Bowie last Wed., watching the Led Zeppelin concert from the side of the stage . While in town, Bowie spent some time at the Electric Lady studios adding the finishing touches to his forthcoming album. He was joined there by John Lennon while working on the old Beatles tune, "Across The Universe." Eddie Kramer was at the board ... Also finishing up his album in New York last week was Todd !Rundgren. It's to be titled "The Initiation" and will feature guest appearances by Edgar Winter, Rick Derringer, John Siomos, and Bernard Purdie. Todd has also been busy working on the new Laura Nyro album for Columbia and doing background vocals for Bette Midler's new LP. Brian Davison, formerly of the Nice, Every Which Way, and Refugee will be the new drummer with Gong when the group embarks on their first American tour this spring. Davison replaces Bill Bruford who played some European dates with the nand after King Crimson split last year ... Bachman -Turner Overdrive return to the road next month after a brief hiatus. Their next album, due in May, will be titled, "Four Wheel Drive." Among the dates slated for the group is the mammoth Palm Beach Raceway Paul, Linda and Denny Laine concert on Mar. 8 where they will appear with J. Geils and Led Zeppelin ... Aretha Franklin has been set to headline a concert tribute to Marian Anderson at the Uris Theater on April 22 ... "Yesterdays," the upcoming Yes LP, a repackage of eight vin- tage songs in a beautiful Roger Dean cover will include the long version of Paul Simon's "America," previously available only as an import. Also included will be "Dear Father," the B side to their "Sweet Dreams" single. Expect the album in about a week along with Alice Cooper's "Welcome To My Nightmare." MORE ROCK AND ROLL: At a luncheon held at Le Champignon last week, Guy Paellart's last rock dream, the cover of the new album by Les Variations entitled "Cafe D'Paris," was unveiled before a small gathering of New York's rock press. The fourth album for the group is a departure from the rough and tumble switchblade rock of their Mediterranean flavored "Moroccan Roll" LP. The group's first personnel change in eight years, which saw French personality Robert Fitoussi replace singer Jo Leb has accounted for a more refined, sleek execution of their music which should ac- count for wide commercial acceptance. The mid -eastern strains are still deeply root- ed in the music, but the group has reverted back to a more mainstream approach typified by the glowing number of possible singles including "Superman, Superman," "Everybody's Got The Blues," and "Berberian Wood." Fitoussi's voice is a flexible in- strument as evidenced by his extraordinarily dulcet reading of "It's Alright" and com- pliments the much improved and tasteful guitar playing of Marc Tobaly. The album, which has already begun to generate much airplay is due next week to coincide with a tour in which Les Variations will be playing dates with Average White Band and Bachman -Turner Overdrive. ODDS & SODS: The next James Gang album, "Newborn," will feature cover artwork by Salvador Dali. The Dali reproduction to be used, "Geopoliticus Child Watching The Birth Of The New Man" was taken from the Salvador Dali Museum in Cleveland. The album has a March release date ... When Bonnie Bramlett rolls into town next week she will be fronting a band that includes former cowboy drummer Bill Stewart; guitarist Buzzy Feiten who formerly played in Paul Butterfield's band and later his own group, Full Moon; bassist Kenny Tibbetts; and a three man horn section. Her new single, taken from her album, will be "Higher and Higher." ... A tour by Emerson Lake and Palmier is expected to be preceded by a Keith Emerson solo album in April .. LAS VEGAS GALA DEPT. - "Wait till this kid gets bigger," joked Liberace, joining 11 year old Carrie McDowell after the little gal belted out a handful of mighty, mighty tunes midway in Mr. Glitter's act Friday -last at the Vegas Hilton. Carrie, one of those wunderkind who make you look at your kids and wonder "how come you can't sing like that?", is already signed to ABC Records and according to its chairman Jerry Rubinstein (in attendance for the opening with own wife and kiddies), she'll be in the studio in a matter of weeks soon as a producer is selected. Carrie's one of those marvelous prodigies whose musical understanding and vocal acrobatics amaze and entertain grownups a la Brenda Lee and Lena Z. Her rendition of 'Top of the World' and 'Keep on Singing' sealed her fate with the Vegas crowd as a rising star, maybe a bit too young but coming up anyway Jerry, Mary Helfer, Otis Smith et al hosted an ABC -Valentine party Sat. after the opening for trade kids (their folks were allowed in) complete with hot dogs, coke and ice cream sundaes. Nice touch for a nice gal who's legitimately unaffected by all the fuss. Oh yes, Liberace ... he glittered, as always. Marvelous good fun. david budge March 1. 1975 23 www.americanradiohistory.com

cash box,- album reviews LOVERS - Mickey Newbury - Elektra 7E-1030 - Producer: Chip Young The haunting and compelling melodies of Mickey Newbury once again echo like the winds across the desert at sunset on the artist's incom- parable new Elektra album. Newbury has gained a sense of soulful expression that is perhaps even more profound than the one he dem- onstrated on his last record. We really enjoy songs like "Apples Dipped In Candy," "How's The Weather," "If You Ever Get To Houston," "Good Night" and "Lead On." A class LP in every sense of the word. LET THERE BE MUSIC - Orleans - Asylum 7E-1029 - Producer: Charles Plotkin Orleans, one of the most inventive and strongest bands recording today, has a tremen- dous new Asylum LP of which they have every right to be proud. The group's latest effort reflects not only the individual strengths of its four members, but also the collective strengths of the band as a unit. The dynamics and arrange- ments of each tune are singularly impressive and the overall effort sparkles with finesse and in- genuity. We like "Fresh Wind," "Dance With Me" and "Business As Usual." COSMIC TRUTH - The Undisputed Truth - Gordy G6 -970S1 - Producer: Norman Whitfield There will be thousands of smiling faces when The Undisputed Truth's latest Gordy disk hits the racks this week. The LP, a tour de force by one of the most inventive and creative groups working today has every ingredient to make it a monster hit, including sensational harmonies, meaningful lyrics and clever production. Our special faves include "Earthquake Shake," "Spaced Out," "Got To Get My Hands On Some Lovin'," "Down By The River" and "UFOs." A stone hit. ORCHESTRA LUNA - Orchestra Luna - Epic KE 33166 - Producers: Jeff Lesser, Rupert Holmes. Though fairly new to the music scene. look for Orchestra Luna to take its futuristic sounds and blend them with the traditional forms of rock they employ into a solid force for the future. The group has all the necessary ingredients to be a major tastemaker in '75, including precision ar- rangements. tight harmonies and impeccable production. Particularly enjoyable selections from this stunning disk include "Were You Dan- cin' On Paper." "Boy Scouts," "Doris Dreams" and "Little Sam." DRUICK & LORANGE - E.A.R. L 2701 - Producer: Marty Lewis This excellent songwriting/artistic team has a bright and good-looking future ahead on E.A.R. and this debut LP has all the ingredients to launch them into the public eye in style. Ob- viously, the song selection was carefully con- sidered because the results are dramatically stunning. Each cut sparkles with its own in- dividual flair. We really dig "Third City Blue," "Sunday Shouldn't Make No Difference," "Lady Marielle" and "Dark End Of The Rainbow." WILLIE BRYANT & JIMMIE LUNCEFORD & THEIR ORCHESTRAS - Bluebird AXM2-5502 A classic two record set harkening back the good old days of swing music is presented on this great Bluebird set which features such greats as Edgar Battle, Jack Butler, Benny Carter, Taft Jordan, Sy Oliver, Glyn Paque, Ram Ramirez, Johnny Russell, Willie Smith, Tommy Stevenson, Joe Thomas, Ben Webster and Ted- dy Wilson. Special cuts include "Throwin' Stones At The Sun," "It's Over Because We're Through," "Cross Patch" and "Is It True What They Say About Dixie?" 10f «mu doux M03`762 WHEW pop picks e`o ,,. w(( t 1I BRIAN' a.d HRRd1E LI NCI I()RD .,d íHllit MU. 1ºiRI2qS CAUGHT IN THE ACT - Commodores - Motown M6 -820S1 - Producers: James Carmichael, Commodores For all of you who were floored by "Machine Gun," the Commodore's last LP, this new disk should provide an extra special treat. The sextet hits new dimensions in soulful pyrotechnics with this record and each cut reflects the growing maturity that has made the act one of the tops in their field today. Our own favorite cuts from this superlative LP are "Wide Open," "You Don't Know That I Know" and "Slippery When Wet." This disk is hitbound without a question. ROLLER COASTER WEEKEND - Joe Vitale - Atlantic SD 18114 - Producers: Ron Albert, Howard Albert, Joe Vitale Joe Vitale is an explosive commodity and the impact of his talent can be felt on his new Atlan- tic LP, one that offers the rock aficianado all he could ask for and then some. Vitale's strengths are many, but can be pinned down to catchy lyric lines, strong lead guitar riffs (some by Rick Der- ringer) and tight harmonies. Especially good cuts include "Roller Coaster Weekend." "Shoot 'Em Up," "Interlude" and "Take A Chance On Love." Look for Joe to do well in the near future. THE DRAMATIC JACKPOT - Ron Banks & The Dramatics - ABC ABCD-867 Ron Banks & The Dramatics have always represented class in r&b recording and this ABC collection is no exception to the high standards they've always stood for. If you're a harmony freak, this LP will send chills down your spine. The group is at its level best on such choice tracks as "(I'm Going By) The Stars In Your Eyes," "A Thousand Shades Of Blue," "I Cried All The Way Home." "Good Things Don't Come Easy" and "Never Let You Go." ILLUSION - Isotope - Gull GU6-402S1 - Producer: Poli Palmer The debut effort by the newly acquired Motown label Gull and that label's brightest prospects, Isotope's new record is an earful to say the least. A futuristic approach combined with the various hard core rock and jazz motifs gives Isotope a great starting block from which to take off and run to daylight. Great tracks on the album include "Rangoon Creeper," "Sliding Dogs, Lion Sandwich," "Marin County Girl" and "Illusion." To say the least, the group's future is extremely bright. WHO IS THIS BITCH, ANYWAY - Marlena Shaw - Blue Note BN -LA 397-G - Producer: Benard lghner Marlena Shaw is going to have a tremendous impact on the music scene in a hurry once this class disk starts getting some airplay and much deserved recognition. Make no mistake, this lady can sing each song as if it were just waiting for her to sing it. Actually, that's where this LP is at and Marlena's performance is stunning, in- corporating a professional capacity few possess. We really like "Davy," "You Been Away Too Long," "The Lord Giveth And The Lord Taketh Away" and "You." TWO SLEEPY PEOPLE - Philip & Vanessa - Anchor ANCL-2003 An amazing duo with an incredible sense of in- sight and thoughtfulness, Philip & Venessa are pure delights on their new Anchor album, one which displays an incredible amount of poise and professionalism. They are as adept as stylists as they are as interpreters and both attributes stand them in excellent stead here. We really enjoy "Two Sleepy People," "If I Fell," "Best Thing," "Baby I Loved You," "Ventura Highway" and "Dancing Jones." 34 March 8, 1975 www.americanradiohistory.com
