Famous Music Names Gardner To Promo Post NEW YORK — Marvin Cane, chief operating officer of the Famous Music Publishing Companies has announced the promotion of Ms Ann Gardner to the position of national director of promo- tion. Cane points to this decision as the result of a program instituted by Famous Music three months ago to examine the value of a publishing firm personalizing local promotion. Ms. Gardner, who joined the company as a part of the promotion program will be coordinating her efforts with record labels as well as making direct contact with radio stations via extensive travel, phone and mail She is currently coordinating an extensive promotion campaign with ABC-TV, MGM Records and Phil Gernhard Enterprises for Jim Stafford's current MGM album “Not Just Another Pretty Foot," and his ABC-TV summer replacement show Blue Note Plans Jazz Re-Issue LOS ANGELES — The June Blue Note re-issue Series release includes: Lester Young, the complete Aladdin combo re- cordings in one package, rare Yound sides; Ornette Coleman, unreleased tapes from the historic December 21, 1962 Town Hall concert, considered the pinnacle of Coleman's career, with sup- port from David Izenzon on bass and Charles Moffet on drums; Cham- bers/Coltrane, recordings by the top jazz team o the late fifties, including a newly- discovered session released for the first time; Gil Evans, two long Pacific jazz dates by such top performers as Cannon- ball Adderley, Art Blakey, Chambers, Curtis Fuller and Steve Lacy; Andrew Hill, three previously unreleased sessions, including one featuring a uni- que combination of jazz quartet coupled with string quartet; Jackie McLean, two previously unreleased sessions with the saxophonist in quintet and sextet set- tings — sidemen include Lee Morgan, Charles Tolliver, Larry Ridley, and Jack DeJohnette; Sam Rivers, two previously unreleased sessions by the top sax- ophonist, with support from Donald Byrd, Julian Priester, Ceil McBee and the Andrew Hill Quartet; Cecil Taylor, two rare albums by one of the most in- fluential leaders of the new music — the Transition and United Artists albums brought together for the first time, with one original tune previously unreleased anywhere. Jerry Fuller To Produce Rick Nelson LOS ANGELES — MCA Records has contracted producer Jerry Fuller to re- cord the next album release by Rick Nelson and the Stone Canyon Band Fuller's first break in music came in 1961 when he wrote "Travellin’ Man" for Nelson, who at the time was recording for the Imperial label. That number one single was followed with the Fuller- penned hits "Young World," "It's Up To You." and "A Wonder Like You.” as well as sixteen other songs recorded by Nelson. Later, Fuller went on to write and pro- duce gold records for Gary Puckett and the Union Gap. O C Smith and Al Wilson Production of the album, under the aegis of Fuller's Moonchild Productions, will begin here after Fuller completes post-production of his own solo album. "Welcome To My Nightmare” is in fact turning into a pleasant if exacting dream for the controversial Cooper The gold award, over 500,000 units sold, is his first as a solo performer — the other five gold albums in his collection were given to him as a group member and account for sales of more than 10 million albums. Cooper's producer on "Welcome To My Nightmare” is Bob Ezrin, a long time associate in this field, and the album represents the first time Alice Cooper and Atlantic Records have joined forces. Blue Note Records, have announced the signing of singer Carmen McRae to an exclusive recording contract with Blue Note Ms. McRae has completed her first album for Blue Note. “I Am Music,” pro- duced by pianist-composer-arranger Roger Kellaway The album will be re- leased by Blue Note in July Carmen McRae, who has received awards as best female vocalist in many polls, grew up in Manhattan and later performed with such big bands as Mercer Ellington, Benny Carter and Count Basie An international favorite, she has appeared literally all over the world, having just completed a suc- cessful tour of Holland, Belgium and Sweden. Jack Rael, Carmen McRae, Roger Kellaway, Dr. George Butler See Page 20 For Pictorial Coverage Of BMl Dinner Disk Buying Habits; 3rd In Four-Part Series: 14-Year-Old Wants Greater Radio Play The third subject in Cash Box’s four- part study of the record buyer is Alan Dorfman A 14-year-old student at PS 22 Dorfman lives in lower Manhattan. CB: What kind of music do you like 7 AD: Rock music, mostly CB: Whom do you have in mind? AD: "The Wiz,” The Jackson Five, the Osmonds, people like that. CB: Do you try to see these people when they come into town? AD: Not too often I really don't go to too many concerts because the prices are too high CB: Turning to records for a minute, could you tell me why you might buy a particular record? When you go into a Private Stock Signs Lopez NEW YORK — Tmi Lopez has signed with Private Stock Records, an exclusive long term wide world deal His first single is "Somethin' Bout You Baby I Like" produced by Stan Silverburg in as- sociation with Tri-Lo Productions, a new firm. Lopez's agreement with Larry Uttal's Private Stock label provides for him to record in Spanish for distribution to Spanish speaking countries. Silverburg, Uttal, Lopez shop, what turns you on to a record? AD: It’s mostly because everybody likes a record and it keeps you "on " I buy the records because they’re good music and I like them So instead of waiting to hear it on the radio, you can buy it and play it anytime that you want for as long as you want and no one can bother you. CB: Could things like t-shirts, posters in- terest you in a record? AD: Yeah, some Those things usually have pictures from the record and peo- ple come up and ask where you got them from, ’cause they like the way they look. If you see something nice, you go buy the record. CB: Do you look at the ad pages in the Sunday Times? AD: I read them each week right after the sports pages My friends also and we talk about the new records Sometimes we'll hear an ad on the radio. If it's interesting, I usually try to buy it when it's on sale. It costs too much to buy LPs, I mean five, six, or seven dollars is too much. CB: Several record companies have cut the price of their catalog by offering a cheaper line of product. Do you buy these disks Are you, in short, aware that there is a conscious effort being made by some of the record companies to lower their prices? AD: Yeah, I've bought more recently than I "ve ever bought I guess that's true for everybody. CB: How many records have you bought in the last several months? AD: About ten LPs and 30 singles. I don't really buy too many LPs though, I like the 45s. Usually the LPs have songs you've never heard before and why buy them if you only what to hear one song. When a record first comes out, you go crazy try- ing to hear it. If someone walks down the street with a cassette recorder playing something you like, you kinda follow him to hear the music. L A — A star- tling transformation took place recently as the Long Beach Arena took on the trappings of ground zero to the thermo- nucleur rock fallout called Kiss. The New York based blitzkreg suc- ceeded far beyond the normal level of a rock and roll band by virtue of overkill. Blowtorches, smoke bombs, rockets and all manner of pyrotechnics slammed together in the most haphazard manner imaginable and. yet, seemed to fit. Musically the band continued to rely on the lowest common denominator of rock as Ace Frehley and Paul Stanley gathered the most mileage out of three rock and roll chords. Of particular theatrical note was Frehley 's passionate affair with his guitar which ended with him shooting his wad, in the form of a skyrocket, into the arena's upper reaches. Kiss's shades of hades performing stance, spearheaded by outer space cos- tumery and supernatural makeup, is best exemplified by the antics of bassist Gene Simmons During the course of the set Simmons, who possesses the most exag- gerated stage gyrations in rock and roll fed the more hostile fantasies of the au- dience by spitting fire and blood into the audience The band’s continued assault on the primordial shifted into high gear as Sim- mons (reputed to have the longest tongue in the world), alternately tongue bathed the mike stand, his axe, Ace Frehley and an over-excited fan who happened to get too close to the stage The very nature of Kiss's overtness was summed up by another critic who after the show remarked: 'I'd bet that the kids that go to see Kiss are the same ones who go to a Dodger game for no other reason than to sit in the center field bleachers and spit on Jimmy Wynn." Kiss; good clean (?) fun that’s got to be seen to be believed The latest and tightest ever incarna- tion of the James Gang kicked off the evening's proceeding with a roof-shak- ing set of rockers. Gang stalwarts Dale Peters and Jim Fox laid a threadbare rhythm groundwork for the taut lead riffs of Richard Shack and the classic punk vocal stand of Bubba Keith Highlighted were James Gang stan- dards “Funk #49" and a truly metallic "Walk Away " The Gang's newer material fared equally well as the primitive rum- blings of "Merry Go Round' and "Earthshaker” weaved their hard as nails spell. NEW YORK — With two gold LPs and several hit singles to their credit a little more than a year after their formation, Bad Company is obviously something of a phenomenon When the tour hit the Garden last week, marking the first time a group has sold out a venue on their first headlining tour, the air of expectancy was understandably high. Fortunately, Bad Co by and large rose to the oc- casion. The undisputed star of the Swan Song group is vocalist extraordinaire Paul Rodgers, who undeniably has one of the premiere voices in rock In the first part of the set, he led the groop through such tunes as "Rock Steady," "Ready For Love.” "Feel Like Makin' Love” and "Shooting Star " Although suffering from an injured finger, Rodgers did play a lit- tle guitar and piano throughout the eve- ning. Mick Ralphs naturally played his guitar with characteristic intensity and fluidity, ably supported by bassist Boz Burrell and drummer Simon Kirke. Curiously, their set took awhile to build up steam, a situation compounded by the strategic placement of all the “hits” at the close of the show for maximum effect Starting with "Easy On My Soul." the pitch of excitement rose rapidly, this tune featuring an audience sing-along which effectively built up rapport between the group and the crowd. Mov- ing from there into the very impressive "Stealer," "Movin' On,” "Good Lovin' Gone Bad," and "Bad Company” (the BOTTOM LINE, NYC — "Hello mothers, hello others. Were the Pills brothers." The Pills Brothers are in fact David Proc- tor and Peter Bergman, the Yale portion of the Firesign Theatre The two zany bozos performed bits from their "TV or Not TV" Columbia LP and reaffirmed the fact that everything we know is really wrong. The problem, Proctor and Bergman tell us, lies not in our stars but in our conception of ourselves. Their humor is based upon subtle shifts in our perception of reality and an exaggera- tion of modern man's mutilation of language. As Bosco Hern, one of Bergman's characters said, "What was one is now none." The duo, in this respect, are the true heirs of Charlie Chaplin and the Marx Brothers. For Proc- tor and Bergman, our world is like the crystals in a kaleidoscope By twisting the handle, what we think is becomes first encore), the audience demanded a final encore which they received in the not unexpected "Can t Get Enough." Bad Co.'s success is due in large measure to the refreshing sparseness of their sound, which needs to be played with just the right spirit to be impressive. As a relatively new group thrust into superstar status, what they seem to need most is more experience in communicat- ing their basic rock and roll to arena-size crowds. With more dates under their belt, Bad Company will continue to be the#1 attraction they already are. Preceding Bad Company was the first lady of British blues-rock, Maggie Bell Featuring tunes from her latest Swan Song LP, "Suicide Sal,” Maggie, clad in shiny black dress and heels, belted out fast rockers and slow blues numbers (notably her trademark, "Penicillin Blues" from her Stone The Crows days). She has yet to receive the recognition in the U S. that she has in England, but the exposure she is receiving on this tour will hopefully elevate her to that status here in a short time By the end of her fine set, the audience demanded a richly deserved encore from the raspy-voiced queen of the night. The unannounced opening act was 20th Century artist Catfish Hodge, whose 15-minute set depended on drug humor for its effect Unfortunately, his tunes bordered more on bad taste than anything else, and the audience knew it. b.k. what, in reality, is not. The high point of the set was "The Declining Fall of the Roaming Umpire," a parody of the Gibbons' masterpiece. Puns, spoonerisms, and homophonic word-play carried the listener into a world which reminded him of his own, yet sounded strangely different. The duo used props and sound gags particularly well on this night Those fans who are familiar with group solely through their records must try to catch them live But, be prepared to listen. And now for something completely dif- ferent Tom Waits, Eiektra comic, opened the show. He was recently re- viewed in Cah Box on Mar 1 and Mar. 29 His set was particularly effective because the audience was receptive to good humor. The bill was arranged in- telligently. s.m. talentonstage Pat Martino Dave Liebman THE BOTTOM LINE, NYC — One can- not be quite sure how to approach Pat Martino's latest gig at the Bottom Line. The Muse guitarist has made his act "contemporary" and it's difficult to say if it really works To be sure, Martino is one of five or six top jazz guitarists perform- ing now in the world. However, he has, in the past, been a relative unknown out- side jazz circles, save for his redoubt in Philadelphia Martino's music was a veritable cornucopia of jazz textures and colors The pieces always forged in- telligently and never lapsed into academic formality, Martino now seems to be following in the footsteps of his musical compatriot Larry Coryell by working with younger musicians and by integrating rock structures into his act. It is difficult to say if Martino is merely try- ing to attract a broader commercial following or really enjoys playing fusion music. The truth is probably some com- bination of the two. If Martino's artistry did not suffer, then there would be no problem On this date, however, the older material worked best. The jazz- rock pieces were excessively loud and tended to collapse into repetition One can only hope that Martino's experiment with the new music does not lower that level of emotive virtuosity his music has always attained. Miles Davis has said that Dave Lieb- man is one of the finest saxophonists around Part of the reason for Liebman's reputation is his thorough schooling in all of the reed instruments and his mindboggling mastery of iazz and pop standards. Leibman and Larry Coryell used to play the borscht belt and such wedding factories as Leonard's of Great Neck. All of those gigs served as the woodshed in which Liebman developed the tonal control of his instruments. Lieb- man can articulate the traditional tenor voice of Coleman Hawkins as smoothly as the guttural sad wail of Ornette Coleman In both cases, the sharpness and clarity of the music pierce the listener to the quick. One feels emo- tionally drained after a Liebman set for the sensuous power of his horn plays on the listener's ear like an irrepressible siren song His compositions, moreover, place traditional forms in freer structures in such a manner that the old and the new jazz components mutually inform each other. Liebman should soon, hopefully, get the attention his talents deserve s.m. Stephen peeples stationbreaks The legendary Wolfman Jack will be taking his radio show on the road for a 31-city tour beginning June 1 1 in Akron, Ohio, jumping out of the studio and onto the stage with a multi-piece band, dancing dancers, and three fine ladies backing his vocals. “We want to remind our live audiences that radio has been immeasurably instrumen- tal in the development of rock 'n' roll," the Wolf told me during a short break in re- hearsals last weekend at North Hollywood'sM.O.R. Studios. The road show, true to that concept, will be formatted as a visual Wolfman Jack radio show, set with two huge mock transmitting towers and a huge table radio com- plete with knobs and oversized am-fm slide-tuning dial "Consider the stage as a radio and the band members as tubes," quipped Tommy Getz, who conceived and designed the entire set. Looking rather electric himself, Tommy beamed as we inspected the set, which was built with incredibly meticulous attention to style and craftsmanship by world-famous set builders R. L. Grosh and Sons here in Hollywood. Getz also will be staging the lighting for the live show using some dynamically creative effects de- signed to augment rather than overshadow the music and performer. Written by Brad Hammond and choreographed by Buddy Schwimmer, the produc- tion also hopes to project the part rock 'n' roll disk jockeys have played by injecting personality and creativity into their programming, a role seemingly ignored by the de- pendence of some radio stations on sterile automated formats. "Alan Freed (WINS disk jockey in New York during the early-to-mid-fifties) was the first to play 'race' music on a white station and he coined the phrase 'rock 'n' roll,” explained Wolfman. Rock n’ roll, a fusion gospel/blues and bluegrass/ country, was born on American radio because Freed broke the race barrier "It's this kind of originality that gets lost on a Drake-Chennault type format. Disk jockeys in general are restricted by many conceptual boundaries, and are not respected nor paid relative to their impact." I spoke with Don Kelley (Wolfman's manager) and with individual members of the production and everyone was totally involved in the spirit of the show. It's one hell of an undertaking that has the right combination of people and energy to simultaneously get the audience jumping and accurately convey a very important message. Media Communications For Radio Marketing HOLLYWOOD — A new concept in radio programming for stations in all markets is being introduced by the newly-formed Media Communications, Inc., a Los Angeles organization headed by presi- dent Gerry Peterson With headquarters at 9200 Sunset Blvd., Peterson and his staff will provide individualized guidance for stations of all sizes Peterson, formerly of KHJ radio, said, "We feel these new services will benefit not only the major stations, but also the smaller market groups that have difficul- ty competing with the dominant sta- tions." Among the specialized services to be offered is a special package geared to the sale of local advertising. In addition, the stations will receive consulting services directed to their special market situations to provide guidance on format changes and other activities, including market research Peterson, who served with stations in Boston, Phoenix, Denver and Daytona before joining KHJ, said the Media Com- munications service will be provided on a national basis with the assistance of re- gional representatives. Aretha Franklin To Headline Kool Show SAN DIEGO — Aretha Franklin, the "First Lady of Soul," will be making her first appearance in San Diego in nearly a decade at the 1st Annual Southern California Kool Jazz Festival to be held Fn and Sat , July 25 and 26 at the San Diego Stadium. Miss Franklin has had the unique honor of being the only artist to ever re- ceive Grammy nominations for 10 con- secutive years in a row. Some of her big- gest hits include, “I Never Loved A Man," "Respect," “Chain Of Fools,” "Spirit In The Dark," "Ain't Nothing But The Real Thing.” and many, many more Aretha will be joined by Gladys Knight & the Pips, Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes, New Birth, Freddie Hubbard, Donald Byrd, Bobbi Humphrey, The Isley Brothers, Ramsey Lewis, Stan Getz, and Toshiko-Lew Tabackm Big Band on the two-day event. Four giant closed-circuit TV screens will flank the stage enabling all fans to have a close-up seat. Ron Townson Honored by Lincoln U. HOLLYWOOD — Ron Townson, member of the 5th Dimension, was honored by his alma mater. Lincoln University, at the school's spring com- mencement exercises, held in Jefferson City, Missouri Townson was awarded "The Dist- inguished Alumni Award of 1975,” which honors the recipient for achieving ex- cellence in his chosen field, and for aid and assistance extended to Lincoln University. Past recipients of this annual award have included people from the arts, the entertainment field and politics. Also honored this year was Stanley Scott, special assistant to President Gerald R. Ford. The 5th Dimension is currently on the second leg of their national U S. tour, having just concluded an engagement at the Riviera Hotel in Las Vegas. June 14. 1975 39

of international renown. "Right now we re looking for an artist to kick off the new company with," said Russell. "And, as always, we're looking for a new artist. We encourage singers and musicians to send in demo tapes." Los Angeles, Calif. 90028 The number is (213) 466-4355 War Gets Burned In Madera HOLLYWOOD — On Saturday, May 31 War headlined a rock festival and played to near exhaustion in a blistering 101 degree heat The festival was held at Madera Raceway in Madera, California with six other groups participating in the day's activities During the four hour bus ride to Madera spirits were solemn but quickly — err — literally warmed up as the bus door opened and the not so towering in- ferno was at hand Apollo Lunar promoters did however try to lighten the load of the crowd by in- stalling outdoor air conditioning. The air- conditioning was a group of four "Hur- ricane" fans that blew a cold mist over 25% of the track The system successful- ly lowered the temperature by 20° but after four hours use had to be aban- doned because of the mud and puddles it was causing. 40 June 14, 1975

emmhbox/news 0 [Her/) Alpert Returns To Music Scene Via Midnight Special, Gig HOLLYWOOD — Herb Alpert and the Ti- juana Brass have been an on again off again musical institution since the forty year old band leader's initial retirement from performing in 1969. Now Alpert and the Brass are back and cooking on all fourburners. Alpert recently served as host of The Rosica Named RCA Product Director NEW YORK — John Rosica has been named to the post of director of product merchandising for RCA Records, it was revealed by Jack Kiernan, division vice- president of marketing. "Rosica's responsibility will be to develop total merchandising concepts,” noted Kiernan, "supervise the work of all prod- uct managers . . . and smoothly coordinate the product merchandising efforts with that of the advertising, sales, promotion and publicity functions at the [ company." During the past three years, Rosica has held the position of vice president of marketing at both ABC Records and CTI Records. Prior to that, he served in a sales and promotion capacity with A&M Records. From 1959 through 1967, Rosica worked for RCA, where, in his last post for the company, he was simul- taneously national promotion manager and national singles sales manager. Rosica George Butler New Blue Note Vice President LOS ANGELES — Dr George Butler has been appointed to the newly-created post of vice president, Blue Note Records In his new position Butler will be responsible for the acquisition and de- velopment of artists for Blue Note as well as the supervision of all Blue Note re- cording activities Butler had most re- cently served as general manager of Blue Note Butter Midnight Special (to be aired June 20) and last week took the Brass down to Camp Pendleton for a gratis performance for the Vietnamese refugees. In the latter case Alpert's musical message proved to be a un- iversal language and a crowd of approx- imately 6,000 applauded his efforts. Commenting on his nearly six year hiatus and his sudden return to the performing scene. Alpert said “I stopped working because it got to the point where I wasn't having fun musically. I needed time to think and reevaluate. At that time I found myself missing the energy I had when I first began." Last year, Alpert reformed the Tijuana Brass and, in the space of one year, cut "You Smile, The Song Begins" and "Coney Island." Alpert is particularly proud of "Coney Island": "When I was producing good albums with The Brass, each was a pot- pourri. But "Coney Island" not only has the same dimension, it also has different colors to it; colors I've never seen before." "The album has guts,” continued Alpert. "It's very spontaneous. It wasn't assembled from my producing ex- perience; it was recorded live in the space of three days. It’s real and it has things in it that actually happened." During the course of the conversation Alpert remarked that compromise, or in this case the lack of it, played a major part in the artistic success of the album "This album is purely the result of what I'm doing and feeling today. Good or bad, that's the way it is. I feel like I'm get- ting in there, doing what I can do. In a way the album was therapeutic because I know now that I have a lot more to say musically and creatively " "The group is now much more excit- ing, much heavier, I feel much freer, more open I'm no longer limited by things that used to concern me." This freedom was much in evidence during the course of the Camp Pendleton show as Alpert led the band through slices of TJB history with spirit- ed renditions of "The Lonely Bull," "Zorba The Greek” and a strong vocal outing by Alpert on "This Guy's In Love With You." The setting for the show was obviously makeshift but in Herb Alpert's hands a flatbed truck in a parking lot quickly took on the vicarious setting of the Hollywood Bowl. According to Major Pat Cunningham, commander of one of the eight camps at Pendleton, the concert was "spec- tacular" for the refugees. "We know it was a great morale booster." said Major Cunningham “These people are starving for entertainment and Herb Alpert's donation of time will fulfill their needs for quite a while." Black Oak Enters Into Publishing Pact HOLLYWOOD — Black Oak Arkansas has entered into publishing agreements with Ivan Mogull Music Corp . in the United States as well as affiliated com- panies in Mexico, Argentina, Guatemala, Brazil, Spain and South Africa. Virtually all songs performed by the group on its Atco Records albums are Black Oak compositions. The agreements were negotiated by Black Oak manager Butch Stone and Mogull. Cash Box Preview: ‘Musical Chairs’ NEW YORK — "Musical Chairs," the Don Kirshner-produced TV show, premieres this week on the CBS network. Cash Box caught a taping of the program recently, and for the benefit of those without easy access to afternoon TV, herein presents a capsule preview "Musical Chairs” is a game show which uses four laymen contestants and three celebrity performers presenting the musical questions. MC'd by the first black game host, Adam Wade, its primary device is the correct completion of a song verse. While more easily un- derstood in viewing than by verbal description, the basic format involves three rounds of questions, each round being worth progressively more money ($50. $75 & $100 per question). The musical chairs concept is put to use through the elimination of individuals from the running in each round by the re- duction in number of permissible correct answers (those who press their answer buttons first get first crack at an answer). In the final round, those who are eliminated in each question are out of the game for good At the taping we viewed, the three celebrity guests were The Tokens, Kelly Garrett and Ernestine Jackson, alternat- ing questions between them, with host Wade occasionally joining in For exam- ple, one of the questions involved The Tokens, dressed in camp gear, singing a part of "Camp Granada," followed by three possible completions. Several straight factual questions are also used in the course of a show. The program ap- pears to be basically middle-of-the-road oriented, with other numbers performed including "Hey, Look Me Over,” "Killing Me Softly,” "The Casson Song." and Hernando's Hideaway." Simple but relevant costuming and sets compliment each song The last person left at the end of the third round is the winner, and gets to try to complete 10 song verses (from a choice of categories) in 60 seconds, with $50 given for each correct answer and $1000 if all ten are correct With the ex- ception of a few subtleties not noted, that is the essence of “Musical Chairs.” The show is airing from 4:00-4:30 week- day afternoons in all areas of the country except New York, where it will air from Ron Saul Named Motown Pop Dir. HOLLYWOOD — Ron Saul has been ap- pointed to the newly created position of national director of pop music at Motown The appointment was an- nounced by Paul Johnson, vice presi- dent of promotion at the label. Saul will be responsible for the national direction and management of all pop promotion. A twelve-year veteran of the music in- dustry, Saul headed Warner Brothers promotion for five years and was pre- viously employed by ABC Records in Los Angeles, Saul graduated from the University of Washington with a degree in radio-TV. and most recently was general manager of Warner/Spector Records. Commenting on the addition. Johnson said. "The addition of Ron Saul is a de- mythologizational move that will confirm Motown's venture into the pop fields. The ostentatious professionalism of Saul will galvanize Motown's future en- deavors in the vastitudinous spectrum of this area.” Cossette, CBS-TV Ink ’76 Grammy Deal HOLLYWOOD — It may seem like yesterday that we were toasting 1975s Grammy winners, but last week the Pierre Cossette Company firmed a deal with CBS-TV to present the 18th annual Grammy Awards telecast on Feb. 28, 1976 Cossette’s agreement also gives the network options for the 1977 and 78 awards shows, which he first originated for live teievision six years ago in as- sociation with the National Association of Recording Arts and Sciences. Dis- cussions are now underway to determine the point of origination with Los Angeles, New York and Chicago among top con- tenders to host the Grammy telecast. Minor changes in format are also in the works, with the final decisions being based upon production facilities in the prospective cities. Stature of the Grammy Awards has in- creased noticeably since its inception as a TV special, according to producer Cossette who notes more and more ma- jor recording industry names have been scheduled to appear each successive year. 1:00-1:30 p.m WELCOME BACK— Chrysalis Records president, Terry Ellis. (I.) hosted a "welcome back to America" reception for famed record producer, George Martin, last week (Tues , June 10) at the Bistro in Beverly Hills. Joining Ellis for the festivities included (from I.) Al Teller, UA Records; Joe Smith, Warner Bros. Records; Mike Maitland, MCA Records and Mike Stewart, UA Records. Chrysalis is the majority stockholder in Air (London) companies controlling the record production services of Martin, Peter Sullivan and John Burgess. 9 June 21 , 1975

ALBUM PREVIEW: Now that several New York courts have ruled in Larry Coryell’s favor, the doyen of the jazz-rock guitar can place the business problems which have haunted his career behind him and begin concentrating again on his music. Next week. Arista will release his band's latest effort. Level One ." The 1 1th House has been radically revamped since the group recorded its first LP on Vanguard. John Lee has replaced Danny Trifan on bass and Mike Lawrence fills the trumpet gap created by the departure of Randy Brecker. Just to demonstrate how long ago it was that the 1 1th House released its only other record, consider that Ran- dy Brecker left the band to join Billy Cobham’s “Crosswinds" group 1 "Level One” is divided into two complementary thematic sections Side two has several outstanding acoustic moments which rival many of Coryell's top composi- tions Consider in particular his three part "Suite ' While it does not have the standard possibilities of his “Wrong Is Right," it is marked by a subtle mixing of assorted colors and textures which place the jazz and rock sections in a creative conflict with each other. Lawrence, in particular, shines on this piece. His tone is impeccably crisp and clear and his phrasing avoids the monotonous repetition of equally timed notes which jazz-rock trumpeters seem to delight in. Coryell, too, has several lush sections equal to his best acoustical work. His playing is always provocative because he is basically a jazz musician and, as such, is a master improviser. With only the bare framework of the composition in his head. Coryell can spin an intelligently tasteful, coherent web of music. Note, in this regard, his work on the second section. "Repose." Side one is composed of pieces by the various members of the band. While they don't match up to Coryell's "Suite,” the works are successful jazz-rock tunes because, like many fusion pieces, each composition combines several different sonorities within its structure. barry taylor steven s. marks June 21. 1975 21

§TJSf.9hfo@X;iWWS B’NAI BRITH AWARDS DINNER — Don Kirshner, who received the B'Nai Brith Creative Achievement Award is pictured here (center) at the annual awards dinner. Pictured here are (l-r): lodge president and MC William B. Williams, Toby Pieniek of RCA, Kirshner, dinner chairman Errol Gershfeld of Gershfeld advertising, co- chairman Marty Olenick of RCA, and the lodge's executive vice president Ken Rosenblum of Shorewood. 6 Albums Due From Warners RCA ‘Heart of Soul’ Cmpgn Underway NEW YORK — In the second stage of its June release schedule, Warner Bros, is currently shipping six new albums on the Warners, Reprise, Brother, Chrysalis and DiscReet labels, including works from Neil Young, Uriah Heep, Ron Wood, The Beach Boys, Frank Zappa and Sassafras. Uriah Heep’s latest LP, "Return To Fantasy," was produced by Gerry Bron, and marks the first recorded effort with ex-King Crimson/Roxy Music bassist John Wetton. "Now Look," the second solo LP from the Face and temporary Rolling Stone Ron Wood, was produced by Wood with Bobby Womack and fellow Face Ian McLagen. The Reprise release is highlighted by the new Neil Young album, "Tonight's The Night." It was produced by David Briggs and features Crazy Horse. "Good Vibrations — The Best Of The Beach Boys" appears on the groups' Brother label and includes such tunes as "Sloop John B." "Sail On Sailor,” plus the title track. "One Size Fits All" is the new disk from Frank Zappa and The Mothers Of Inven- tion, released on the DiscReet label and including new Mother Captain Beef- heart. Finally, Chrysalis Records is pre- senting the debut LP from the Welsh band Sassafras, entitled "Wheelin' N Deal in'.” PIP Launches Whistle Promo NEW YORK — RCA Records has begun an extensive merchandising campaign using the theme "We've Got A Heart Of Soul" as its focus, and designed to sup- port both new and r&b catalog product throughout the summer The initial thrust of the program will spotlight The Main Ingredient, The Hues Corporation, The Choice Four, The New Birth, and album debuts by The L.T.G. Exchange, Buari and Musical Impressions. Ray Harris, RCA product manager for r&b, noted that “this program was instituted to continue and expand upon a momentum we believe we've achieved in the soul market, whose growth we've all seen re- flected on all of our industry charts, of late." The summer soul push will make use of a variety of marketing tools, including radio spot announcements, print ad- vertising, point of purchase displays, special dealer order forms and na- tionwide in-store and radio contests. A four-color press kit has been prepared Vanguard Slates Six June LPs NEW YORK — Vanguard will ship six records during the last week of June highlighted by the release of Elvin Jones' label debut, "New Agenda," which also features Steve Grossman, Roland Prince. Dave Williams, Joe Far- rell, Frank Foster, and Kenny Barron among others. The other popular release will be from the jazz rock group, Flying Island. The four classical LPs which round out the re- lease are Handel's “Solomon" performed by the English Chamber Orchestra, Mozart's "Die Entfuhrung aus dem Serail" with John Pritchard con- ducting the London Philharmonic Orchestra, Purcell's "The Fairy Queen" performed by the Dellar Consort, and “Paula Robison Plays Flute Music of the Romantic Era," Robison's first recording for the label containing information on the new artists as well as a tank top t-shirt imprinted with the campaign theme. The in-store con- test will reward store personnel for on- premises use of the campaign material. The consumer-directed radio contest will ask listeners to name their choice of "The Greatest Black Man In History" and tell why in an essay of fifty words or more. There will be local and regional winners, as well as a final national winner to be selected by a team of prominent black writers currently being sought to serve as judges. The prize for the na- tional winner will be a week-long trip for two to the Bahamas. America Receives Hearts’ Of Gold NEW YORK — America's latest Warner Bros album, "Hearts," has been certified gold by the RIAA signifying sales in ex- cess of 500,000 units America has pre- viously received gold awards for the LPs "Holiday,"' "Homecoming'' and "America," and for the single "A Horse With No Name.” "Homecoming” and "America" also achieved Warner Bros, platinum status for sales over one million units The "Hearts" LP contains the cur- rent single "Sister Golden Hair." Ember Releases Five LONDON — Ember Records this week released five new albums including works by Count Basie and Louis Armstrong. Albums released this week include "Basie's Best” by Count Basie and his Orchestra, "Mostly Blues" by Louis Armstrong (with Jack Teagarden and Fats Waller) and "The Glorious Gabrieli" by the New York Brass Ensemble, Samual Baron conducting. Also released are "The Golden Sound of Jean-Pierre Rampal ” and "Ignace Jan Paderewski — Volume One." New Jersey Label Bows NEW YORK — Century Productions, a Sayreville, New Jersey-based recording studio has formed its own label, Conpro Records. First artist to record is Judy Stevens with a bicentennial single, "Happy Birthday America,” backed by 1 "New Jersey To Thee.” Conpro officers are Roger Bangert, president, Lou Cyktor, vice president, Michael Yannich, secretary, and Robert Ligotino, chairman. NEW YORK — In support of their current single "7-6-5-4-3-2-1 (Blow Your Whis- tle)” by the Gary Toms Empire, PIP Records (a division of Pickwick Interna- tional, Inc.) has initiated a “whistle- blowing" promotion. The label is dis- tributing over 25,000 whistles of varying size and shape to radio stations, dis- cotheques and television stations around the country. So far, the whistles have beep used in radio station contests, passed out to discotheque dancers while the record is being played, and used in a promotion on the “Soul Train" TV show in Chicago. New Dist. For Boot NEW YORK — Boot Records, Inc. has re- ported the addition of four new dis- tributors for their product. They are: Pacific Record & Tape Dist., Inc. of Oakland, Calif., All South Dist. Corp., New Orleans; R. R. Record Dist., Glen- dale, Calif.; and Alta Inc. of Phoenix. Kiss: Defending Three Chords To those included to the mechanics of heavymetal, the mastabatory rock and roll of Kiss is more than mere fodder for your less discriminating cheap wine and reds out- ing. It is, in fact, a most notable experiment as these crusading musical throwbacks from New York attempt to pave new musical ground while setting themselves a limit of the three basic rock chords as tools. Of course there's more to Kiss than music Blood, fire, smoke, bizarre makeup and various attacks of the elements combine in a theatrical tour de force worthy of an au- dience's most warped visions. But what it all boils down to is music and in a recent in- terview with Kiss, that point proved the major topic of conversation. Bassist Gene Simmons (by the way of a Pretty Things-Kinks childhood) conceded that the band, musically wasn't doing anything new. “You can't be totally original. What we do is original for us because we re taking bits and pieces of what we've heard in the past and putting them into our own style of playing. What we play is straightforward, danceable rock and roll. There's no hidden punches or double entendre. Whatever’s in our music is meant to be there .” Those thusly inclined have been prone to hang the deceptive tag of three chord jerkoff on the band's music. Guitarist Paul Stanley seemed non-plussed by the attack. "Most of the time people have a tendency to look at something and say it looks a lot easier than it is. Nobody in this band started playing last winter To do something well you have to go at it for awhile” "If people want to call the music three chord jerkoff it's alright with me The band is here to entertain and as long as we re doing a good job of entertaining who cares what people think.' 1 The band's earliest press rumblings described Kiss' sound as macho glitter-rock for those into blowing up buildings and destroying cars This brought instant laughter from drummer Pete Crise who recovered his composure long enough to explain Kiss' concept of violence in music "Usually you associate violence with people doing things to other people Kiss music is violent in the sense that it makes people want to get up and do something but it’s not violent in the sense of people doing things to other people. It’s move music. We don't play this music for people to sit It's music for people to be looser and a bit less contrived. ” Crise continued "In a sense we've taken a musical step backwards. We don't jam and all of our songs are right around the three minute mark. What we re trying to do is bring the punch back into rock and roll music. All our music is concisely worked out We make our point on stage and it’s over According to Stanley this economy in music is in keeping with the desires of the au- dience that Kiss plays to. "It wouldn’t be giving the audience a fair break to subject them to experimentation We work on the music until we find the parts we like and that sound good It s what is left after we cut the extraneous material that we play to the audience " By Stanley's own admittance the sound of Kiss is one that happens and not one that is thought about. The immediacy of the music also extends to the group's musical structuring as explained by Gene. "As we go through a song everybody gets a part The way a song happens is that its theme lends you ideas and you take what's obvious and add to it. We re all creative enough to know what fits and what doesn't. Kiss' killer approach to rock music belays much time spent on the torturous New York club circuit in such breeding grounds of metal and theatrical madness as Kennys and The Diplomat. This led, in turn, to discussing the validity of the emerging New York sound. Gene dismissed it as an attitude rather than a sound ( "something very black and white") while Paul, in elaborating on this attitude, stated the importance of theatrics in east coast rock. "The most important thing happening in New York is that 16 and 17-year-olds that are forming bands are beginning to pay attention to the stage as a viable means of communication. If an audience only wants to listen to music they can sit home and listen to the music. But as long as an audience is going to pay to see us we figure we owe their eyes as well as their ears. Guitarist Ace “The Space” Frehley, until now rather noncommittal to conversation, appropriately stated the band's reason for being when he remarked "Our purpose is to entertain. A kid goes to a concert and pays six bucks for a ticket If he gets off on the music and the weird shit we do on stage he’ll leave that concert with a smile on his face.” "When that happens we know we've done our job. " marc shapiro cashbox/mssght&mmmd James Gang: A Lot Of Years On "Okay the man wants to know our influences. On your mark, get set, go! The Yardbirds, Hendrix, Buffalo Springfield, Cream, the Beatles, Lonnie Mack If you multiply guitarist Richard Shack’s countless musical influences by four you’ve got 1 975's answer to musical interaction; the James Gang. The Gang, anchored by founding members Jim Fox and Dale Peters, have gone through a whole lot of changes with a whole lot of faces since their mid-sixties Cleveland breakout with the resultant survival, near ten years on, serving as testa- ment to their durability as a rock and roll band. According to Fox, progression in experience as well as in music has been responsi- ble for the band's survival. “I think it's always been the same music but it’s progressed as far as quality and diversification. It’s been more a matter of progressing through the experience we’ve picked up over the years. It's still pretty much rock and roll but it's rock and roll that's applicable to today's audience." Bassist Peters echoed Fox's comments on the band over the years with the brunt of his remarks centering on the new direction of the band. "It’s not the same hit all the time. There's new tunes, new faces. It's always different. We've probably come up with more new material over the years than most groups because of the turnover in personnel. And what a turnover that’s been. The James Gang has been notorious for being hard on axemen with Joe Walsh, Domenic Troiano and Tommy Bolin taking turns on lead riffs at various junctures in the band's existence Looking back on the musical chairs that have taken place over the years, Dale re- marked: "A lot of times Jim and I would think about junking it when something got weird but as long as the music was good and we kept getting people that it was fun playing the music with, we felt it was worth keeping the band together. " The "fun people" this outing include Shack and vocalist Bubba Keith who have taken on the bulk of the Gang's songwriting chores as well as adding firepower to the rock and thunder leanings. But lost in the rush to praise such cloud of dust power numbers as "Walk Away" and. of more recent vintage, "Merry Go Round” and "Earthshaker" is the fact that the James Gang have been ardent practitioners of the country flavored ditty since the days of "Thirds. " This fact of life outlook was explained by Jim "Let's be honest about it; we do some stuff that is just downright heavymetal rock. But I don't think we’ve based our entire career on that. If we had I don't think we would have lasted as long as we have. Our big hits have been the harder songs but we've never really had a heavymetal hit Unfortunately when a band plays both hard and acoustic songs your major success usually comes on the hard stuff. But like it or not the name James Gang has become synonymous with raw ballsy rock and roll; a musical style well suited to the songwriting talents of Keith and Shack. Shack commented on this in stating the process by which a James Gang song is born. "It definitely boils down to a state of mind; especially when you're writing a hard rock song. I get this "move” kind of feeling when I'm doing the music while Bubba gets into the same kind of thing with the lyrics. With ballads it becomes a whole dif- ferent process. It's a whole different kind of feel. I mean you can t really get musically light behind a hard rock song and, on the other hand, you can t sing a soft ballad the same way you'd sing "Earthshaker.” A telling point in the history of the James Gang has been their association with Joe Walsh. After Walsh's departure there were those who felt that the “guts” of the band had flown, leaving a mindless musical vegetable in its wake Having proven the skep- tics wrong, Jim was given to talking about the past association "Joe was a talented guy and it was inevitable that he would split But it was really the best thing that could happen as far as the overall identity of the band was con- cerned We re taken more as a band now as opposed to being Joe Walsh’s backup band Now there's more of a group feeling than there was towards the end of Joe's stay with the band. The direction of the band is more defined now than it has been in a long time ” Speaking of direction, the band’s latest LP "Newborn" ranks high in terms of tight- ness as riffs and instrumental jams make their points with regularity. According to Shack the band's future recording plans are something like this: “Right now it’s a mat- ter of getting into the studio twice a year. I think you’ll find that the overall sound will be getting tighter and more concise. We’ve got an advantage over other bands in that all four of us are good at different things as opposed to only being able to do one thing well. So the only thing we can do is progress." There are a hell of a lot of rock and roll bands around and, in closing, I posed the ob- vious question to Dale about the James Gang's validity as opposed to any other band "I can't really answer that. I don’t think there's any rhyme or reason to music these days. I don't really know what better or worse is. We just do the best we can If the kids like us fine; if they don't, they don't ” The James Gang waxes philosophical and consistent. marc shapiro June 28, 1975

Buddah Showcase Called Success NEW YORK — Buddah Records spon- sored a weekend musical event recently at New York's Apollo Theatre, show- casing nine of its r&b acts. Billed as the "Soul Of The Buddah Group,” the 3-day festival was introduced as a non-profit venture aimed at presenting artists at re- duced prices The company rented the theatre for the program, paid the ex- penses for the acts, and donated quan- tities of tickets to community charitable organizations. Headlining the bill was Melba Moore, with special guest artists Black Ivory. Supportive performances were given by The Modulations, Bobby Wilson, Jae Mason, First Class. Fifth Avenue, Jimmy Jackson, and the Sound Experience "Our goal was to bring a low-priced, top quality show to the Apollo communi- ty,” noted Buddah president Art Kass. "It was an excellent showcase for some of our relatively new acts, as well as provid- ing the entertainment of established talents. The people turned out — we were very pleased with the response." Radio time buys on three of New York’s r&b stations (WWRL, WBLS, & WLIB), newspaper ads, as well as posters and flyers, were used to advertise the event In addition, tickets were given to the radio stations for donation to their favorite community charities. Pictured at the event are (I. to r.): Alan Lott, director of r&b operations for Bud- dah; Ron Early, east coast regional pro- motion; singer Jimmy Jackson; Melba Moore; Art Kass; Bill Able, director of artist relations; Earlean Fisher, midwest regional promo director; Caesar Han- cock, Texas area promo director; and Bil- ly Hendricks, local promotion (Phila.). |WELCOTUrac; Leon Haywood Inks With Ajaye Signs With Gemini Artists Little David HOLLYWOOD — Ira Okun, executive vice-president of Gemini Artists Management Ltd has announced the ex- clusive worldwide representation of Leon Haywood. KGAB is basically an LP orientated station but plays singles during its Disco Power Shop. Dis- co Power rocks the soul waves every day from 10 p.m. to midnight. Hot new LP’s on KGAB-FM are Ray Charles’s "Renaissance," "Come Get To This,” by Nancy Wilson and War’s, "Why Can't We Be Friends " Crossover product is an important mainstay to the station with Chicago, Blood, Sweat and Tears, Melissa Manchester, Lani Hall, Gino Vannelli and Frankie Valli just a few of the artists being broadcast. ===== PAGE 21 =====
POINTS WEST — Ozark Mountain Daredevils manager Stan Plesser, who also manages Brewer & Shipley out of his Cowtown Productions offices in Kansas City, was in town on business last week and got together to rap about what the A&M Ozark-ers are up to. Seems as though the band, whose single “Jackie Blue" went to #1 on the Cash Box charts, are in Nashville recording what Stan refers to as being a “very suc- cessful album." A&M plans release of a single in two weeks, with the LP due around the first of September. Brewer & Shipley, on the other hand, have a new 45 out called “Brain Damage.” I guess that’s somehow related to their previous hit “One Toke Over The Line!” Anyway, good to see Stan in town — managers of his sincerity and ability don't grow on trees. And the Daredevils have a lot of songs in the works — sounds perfect. Apologies Up Front — Did I really forget to thank Alice Cooper’s Shep Gordon and the Alive organization specifically in last week's column? Shep — I love you! And, as I explained, Alice s bash was one of the greatest in recent memory. Can’t wait for the next tour! Many thanks are also due this week to my colleague Harvey Kubernik, writer for Britain's Melody Maker Magazine, for having been our eyes and ears this past weekend (June 21) for Elton John’s Wembley Stadium gig with Joe Walsh, the Beach Boys, Eagles, Rufus and Stackridge. Now that Elton’s formally introduced his new ensemble (sans permanent Doobie Brothers guitarist Jeff Baxter) we can only as- sume the next major news from the Rocket-MCA artist will be regarding his upcoming rumored Southern California dates. S-e si has acquired the first Monty Python album for U S. release on ATV/Pye Records. The album, "The Worst Of Monty Python's Flying Circus" was originally released in 1 9 ? on the BBC label in England. The LP was never released in the U.S., though it con- tains their most popular comedy sketches, many of which have recently been run on the NET-TV series. "The Worst Of Monty Python” answers such vital questions as "What is brown and sounds like a bell?" and introduces such memorable personalities as the man who puts bricks to sleep by hypnosis. The album will be available in two weeks. cashbox/album reviews TRAILWAYS EXPRESS - Philly Joe Jones - AFE Black Lion 142 — Producer: Alan Bates — List: 6.98 Recorded at Trident Studios, these sessions document the drummer's 1968 London visit. Each of the six tracks here contain a drum solo which brings out another side of his consummate skills. Listen for example to the way he changes from brushes to sticks during the drum solo on "Baubles, Bangles, and Beads.” Jones’ two originals, the rhythmic “Mo Jo" and "Trailways Express” perk as his talents as a composer are brought to the fore. The excellent musicians on these sessions including Kenny Wheeler, Les Condon, Chris Pyne, Peter King, Harold McNair, are all given the opportunity to solo, yet Jones remains in the spotlight throughout. RING — Gary Burton Quintet with Eberhard Weber — ECM 1 051 — Producer: Manfred Eicher - List: 6.98 Burton showed that he was finally back on track with his "New Quartet” LP (ECM 1030), but his latest even surpasses that exemplary 73 re- cording. Only guitarist Mick Goodrick remains from that group, but Burton is now reunited with his former accompanists, Steve Swallow and Bob Moses. Pat Metheny and noted bassist/ composer Eberhard Weber round out the 74 session. The LP shows tremendous depth with the two guitarists demonstrating a sympathetic relationship under and around Burton’s darting vibes. Perhaps Carla Bley's "Silent Spring” best shows off the textured workings of the group, with the double guitars and basses forming a network under Burton’s insistent strokes. DRUM ODE - Dave Liebman - ECM 1046 - Producer: Manfred Eicher — List: 6.98 Dave Liebman’s second album for the ECM label further establishes him as one of this generation’s brightest young saxophonists. Lieb- man has played with such notables as Miles, Elvin Jones, and John McLaughlin, but his style owes more to Coltrane, especially on his soprano work. No less than seven percussionists have been added to his Lookout Farm quartet on this "celebration" of the drum, making for a highly rhythmic foundation under Liebman’s sonorous flights. As on their debut, the group covers many moods and styles. Listen to the Liebman-John Abercrombie voicings on the electric "Iguana Ritual" and for contrast, the dulcet acoustic tex- tures of "Satya Dwani.” A very satisfying second effort. PHENIX - Cannonball Adderley — Fantasy F 79004 — Producer: Cannonball Adderley, Nat Ad- derley & Orrin Keepnews Adderley steps lightly this outing as this two record package on Fantasy allows him room to stretch out and flex his creative muscles a bit. On "Phenix” the likes of "The Sidewalks Of New York" and “Stars Fell On Alabama” get a sup- perior workout from Adderley and company. Other fop cuts include "Mercy, Mercy, Mercy," "74 Miles Away” and "High Fly.” The Adderley touch continues to one of the velvet glove as his handling of material makes him a prime can- didate for Phenix of the jazz age. MOVIES IN ME — John Dankworth and his Orchestra — RCA LPL 15092 — Producer: John Dankworth The intelligent and darting use of horns over an orchestrated setting highlights John Dank- worth’s interpretation of movie themes on "Mov- ies In Me.” His jazzical-pop approach to re- creating movie magic makes for a sound at once intimate and mellow. Top cuts on this album in- clude "Return From The Ashes," "East St. Louis Boogaloo" and "Herbie Walks Again." Produc- tion values on this album run smooth as silk and contribute to the overall listenability of all com- positions. HIRTH FROM EARTH - Hirth Martinez - WB BS 2867 — Producer: Robbie Robertson— List: 6.98 Hirth Martinez’s approach to music is laidback without being comatose, aggressive without be- ing blaring. On "Hirth From Earth" Hirth gets into some lighthearted storytelling that fits in well with the simplicity of his musical structuring. Top excursions into the mind of Hirth include “Cornin’ Round the Moon,” "That's The Way It’s Gotta Go” and "I Don't Know Why The Hell.” Good production abounds on this album and goes a long way towards making "Hirth From Earth" a collection of out of this world music. Dave Liebman Drum Ode poppicks (m , \m Im TIMELESS — John Abercrombie — ECM 1047 — Producer: Manfred Eicher - List: 6.98 John Abercrombie’s first LP as a leader is an impressive one for the young musician who has already served with Dave Liebman, Billy Cobham, and Gil Evans among others. Abercrombie mades the transition from studio musician to leader of this lifetime-ish trio with relative ease. Along with Jan Hammer and Jack DeJohnette, the trio work as a harmonious unit capable of creating a melodic statement in a variety of moods without sounding clinical. Listen to the high energy of "Red and Orange” which stands in contrast to the dulcet piano- acoustic guitar duet, “Remembering” and the drone-like quality of the titletrack. MOBIUS - Cedar Walton - RCA APL 1-1009 - Producer: Mike Lipskin — List: 6.98 Cedar Walton alternates between keyboards and synthesizers on his first LP for the label , cov- ering material that ranges from Coltrane’s "Blue Trane" to Monk’s "Off Minor” with a couple of his original compositions sandwiched inbetween. With a stellar group of musicians including Gordon Edwards on bass, Steve Gadd on drums, Ryo Kawaski on guitar and Frank Foster on tenor sax, Walton’s group has a decidedly contem- porary sound. A veteran of J.J. Johnson’s band and once a member of Art Blakey’s Jazz Messengers, Walton has made the transition to the 70s with this disk. BLACK GIANTS — Various Artists — Columbia PG 33402 — Producer: Teo Macero — List: 7.98 A compilation of mostly previously released jazz material ranging from the indispensible creativity of a 1927 Louis Armstrong ("Potato Head Blues”) to a 1972 all electric Ramsey Lewis ("Kufanya Mapenzi”). In between are tracks from Horace Silver, Charlie Mingus, Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Bud Powell, etc. Intelligently pro- grammed, two unreleased cuts are Miles Davis’ 1958 "Love For Sale," before youth culture and with Cannonball Adderley, and "Blues In Hoss’ Flat" which mixes the bands of Ellington and Count Basie. Should have appeal and merit to a rocker seeking wide horizons and the many forms of jazz. LIES LIES LIES - Bill Horwitz - ESP 3020 - Producer: Bill Horwitz and David Butler It’s been a while since contemporary music has unleashed a social commentator with any bite. Such a musical study is Bill Horwitz who on “Lies Lies Lies” puts the lyrical boot to a whole lot of people, places and things. His simple musical ac- companiment and laid-back vocals serve well in driving his well delivered points home. Top musical barbs include "Consumption,” “New American Guilt Trip" and "If I Had A Friend Like Rosemary Woods.” Most people think about it. Billy Horwitz says it. FUEL — Larry Young — Arista Al 4051 — Producer: Larry Young & Terry Philips Larry Young has built up quite a reputation as a keyboardist. He only plays with the best. And so when it was time to get his own thing together you knew a large amount of that creative energy would make its presence felt. Young's ex- cursions into the realm of native based jazz makes good use of the playoff between keyboards and vocals for that proper flighty ef- fect. Top cuts include “New York Electric Street Music,” “Turn Off The Lights” and a racing "Fuel For The Fire.” Larry Young's “Fuel" is high oc- tane music. RUN TELL THE PEOPLE - Daniel Boone - Pye 12105 — Producer: Larry Page — List: 6.98 Lightweight rock and roll music that purports to be nothing more than good entertainment and a good listen. “Run Tell The People" is all that and much more as Daniel Boone takes us on a bouncey good time musical journey that is as polished as it is entertaining. High on this album’s list of good listens are "Singing Backing Vocal With A Rock N' Roll Band,” “Who Turned The Light Out Of My Life” and "Running Around With The Boys Again." “Run Tell The People” that good music is on the way. July 5, 1975

A. LA 3536) 45 EUROPEAN SOUL — Shown takin' a break from a recent recording session are American Gypsy, an American soul band exported to Europe. Pictured from left to right are: Lorenzo Mills, Richard James, "Skeeter” Lee Jordan, Michael Hamane, Joe Skeete, Steve Clisby and Dale Harrell. By playing 360 degrees of music Rod McGrew, station manager at KJLH-FM Los Angeles has come a long way from his early days back in 1968 as the midnight to six jock on KCBA. “When I got back into radio in 1972 after manufacturing shirts, promot- ing concerts and going into politics I wanted to approach the station management with a whole new concept in programming. I came in and rapped about universal pro- gramming, multi-sounds of music, ethnic sounds and different patterns and concepts concerning jazz, pop, r&b, mor, and top 40. I knew it could be done if programmed properly. At first it sounded foreign, but it sounded so good that they gave me a show.” In six months Rod was getting such favorable response from listeners that the sta- tion made him program director. Rod’s programming techniques are based on the fact that all people are universal beings. Rod said, “Just because we live in the United States doesn't mean that we are right and unapproachable to new ideas. We can learn something, anything from anybody, and we as people need to go beyond the boun- daries that society puts on us.” Rod related back to his own childhood in L.A. saying when he was growing up all he listened to on the radio was jazz and r&b and that artists like The Beatles and other contemporary groups of the time were foreign to him because they were not played on black radio. So Rod decided when he went into radio that he wanted to expand the base of people’s consciousness in music. “I didn’t want to have just an r&b or jazz sta- tion, but I wanted to have a radio station that programmed music, because music is the common denominator. I felt that all kinds of music could be incorporated into one kind of show if there was a happy medium, and the happy medium turned out to be mellow music. After Rod started training other jocks with his programming concepts, he found that he was moving even farther away from the mor program concept. He found even more music that fit into his 360 degree concept. “There was a lot of music out there that was harder but still maintained a melodic line without getting into avant garde. “I found out that groups like Chicago, AWB, Weather Report, Steely Dan and others could be programmed in if they were put in the proper context. So now I am finding that my circle keeps getting larger but that it is still perfect, but it is getting more un- iversal in scope.” Rod sees the music of today stripping away all barriers and misconceptions regard- ing people. “Forty percent of the playlists of pop stations are now occupied by black artists. Black records are now selling better than ever. It doesn’t matter as much who the artist is, but more importantly on his music and what he is saying with his music.” When questioned about the resistance of black stations to play white artists. Rod said, "Fair exchange is no robbery and that black stations shouldn't use reverse racism as their criterion. The criterion is the concept of music, music educates peo- ple.” For example Rod said that the J-5 can go over to Japan and tear everybody up with their music even though the people there don’t understand the lyric content. The most important thing is that the music is vibrant and alive and this is what people all over the world understand. “Why should I limit myself to a corner. When you limit yourself to a corner that is all you’ll ever know. One has to take it upon himself or herself to be out there, aggressive and inquisitive and have the ability to be able to go beyond and see what else is out there that you like. When I was younger I had no idea that I would love Barbra Streisand, or a Helen Reddy, Dusty Springfield or a Jack Jones. I didn’t understand the heaviness of the lyric content of somebody like John Lennon and Paul McCartney. Those two guys were out there giving people messages that were relevant to the sixties. The problem lies in that blacks have been isolated in Los Angeles, they have for the most part been unexposed to other cultures. Rod feels that radio is an essential tool in spreading communication and he feels it is his obligation as a communicator to let blacks know not only what is happening in their own community, but in the world. “There is a definite need for people to know of the total ity of music. More people are buying black product such as Leroy Hutson and Voices Of East Harlem because they are listening to more stations than KHJ. Rod added, it’s a proven fact that when people hear things that they are the true judges as to what they I ike, what they relate to, and what they buy. To be a good programmer, Rod feels an individual has to have a good knowledge of all kinds of music and the ability to be able to put it together in a format. Rod calls it the ability to paint pictures with words and music. “You have to do more than play records and tell people to have a good time. “The O’Jays ‘Love T rain’ is a good tune to use as an example. What the O'Jays are talking about is love. They are talking about life. Before the cut goes on, I feel a need to tell the people to listen to the message whle they are dancin’ and doing the bump.” What Rod looks for in a good jock is his ability to know music, to put together a pro- gram and to be intelligent, articulate and sincere. Rod doesn't see too much difference between FM & AM radio, only that the quality of FM with stereo gives the listener a better sound. However regarding programming he feels that for the most part AM radio lacks creativity, is irresponsible, only interest- ed in the commercial dollar and unconcerned with the need to convey education to the community. He also sees AM radio taking money out of the community and put- ting very little back. Rod would like to see more of a blend of education and entertainment. "Not to make the education boring, but trying through music to learn and grow, somewhat similar to the television show “Sesame Street.” “I think that through music and radio one can get exposure to life problems which you don’t get sitting in school.” Rod said he is very disgusted with tight playlists and feels that programmers are basically lazy. “There is no reason why a record should be played more than once every three hours. Our station moves a lot of product. A lot of artists are exposed, everybody should get a break — the artist as well as the listener. People don’t know that they can stop stations from broadcasting what they are broadcasting by writing letters to station managers, programs directors and the government. I know many of my peers may not be happy with some of my statements but I have to be honest and truthful and more importantly live with myself. I have a conscience and it lets me know they’re only concerned with money and not quality. Kids listen to the radio and kids want to know. We have to prepare our children for today and tomorrow. jess levitt

Katy Lied — Steely Dan — ABC 7. It’s Only Rock & Roll — Rolling Stones — Rolling Stone 8. Playing Possum — Carly Simon — Elektra 9. Ian Hunter — Ian Hunter — Columbia 10. Matching Tie & Handkerchief— Monty Python — Arista PHIL ALEXANDER This year's answer to the age-old ques- tion “Who's at number one?” yielded some interesting replies, among them David Bowie, Ringo Starr, Ace, Linda Ronstadt, Ozark Mountain Daredevils, Earth Wind and Fire, Neil Sedaka and Paul Anka. And to the unsung heroes of the record business, musicians in base- ment studios sweating out the fifteenth take on their first demo, artists whose disks provide the enthusiasm and vital spark that make the industry an exciting place to make a living, a tip of the Cash Box hat. For those people, the relative ease of an Elton John breaking an LP on- to number one the first week out remains an elusive, unbelievable dream. In the end. everyone's a superstar. This year has produced brilliant disks that account for any peculiarities in my top choices. Musical and studio artistry are the bottom line in determining favorites, and year's not over yet! JESS LEVITT This past year continues to show a very strong trend toward disco and r&b flavored records. Middle of the road pop is still strong but danceable music is making strong in-roads into the pop charts Harold Melvin and the Blue Notes are leading the way followed closely by Earth, Wind & Fire and Kool & The Gang. This was also the year of comeback artists with Paul Anka, Neil Sedaka and Frankie Valli having big singles. Electronic jazz broke out big this year with Chick Corea, Billy Cobham and Herbie Hancock coming out with fine LP's. Probably the most interesting new trend on the pop scene has been the re- birth of acoustic jazz. Artists like Grover Washington, Jr., George Benson, Les McCann, Herbie Mann, Stanley Turren- tine and Eddie Harris are gaining more widespread acclaim with pop audiences. Bad Luck — Not Really Harold Melvin And The Blue Notes BEST OF THE NEW-IES BEST NEW GROUP — From the virtual obscurity of San Pedro. California has come a group that combines the musical virtuosity of Emerson, Lake, & Palmer, the lyrical and vocal abilities of Yes, and a rhythmic sensitivity that rivals the com- plexities of a Ravi Shankar! Twentieth Century's Ambosia are innovators in every sense, drawing on the talents of novelist Kurt Vonnegut, Jr., for their spectacular “Nice, Nice. Very Nice." An apt description of their music! Janis Ian BEST NEW MALE ARTIST - Atter a highly successful, albeit faceless career creating some of America's best-known commercial jingles Barry Manilow has broken out with two major hit singles. “Mandy" and "It s A Miracle. ' and two top chart LPs. Barry posseses a high- energy on-stage charisma and composi- tional genius that makes him one of the freshest, brightest prospects on the music scene today. Sing it. Barry! Supertramp BEST NEW MALE ARTIST — This is another hard choice but Major Harris seems the one who'll break out and become one artist with a very bright future in show business. Formerly with the Delfonics, the Major has been burn- ing up the charts with his hit single. "Love Won't Let Me Wait” on Atlantic from his LP "My Way." The Major will be a major star. Major Harris “Captain Fantastic Elton John Ambrosia BEST NEW FEMALE ARTIST - Seven years have passed since Leonard Bernstein proclaimed Janis Ian’s “Society's Child" as one of the most im- portant pop records ever written. From that stigma of success at fifteen has emerged a sensitive woman, now 23. with an album and single for Columbia that makes her period of self-imposed musical abstinence meaningful. We can expect many good things to come from Janis. Barry Manilow BEST OF THE NEW-IES BEST NEW GROUP — There were many new hot groups this past year, but A&M's Supertramp from England seem destined to stardom if their "Crime of the Century" is any indication. With tasty lyrics and polyrhymic music this group is headed for bigger and better things and should join the ranks of England's other superstars like the Moody Blues, Yes, Pink Floyd, and Genesis very quickly. Phoebe Snow BEST NEW FEMALE ARTIST - Learning to play the guitar to impress a boy she had a crush on has brought Phoebe Snow to the top. With her LP on Shelter. Phoebe possesses a clear shin- ing jazz-blues voice that sends tingles up spines. It no wonder that her LP Phoebe Snow and the single. "Poetry Man," went gold because, she may soon have more gold than Fort Knox.

sashbmx/news Rollers On 1st Cosell Show NEW YORK — U.K. group, the Bay City Rollers will make their U.S. debut on the first show in the new ABC-TV variety series built around sportscaster Howard Cossell. The show will be screened Sept. 20 and will present the Rollers by satel- lite, probably from their home city, Edin- burgh. This will be followed one week later by another appearance on the Howard Cossell show, this time live in New York. Those appearing in- clude Kelly Garrett, Ernestine Jackson, The Tokens, Jane Oliver, Lynn Kellogg, Sister Sledge, Lee Kirk, Marilyn Sokol, Larry Kert, Donny Theodore and the Flashy Ladies. Isley’s ‘Heat’ LP Goes Gold NEW YORK — The Isley Brothers’ latest LP, “The Heat Is On," has been certified gold by the Rl AA (signifying sales in ex- cess of one million dollars). This repre- sents the fourth gold record (including two LPs and a single) for the T-Neck group since the label joined the CBS Records Custom label family. The Isleys also have seven additional gold records to their credit over the years. Bluenotes’ ‘True’ Gold NEW YORK — “To Be True," the most recent LP from Harold Melvin & The Bluenotes, has been certified gold by the RIAA (signifying sales in excess of one million dollars). This marks the third gold record for the Philadelphia Interna- tional group, and their first LP to attain that status. The group’s current single is "Bad Luck." Committee Named For Gershwin Tribute HOLLYWOOD — A roster of society, film, television, theatre and songwriting personalities has come together as an honorary committee to assist the Reiss- Davis Child Study Center in its “Tribute to Ira Gershwin" benefit, July 27 at the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion of the Music Center. Directed by Gower Champion, the one-night performance will star Frank Sinatra, Tony Bennett, Liza Min- nelli. Ethel Merman, Rock Hudson, Nan- cy Walker, Ben Vereen, Jack Lemmon, the Ray Charles Singers and musical director Jack Elliott.
